author: Andrés
title: “Justicia es que no vuelva a pasar”: el juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas se acerca a su final
content:
Foto: Sol Erazo




El juicio por el triple lesbicidio de Barracas se acerca al final y convocan a seguir las audiencias. El 6 de mayo de 2024 Justo Fernando Barrientos lanzó un explosivo a la habitación de Barracas donde dormían dos parejas de mujeres lesbianas: Pamela Cobas, Roxana Figueroa, Andrea Amarante y Sofía Castro Riglos. Sofía es la única que sobrevivió. La causa judicial derivada de ese ataque lesboodiante y misógino llegó a Tribunales el pasado 18 de mayo caratulado como “homicidio”. Fue por  impulso de las querellas que ahora se juzga más precisamente como lo que fue: un triple asesinato cometido por el “odio a la orientación sexual de las víctimas, mediando violencia de género”. 

Por Sol Tobia, para ANRed. 







Ahora el juicio está por llegar a su fin. 

El jueves 15 de octubre declaró el lesbofemicida y restan tres audiencias de alegatos. El lunes 26, protagonizada por las representantes de las víctimas; el miércoles 28, con declaración de la querella colectiva que impulsó la FALGBT, y la tercera con fecha a definir, donde se presentará la defensa del asesino.

 Después, los jueces darán su veredicto y la expectativa es que dicten prisión perpetua. “Sin embargo, más allá de la pena en números, lo que está en juego acá es que se consideren los agravantes por odio a la orientación sexual y por razón de género, además de la alevosía”, explica 

Miriam Djeordjian, integrante de la Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más.




“Se demostró que hubo premeditación para lanzar el artefacto incendiario, que aparentemente fue algún tipo de pintura con un acelerante, y 

la saña con la que el agresor, después de arrojar el objeto, bloqueó la puerta para evitar que las compañeras pudieran escapar. Las golpeó para que volvieran a quedar encerradas, y trabó la puerta. 

Si no hubiera sido por la intervención de los vecinos, no hubieran ni siquiera logrado salir de la pieza”.




La Coordinadora que integra Djeordjian se formó poco antes del comienzo del juicio y, desde entonces, las mujeres que la integran 

concentraron frente al Palacio de Tribunales durante cada audiencia 

y realizaron otras actividades de visibilización, tales como llevar la causa al reciente Encuentro Plurinacional que se hizo en Córdoba

. Una de sus principales consignas es que este crimen de odio no se repita más, entendiendo que

 justicia es que no vuelva a pasar

”, detalla la activista.




Foto: Miriam Djordjian




El triple lesbicidio en contexto: misoginia, lesboodio y precarización




Los crímenes como el triple lesbicidio nunca son casos aislados. La misoginia propia de la cultura patriarcal se materializa, entre muchas otras maneras, en los femicidios que los hombres cometen todos los días, y suele tener un agregado específico contra las lesbianas: el odio que despierta en los agresores el hecho de que las mujeres rechacemos el mandato de la heterosexualidad, pilar fundamental del patriarcado.




“

Existió otro ataque en Cañuelas, unos seis o siete meses después

”, recuerda Miriam. Se refiere a lo ocurrido el 29 de enero de 2025, cuando 

Orlando Alcides Lutz Fogar, “un nazi que venía amenazando a dos madres lesbianas con una niña”, terminó incendiándoles la casa. 

Aquel día “ellas, por sentir miedo, decidieron no pasar la noche en la casa y por eso salvaron su vida”, recuerda la activista y añade que 

el juicio por este otro caso está por comenzar en La Plata.




Destaca también

 el asesinato de la Pepa Gaitán en Córdoba, en 2010. 

Entonces “no existían en el Código Penal las agravantes que hoy sí existen. El padrastro de su novia, 

Daniel Torres, que la fusila con varios disparos a corta distancia, fue condenado a 14 años de prisión, de los cuales terminó cumpliendo solo ocho, y hoy está libre”. A continuación, menciona

 “el ataque que sufrió Higui”, quien estuvo presa por defenderse de “una violación correctiva”,

 y salió en libertad gracias a la lucha de las organizaciones que la acompañaron.




Sofía Castro Riglos, única sobreviviente de la masacre lesboodiante, presenciando la audiencia virtual de la defensa del asesino frente a Palacio de Tribunales el pasado 15 de octubre. Foto: Sol Erazo




El anhelo de quienes integran la Coordinadora es que el triple lesbicidio de Barracas se reconozca como parte de un continuo de violencia lesboodiante, sirviendo además para el futuro: “

Se pretende sentar antecedentes judiciales que puedan servir de jurisprudencia, inspirar fallos

. Ojalá que no sean necesarios, pero que se pueda nombrar, porque lo que no se nombra no existe. Y además, con el caso de Cañuelas, también el veredicto que salga de acá sin dudas va a ser inspirador y referencial”.




Finalmente, la referente resalta la relación entre la violencia contra las lesbianas y otros dos factores de peso: 

el discurso oficial y la emergencia habitacional.

 Tres meses y medio antes del triple lesbicidio, el presidente hizo una síntesis bruta de la forma en que los personajes de derecha perciben a las mujeres y al colectivo LGBT, despotricando contra el feminismo y asociando directamente a la homosexualidad con los crímenes de abuso sexual en la infancia. 

“En el contexto de derechización las diversidades quedamos expuestas, no solo por lo que dijo el presidente, sino porque al hacerlo él quedan todos los violentos habilitados para atacar”, 

señala Miriam.




Foto: Miriam Djordjian




Además, agrega, “decidimos hacer foco en la precarización y en

 las condiciones habitacionales que se viven en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires

: en el caso de Andrea y Sofía, estaban en situación de calle. A través del juicio se develaron las condiciones previas de violencia existentes antes de esta violencia final; violencia que vivieron en los paradores que la Ciudad tiene para personas en situación de calle, en donde por su condición de lesbianas no les estaba permitido dormir juntas, por ejemplo, y otras denuncias que habían hecho que quedaron registradas y también se plasmaron en el juicio”. 




“Queremos poder hablar de nuestra existencia con alegría”




Durante su declaración, Barrientos desempeñó un papel “predecible” a los ojos de

 Samanta Pedrozo, abogada de la querella colectiva

. “Fue bastante obvio lo que hizo: tratar de despegarse de alguna manera de la autoría, tratar de justificarse diciendo que perdió la cabeza, que no se acuerda de nada, que se despertó en la comisaría; cosa que es totalmente falsa porque lo sacaron consciente del edificio”, detalló en un audio que difundió la Coordinadora en sus redes.




La abogada también subrayó las “contradicciones” del relato del lesbofemicida, y destacó que “se notó muchísimo la preparación del defensor”, cuya estrategia parece apuntar hacia la presentación de Barrientos como una persona inimputable o al menos digna de una pena reducida por haber “perdido la cabeza” y ser “una persona mayor”. Frente a esto, Pedrozo enfatizó en que “

todas las evaluaciones psicológicas y psiquiátricas que le hicieron acreditan que es un hombre totalmente sano, que no tuvo ningún problema, ninguna patología, ninguna situación que lo exima de la responsabilidad

”.




Foto: Sol Erazo




¿Qué queda por delante? Por un lado, la expectativa de la pena máxima y, sobre todo, que los agravantes que reconocen un contexto social, político e histórico sirvan para futuros procesos, como el que se abre por el caso de Cañuelas. Por el otro, queda también el horizonte que da nombre a la coordinadora: 

que los lesbicidios no sucedan nunca más.

 “Queremos dejar de hablar de lesbianas y disidencias atacadas por odio, queremos poder hablar de nuestra existencia con alegría, queremos poder hablar de nuestro amor con orgullo, sin sanciones.”




“Queremos poder hablar de nuestras creaciones, como tantas referentes que quizás de manera no del todo pública pero son parte de nuestra cultura, tales como María Elena Walsh, Leda Valladares, María Herminia Avellaneda, Lita Stantic, Sandra Mihanovich. Y tantas más que  son menos conocidas, y están en cada lucha. 

Porque estamos, somos parte de nuestra sociedad y queremos poder hablar de nuestros logros, de nuestras creaciones, y dejar de hablar del odio y de cómo matan a nuestras hermanas

”, cierra Miriam Djeordjian.

author: Unknown
title: Alevi Bektaşi Federasyonu'ndan Kıraç Cemevi için tahliye tepkisi: Alevi toplumunun bu tahliye kararına rızası yoktur
content:
Alevi Bektaşi Federasyonu, İstanbul Esenyurt’un Kıraç semtindeki Kıraç Cemevi’ne yönelik tahliye sürecine tepki gösterdi. Federasyon, cemevinin halkın emeğiyle var edildiğini belirterek, "Alevi toplumunun bu tahliye kararına rızası yoktur. Alevilerin ibadethanelerine antidemokratik kararlarla kayyım atamaktan vazgeçin. Cemevlerimiz ticarethane değildir" açıklamasını yaptı.

Alevi Bektaşi Federasyonu, Kıraç Cemevi’ne yönelik tahliye süreci hakkında yazılı açıklama yayımladı. Açıklamada şu ifadelere yer verildi:

"İstanbul Esenyurt ilçesinin Kıraç semtinde bulunan Kıraç Cemevimize yönelik başlatılan tahliye ve gasp sürecini büyük bir endişe, öfke ve kararlılıkla yakından takip ediyoruz. İnancımızın en temel ilkesi olan rızalık esasını yok sayan, toplumsal barışı ve inanç özgürlüğümüzü hedef alan hiçbir dayatmayı kabul etmiyoruz. Bu cemevini var eden; taşına, toprağına emeğini veren, lokmasını paylaşan, çerağını uyandıran, cemini yürüten, hizmetini gören Kıraç halkıdır. O bölgede yaşayan canların rızası olmadan yürütülen hiçbir hizmetin Hak katında da toplum vicdanında da karşılığı yoktur, olamaz. Alevilerin inançsal ve toplumsal sorunları, kamu zoruyla ve devlet mahkemelerinin koridorlarında değil, yüzyıllardır süregelen tarihsel ilkelerimiz ve Alevi hukuku temelinde çözüme kavuşturulmak zorundadır.

Kamu gücünü arkasına alarak atılan her hukuk dışı adım, yalnızca toplumsal huzursuzluğu tırmandırmakla kalmayacak, Yol'a ve adalete olan inancı da derinden sarsacaktır. Cemevleri, resmi evraklarda hangi kurumun üzerinde görünürse görünsün taşını döşeyen, kapısını açan, aşını pişiren Alevi toplumunun öz mülküdür. Alevilerin binbir emekle, helal lokmayla ve alın teriyle var ettiği cemevlerimizin geleceği kamu gücünü arkasına alan vakıfların, bürokratik makamların, mahkeme kararlarının ya da herhangi bir kişinin tasarrufuna bırakılamaz. İbadethanelerimiz rantın, tahakkümün ve siyasi hesapların alanı değildir.

Kıraç halkının büyük özverisi ve gönüllü hizmetleriyle bugüne taşınan Kıraç Cemevi, halkın iradesi ve rızası dışında, başka hiçbir kuruma devredilemez. Alevi toplumunun bu tahliye kararına rızası yoktur. Bu vahim hatadan derhal dönülmelidir. İnancımızı, birliğimizi ve ibadethanemizi kirli çatışmaların içine çekmeye çalışanlara açıkça sesleniyoruz: Alevilerin ibadethanelerine antidemokratik kararlarla kayyım atamaktan vazgeçin. Cemevlerimiz ticarethane değildir. İnancımız pazarlık konusu yapılamaz. Yolumuza, erkanımıza mekanımıza ve geleceğimize sahip çıkacak, halkın rızalığı olmayan hiçbir dayatmaya boyun eğmeyeceğiz."

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Moussa Traoure
title: The Palace Guard Against the Trenches : What the Mutiny in Niamey Revealed
content:
The mutiny that broke out in 

air base 101 in Niamey

 in the night of 29 August 2026 failed. The real question now is to understand why it took place. Those who took up arms against General Abdourahamane Tiani were young soldiers from the front lines, those who fought the ‘jihadists.’ For all of the Sahel, it’s a much more worrying sign than any plot from the army high command.




Until Saturday morning, fighting took place in the Nigerien capital near to Diori Hamani airport, the presidential palace, and the public television channel RTN. 

Loyalists retook control only with the support of the Russian Africa Corps

. 

The state television broadcast

 the live arrest of several tens of soldiers being arrested, most of them extremely young.




Three juntas, one promise




In Mali, in Burkina Faso, and in Niger, soldiers took power putting forward the same argument: civilian leaders had failed in front of the ‘jihadists,’ and the army would now do better. Assimi Goïta carried out two coups in Mali in 2020 and 2021. Ibrahim Traoré took control of Burkina Faso in September 2022 and overturned another putschist, Paul-Henri Damiba. Tiani deposed President Mohamed Bazoum in July 2023.




The French were asked to leave, and the Russians invited to come in. The three countries concerned founded the Alliance of Sahel States and 

withdrew from ECOWAS in January 2025

. Each then solidified its grip on power through legislation. In Mali, 

political parties were banned in 2025

, and the leadership was granted a 

five-year renewable term in office

—without elections. 

Until 2030, Tiani will remain president of the transition

. In Burkina Faso, 

all political parties were dissolved in January 2026

, clearing the way for the regime to consolidate control.




The promised security, however, never materialised. This gap between promises and actions has fuelled anger—an anger that is now festering in the barracks.




Two armies in one




Niger effectively has two armies

: the Presidential Guard, and everyone else. Tiani commanded the Guard for twelve years; since the coup, it has received the best equipment and the most secure and comfortable postings. Meanwhile, regular units stationed in the southwest and along the Nier’s borders are losing personnel in the fight against the Islamic State in the Sahel and the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM.




According to observers, it is these soldiers who have mutinied. US researcher 

Alex Thurston 

 that most accounts align: regardless of infighting at the top, it is the anger of the rank-and-file that has driven the revolt. 

Paul Melly, of Chatham House

, aptly summari the sentiment among young officers: three years ago, things seemed to be improving; today, the opposite is true.




When dealing with generals, a regime can either negotiate or simply swap out loyalists for other trusted figures. But for soldiers suffering from a lack of ammunition and reinforcements, a reshuffle within the high command changes nothing.




Niamey, Niger.




How the juntas protect themselves




The first pillar: the purges. In Mali, following a 

reported coup attempt in August 2025

, two generals and more than fifty military personnel were arrested. At the end of December, 

a decree mandated the forced retirement

 of several high-ranking officers, including the former intelligence chief. In Burkina Faso, after a plot was uncovered in January 2026, Damiba—identified by Ouagadougou as one of the organizers—

was extradited to Togo

. Tiani has taken a more cautious approach: on 11 September, 

he replaced Chief of Staff Moussa Salaou Barmou with Mamane Sani Kiaou

. Former Defense Minister 

Kalla Moutari has been arrested

, and former RFI journalist 

Moussa Kaka

 has been shot. According to Thurston, this reaction suggests that 

Tiani does not wish to appear fearful

.




The second pillar is the law. With political parties banned and terms of office extended, the opposition has no remaining legal path to power.




The third pillar is an external protector. 

Between 200 and 300 fighters

 from the Russian African Corps are stationed in Niger, with their headquarters located south of Base 101. Russian Ambassador 

Viktor Voropaev maintains that Niamey merely requested assistance

. According to Thurston, 

the Algerian air force also provided support

 to the loyalists. For the first time, forces tasked with fighting jihadists have openly opened fire on soldiers from the very countries that employ them.




Does a failed coup strengthen a regime?




Many analysts, including 

the editorial team at 

, believe that every thwarted coup serves to consolidate the junta: the leadership eliminates its rivals and ties its security even more closely to Moscow. In the short term, this is true. Goïta, Traoré, and Tiani remain in power, and the failed attempts have resulted in reshuffles that worked to their advantage. However, a purge works against individual conspirators who can be named, but not against the collective anger of entire units—you cannot simply dismiss a battalion that is holding the front line. Furthermore, every instance of calling in foreign forces to suppress one’s own soldiers undermines the very foundation of the regime: the image of a sovereign army.




Moreover, the ‘protector’’ is not all-powerful. In April 2026, jihadists and Tuareg separatists 

drove the Russians out of Kidal, Mali

; Defence Minister 

Sadio Camara was killed

, and 

Goïta took over the ministry himself

. A regime that relies on a single external backer becomes vulnerable when that support begins to falter.




Calm in the capital, fire on the periphery




While the juntas fortify their palaces, the war draws ever closer to the capitals. 

Niamey faced attacks in January

 

and June 2026

, including at the airport. 

Analyst Rida Lyammouri 

 that armed groups are gathering along the borders with Benin and Nigeria. In Mali, the JNIM and Tuareg separatists 

struck near the Bamako airport in late April

, and 

again in September at Diouri and Sévaré

. 

On September 20, Goïta convened an emergency meeting

.




It is a vicious cycle. With the best soldiers stationed in the palace gardens, the front line is left neglected. Casualties mount, and anger grows. By shielding their power from the army, the juntas end up weakening the army itself.




What will the autumn bring?




The crucial question is not whether Tiani can survive another night of gunfire, but whether he understands where the shots came from. The first real test concerns resources for the front: if equipment, pay, and troop rotations continue to be diverted to the presidential guard, it will be clear that the mutineers’ grievances have not been understood.




The post 

The Palace Guard Against the Trenches : What the Mutiny in Niamey Revealed

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: Perseus
title: Αυτό το ζωντανό τίποτα που πετά στα τυφλά δακρυγόνο στο μετρό στην Ομόνοια ενσαρκώνει τη φράση του Χρυσοχοΐδη (Βίντεο)
content:
Αυτό το ζωντανό τίποτα που πετά στα τυφλά δακρυγόνο στο μετρό στην Ομόνοια ενσαρκώνει τη φράση του Χρυσοχοΐδη (Βίντεο)




Με βίαιη καταστολή ολοκληρώθηκε το πανεκπαιδευτικό συλλαλητήριο την Τετάρτη 21 Οκτώβρη 2026 στην Αθήνα, με τις αστυνομικές δυνάμεις καταστολής να εξαπολύουν επιθέσεις με χρήση χημικών και χειροβομβίδων κρότου-λάμψης κατά των διαδηλωτών.








Μάλιστα στα πλάνα που αναρτήθηκαν στο instagram από τον χρήστη pi_kappaa, αστυνομικός των ΜΑΤ πετά στα τυφλά δακρυγόνο μέσα στην είσοδο του σταθμού του μετρό στην Ομόνοια, εν ώρα λειτουργίας, με προφανή σκοπό να τραυματίσει όποιον ή όποια εισερχόταν ή εξερχόταν του σταθμού εκείνη τη στιγμή.










Σε μια επίδειξη προκλητικής αδιαφορίας, ο αστυνομικός εμφανίζεται στη συνέχεια να προβαίνει σε έναν ειρωνικό χαιρετισμό, περήφανος για την εγκληματική του πράξη μπροστά στις κάμερες των φωτορεπόρτερ και των δημοσιογράφων.













Το γεγονός ότι ο αστυνομικός ένιωσε ασφαλής να επιτεθεί έτσι, εν γνώσει του ότι καταγράφεται, αποκαλύπτει και κάτι χειρότερο: ότι δε φοβάται. Δε φοβάται οποιαδήποτε τιμωρία, αλλά υποδηλώνει μια βαθύτερη πεποίθηση ότι μπορεί να ενεργήσει, χωρίς συνέπειες. Αυτή η αίσθηση της ασυλίας είναι το πιο επικίνδυνο στοιχείο της συμπεριφοράς του, γιατί γνωρίζει πως το σύστημα σπάνια αγγίζει τους «δικούς του». Ίσα, ίσα κιόλας που κάθε τρεις και λίγο τον ανταμείβει με νέα επιδόματα. Αυτή η αίσθηση ατιμωρησίας και επιβράβευσης της 

βίας

 αποτελεί το υπόβαθρο για την κλιμάκωση της αστυνομικής αγριότητας. Το συγκεκριμένο παράδειγμα ενός ακόμα περιστατικού αστυνομικής βίας, δεν είναι επιβολή της τάξης, αλλά εγκληματική βία στην πιο ξεκάθαρη μορφή της.










 










Το άλλο κρίσιμο ερώτημα όπως και κάθε φορά είναι: αφού δεν είναι όλοι οι αστυνομικοί ίδιοι, τι έκαναν οι συνάδελφοι του όταν είδαν να συμβαίνει αυτό; 










 










Και τέλος, το πραγματικό ερώτημα, δεν είναι «ποιος και αν θα τιμωρηθεί», αλλά εμείς τι ανεχόμαστε. Γιατί όσο μένουμε σιωπηλοί, όσο μένουμε σιωπηλές, όσο το βίντεο παίζει για λίγα λεπτά στα social media κι έπειτα χάνεται μέσα στη ροή των ειδήσεων, τόσο θα βαθαίνει το ρήγμα στην αξιοπρέπεια μιας κοινωνίας που έχει πάψει να εξοργίζεται με αυτά που βλέπει, με αυτά που ζει, με την πραγματική απεικόνιση της φράσης Χρυσοχοϊδή “περνούν οι αστυνομικοί και ο κόσμος τους χειροκροτεί”.

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Domestic Violence and Femicide in Afghanistan: Women Are Denied Protection and Justice
content:
Domestic violence has intensified under Taliban rule since August 2021, as the regime has imposed more than 160 edicts and directives restricting the rights and freedoms of women and girls. By barring women from education and employment, severely limiting their freedom of movement, and denying them meaningful access to justice, the Taliban has deepened women’s dependence on their families and left many with fewer ways to escape abuse or seek protection. In this climate of systemic oppression and impunity, domestic violence can go unchallenged, while women and girls face the devastating risk of femicide.

Reports from The Guardian and Zan Times have recorded 231 cases of femicide across just ten provinces -there are 34 provinces – in Afghanistan since 2021. However, it is important to note that these reports emphasized the fact that these cases of femicide do not represent all of the cases in the country since 2021, given the fact that it’s difficult to record these instances of domestic violence after the Taliban has removed avenues to report these crimes.

The Taliban has dismantled the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, the prosecutor’s office that handled violence against women, and women’s shelters all together. Additionally, women judges and men judges that were trained on domestic violence issues and supported women, have all been removed. With the Taliban’s return to power, roughly 250 female judges lost their jobs and were banned from practicing. All those positions were filled with Taliban members, most of whom have no official training in law. The complete dismantling of all legal protections for women in Afghanistan has contributed to the increased rates of domestic violence in addition to a lack of legal accountability for men who commit domestic violence.

Even worse, the victims of just the recorded cases ranged from 5 to 65. Of these 231 cases, only 58 cases resulted in arrests of the suspect committing violence, only roughly 25% of cases. The lack of accountability for domestic violence is reinforced by the Taliban’s astonishing new Criminal Procedure Regulation of the Courts released in February 2026. In these regulations, it “allows husbands to physically punish their wives as long as the violence does not result in ‘broken bones or serious visible injuries.’” This regulation is evidence of the Taliban’s disregard for the rights, safety, and wellbeing of women. This new regulation just allows domestic violence to occur with no repercussions, and women are left paying the consequences with their dignity and lives. Liza Shams, a victim of domestic violence, passed away after going to the hospital for “being severely beaten” with “multiple fractures to her facial bones.”

The systematic oppression of women has left a huge burden on Afghan women not just physically, but also mentally and emotionally. With the lack of support or possibility to leave a relationship of domestic violence, there has been an increase in suicide due to psychological pressure. According to data from the UN, 7 in 10 women “describe their mental health as ‘bad’ or ‘very bad.’” Hasina, a young woman who was just 22 years old, took her own life after experiencing domestic violence from her husband and his family. Her uncle spoke out and said her death was “a killing caused by violence and oppression, even if the final act was carried out by her own hand.” He goes on to say “at such a young age, she had already gone through so much. She should have been studying, growing and preparing for a brighter future. Instead, she found herself in circumstances where, from her perspective, ending her life appeared to be the only escape.”

There is enough evidence to demonstrate that domestic violence is not just a household issue, but one compounded by a political system that strips women of their autonomy, protections, and opportunities. When women are banned from going to school, earning an income, seeking justice, or becoming independent – escaping an abusive situation is incredibly difficult. The consequences leave women isolated, psychologically distressed, and in the most tragic cases – dead.

Afghan women have repeatedly made clear that they deserve more than expressions of international concern. Their suffering must not remain hidden behind the closed doors of abusive households and be further obscured by the Taliban’s systematic efforts to erase women from public life and silence their voices. Without access to legal protection, education, economic independence, and meaningful avenues to seek justice, women will remain trapped in cycles of violence and impunity. The international community must move beyond words and take action to ensure Afghan women can live free from violence, exercise their fundamental rights, and access the protection and justice they deserve.

Sources: Zan Times, The Guardian, Equality Now

title: Ephéméride des luttes : 21 octobre
content:
L'éphéméride des luttes du 21 octobre, comme toutes les autres, sert à se nourrir des luttes passées pour comprendre celles que nous menons au présent et au futur. L'Histoire est une matière qui peut être modelée, alors souvenons-nous de notre histoire, ou de nos histoires.




1894 :

 Révolte des forçats du bagne des Îles du Salut : "

En septembre 1894, au bagne des Îles du Salut, un surveillant tue le forçat anarchiste François Briens. Celui-ci déclare, avant de mourir :"Je meurs pour l'anarchie, les anarchistes me vengeront".


Le 21 octobre 1894, le surveillant est tué à son tour, à coup de poignard, ainsi que trois autres gardiens. La révolte se propage, mais la répression ne tarde pas. Le lendemain, 22 octobre 1894, 11 forçats seront tués dont des anarchistes connus comme Jules Léauthier, Pierre Meyrveis, Benoît Chevenet, Simon (dit Biscuit), réfugié dans un arbre, abattu après avoir crié "Vive l'anarchie". Edouard Marpeaux, sera tué au matin du 23 octobre

".




Repris de l'éphéméride anarchiste.




1902 :

 Aux USA, une grève de mineurs prend fin après cinq mois de mobilisation.




1928 :

 Naissance à Milan de Giuseppe Pinelli, cheminot anarchiste qui sera accusé en décembre 1969 d'avoir posé la bombe de Piazza Fontana, qui avait en réalité été placée par un groupe néofasciste. Pinelli mourra jeté par la fenêtre du commissariat de Milan, le 15 décembre 1969.




1964 :

 A Copenhague, une bombe explose dans l'ambassade espagnole pour lutter contre la dictature franquiste. La FIJL et le groupe anarchiste Primero de Mayo sont derrière tout ça.




1967 :

 A Washington, plus de 100.000 personnes participent à une marche contre la guerre du Vietnam. Celle-ci sera suivie d'une marche sur le Pentagone, où de durs affrontements auront lieu contre la garde nationale.




1970 :

 En Argentine, les FAR (

Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias

) incendient un patrouille de police à l'aide d'un lance-flammes.




1972 :

 - Dans la banlieue de Barcelone, le Mouvement Ibérique de Libération (MIL, entre anarchisme et conseillisme) braque la Caisse d'Epargne de Mataro et repart avec un million de pesetas, qui serviront à alimenter une imprimerie clandestine.




 A Latina, des explosifs sautent sur les marches du Palais de Justice.

 A Roccella Jonica en Calabre, deux répétiteurs téléphoniques sont endommagés par des explosifs.




1976 :

 A Rennes, le Front de Libération de la Bretagne/Armée Révolutionnaire Bretonne (FLB/ARB) fait sauter une bombe au centre des impôts.




1977 :

 - A Paris, plusieurs manifestations de soutien à la Fraction Armée Rouge (RAF) ont lieu suite à la mort 

quelques jours plus tôt

 de plusieurs de ses militants en prison. Le soir, des groupes autonomes incendient des bus de tourisme allemands. Enormément d'actions ont eu lieu les jours précédents (

19

 et 

20

 octobre).




 A Trento, un concessionnaire Volkswagen est attaqué au cocktail molotov. Dans l'après-midi, un bus de touristes allemands est incendié dans le centre-ville.

 A Vicenza, une bombe fait sauter les locaux du concessionnaire Mercedes, tandis qu'un magasin de Volkswagen est attaqué de 3 molotov.

 A San Sebastian/Donostia, un groupe anarchiste fait sauter deux bombes contre le consulat d'Allemagne de l'Ouest.

 Les NAPAP (Noyaux Armés Pour l'Autonomie Populaire) font sauter un hangar Mercedes dans la nuit.




1979 :

 Dans l'Aude, en Haute-Garonne et dans l'Hérault, trois futurs pylônes de THT sont endommagés par des charges d'explosif (à La Gaudière, Lanta et Saint-Gélydu-Fesc).




1992 :

 A Bangor en Irlande du Nord, l'IRA fait sauter une grosse bombe dans une des rues principales, causant de gros dégâts alentours. La rue avait été évacuée avant explosion.




Voir aussi 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 21 octobre.

title: Buchlesung: Land und Freiheit von Aurélien Berlan
content:
Warum und wie sollen wir uns gegen ein System auflehnen, das Freiheit verspricht, von dem wir aber für den eigenen Lebensunterhalt abhängig sind?




Dieser Frage geht Aurélien Berlan in seinem Buch nach. Dafür kritisiert und analysiert er den kapitalistischen Freiheitsbegriff und stellt diesem ein Verständnis von Freiheit als kollektive Autonomie gegenüber.




Kollektive Autonomie bedeutet u.a., asymmetrische Abhängigkeiten abzulehnen, sich vom blinden Glauben an technische Problemlösungen zu befreien und das eigene Leben möglichst mit den Ressourcen der eigenen Region zu gestalten.




Aurélien Berlan ist Philosoph, Gärtner und Teil der „Soulèvements de la Terre“-Bewegung. Er hat sich in den vergangenen zehn Jahren mit Digitalisierung und der ZAD-Bewegung auseinandergesetzt.




Kurzweilig und auf Deutsch liest Aurélien aus seinem nun auf Deutsch herausgegebenen Buch „Land und Freiheit“.

author: Amadou Diarra
title: Wood for War: How Wagner Was Paid in Central African Forest
content:
On 9 February 2021, as government troops and Russian mercenaries pushed rebels back from Bangui, the Central African Republic (CAR) signed Decree No. 21.044. It gave a young company called Bois Rouge a forestry permit covering 186,596 hectares in the south-western Lobaye region – 

roughly 1,866 km² of tropical forest, an area larger than Greater London

.




Bois Rouge had never logged a tree. What it had, according to the 

US Treasury

, was a patron: the concession was granted in exchange for services the Wagner Group provided to the CAR, at about the same time Wagner fighters and government forces were recapturing territory from the rebels.




Pieced together from sanctions files, customs data and transparency reports, the story shows how Wagner turned battlefield gains into commodities – and why timber proved a poor currency for a sanctioned militia.




A Russian Company with a Central African Face




Flag of the Central African Republic




Bois Rouge SARLU was 

registered in Bangui in March 2019

. On paper it was a local firm with a Central African boss. 

By October 2019

, at a forestry forum in Shanghai, Bois Rouge was listed under ‘Russia’, represented by Russians Artem Tolmachov and ‘Mike’ Vdovin.




A 

UK parliamentary inquiry into the Wagner network

 later named Tolmachov as Bois Rouge’s commercial director. The research group All Eyes on Wagner 

found he was also paid

 by two other companies tied to Wagner founder Yevgeny Prigozhin: Service K, which also financed the diamond firm Diamville, and Ferrum Mining, active in Madagascar. The pattern is familiar: a local shell in front, Russian managers behind.




The paperwork moved fast. The 

CAR’s 2021 report to the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI)

 and a 

forestry sector review

 record the permit, PEA 193, with 137,585 exploitable hectares and a management plan approved on 28 April 2021 – less than three months after the decree. The terms were generous: the newcomer received a moratorium on concession rent and export tax, which researchers consider unlawful and which cost the state and communities revenue.




The company built its sawmill in Boda, a town 

government forces and Wagner had cleared of rebels

 shortly before the permit was issued. This sets the case apart from ordinary illegal logging. The wood was not smuggled out of a lawless forest. It was licensed by the state, as payment for war.




From Boda to Douala




The export route, as reconstructed by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), ran from Boda to the ‘Kassaï’ military base in Bangui, then by road through Cameroon to the port of Douala. A GI-TOC photograph from 7 June 2023 shows a loaded company truck at Kassaï. That logs were staged at a military base says much about who ran the business.




The Treasury lists the species exported: azobé, iroko, mukulungu, tali and, above all, sapele. Supplies flowed the other way through Broker Expert, a St Petersburg firm long used by Prigozhin, which made dozens of deliveries for Bois Rouge and, according to the Treasury, also moved the network’s money. Trade data showed 

hundreds of imports

 of Russian machinery and logging equipment.




Most timber went to Turkey, the UAE and China, but some reached Europe. 

Earthsight found

 that in 2022 the Danish firm WoodGroup ApS, a subsidiary of London-based Woodbois, took six shipments – 465 m³ of sapele worth an estimated €3.4 million at retail. One shipment was recorded as going to France’s Tropica-Bois, whose manager 

told Earthsight

 the company had never bought the wood – a discrepancy, not proof of complicity.




New Names, Same Wood




After All Eyes on Wagner began publishing in 2022, Bois Rouge became Wood International Group (WIG) and 

hired a new Central African director and a new Russian commercial director

. It did not help. In 2023, 

CBS News filmed

 timber convoys heading from a Wagner-linked base to Cameroon and obtained about 100 WIG export documents whose details matched those of Bois Rouge.




OFAC, the Treasury’s sanctions office, 

designated the company in September 2023

. In March 2024 the Treasury detailed its Wagner ties and sanctioned Broker Expert, after a joint probe with 

Homeland Security Investigations

. Britain followed on 13 June 2024 (

UK sanctions list

; notices in the 

Isle of Man

 and 

Guernsey

). In Douala, WIG cargo was already being held up in June 2023.




GI-TOC counts 839 m³ exported in 2022 and a peak of 5,810 m³, worth $1.37 million, in 2023 – about 3% of the CAR’s timber exports. The last shipment under the WIG name left in October 2023. In 2024 two proxies moved just 550 m³, possibly leftover stock. Renamed again as Société Industrielle Forestière, the company is inactive, according to the 

latest EITI report

. By September 2024, satellite images showed the Boda sawmill abandoned.




Profit, by GI-TOC’s estimate, was at least $1 million, perhaps $5 million at Asian prices – far below early forecasts of $36 million. The widely quoted $890 million figure was an estimate of the forest’s total resource value, never actual income; All Eyes on Wagner 

later put potential earnings

 at about €2 million a year.




Gold fits in a suitcase; sawn sapele needs trucks, borders, ports and paperwork – each a point where scrutiny can bite.




The Next Concession




In January 2023 another firm, Forest Consulting Company (FCC), received permit PEA 194 in Sangha-Mbaéré. GI-TOC found indirect links to Wagner: FCC banks alongside Wagner-linked companies and buys chemicals from the same Chinese supplier as First Industrial Company, believed to be controlled by Dmitry Sytyi, head of the ‘Russian House’ in Bangui. Satellite images show no logging. FCC did not respond to GI-TOC. A 

reported successor

, Ripperwood SARLU, apparently never operated.




Is this timber stolen? Legally, it was licensed. But a concession paid for with military services, in territory taken by force, on unlawful terms, fits what researchers call ‘conflict timber’. Elsewhere in Africa – Sudan, Mali, Madagascar – the network’s prize was minerals, not forests.




The Model Survives the Sawmill




After Prigozhin’s death in August 2023, Moscow began folding Wagner’s African operations into 

Africa Corps

, run by the Defence Ministry and GRU military intelligence. In Mali the 

handover is complete

. In the CAR it is not: President Faustin-Archange Touadéra and former Wagner commanders are resisting Moscow’s demands to be paid in cash rather than concessions and to accept direct GRU command (

ISPI

; 

Inkstick

). Commanders such as Andrei Ivanov, callsign ‘Kep’, reportedly fear losing their assets and facing prosecution at home.




Claims aired in a video investigation

, not independently verified, allege the Russian House network under Sytyi diverts Defence Ministry resources with the consent of Deputy Defence Minister Yunus-bek Yevkurov, who oversees Africa Corps.




Touadéra, re-elected in a disputed December 2025 vote secured by fighters still wearing Wagner insignia, visited Moscow in March 2026 to reaffirm security ties. GI-TOC describes the CAR as a key logistics hub for Africa Corps across the continent.




As for the timber, GI-TOC concludes that extraction has stopped. But the forest business was never really about wood. It was about a model – resources as payment for protection – that remains embedded in the presidential circle and among the remnants of Wagner’s Bangui team, who have little interest in surrendering it to the Defence Ministry. The sawmill in Boda stands empty. The arrangement that built it is still standing.




The post 

Wood for War: How Wagner Was Paid in Central African Forest

 appeared first on 

African Arguments

.

author: Andrea DiP
title: Que a injustiça não te entristeça, que te radicalize
content:
Cerca de 500 mil pessoas foram às ruas em protestos na França nos últimos dias, em atos que começaram pedindo reformas no sistema educacional e evoluíram para reivindicações sociais mais amplas, que já influenciam outros países da Europa.




Os protestos começaram em setembro, quando estudantes bloquearam o acesso a uma escola na região de Paris para exigir mais recursos para a educação. Rapidamente, alunos de outras escolas aderiram, e as manifestações se espalharam pelo país, reivindicando mais professores, mais recursos e a melhora da estrutura dos prédios. 

A demanda escalou, e se transformou na manifestação de uma insatisfação generalizada com o alto custo de vida, a queda na qualidade dos serviços públicos e com o governo.




O governo tem falado em atos de violência, depredação de patrimônio e incêndios. As autoridades francesas detiveram mais de 6,8 mil pessoas – mais de 5 mil menores de idade.




As manifestações inspiraram levantes na Itália, Albânia e Portugal.




Na Grécia, os estudantes reclamam do custo de vida e do aumento de mensalidades e taxas. Na Espanha, professores exigem melhores salários. Na Albânia, estudantes protestam contra as condições nas universidades, os custos do ensino superior e a falta de apoio financeiro. Em Portugal, a demanda é também por custos mais baixos de taxas nas universidades. 




Na Argentina, milhares de estudantes e professores foram às ruas na última quinta-feira, 15 de outubro, em protesto contra o governo de Javier Milei.




Essa onda de protestos também tem sua contrapartida no Brasil. “Estamos na rua contra a extrema direita e, sobretudo, contra o que ela representa de retrocesso no nosso país” me disse em entrevista 

no último Pauta Pública

 o vice-presidente da União Nacional dos Estudantes, Gutemberg Rodrigues, sobre os atos e assembleias que têm sido organizados de forma espontânea por todo o país desde o dia 5 de outubro, sobretudo em apoio à reeleição de Lula, e que têm levado milhares de pessoas às ruas.




É sempre muito bonito ver os estudantes ocuparem os espaços públicos, e o Brasil tem momentos históricos importantes nesse sentido – seja na época da ditadura militar, com a Passeata dos Cem Mil em 1968, o movimento pelo Passe Livre em 2013, ou quando os secundaristas ocuparam as escolas de São Paulo em 2015.




Neste momento, em que tanto está em jogo no futuro do país dependendo do resultado das eleições que acontecem em poucos dias, e que ouvimos apenas que a juventude tem se radicalizado à direita, que há uma apatia na GenZ, que o elo de rebeldia com a esquerda se desfez e que não há mais pensamento crítico ou pautas coletivas, esse levante jovem no mundo é um alívio para nossos corações cansados.




Que esse levante dos estudantes, no Brasil e pelo mundo, nos sirva de inspiração  e nos dê energia nestes poucos dias que faltam para o segundo turno, em que nossas cabeças estão cheias, nossos corações estão pesados e parece que a energia vai acabar a qualquer momento. 




Mas que nos inspire também para além destas eleições, porque a luta não acaba com a apuração de votos, seja qual for o resultado.




Tem aquela frase bonita que o artista mexicano Enrique Cedillo criou para o Partido Comunista Mexicano e que eu gosto de lembrar sempre: “Que a injustiça não te entristeça, que te radicalize”.

title: Jugendstreik Basel
content:
Aufruf zum Jugendstreik am 20.11. in Basel




Als Jugendorganisationen aus ganz Europa, und darüber hinaus, rufen wir Unter dem Motto «FIGHT FOR OUR FUTURE, NOT THEIR WARS» zum Internationalen Jugendstreik auf.


Auch in Basel gehen wir am 20. November auf die Strasse.




Demo: 14:00 De-Wette Park


Fest: ab 17:00 (Genauere Infos werden über die Instagramkanäle bekanntgegeben)




Wieso streiken wir?


Unsere Staaten rüsten auf. Die Jugend wird darauf vorbereitet, in den Krieg zu ziehen. Während die Regierungen Milliarden in Aufrüstung investieren, wird der Sozialstaat kaputt gesparrt.


Auch die Schweiz macht mit. So plant der Bund zum Beispiel einen Rüstungsfonds in der Grösse von 24 Milliarden Franken. Das Budget für die Armee für den Zeitraum 2025–2028 wurde bereits um 4 Milliarden Franken erhöht. Gleichzeitig wird mit dem Entlastungspaket 27 in über 60 Bereichen gespart, unter anderem bei der Bildung, der Gesundheit und beim Klimaschutz.




Es zeigt die Priorität dieses Systems: Die fortlaufende Erweiterung des Kapitals.




Der Kapitalismus kann der Jugend keine Zukunft garantieren!


Die Armee dient der Interessen der herrschenden Klasse. Die neuen militärischen Kapazitäten erweitern dabei den Handlungsspielraum zur Durchsetzung dieser Interessen.


Beispiele dafür sind der Einsatz des Militärs an der Demonstration gegen den G7 Gipfel, die laufende Grenzmilitarisierung oder die Waffenexporte nach Israel.




Wir sterben nicht für ihre Kriege!


Wir schauen solidarisch nach Deutschland und Frankreich wo sich bereits hunderttausende Jugendliche gegen die Militarisierung und Kürzungen wehren.


Für uns ist klar: Unsere Antwort auf die Militarisierungsspirale muss international sein. 


Wir sterben nicht für ihre Kriege – Wir streiken!




Basel: 


Demo 14:00 De-Wette Fest ab 17:00 (Infos werden auf Instagramkanälen publiziert)




Streiken ist ein Grundrecht. Wenn du aber aufgrund von allfälligen Repressionen deines Betriebes, der Schule oder Polizei verhindert bist, ist es auch möglich, deine Solidarität in Form eines Banners zu zeigen.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Casual student support staff approvals in Nunavut drops from 75 to 15
content:
Nunavut’s Education Department approved 15 requests for casual student support assistants this school year, one-fifth of the number it approved the school year prior.




Of those 15, a total of 11 have been hired, according to figures the department provided Nunatsiaq News Wednesday.




The department is recruiting workers for the remaining four positions, spokesperson Kuthula Matshazi said in an email.




He said some positions couldn’t get filled despite recruiting efforts. Others remained vacant due to relief employees filling in or workers going on leave.




Student support workers join classroom teachers to help them deliver the curriculum. They work with individual students who require accommodations and those who follow unique education guidelines. School leaders can submit requests for casual support staff when they don’t have enough permanent staff to meet demand.




There is currently 206.5 support positions allocated to the territory, Matshazi said, 161 of which are being filled indeterminately. The department has also hired 164 on-call relief employees this year, to fill in for support workers who are on leave.




In the 2025-26 school year, the department approved 75 requests for casual support staff, resulting in 36 hires.
















There are fewer casual support staff 

assigned

 to Nunavut’s classrooms this year after Inuit Child First Initiative policies changed in February 2025.




That’s when Indigenous Services Canada disqualified funding requests through the initiative for student support assistants. Requests can still be submitted, but they are now considered on a case-by-case basis and approved only in exceptional circumstances.




During the 2024-25 school year, the funding program allowed district education authorities to hire 88 casual student support assistants, adding an extra number to those the Government of Nunavut regularly employs.

author: By Sean Summers, Unicorn Riot
title: Line 5 Opponents Confront Wis. Gov. Evers: ‘Drink the Future Water of Lake Superior’
content:
Milwaukee, WI — As Governor Tony Evers took the stage during the annual Wisconsin Association for Justice dinner, an audience member rose to lead a toast for the state’s leader.




But rather than honoring Evers’ accomplishments, the patron issued a challenge. Thrusting a glass of thick black fluid into the air, Tom Hoy asked Evers to drink the liquid which served as a representation of Lake Superior’s waters which protesters say will be contaminated by oil and other hazardous waste from Enbridge’s Line 5 pipeline if the state, and Evers specifically, doesn’t revoke the company’s construction permits.
















“I have a glass of water with crude oil,” Hoy announced, holding aloft a cup filled with liquid resembling oil-laden water. “Will you drink the future waters of Lake Superior, sir?”




Hoy, an activist with the group 

Climate Defiance

, continued to challenge Evers to have a drink as attendees, security personnel and police shoved them out of the audience and toward the door.




Protesters attended the dinner calling on Evers to reject the pipeline not on vague objections to the project but under specific conditions spelled out in the state’s agreement with the company.




See all of Unicorn Riot’s Line 5 Coverage




Under the Line 5 reroute 

permit issued

 in 2024 to Enbridge by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, or DNR, the state has the right to terminate the project for good cause, including if the project is not completed according to the conditions of the permit.




Activists, and increasingly the state itself, say that Enbridge’s work has fallen outside the scope of the original permit and violated numerous state regulations.




On October 13, the Wisconsin DNR issued a 

Notice of Violation

 to Enbridge for what it calls a “persistent pattern of non-compliance” stretching back to at least March of this year.




The violations listed in the notice include unpermitted construction, unpermitted activity in wetlands and other waterways, and violations of air quality laws, among others.




Language in the permit says that no work outside the originally approved plan the company submitted is allowed, but in September the company 

began construction on an unpermitted reroute

 for the pipeline in response to a rupture this summer. 




And on August 25, the company was responsible for what’s been called the state’s 

largest oil spill

 in more than 50 years when an unoccupied truck rolled into a section of Line 5 at a work site. The 

line ruptured

, leading to 31,000 barrels, or 1.3 million gallons, of natural gas spilling just east of the Bad River Reservation in Iron county.




Related: 

Enbridge Line 5 Spills Natural Gas Liquids in Northern Wisconsin




In light of the violations and pattern of not complying with state rules, opponents are calling on Evers, the state’s top executive, to exercise his power to revoke the permit.




“If he has a conscience, he needs to act now on the power he has right now to cancel the Line 5 permits,” Hoy, the oil-toasting protester, said in a recorded statement shortly after the disruption happened.




Immediately after Hoy was ejected, another Climate Defiance activist approached the stage calling on Evers to reject the Line 5 permits. They were quickly confronted by an attendee, but resisted removal while demanding the governor consider his legacy and stop work on the pipeline.




The action is the latest in an ongoing battle against the Canadian oil company’s reconstruction of the Line 5 pipeline. For years, organizers have opposed the project on the grounds that it violates Native sovereignty and poses a dire threat to the region’s fresh water, all while accelerating climate change by propping up fossil fuel infrastructure.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Austerity under fire as Godongwana pauses fuel levies and low-cost housing
content:
Residents, activists, members of trade unions and civil society groups took to the streets of Cape Town earlier today against budget cuts. This was before the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement was delivered by the Minister of Finance, Enoch Godongwana. Led by Cry of the Xcluded, some of the protesters’ demands included the right to decent work, an end to exclusionary access to free basic services, an end to privatisation, an increase in health, education and policing, and an universal basic income amongst others.




Equal Education’s secretary general, Itumeleng Mothlabane said that the budget cuts in education have resulted in the existence of plain pit latrines in schools, overcrowded classrooms and learners having to walk on dangerous roads when they go to school.




“We reject a budget that continues to deprioritise the education of a poor black learner. We demand an increase in the allocation that is given to each and every learner. We demand an increase in the school infrastructure budget in Limpopo, KwaZulu-Natal, the Eastern Cape and all the rural provinces,” Mothlabane said.




Lusanda Dyan from Rural Women’s Assembly said they are calling for the allocation of land to women and youth in rural areas and funding of centres that offer assistance to victims of gender-based violence in the rural areas. “Give us 2 hectares of land, seeds and access to water and we will feed this country,” she said.




The protesters also demanded land with water redistribution, and for the government to deal with the housing backlog.




Member of the Movement for Change and Social Justice, Lindiwe Mvandaba said the austerity measures that are implemented by the government are a political choice. “We reject the R370 SRD [social relief of distress] grant because it is not enough for us to feed ourselves and families,” she said. 




Speaking to 

Elitsha

, SRD grant recipient, Bernice Benjamin from De Doorns said that she is only able to buy bread, electricity and a few toiletries with the R370 that she receives. Benjamin is currently unemployed and gets support from her parents who receive an old age grant. “My R370 and my parents’ old age pensions only allow us to buy food for two weeks. For the rest of the month, we have to buy food on the book [credit] and we have to get loans for electricity and other stuff that we need. If you borrow R100, you must return it as R150,” she said.




Another SRD grant recipient from Ceres, Wendy Samson said that her R370 is enough to pay her municipal bill only. “We demand that the grant be increased,” she said.




Protesters called for an end to budget cuts because of their negative effect on the poor. Photo by Mzi Velapi




The South African Communist Party leader in the Western Cape and former provincial legislature member for the African National Congress, Benson Ngqentsu told the crowd that the aim of the budget cuts is to hollow the capacity of state entities so that the government can privatise them. “All police stations in this province and around the country do not have enough detectives and police vehicles,” Ngqentsu complained. He was a member of the standing committee on police oversight in the Western Cape legislature.




“We know that Godongwana will announce neo-liberal policies in local government in order to pave the way for privatisation. We therefore say no to the auctioning of solid waste, and water and sanitation departments,” he said.




Cosatu and Saftu united




Zwelinzima Vavi, the general secretary of the South African Federation of Trade Unions (Saftu), called for unity between the federation and the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu). Vavi shared the stage with the newly elected president of Cosatu, Mike Shingange.




“I want to propose that we have a meeting now in October and next month with Cosatu that will result in a joint 77 notice to the government and inform them that in February next year, during the budget speech, all workers in the Western Cape and around the country, will demand an end to austerity measures and we say voetsek Godongwana,” Vavi said.




Shingange said that the next austerity protest in February should lead to a national shutdown. “Workers have no luxury to be divided because of the badge on their T-shirt or colour of their T-shirt. The enemy knows no name of the union, colour or badge. They only know exploitation and will exploit workers irrespective of the union they belong to,” he said.




Minister Enoch Godongwana presenting the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement in parliament. Photo by Phando Jikelo/Parliament of RSA




‘Mini-budget’ pauses fuel levies and low-cost housing




During the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement presentation, Godongwana announced that the SRD grant will be extended until March 2028. The former trade union leader turned finance minister told parliament that just over 5-billion is to be allocated to combat gender-based violence over three years, with most of the money going to the employment of more than 3,500 social workers.




From 4 November to 1 December, according to Godongwana, the fuel levies on diesel will be cut by R3 and on petrol by R1.50 per litre. Between 1 December and 5 January 2027, the levy will be R1.50/litre lower on diesel and R1/litre lower on petrol.




When it comes to low-cost housing, Godwongwana announced that the human settlements development grant, is to be paused while a new delivery model is designed.

author: Chris Walker
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid to Halt Care for Incarcerated Trans People
content:
The decision is a rare win for transgender rights at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The U.S. Supreme Court has denied an emergency petition from the Trump administration, which sought a stay on a lower court’s injunction on a policy that would have denied gender-affirming care to federally incarcerated transgender people.

That policy was implemented by the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 that denied the existence of transgender people. The order also directed federal agencies to take steps that would be consistent with that view, and included specific instructions for the BOP.

“The Attorney General shall ensure that the Bureau of Prisons revises its policies concerning medical care to be consistent with this order, and shall ensure that no Federal funds are expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex,” the order reads.

After the BOP conformed to the order, a group of incarcerated trans people who had been receiving gender-affirming care sued the administration. The group is being represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), which argued that their Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment were being infringed upon.

A federal judge agreed, and, in August, ordered the policy to be blocked. The Trump administration challenged that finding, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld it, prompting Solicitor General John Sauer to submit an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.

The court has regularly ruled against transgender people, allowing state bans on trans athletes’ participation in sports, ruling in favor of a ban on transgender people in the military, and upholding state laws that bar gender-affirming care for trans children and teens. Yet on Wednesday, the court denied the Trump administration’s request.

“The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied,” the order read, giving no further explanation. Two justices for the court — Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas — would have granted the Trump administration’s request for a stay, the document said.

The ACLU heralded the high court’s denial of the emergency petition, stating, “This ruling affirms that federal prison officials can’t deny transgender people essential health care.”

Around 1,000 federally incarcerated trans people have also been diagnosed with gender dysphoria. The ruling means these individuals can continue receiving gender-affirming care while they remain in federal prisons or jails and the case moves forward in the lower courts.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

In nine days, on 30 October, dockworkers in more than 100 ports across Europe, Asia, Africa and America are taking action together, under the slogan: Dockworkers do not work for war. The unions call it one of the biggest coordinated workers’ actions the docks have ever seen.

Dockworkers who act without people at the gates will bear the brunt of the repression that follows, so stand with them.

We’ve built a tool to help you find the action nearest to you. Use it at the link in bio.

The map shows every port we can name so far, grouped by country, with times and meeting points added as unions confirm them. Check back before the 30th; the list is still growing.

It also tells you what passes through your port. We have documented 315 shipments of Elbit Systems components through 56 commercial ports and 3,400 shipments supplying US military bases through 67 ports. Where we have documented transfers from this database or the press for 2025-2026, the port’s entry says so.

Not near a port? Join a solidarity action in your city, push the Istanbul Declaration, share the poster. If you are a union member, dockworker, port worker or seafarer, use our template to write to your union. If you live in a port city, use our template letter to write to your port authority.

Organising something on the day that isn’t on the map yet? Tell us through the form on the page and we’ll add it once it’s confirmed.

Translations of the templates are coming soon.

author: labor4pal
title: As More Unions Oppose ICE and Israel, the Right Is Cracking Down (Truthout)
content:
The right is trying to gain access to labor unions’ minutes, membership lists, and Zoom chats.By Blanca Missé , Truthout Published October 21, 2026

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On September 22, The Free Press attacked the California Faculty Association (CFA), which represents about 29,000 faculty, librarians, counselors, and coaches across the California State University (CSU) system. Drawing on private discussions about a proposed Jewish caucus, including communications from a union Zoom meeting, the article accused CFA of antisemitism. How those communications reached the publication remains unclear. Two days later, the Jewish Journal amplified those allegations, urging Gov. Gavin Newsom to consider them as he weighed California Assembly Bill (AB) 2551, CFA-sponsored legislation challenging campus protest restrictions imposed after the 2024 Palestine solidarity encampments. Less than a week after The Free Press story was published, Newsom vetoed the bill.

Pro-Israel and Jewish advocacy organizations had already campaigned against AB 2551 before the union’s internal deliberations were targeted, arguing that greater scrutiny would weaken rules needed to protect Jewish students from harassment and intimidation. Newsom’s veto does not prove coordination, but the campaign portraying CFA as hostile to Jewish students had become entangled with the union’s fight against campus protest restrictions.

The CSU’s systemwide policy prohibits encampments, overnight demonstrations, and unauthorized structures. The CSU Academic Senate immediately condemned the restrictions as undermining academic freedom when it was instituted in 2024, while CFA warned that vague definitions of disruption threatened constitutionally protected speech, assembly, protest, and future strike activity. A major 2026 ACLU-Amnesty study, investigating 80 campuses over two years, documented sweeping repression of Palestine solidarity protests. As the report found, universities “have imposed sweeping restrictions on student speech, initiated disciplinary actions against students, and imposed severe punishments, including expulsions and suspensions.” The ACLU has insisted that even legitimate time, place, and manner restrictions “must leave ample room for students to express themselves.”

The controversy reaches beyond CFA and CSU. Unions and rank-and-file organizations committed to Palestine solidarity have been forced to relitigate, again and again, whether anti-Zionism and solidarity with Palestinians constitute antisemitism — and whether such organizing should be systematically policed, investigated, or surveilled. At stake is a more fundamental right of the exploited: Can workers democratically connect economic struggles with Palestine solidarity, resistance to anti-immigrant and anti-Black racism, and the defense of civil liberties without exposing their organizing and deliberations to external pressure or repression?

We already have a word for the use of legal process as a political weapon: lawfare. You do not necessarily have to win. Investigation, expense, compelled disclosure, and possible sanctions can exact their own price.

Call its media counterpart pressfare: leaked material, selective or doctored quotations, and public identification can turn people into political targets and invite pressure on employers, universities, or government agencies.

The leaked CFA meeting should not be adjudicated through fragments selected for publication, especially when CFA’s statewide record contradicts the portrayal of a union indifferent to antisemitism. During the 2024 encampments, CFA opposed antisemitism and Islamophobia “in all forms” while supporting the encampments. Amid a 2025 federal antisemitism investigation, it stated that “as CFA members, we are united against antisemitism; it has no place in our communities,” while defending members’ academic freedom. CFA’s Palestine, Arab, and Muslim Caucus likewise defines its mission as confronting racism “in all its manifestations,” explicitly including antisemitism. The Free Press story — a clear example of pressfare — sought to overwrite this legacy with weaponized accusations, undermining the trust that workers place in the sanctity of their union spaces and processes.

Antisemitism demands to be taken seriously — which is why accusations of anti-Jewish discrimination should not be instrumentalized. Kenneth Stern, director of the Bard Center for the Study of Hate, has warned that using the International Holocaust Remembrance Association (IHRA) definition of antisemitism as a regulatory code threatens academic freedom by equating criticism of Israel with antisemitism, while the Jerusalem Declaration warns that the definition’s ambiguities have generated confusion and controversy, “hence weakening the fight against antisemitism.” And as Jewish Voice for Peace and Jerusalem Declaration scholars have argued, combating antisemitism is not helped by conflating hostility toward Jews with anti-Zionism, criticism of Israel, or Palestine solidarity. Requiring Palestinian and anti-Zionist unionists to prove otherwise reverses the burden of proof, allowing accusations to substitute for evidence and cultivating fear and suspicion that inhibit collective action while fueling an ever-expanding search for evidence.

That ever-expanding search has taken the form of several federal antisemitism inquiries targeting universities and their workers.

Federal antisemitism investigations have extended scrutiny to faculty speech and Palestine solidarity organizing, with consequences for unions. At Cal State LA, CSU disclosed employees’ personal information to federal investigators, prompting CFA to sue over violations of workers’ privacy.

What drove these federal inquiries on antisemitism? A 2025 study from the American Association of University Professors and the Middle East Studies Association examined 102 complaints that prompted federal civil rights investigations; pro-Israel and right-wing organizations were involved in 78 percent. All but one of the complaints concerned speech critical of Israel, and in 80 percent, complainants characterized criticism of Israel or Zionism that made no reference to Jews or Judaism as antisemitic. In at least half, the complaint rested solely on constitutionally protected political speech.

The study separately examined 28 Title VI antisemitism lawsuits brought against universities by pro-Israel groups. As of its cutoff, not one had produced a final judicial finding of discrimination in favor of the plaintiffs, although some resulted in settlements imposing new restrictions on campus speech and protest.

CFA’s political commitments long predate the renewed Palestine solidarity movement. In 2023, the union challenged CSU administrators on First Amendment grounds for restricting classroom discussion of strikes. In 2020, after years of organizing, CFA helped secure passage of AB 1460, the landmark law making Ethnic Studies a graduation requirement across the CSU system — a major victory for racial justice and educational equity in one of the nation’s most racially and ethnically diverse states. Since then, it has continued fighting CSU over its implementation, defending faculty control over curriculum and the integrity of Ethnic Studies programs.

Now, at the bargaining table, CFA is seeking protections against retaliation for faculty speech, assembly, and protest through an academic freedom article that would make those protections enforceable through the union contract.

Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity?

The Free Press article published names and private union messages, exposing faculty, particularly faculty of color vulnerable around employment and tenure, to potential retaliation. Among those identified was Omar Zahzah, whose scholarship includes the book Terms of Servitude, on U.S. technology companies and Israeli settler colonialism. He had also recently written about the “Michigan 8,” warning of “a broader targeting of the pro-Palestine movement.” Whatever the intent, the chilling message is clear: Continue this scholarship, political writing, or union organizing, and you, too, risk public exposure and targeting.

The consequences of this attack reach into union democracy itself: Fear of exposure changes what members dare to say, whom they trust, and how they are willing to organize together. In 2025, CFA sued CSU after Cal State LA disclosed faculty and staff members’ personal contact information to federal investigators conducting an antisemitism inquiry. The union secured a January 2026 settlement requiring CSU to notify employees before complying with any specified federal demands for personal information, unless legally prohibited.

The exposure of CFA’s internal deliberations raises a question beyond leaked communications: Why are state agencies and outside political organizations seeking access to the networks through which workers organize political solidarity? In Minnesota and Michigan, that scrutiny has taken a more coercive form: undercover surveillance and federal subpoenas.

In Minnesota, federal agents infiltrated political meetings and activist chats under “Operation Puppet Master,” a surveillance operation exposed during the prosecution of the “Minnesota 15,” activists charged with conspiracy to impede federal officers. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) slide titled “The Conspiracy” mapped 18 organizations, including unions, while Homeland Security Investigations used administrative subpoenas — requiring no judicial approval — to obtain years of financial records connected to Service Employees International Union (SEIU) and Communications Workers of America (CWA). Defense attorney Kevin Riach challenged the surveillance as lacking any “articulable criminal predicate” and violating constitutional protections; federal prosecutors maintained that the charges concerned criminal conduct alone.

At a February workers’ assembly at Minneapolis’s United Labor Centre, roughly 400 workers debated labor’s response to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). One undercover agent reported “no real threats”; another sought to “get phone numbers.” Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration and whether anti-ICE activists were selectively prosecuted.

Defense attorneys are seeking federal surveillance reports, undercover device downloads, and communications between local prosecutors and Washington to establish the extent of infiltration.

In Michigan, following the indictment of the Michigan 8 — eight Palestine solidarity activists accused of conspiracy — a federal grand jury subpoena demanded Graduate Employees’ Organization (GEO) records dating to January 1, 2023: current and former membership information, officers, meeting minutes, personnel, and finances.

GEO President Hiab Teshome faced felony embezzlement and false-pretenses charges over alleged misuse of student organization funds. University police also sought to bar her from campus, potentially excluding a member of the union’s bargaining team from her workplace. Both charges were dismissed on August 6 — the day the federal subpoena was signed. GEO denounced the prosecution as politically motivated and moved to quash the subpoena. The dismissal does not establish a political motive behind the federal investigation, but the juxtaposition is striking: The charges against one union leader collapsed, yet federal scrutiny extended to the entire union — who belonged to GEO, who led it, what its members discussed, and how they spent their money.

Those records could reveal how solidarity was organized. Meanwhile, GEO says university management struck proposed contract language barring disclosure of workers’ union membership to the federal government. The constitutional stakes are hardly new: In the 1958 case of NAACP v. Alabama, the Supreme Court recognized that compelled disclosure of membership lists can expose people to retaliation and deter lawful political association.

Membership lists, meeting minutes, financial records, and private communications reveal who organizes with whom. Historian Ellen Schrecker identifies a disturbing historical precedent in McCarthyism’s system of “guilt by association”: Private groups compiled dossiers, government investigated political affiliations, and employers and universities imposed punishment. She sees today’s assault on higher education as even more dire: “Today, what’s happening is worse, so much worse that we have to really find a new phrase for it,” she told Democracy Now!.

Labor has its own answer to “guilt by association”: solidarity by association — where association is not a risk to be feared, but a means of repairing what injustice or oppression has torn apart. In the words of the Minnesota 15 solidarity campaign, “Community Is Not Conspiracy.” Rather than accept the social hierarchies that divide and oppress workers, union organizers build relationships that can dismantle and transform them. In organizing with those under attack, workers discover capacities for collective action that none could exercise alone. An injury to an immigrant family facing deportation, a Black community confronting police violence, or Palestinians facing repression thus becomes a concern for workers beyond those immediately targeted.

“An injury to one is an injury to all” means little if solidarity becomes competitive or selective — if defending Jewish workers requires silence about Palestinians, if defending citizens means abandoning undocumented workers, or if wages are labor’s concern while police violence, deportations, and attacks on civil liberties belong to somebody else.

Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate.

Union meetings, caucuses, and other forms of association create spaces where workers connect economic and political struggles, building solidarity across sectors rather than dividing struggles against racism, gender oppression, political repression, and exploitation into separate constituencies. Through these relationships, workers build collective power, expanding their capacity to think, feel, and act together beyond the narrow and isolated roles assigned to them in the workplace and, more broadly, under capitalism.

Yet none of this is possible without preserving unions’ internal democracy and political independence. Workers need room to reflect, make mistakes and acknowledge them, disagree, organize, persuade one another, and make collective decisions without employers, the state, or outside political organizations dictating the limits of debate. Pressfare undermines that democracy when unproven allegations and internal deliberations become material for public targeting; lawfare erodes the independence of unions when accusations and investigations impose political costs before wrongdoing is established. Undercover agents mapping worker assemblies and prosecutors demanding years of union records bring far greater coercive power to bear on those same democratic spaces.

These methods differ in form and intensity, but they reproduce the same political effects: fear, suspicion, sadness, and isolation. These are effects that weaken the relationships through which workers might act together and change their circumstances. Solidarity, by contrast, nurtures compassion, courage, and the joy of gathering in assemblies, discovering what we can accomplish together. It strengthens our capacity not only to resist oppression and exploitation but to transform the social relations that sustain them. Perhaps that is what those who fear organized labor solidarity find most threatening.
