author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Juan Francisco Solórzano Foppa: Prominent Anti-Corruption Lawyer in Guatemala Assassinated
content:
The prominent Guatemalan anti-corruption lawyer Juan Francisco Solórzano Foppa was fatally shot along with another man on Saturday at a sports center in Guatemala City. For years, Solórzano Foppa had been outspoken against Guatemala’s most powerful politicians, business leaders and companies. He was known for his anti-corruption work as head of the Criminal Investigations Directorate within the Public Prosecutor’s Office and later as head of Guatemala’s tax authority, when he helped prosecute dozens of powerful Guatemalan business figures.




“In more recent years, he developed a social media presence, and he was forcefully denouncing corruption,” says Roman Gressier, a journalist based in Guatemala City. “We were thinking about [the killing of Solórzano Foppa] not only as an assassination, but also having a deep effect on freedom of expression.”




“Juan Francisco was a young lawyer coming from a background of pro-democracy and revolutionary activists,” says Silvia Solórzano Foppa, Juan Francisco’s mother. Her son was 43 years old when he was killed.

author: Lana Harb
title: Lebanon’s ‘pilot zone’ experiment: The case of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah
content:
Ihsan Yaghi’s house in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah is scorched from the inside. Piles of rubble fill the rooms she and her husband walk through to see what remains. What was not demolished by nearby Israeli strikes has been blackened by fire, with soot covering the interior walls. But Yaghi refuses to leave.




“Despite everything, this is still my land, and we have a very strong attachment to this land that we can’t let go of,” Yaghi tells Mada Masr.




Yaghi’s is one of roughly 100 families that have, since July, returned to Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, one of around 70 villages in southern Lebanon still under Israeli occupation, its residents displaced, its homes destroyed, its fields unreachable. The question of what should be done for the south, how to rebuild and how to return people to their land under continued occupation, has become one of the most pressing political questions in Lebanon. The answer currently on offer from the Lebanese government and its international partners is the “pilot zone.”




On July 21, the United States announced 

the official commencement

 of pilot zone operations in three villages in southern Lebanon: Froun, Srifa and Zawtar al-Gharbiyah. The model emerged from the framework agreement — a US-mediated trilateral framework signed by Lebanon and Israel on June 26, under which the Lebanese military is to restore sovereign authority over all Lebanese territory pending Hezbollah’s disarmament. The implementation of pilot zones was to mark the agreement’s first practical step. The idea was that the Lebanese military would deploy to select villages in coordination with a limited Israeli withdrawal, allowing residents to return while reconstruction and services would be concentrated there. Those villages would serve as templates, proof that return and rebuilding are possible, and the model could then be replicated elsewhere in the south.




Mada Masr spoke to residents, municipal officials and others involved with the project to assess whether this is indeed a workable model for the south.




Two months in, it is falling short on nearly every measure residents say matters. People are returning to villages without water, electricity, schools or livelihoods, the prefabricated homes promised as a temporary fix have arrived at a fraction of the numbers requested, and there is no guarantee of safety so long as Israeli forces remain in position nearby and have not withdrawn.




Children walking by destroyed houses in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, July 26. Photo by Ammar Ammar.




The model also treats villages as isolated units, when in reality they depend on one another for schools, shops, hospitals and work, activists say. While experts on the South’s history of war and reconstruction say the current process marks a fundamental shift from previous rounds of war, for those in the south adopting a more radical position on resistance, another pathway must be found.




***




The pilot zone is a new model for the south. Political historian Nassib Chams tells Mada Masr that it emerged from a major shift in Lebanese politics: direct talks with Israel.




Such talks were not the case during the 2000 Israeli withdrawal, after 20 years of occupation, or after the 2006 war. That shift, he says, is what allowed the pilot zone project to come into being, and it gives Israel agency and authority over the return of southern Lebanese.




“This is the first time in Lebanese history that we see many Lebanese expressing that they want peace with Israel. So, while Israel was always stronger militarily, it is the first time there is this much political support for Israel,” he notes.




He adds that the project remains loosely defined, with the government yet to give residents a clear account of what the pilot zones entail.




“We may not know what is in it. We don’t know the details of what is happening in the negotiations. So far, we have not seen an Israeli withdrawal or anything. Israeli military operations are still continuing,” he says. “Are the people supposed to test if their villages are still habitable? It is unclear what they are trying to achieve when it is not even contingent on a full Israeli withdrawal,” he says.




Israeli forces in Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, September 24. Photo by Ammar Ammar.




A resident of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, speaking on condition of anonymity, tells Mada Masr that Froun and Srifa have no Israeli presence at all, while Zawtar al-Gharbiyah has a relatively limited presence of Israeli troops compared to its twin village, Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, which remains under occupation and continues to face airstrikes, artillery shelling and the demolition of homes. The two villages sit in the Nabatieh District, on elevated terrain north of the Litani River, overlooking its valley, with Zawtar al-Sharqiyah immediately to the east of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah and with Mayfadoun to their north and Qaaqaaiyet al-Jisr to the west.




Following the July 21 announcement, the Lebanese military 

deployed

 to Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, and residents were allowed to return. What they found was widespread destruction of residential buildings, infrastructure, schools, supermarkets, hospitals and government offices. To the west of the village, Israeli forces remain positioned behind an earthen berm, blocking access to the rest of the village.




Earthen beam Israeli forces placed between Zawtar al-Gharbiyah and Zawtar al-Sharqiyah. Photo by Ammar Ammar.




Israeli forces are now 300-400 metres away, according to Yaghi. The Lebanese military has set up a checkpoint some 20 metres from the berm, which gives residents a sense of security and protection, she adds.




“The thing that encouraged people to return is the presence of the Lebanese military,” Abed Ezz Eddin, Zawtar al-Gharbiyah’s mayor, tells Mada Masr. “People feel safe knowing that the Lebanese military is present among us,” he says.




Lebanese military assisting residents’ return to Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, July 24. Photo by Ammar Ammar.




***




Two months into the start of the pilot zones, only 16 out of 263 requested prefabricated homes have reached Zawtar al-Gharbiyah, according to Ezz Eddin. The units were secured through a joint project between the Council of the South, a governmental institution tasked with providing assistance and compensation to the people affected by war and disasters in southern Lebanon, and the government’s High Relief Committee (HRC).




Bassam Naboulsy, the high committee’s director, tells Mada Masr that the government tasked the committee with securing 150 units, sourced through a mix of locally purchased units funded by the HRC and units brought in from East Asia by a private Swiss organization, whose name Naboulsy did not disclose.




“These houses will be distributed between Zawtar al-Gharbiyah and nearby villages, such as Merouaniyeh and Froun,” he says. Naboulsy adds that the distribution process is being handled by the southern council and local municipalities.




Prefabricated homes can cost around US$5,000 per unit, according to Naboulsy, a figure that he says exceeds the government’s limited budget and has thus necessitated having to rely on foreign assistance. As a result, there are no guarantees on how many units will arrive or when. In late July, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met with Turkish President 

Recep Tayyip Erdoğan

, who agreed to provide prefabricated homes to Lebanon, with no guaranteed timeline.




Even when the units arrive, they need to be made ready. Ezz Eddin says the land beneath them must first be cleared of debris and prepared before the winter rains, a process overseen by the Council of the South. The units also need solar panels, water tanks and kitchen appliances, for which Zawtar al-Gharbiyah’s municipality is seeking support from nongovernmental organizations.




A prefabricated home in place of a destroyed house, October 14. Photo by Ammar Ammar.




Much of the work of return has fallen on the municipality and on residents themselves. Ezz Eddin says the municipality has been left to restore power lines, work on water infrastructure and seek foreign funding for both.




“People are paying out of pocket to fix their houses to be able to stay in them,” he says. “But even then, people are hesitant to put glass in their windows and are just using plastic wrap instead.”




For those who have returned, making a living remains difficult. Zawtar relies on agriculture, but venturing into fields, particularly those farther from the village center, has become risky. Residents need permission from the 

Mechanism

, a committee comprising Lebanon, Israel, France and UNIFIL tasked with overseeing the ceasefire. The Lebanese military communicates residents’ requests to the Mechanism, Ezz Eddin says, but so far, they have not received permission to access their fields.




“Even if I wanted to plant my own field around the house, I need to remove the debris on my own. So my husband and I are having to rent a bulldozer to do that ourselves,” Yaghi says. She currently comes to the village only during the day and leaves for a nearby village at night, as her house remains unrepaired and unlivable.




***




The limits of the pilot zones are already clear in villages it has yet to reach. Tarek Mazraany, an activist and the founder of grassroots initiative the Gathering of the Children of the Southern Border Towns, says the model would be difficult to replicate because it treats each village separately and overlooks how much residents depend on neighboring villages for schools, shops, hospitals and work.




“Zawtar al-Gharbiyah is a relatively small village, and it took two months to start securing prefabricated houses,” Mazraany says. “This can’t be sustainable in other villages, particularly those near the border, where the scale of destruction is much greater and many have become totally isolated,” he adds.




Zawtar al-Gharbiyah also has an advantage because of its proximity to Nabatieh, which gives residents access to shops, schools and government offices. In villages closer to the border, where destruction is far more extensive, clearing the rubble alone could take years.




Rebuilding homes will not be enough, Mazraany says. Residents also need schools, shops, hospitals and law enforcement services to return before they can fully resume their lives.




He argues that reconstruction should instead be organized by district, with neighboring villages rebuilt together so they can share services and speed up residents’ return.




“The best model would be to work district by district as pilot zones, because villages in the broader South depend on each other. One can have the school, the other can have the shops, so that the process is quicker and more residents can return,” he says.




Reconstruction in some of the larger towns, such as Bint Jbeil and Khiam, could take up to 20 years, Mazraany says, adding that time is not on southern residents’ side if the government continues to delay their return.




***




While those Mada Masr spoke to see the pilot zones as a failed approach to reconstruction, those committed to a more radical position on resistance reject the project altogether, refusing to recognize the agreement on which it is based.




“We consider all the land to be our land, and it is our right to be in any place in southern Lebanon and in any village in southern Lebanon, regardless of whether the enemy withdrew under conditions or without conditions,” Afif Shuman, the director of NGO Wa Taawano, tells Mada Masr. “We do not turn to and we are not ready even to coordinate with the Mechanism or any party that may be coordinating with the Israelis.”




Wa Taawano is one of the most active charities in Zawtar al-Gharbiyah. But Shuman says the security situation, particularly the constant presence of Israeli drones overhead, has made it difficult for activists and NGOs to operate safely.




Shuman also points to political and security pressures that he says are preventing aid from reaching southern residents. He says some charities affiliated with Lebanese political figures withheld assistance to appease the US, while others refrained from operating in areas affected by the fighting for fear of security repercussions and possible sanctions.




For Shuman, the pilot zones are not a reconstruction model but a way to determine who is allowed to return. He argues that the project is designed to exclude families Israel does not want back in their villages, including the families of those killed in the fighting and the fighters themselves.




He says residents would not accept a system that prevents them from returning to their homes, making the project unworkable in the long run.




Hajj Ali Khazaal, the head of the municipality in Ainata, a border village in the Bint Jbeil district, and the head of Hezbollah’s municipality affairs for the south, holds a similar position. “I do not fundamentally recognize the framework agreement that this project came out of,” Khazaal tells Mada Masr.




Khazaal says the Lebanese military’s deployment to all southern villages should be the government’s main priority, which would require a complete Israeli withdrawal. He describes the pressure on the region as military, political and financial, arguing that the state has also failed residents by leaving reconstruction unaddressed.




“They want reconstruction without resistance so that they can get rid of the resistance, but that will be futile. There should be a clear focus on reconstruction and people’s immediate return,” he says.




Khazaal also pointed to US President Donald Trump’s proposal for an 

economic zone

 spanning more than two dozen towns in southern Lebanon, focused on development and investment — not the Lebanese people’s return — as more likely to move forward than the pilot zones.




For Khazaal, the first step before reconstruction can begin must be to secure the withdrawal of Israeli forces and regain access to all the land. He says the municipality already has a plan for the process, which he estimates would take around three years. Clearing rubble would take six months to a year, followed by another six to 12 months to reopen roads and restore water and electricity infrastructure. Installing prefabricated homes and making them habitable would then take another year to a year and a half.




In the meantime, he argues, negotiations are wasting time while the decisions shaping southern Lebanon’s future are being made elsewhere.




“The Iranian-American agreement, wherever things go there is reflected here,” he says. “All of this is a waste of time here, until the decision comes from those superior.”




Lebanon and Israel are expected to 

hold a new round

 of negotiations in Florida, around the end of October, where the possibility of a second pilot zone could be discussed.




And while the US and Israel have tried to push forward their plans for the south, Hezbollah and Iran have not remained confined to criticism.




Hezbollah’s Executive Council head Ali Damoush addresses a press conference in southern Beirut, October 13. Courtesy of Anwar Amro/AFP




On October 13, Hezbollah 

announced

 it would begin paying rent compensation to people whose homes were destroyed, with payments reaching as much as $14,000 for housing units in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $12,000 elsewhere, starting with an initial installment of $3,500 in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $3,000 outside those areas.




The announcement of the cash payouts come after Iran transferred $600 million to Hezbollah at the beginning of October via Syrian intermediaries, an Iranian diplomat, a Syrian source with direct knowledge of the transfer and a source in the party tell Mada Masr.




The money, the Iranian diplomat says, aims to help the displaced ahead of the coming winter.




For families like Yaghi’s, promises for support from either side are still yet to materialize, and, for now, there is nothing to do apart from carrying on.




“Seeing how attached our neighbors are to the land,” she says, “and how adamant they are to remain present, gives us the strength to stay and endure.”

The post 

Lebanon’s ‘pilot zone’ experiment: The case of Zawtar al-Gharbiyah

 first appeared on 

Mada Masr

.

author: Unknown
title: Spagna chiama Italia: casa e finanziarizzazione
content:
La lotta per il diritto alla casa negli ultimi trent’anni è sempre stata un’invarianza della rigidità che le classi subalterne hanno imposto al potere nella più generale tendenza neo liberista di attacco alle condizioni materiali di vita delle persone. 




Da mesi però assistiamo ad un ritorno di questa lotta come centralità politica a livello internazionale. Partendo dall’elezione a New York del nuovo Sindaco Mamdani, passando per la vittoria a Berlino della candidata Linke Elif Eralp, fino alle imponenti mobilitazioni spagnole partite dalla vicenda Maricarmen la lotta per l’accesso alla casa ha saputo diventare nuovamente una spina nel fianco delle élites capitaliste, anche aggredendo i nuovi meccanismi che la speculazione immobiliare ha messo in campo.




Si possono infatti delineare delle nuove  invarianze in questa ondata  di mobilitazione, ossia l’attacco frontale ai meccanismi di finanziarizzazione della casa e dell’abitare. 




La trasformazione della casa in “asset finanziario” ha infatti inasprito le difficoltà di accedere ad affitti proporzionati ai salari reali e innalzato la barriera economica che divide i proletari e il ceto medio dalla possibilità di acquistare una casa.




In tutti i contesti europei e d’oltreoceano il rapporto fra salario e spesa per garantirsi un tetto sopra la testa è letteralmente saltato, facendo esplodere una vera e propria “bomba” sociale. Questo meccanismo di finanziarizzazione della casa è recentemente approdato anche in Italia, dove le lotte per la casa sono storicamente centrali, ma che negli ultimi anni hanno subito molti attacchi mettendone  a rischio le conquiste del passato. L’insorgere di questo nuovo fenomeno però allarga di fatto la base sociale coinvolta dalla lotta anche nel nostro paese. Siamo di fronte ad un nuovo ciclo di opposizione sociale e antagonista su questo ambito della riproduzione popolare?




Anche se è difficile rispondere a questa domanda crediamo sia importante partire primariamente dai meccanismi materiali alla base di questa scommessa, appunto la finanziarizzazione.




Milano, Firenze, Roma, Torino, Bologna

 e molte altre città sono investite da meccanismi di speculazione immobiliare portate avanti dai fondi che a loro volta sono gestiti e comandati da colossi detti società di gestione del risparmio. Questo meccanismo si somma a quelli storici della gentrificazione, della turistificazione e della speculazione immobiliare intorno all’abitare studentesco.




Abbiamo preso spunto per spiegare questo complesso fenomeno da un’ intervista al Professor Alessandro Volpi apparsa recentemente 

qui

.







Il mercato è mosso dalle società di gestione del risparmio che si occupano di immobiliare. Oggi queste hanno un peso importante e sono in sintesi una settantina ed hanno un patrimonio immobiliare che si aggira intorno 145 miliardi di euro. 




Esiste di fatto una grossa concentrazione nella capacità di gestire il patrimonio, infatti tendenzialmente 10 società detengono quasi metà dell’importo complessivo.




 Le società di gestione del risparmio non gestiscono direttamente il patrimonio immobiliare (es Fabrica sgr, Investire sgr), ma generano fondi immobiliari, i quali sono legati a specifici progetti immobiliari, sia di recupero che di acquisto di aree già edificate o di costruzione di nuovi complessi di edifici.




Esistono più o meno 750 fondi immobiliari legati a queste 70 sgr, le 10 più importanti ne hanno di conseguenza una quota maggiore. Quindi diversi fondi immobiliari, nella stessa città o in diverse metropoli italiane, possono usufruire della stessa strategia dovuta al fatto che una singola società di gestione del risparmio ha molti fondi a disposizione.




Il fondo, in particolare, si occupa di decidere i progetti sull’area urbana di riferimento e della gestione del patrimonio immobiliare che possiede. 




Essendo che una sgr guadagna dalle commissioni che gli pagano i fondi, essi vendono le loro quote per finanziarsi.  Fino a poco tempo fa la  tendenza era quella di vendere anche a risparmiatori benestanti di fascia medio alta, ma comunque a patrimonio limitato, se paragonato a grandi agglomerati finanziari, ora  i fondi vengono frammentati e divisi  in quote vendute principalmente a investitori istituzionali. Questi possono essere ad esempio fondi pensione e casse di previdenza degli ordini professionali o altri con grandi capacità. Così facendo vi è quindi un  allargamento della base di reperibilità delle risorse per il fondo, accentrando grosse porzioni di capitale.




Per fare un’operazione ad esempio, un fondo compra un blocco di migliaia di appartamenti, diventando decisore in ultima istanza dell’andamento del mercato immobiliare nella zona in cui acquista, poi si predispone per avere un rendimento alto delle quote vendute con cui ha investito negli appartamenti. Le quote hanno la necessità di essere competitive economicamente, ossia  la quota parte deve  competere contro tutti i prodotti finanziari come azioni di altri fondi come ad esempio Black Rock o altri colossi che hanno fatto manbassa del capitale nostrano.  Per poter competere ed attirare compratori devono essere remunerativi. Per farlo, come dicevamo, comprano ad esempio un blocco di tanti appartamenti nella stessa zona, li liberano degli inquilini in vari modi, alzando gli affitti come nel caso di MariCarmen a Madrid. Una volta disponibili, una parte di questi appartamenti  vengono tolti dal mercato, per risparmiare sulle ristrutturazioni da una parte e dall’altra per far alzare il prezzo complessivo con la scarsità del bene che controllano. Così facendo vengono messi sul mercato solo una parte degli appartamenti realmente disponibili che possono diventare particolarmente redditizi, se vi si applicano affitti molto alti o venduti a prezzi alti. In questo modo si alza il prezzo medio complessivo della zona in cui il fondo ha investito.




Si tende ad un rendimento massimo in breve periodo in modo da poter ripartire i profitti a tutti gli attori di questo processo economico giocato sulla pelle degli inquilini.




Così facendo si innesca il meccanismo che porta all’innalzamento complessivo degli affitti in in un’intera porzione metropolitana o addirittura nella sua totalità. A cascata vi è un espulsione primariamente delle persone a basso reddito, ma anche di quelle a medio che riparano in zone sempre più periferiche o addirittura in altre città limitrofe e di provincia.







Riassumendo quindi il funzionamento della catena della produzione di  valore è: la società di gestione del risparmio guadagna e vive di commissioni e servizi che le sono pagate e fornite dai fondi: così più fondi crea più commissioni o azioni riesce a incamerare e, quindi, più ci guadagna. I fondi immobiliari remunerano i sottoscrittori delle loro quote in proporzione ai ricavi che ottengono, i quali sono legati tendenzialmente alla possibilità di praticare affitti più alti. L’ultimo anello di questa catena è chi paga la rendita, l’affitto, o meglio chi non riesce a permetterselo e viene impoverito se deve o vuole rimanere nella zona interessata, oppure viene espulso.




Questo processo genera come effetto collaterale una scarsità di immobili disponibili oltre al fatto che quelli disponibili hanno prezzi molto alti. 




Aggiungiamo un 

ulteriore aspetto da indagare che riguarda una tendenza in atto, ossia la forte presenza di colossi immobiliari tra le fila delle società promotrici di progetti di nuovi data center, soprattutto al Nord-Ovest, ma non solo.

 Anche da 

fonti

 del settore viene sottolineato come “una serie di fattori convergenti rende interessante la riconversione degli asset immobiliari come data center”. A Milano ad esempio il primo investimento del colosso americano Hines nei data center ha inaugurato questo processo con un progetto di 95mila mq nell’area del Noviglio; la stessa società ha promosso il data center di Caselle Torinese in Piemonte. Il fatto che i data center necessitino di vaste aree da bonificare o direttamente suoli agricoli significa per le società immobiliari ampliare i propri asset di investimento anche in zone che precedentemente non erano interessanti per alimentare valore. 

Quindi superfici che non erano utili a produrre profitto, perché ex aree industriali dismesse o non collocate nei centri città, ora lo diventano.

 Territori “marginali” possono dunque diventare strategici e alimentare il processo di finanziarizzazione, gli investimenti presumibilmente avranno effetti sul valore che questi terreni potranno acquisire in un futuro e, dunque, aumentano il prezzo al metroquadro sul mercato in generale. 

Questo avviene perché a dare il valore di questo genere di collocazioni per questi specifici immobili è la capacità in termini di megawatt, ossia la possibilità di allaccio alla rete, i tempi di connessione, la disponibilità di energia.

 Un esempio in questo senso viene fornito da questo 

articolo

, dove viene sostenuto che :







“La scala dell’AI spinge il mercato verso territori nei quali terreno ed energia sono più disponibili, [quindi l’hinterland] senza perdere il collegamento economico e digitale con Milano.” Questo chiaramente non significa perdita di centralità dal punto di vista di rendita, investimenti, profitti relativamente alla città, in questo caso Milano. Significa però che se colossi immobiliari si muovono per acquistare terreni brownfield aprono un terreno di speculazione e finanziarizzazione sulla base della ricchezza che l’intelligenza artificiale porterà. Si tratta di una sorta di scommessa sul futuro perché, nel frattempo, viene consumato suolo, risorse naturali, energia e infrastrutture. Questo campo però permette di avviare margini di guadagno per fondi privati, investitori, banche. Seguendo questo ragionamento parrebbe dunque che siamo di fronte a un processo che individua i data center come nuovo asset strategico immobiliare e ne riscrive le regole in quanto la “collocazione” non è più condizionata alla vicinanza con i centri del capitale.







Inoltre questo fenomeno di speculazione ne genera uno proporzionalmente inverso sul mercato prettamente immobiliare, quindi di case da abitare. Intorno ai data center, dunque ai terreni su cui il valore di rendita è aumentato, si genera un deprezzamento degli immobili esistenti adibiti ad abitazioni civili, spesso in aree periferiche perciò destinazione e proprietà di quel vasto proletariato e ceto medio italiano

 che ha un tasso di proprietà di casa intorno al 70%. Questo significa che in  diverse aree periurbane e periferiche già in crisi, ad essere attaccato di riflesso, è la maggior riserva di valore accumulata nella parte bassa della società, ossia la casa di proprietà.




Un altro fenomeno che è utile segnalare, fra le dinamiche che vediamo evolversi attorno alla questione casa, c’è quella delle 

successioni del patrimonio immobiliare familiare e l’insorgere di speculatori detti “instant buyers”.

 In sostanza il nostro paese si trova, per via dell’andamento demografico, davanti ad un aumento di giovani e meno giovani che ereditano case dalla generazione “boomer”. Questi immobili, molto spesso nelle province e nelle periferie metropolitane, sono vecchie, inefficienti a livello energetico a volte fatiscenti. Necessitano quindi di un investimento per poter essere usate o fruttare attraverso una vendita o una rendita. Molte rimangono vuote per problemi di 

successione e burocrazia

, altre perché situate in territori spopolati o in via di spopolamento, altre ancora per mancanza di risorse da parte di chi le eredita. 

Qui si inserisce il ruolo dell’Istant Buyer: un impresario o un fondo che compra deprezzato l’immobile per rivenderlo o affittarlo in breve tempo. Così si assiste ad un fenomeno speculativo, ma anche ad una perdita di riserva di capitale nei ceti bassi della società a favore di una concentrazione di valore, capitale e rendita per la

 

borghesia rentier

.

 




Inoltre alcuni studiosi iniziano ad ipotizzare la nascita di due mercati immobiliari separati: da una parte uno redditizio fatto immobili ristrutturati e ad alto valore, un altro fatto di immobili al limite della fatiscenza con prezzi ribassati destinato a proletari, migranti e non, con basso o bassissimo reddito. 




Parliamo quindi di una situazione a “collo di bottiglia” in cui il maggiore pilastro del welfare familistico del nostro paese viene rapidamente eroso e riportato nelle mani di una piccola borghesia nazionale e internazionale. Va messo in risalto questo passaggio storico poiché è proprio questa forma tutta italiana di welfare, ad aver molte volte fatto da “tappo” e cuscinetto all’esplosione di conflitti sociali dispiegati a livello di massa sull’abitare e sulla precarietà del lavoro.




Vediamo quindi come la finanziarizzazione della casa legata ad altre dinamiche storiche abbia delle ricadute concrete per le persone sia di ceto medio che proletarie.  




Questo processo di finanziarizzazione dell’abitare accomuna e colpisce indistintamente un gran numero di persone, portando indirettamente un attacco che conduce all’erosione dei salari nel nostro paese, fermi da decenni. Gli stipendi bassi e l’iper sfruttamento sono la principale base di guadagno per i padroni nel nostro paese. L’imporsi di grossi colossi, principalmente americani, sia nel comparto pubblico che nel capitale privato, ha come effetto diretto per le persone un ulteriore impoverimento. 

Se si aggiunge a questo l’inflazione, il caro carburante e il carovita di guerra, l’attacco economico assume proporzioni devastanti per le condizioni di vita delle persone, soprattutto perchè a ciò si somma un generale disinvestimento o privatizzazione del welfare nella sua totalità a favore del riarmo.




Le lotte per la casa in questi anni hanno resistito attraverso pratiche di occupazione, sciopero delle bollette, vertenze sulle case poplari e campagne di pressione sulle amministrazioni locali e i governi nazionali di destra e sinistra per calmierare gli affitti. 

Oggi ci sembra però che le condizioni dettate dalla crisi pongano il movimento per l’abitare di fronte ad una nuova sfida che potenzialmente può poggiare su nuovi rapporti di forza a suo favore.

 L’accentramento di capitale immobiliare, come abbiamo cercato di spiegare, coinvolge molte più persone direttamente e indirettamente in questa lotta per la sopravvivenza minima. In più i profitti che questo attacco genera sono portati dai mercati finanziari al di fuori del nostro territorio, accentrando in questo modo il numero di approfittatori della rendita che sulla finanziarizzazione della casa si arricchiscono. 

Mai come oggi è vero che l’1% si arricchisce alle spalle del resto delle persone.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Masked Israeli Settlers Nearly Kill Washington Post Journalist as Attacks on Palestinians Escalate
content:
Israeli settlers backed by 

IDF

 soldiers brutally assaulted Palestinian olive farmers in the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, on Friday. Witnesses say dozens of masked Israeli settlers armed with clubs, sticks, slingshots and guns hurled rocks at Palestinian farmers, set olive trees ablaze and drove people from their fields. Veteran 

Washington Post

 photojournalist Heidi Levine, a 64-year-old American, was documenting the attack when settlers began beating her. She suffered stab wounds, a broken rib, four broken vertebrae and a severe hand injury. Levine was wearing a clearly marked press vest and a helmet at the time of the attack. According to the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din, Israeli settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank since September 27, which marked the start of this year’s olive harvest.




“It looked like they were killing her,” says independent American journalist Jasper Nathaniel, who witnessed the attack on Levine and helped intervene. “The Palestinian youth, the 

shabab

, stepped up. They ran out ahead, and they started beating the settlers back by throwing stones at them, which is the only thing that allowed me to then run out front and grab Heidi.” As the journalists and Palestinians retreated into Abu Falah, “The Israeli military jeep that had been standing by the settlers who were attacking us then drives into the village itself, … and they start firing into crowds of Palestinian people.”

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: ‘Burnout and hardship’: Nunavut teachers struggle with loss of student support workers
content:
Teachers in Nunavut have access to fewer student support assistants this year after school-related requests became ineligible for funding under the Inuit Child First Initiative.




The federal funding program, similar to Jordan’s Principle, is designed to ensure Inuit children across Canada have equal access to health, social and educational supports.




In the 2024-25 school year, the Inuit Child First Initiative allowed Nunavut’s 27 district education authorities to pay the salaries of 88 casual student support workers. The staff worked in elementary and high schools, according to figures provided to Nunatsiaq News by Nunavut’s Education Department.




Last year, the department approved 75 casual workers, said department spokesperson Kuthula Matshazi in an email.




He declined to say how many casual support workers are working in Nunavut schools this year. Instead, he characterized it as a “limited number.”




“When that funding was readily available,” said Nunavut Teachers Association president Justin Matchett in an interview, “there were a lot of schools that were accessing that and getting additional support staff.”




Student support workers join classroom teachers to help deliver curriculum, with a particular focus on students who require accommodations.
















In February 2025, Indigenous Services Canada annoucned that requests for student support assistants would no longer be eligible for funding under the Inuit Child First Initiative, except for in exceptional cases.




Nunavut’s classrooms look very different without that funding, Matchett said.




“There’s a lot of behaviour needs, a lot of medical diagnoses that need and deserve special attention,” he said. “It definitely causes a lot of stress, burnout and hardship on the teachers when they’re trying to manage all of that on top of teaching the curriculum.”




The Nunavut Employees Union, which represents the GN’s permanent student support staff, isn’t opposed to the government hiring fewer casual student support assistants, said president Jason Rochon in an email.




He has been concerned about support staff roles going to non-unionized workers.




“These were casual, lesser paid and non-unionized roles for essentially the same work as unionized [support] positions under our collective agreement with the GN,” said Rochon.
















“All [support] positions should be unionized and covered by the NEU’s collective agreement with the Government of Nunavut,” he added. “We encourage the employer to ensure that enough [support workers] are hired across Nunavut schools.”




Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty promised in November 2025 to revamp Inuit Child First Initiative and make it permanent. She 

announced

 a $115-million, one-year extension in February.




The $115-million top up ensures “continuity” while the department works on a long-term approach for Inuit Child First Initiative, said Carolane Gratton, spokesperson for the department, in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




In the interim, all funding for school-related needs are reviewed on a case to case basis.




“Although the Inuit Child First Initiative can support child-specific education-related requests, such as psycho educational assessments, technology supports, and tutoring to meet individual student needs, it is not intended to replace existing federal/provincial or territorial universal programs,” Gratton said.

title: Ozgul Sakiyê li Metrîsê serdana girtiyên LGBTÎ+ kir: Hevgirtin wan bihêztir dike
content:
Parlementera Stenbolê ya Partiya Wekhevî û Demokrasiyê ya Gelan (DEM Partî) Ozgul Sakiyê li Girtîgeha Metîsê serdana LGBTÎ+yên girtî kir. Operasyonên navborî di 12ê Îlonê de li dijî  rêxistin, aktivîst û cihên LGBTÎ+yan hatibûn kirin. Di wan operasyonan de gelek LGBTÎ+ hatibûn girtin.




Sakiyê têkildarî serdana xwe li ser hesabê xwe yê medyaya civakî daxuyanî daye. Sakiyê diyar kir ku girtiyan ji xizm û heskiriyên xwe re slav şandin.



















Li Stenbolê di operasyonên li dijî LGBTÎ+yan de 20 kes hatin girtin




17 Îlon 2026










Sakiyê da zanîn ku mehek li ser girtîbûna wan re derbas bûye û bertek nîşanî ne berdana wan da.




“Tevî ku tu sedemeke tune ye da ku rojekê tenê jî girtî bimînin, di yekem nirxandina girtîbûnê de jî nehatin berdan.”




“Piştgiriya li derve hêzê dide wan”




Sakiyê ragihand ku mercên girtîgehê li gorî rojên destpêkê baş bûne û anî ziman ku ew bi rêvebirê girtîgehê re jî civiyaye û hin daxwazên girtiyan gihandine rêveberiyê.




Sakiyê diyar kir ku LGBTÎ+yên ku wê dîtiye, bi taybetî bal kişandine ser girîngiya piştgiriya li derve:




“Her yek ji wan bi cihêyî anî ziman ku piştgiriya li derve hêzê dide wan.”




Sakiyê destnîşan kir ku divê girtî di demek nêz de serbest bên berdan û daxuyaniya xwe bi banga piştgiriyê bi dawî anî:




“Lêbelê tişta herî girîng ew e ku em ji bo ku ew di zûtirîn demê de azadiya xwe bi dest bixin, têkoşîn û piştgiriyê kêm nekin.”



















Polîsan bi ser Kaos GLyê de girt: Polîs ketin komeleyê, rêveber hatin desteserkirin




14 Îlon 2026













Çi bûbû?




Di 12ê Îlonê de di çarçoveya operasyonên “Malbata min di ewlehiyê de ye” polîsan li gelek bajaran bi ser komeleyên LGBTÎ+yan, malên aktivîstan û mekânên cuda de girtin.




Di operasyonan de gelek kes hatin desteserkirin. Di heman demê de malperên înternetê yên rêxistinên LGBTÎ+yan û hesabên medyaya civakî yên aktivîstan hatin astengkirin.




Derbarê neh LGBTÎ+ yên li Stenbolê hatibûn girtin de, di yekem nirxandina girtîbûnê ya mehane de biryara berdewamiya girtîbûna wan hate dayîn.







(NÖ/AY)

title: French Gov't Cracks Down on Mass Protests over Cost of Living, Education Cuts; 2,400+ Arrested
content:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters marched in over 140 cities across France on Saturday, demanding relief from the high cost of living, more funding for public services and improvements to deteriorating schools, among other grievances. The demonstrations were the latest — and largest — in a series of protests that began in September with high schooler-led demonstrations against overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure. Some cities saw property destruction, arson and theft on Saturday, with city halls and other symbols of the state coming under attack. Officials said nearly 1,000 police officers were injured and some 2,400 people were arrested.




“What is frustrating to see is how little the police violence is addressed and talked about, which is really the main violence and the real violence today that is taking place in France,” says Rayyan Seriket, a member of the French student union.




“We’re talking about shattered jaws, high schoolers and adolescents who have been blinded,” adds Harrison Stetler, an independent journalist and teacher based in Paris.




This all comes as Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally party is leading in the polls six months ahead of France’s elections. “This situation is essentially what Marine Le Pen hopes for,” says Stetler.

title: De España a Francia y de Portugal a Italia, pasando por Albania: estalla la juventud europea sin futuro
content:
Foto: Martin Barzilai




En alianza con otros sectores y movimientos de otras edades y trayectorias, una juventud politizada y harta de no tener futuro trae a Europa los ecos de las revoluciones de la Generación Z. 

Por Martín Cúneo (@MartinCuneo78), para El Salto Diario.







Desde mayo de 2025 y hasta julio de este año, la llamada Generación Z, jóvenes nacidos cerca del cambio de milenio, impulsaron o se convirtieron en la cara más visible de revueltas que sacudieron la vida política de países tan dispersos y diversos como Bangladesh, Nepal, Indonesia, Marruecos, Madagascar, Perú, Bulgaria, Filipinas, Camerún, Timor Oriental o India.




En 

Nepal

, 

Madagascar

, 

Bangladesh

 y 

Bulgaria

 contribuyeron o causaron directamente la caída del Gobierno. En otros casos, las revueltas consiguieron que se retiraran privilegios (

Timor

 o 

Indonesia

), conquistaron aumentos nunca vistos en servicios públicos (

Marruecos

) o lograron dimisiones de ministros (

India

).




No fueron solo los jóvenes quienes se movilizaron, pero en todos estos casos se convirtieron en el centro de coaliciones más amplias con otros sectores descontentos para protestar contra la desigualdad, los privilegios, la corrupción, el deterioro del nivel de vida, la pobreza y la crisis económica.




Esta fórmula se está replicando este otoño en muchos países europeos, una región que apenas había sentido los movimientos sísmicos de aquellas revueltas.




Aunque las protestas por la vivienda tuvieron en un inicio un carácter intergeneracional, las acampadas fueron protagonizadas por jóvenes que ya nacieron en el siglo XXI y que miran con recelo su futuro




España, al igual que hace 15 años, se ha convertido en foco de inspiración para otros países con la revuelta por la vivienda iniciada por el Sindicato de Inquilinas tras el desahucio de Maricarmen el pasado 23 de septiembre. Aunque las protestas tuvieron en un inicio un carácter intergeneracional, las acampadas fueron y siguen siendo protagonizadas por jóvenes que nacieron ya en el siglo XXI

, 

que no superan los 25 años y miran con recelo su futuro, su capacidad de independizarse o de construir una vida propia.




El movimiento de vivienda —que va mucho más allá de la Generación Z— ha conseguido establecer alianzas con otros grandes movimientos de los últimos años: la lucha por la 

sanidad

 y por la 

educación públic

a. Estas causas han confluido en las últimas semanas en movilizaciones históricas con una importante presencia de trabajadores y pensionistas, pero también de una marea de jóvenes nacidos en este siglo, una diversidad que desafía las definiciones simplistas. Las movilizaciones en el marco de la huelga educativa en Madrid, especialmente en la Universidad Complutense han dejado imágenes de encierros, bloqueos, piquetes, manifestaciones, protestas y 

una represión policial desatada

.




Las alianzas se han extendido también al mundo del trabajo con la convocatoria de la 

huelga general del 11N

 y la creación de centenares de comités para la preparación del paro. Aunque no lo explican todo, tanto en la vivienda como en la educación, la llamada Generación Z y en algunos casos la Generación Alfa —nacidos después de 2010— están jugando un papel determinante con muestras de una juventud mucho más politizada y dispuesta a movilizarse de lo que los estereotipos y los grandes medios apuntaban. Más claro aún es el caso de Francia y la revuelta de los liceos.




Francia




Además de España, el otro 

gran polo de protestas

 en Europa es Francia, donde la respuesta de los estudiantes al paquete de recortes ha vuelto a poner al primer ministro Emmanuel Macron ante una crisis de Gobierno. El movimiento iniciado por los estudiantes de secundaria del norte de París —pertenecientes más bien bien a la Generación Alfa— se extendió a más de mil institutos, llegó a las universidades y prendió en los sindicatos de trabajadores y las asociaciones de padres y madres de alumnos. El martes 6 de octubre, más de medio millón de personas salía a las calles para protestar contra las medidas neoliberales de Macrón.







Le mouvement des lycéens se poursuit et fait naître chaque jour un peu plus une lueur d’espoir pour l’avenir de la France. Merci. https://t.co/XkqQoYJKC7




— Rima Hassan (@RimaHas) 

October 8, 2026







Cuando faltan apenas unos meses para las elecciones presidenciales, con encuestas que señalan una victoria ajustada de la extrema derecha, los bloqueos en centenares de colegios y las manifestaciones que congregan a cada vez a más sectores de la población han cambiado un guion que parecía ya escrito.




Greta Thunberg establecía paralelismos entre la revuelta de los estudiantes franceses, el movimiento Cucaracha de la India y el de vivienda en España, una ola de protestas de jóvenes que ven cómo les “roban el futuro”




En la manifestación del 13 de octubre cientos de miles de personas, jóvenes en su mayoría, volvían a tomar las calles para protestar contra los recortes de 54.000 millones anunciados y demandar mejoras en un sistema educativo que segrega y perpetúa las desigualdades sociales. En la marcha, la activista climática 

Greta Thunberg

 establecía paralelismos entre la movilización de los estudiantes franceses, el Movimiento Cucaracha de la India, que surgió entre estudiantes que pedían reformas en el sistema educativo, y el movimiento de vivienda en España, una nueva ola de protestas de jóvenes que ven cómo les “roban el futuro”.




El movimiento estudiantil francés comenzó exigiendo la renovación de los centros educativos, más personal y más becas, mejores salarios y residencias estudiantiles. Pero la revuelta de los liceos ha trascendido las demandas iniciales para convertirse en una rebelión contra la política austericida del Gobierno de Macron. Se han sumado a las protestas la CGT —el principal sindicato del país—, el Partido Socialista y la Francia Insumisa de Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Las movilizaciones han sido respondidas por una violencia policial que ha dejado, al menos, 

387 estudiantes, manifestantes y docentes

 heridos. Cuatro de estas agresiones han terminado en mutilaciones. En una carga, un joven de 15 años perdió una mano por una granada aturdidora. Desde el inicio de las protestas, el 17 de septiembre, más de 8.000 personas han sido arrestadas, nueve de cada diez menores de edad.







« Macron démission »




Manifestation massive des lycéens et étudiants sur la place de la Bastille à Paris.




Plusieurs dizaines de milliers de personnes.




#BlocusLycées #BlocusUniversités #8octobre https://t.co/P0FeHJsHQd




— Luc Auffret (@LucAuffret) 

October 8, 2026







Este sábado 17 de octubre, una nueva movilización reunió a casi un millón de personas —según los convocantes— en 500 acciones y 90 manifestaciones a lo largo del país entre estudiantes, ‘chalecos amarillos’ y trabajadores convocados por los principales sindicatos. Los enfrentamientos con la policía acabaron en disturbios en varias ciudades. Más de 1.800 personas han sido detenidas. En Lyon, la oficina de turismo fue incendiada. En Limoges, el fuego devoró el edificio del ayuntamiento. Coches volcados, grandes tiendas saqueadas, mobiliario destruido y los clásicos adoquines de las revueltas francesas han marcado una jornada caótica en la que las autoridades locales y del Gobierno central han quedado completamente desbordadas.




De fondo, la tramitación de un proyecto de ley que pretende contener un déficit del 5% utilizando parte del presupuesto de educación para pagar pensiones, a la vez que lleva a cabo un recorte masivo en los servicios públicos. Un proyecto cuya aprobación definitiva cada vez está más lejos después de la oposición desplegada en las calles.







Unbelievable scenes of France burning across cities as students, workers & other groups riot against cost of living and more. Mass looting and arson in different cities including Paris, Marseilles, Lyon, Brussels. https://t.co/9sljz2nM22




— Rajat Srivastava (@RajatSr25883578) 

October 17, 2026







“Las dos oleadas de protestas [Francia y España], lideradas principalmente por jóvenes, ejemplifican un problema creciente para los gobiernos de Europa occidental”, escribía Jon Henley, de The Guardian




El analista y corresponsal de 

The Guardian

 Jon Henley

 establecía una línea de conexión entre las movilizaciones en España y Francia. Aunque tienen orígenes y recorrido diferentes, “las dos oleadas de protestas, lideradas principalmente por jóvenes, ejemplifican un problema creciente para los gobiernos de Europa occidental: una generación de jóvenes que se siente cada vez más privada de la seguridad socioeconómica básica de la que, en general, disfrutaron sus padres”. Mientras el partido de Mélenchon se ha alineado con la calle y aumenta su popularidad entre una juventud que lo apoya masivamente, explica este analista, la extrema derecha de Marine Le Pen “está jugando la carta del orden público” aireando las imágenes de disturbios, incendios y barricadas. Según cifras dadas por la policía, cerca de mil agentes han resultado heridos. La influencia de la revuelta de los liceos se ha extendido a otros países vecinos, especialmente a Italia y Bélgica.




Bélgica




El movimiento de protesta en Francia prendió en la vecina Bélgica, donde miles de estudiantes salieron a las calles para protestar por el aumento de las tasas, las aulas masificadas y la falta de recursos en los centros. En los enfrentamientos del 7 de octubre, 107 jóvenes fueron 

detenidos en Lieja

. Desde el inicio de las protestas en el país, más de 200 jóvenes han pasado a disposición policial. Entre los lemas más repetidos destacaban “Luchamos por un derecho, no por un privilegio” o “Elijo educación, no los Juegos del Hambre”.







 La police belge réprime violemment les lycéens à Bruxelles




 Des images montrent la violente répression policière des lycéens qui manifestent contre la détérioration du système éducatif en Belgique https://t.co/YREiuPpKsJ




— Press TV Français (@fr_presstv) 

October 13, 2026







También acabó en disturbios, cargas y gases lacrimógenos la 

manifestación convocada por los sindicatos

 contra la austeridad del 9 de octubre en Bruselas, que reunió a una multitud de entre 30.000 y 50.000 personas. Al igual que en Francia, el telón de fondo es el debate sobre los presupuestos anuales que pretenden reducir la deuda pública mientras aumentan las tasas educativas, el precio del transporte y el coste de la vida. Los sindicatos amenazan con convocar una huelga general a finales de noviembre si el Gobierno mantiene las propuestas de reforma de la indexación automática de los salarios, de subida del IVA, de cómputo anual de la jornada laboral o los recortes que afectan a las ayudas sociales y los servicios públicos.




En Bélgica, Francia, Alemania, España y otros países, ha sido convocada una 

huelga general educativa para el 20 de noviembre

 para seguir protestando contra los recortes en colegios, institutos y universidades.




Italia




Según informa 

Il Manifesto

, este 17 de octubre, cientos de miles de estudiantes italianos salieron a las calles en una manifestación espontánea contra los recortes en educación, la precariedad laboral y la guerra, uniendo reivindicaciones educativas, sociales y medioambientales en un frente común contra las políticas de derecha. Los choques entre policías y manifestantes acabaron en violencia en Milán, Turín y Bolonia, donde se repitieron las escenas de gases lacrimógenos, cañones de agua y una juventud que protesta por el aumento del coste de la vida y el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni. En 

Roma

, el sindicato CGIL y más de cien organizaciones convocaron una marcha para demandar salarios más altos, servicios públicos, impuestos más justos y menor gasto militar. Han convocado una huelga general para el 20 de noviembre, el mismo día de la huelga general educativa en toda Europa. La capital ya había experimentado un día antes, el 16 de octubre, manifestaciones estudiantiles que protestaban para exigir medidas urgentes frente a la crisis climática y mejoras estructurales en el sistema educativo. Las movilizaciones del viernes también llegaron a Milán, Bolonia, Turín, Génova, Pisa y Nápoles, centradas en denunciar el alto coste de la vida y en rechazar al rearme.







Manifestazioni carovita, a Milano cariche degli agenti sui manifestanti in Piazza Duomo. Scene di guerriglia urbana in pieno centro con decine di persone fermate. Scontri anche a Torino e Bologna, dove è stata chiusa la stazione ferroviaria.


Meloni: “Manifestare è un diritto sacrosanto, ma mettere città a ferro e fuoco non è accettabile. Le opposizioni condannino”.




@ultimoranet




— Ultimora.net (@ultimoranet) 

October 17, 2026







En Roma (Italia), el 15 de octubre, colectivos de vivienda montaron una acampada en la Piazza dei Cinquecento, enfrente a la estación de Termini, rebautizada como “

Piazza Maricarmen Abascal

”.




Serbia




Cuando se acerca el segundo aniversario de aquel 1 de noviembre de 2024, día en el que una marquesina se derrumbó en la estación de trenes de Novi Sad, el movimiento social generado por aquel incidente que provocó la muerte de 16 personas se enfrenta a un nuevo desafío: ganar las elecciones legislativas.




Aquel movimiento descentralizado, sin caras visibles, formado en su mayor parte por jóvenes de la Generación Z, ha organizado acampadas, cierres en las universidades, bloqueos, marchas y manifestaciones para denunciar la corrupción del Gobierno de Aleksandar Vučić, al que culpan del derrumbe de aquella marquesina.




Hace un año

, más de diez mil jóvenes recordaban a las víctimas en aquella estación y demandaban más inversión en sanidad, en educación, responsabilidades penales por las muertes y la dimisión de Vučić. Ahora, cuando se acercan las elecciones legislativas del 25 de octubre, una lista formada por docentes, académicos y activistas lidera las encuestas.




El 22 de octubre se espera una gran movilización para respaldar la candidatura que surge del movimiento estudiantil, una oportunidad histórica para desafiar el poder que Vučić detenta en Serbia desde hace más de una década




El 7, el 10 y el 11 de octubre decenas de miles de jóvenes se manifestaron para mostrar su apoyo a la candidatura Studentska lista – Studenti pobeđuju (Lista estudiantil – Los estudiantes vencen), cuyos representantes 

fueron elegidos

 por los estudiantes en asambleas abiertas. El 22 de octubre se espera una gran movilización para respaldar esta lista que surge del movimiento estudiantil, una oportunidad histórica para desafiar el poder que Vučić detenta en el país desde hace más de una década.




Portugal




El 10 de octubre, con el lema “

Não Dá Mais para Viver Assim

” (No da más para vivir así), más de 30 organizaciones sociales portuguesas convocaron manifestaciones en Lisboa, Oporto, Funchal, Braga y Aveiro. En una movilización inspirada por la revuelta en España y en Francia, miles de personas salieron a las calles para protestar por los altos precios de la vivienda y el costo de la vida. “Ser jóvenes es como entrar en un juego del Monopoly cuando todas las calles ya fueron compradas y todos los hoteles han sido construidos por todos lados”, decía el sociólogo portugués Alessio Motta.




Las 

pancartas 

recordaban a las protestas en Sol y tantas plazas españolas: “Queremos un salario que nos permita pagar la vivienda y vivir”, “Menos turismo. Más barrio”, “Não consegues pagar renda? Então monta a tua tenda” o “Esto no es una crisis. Es una emergencia”. También en los cánticos de “¡Viva Maricarmen!” y “Como em Espanha, todos à rua” quedaba clara la influencia del país vecino.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por Luiz Santos (@lhdosantos)













Los manifestantes protestan por la pérdida de poder adquisitivo, pero también contra la

 reforma de la ley de alquileres

, que pretende dar más aún más libertades a los caseros para subir los precios y facilitar los desahucios.




Al terminar la marcha de Oporto del 10 de octubre, en la que participaron cerca de 2.000 personas, los manifestantes instalaron tiendas en la Praça D. João I, en el centro de la ciudad. Dos días después, la policía desalojó la plaza y desmontó las tiendas, pero los manifestantes no tardaron en volver a la plaza con sacos de dormir para ocupar el espacio y pasar la noche allí.




En asamblea, los ocupantes de la plaza decidieron desobedecer la orden del Ayuntamiento y volver a montar las tiendas. En la madrugada del 15 de octubre, a las 3h, la policía cargó contra la acampada. La brutalidad de la actuación policial ha quedado registrada en decenas de vídeos. Al menos 37 personas resultaron heridas por la violencia policial. La respuesta de la población de Oporto fue masiva y reconquistó la plaza con una masa humana de apoyo. El 17 de octubre, miles de personas se manifestaron en Lisboa por el aumento del coste de la vida y por el derecho a la vivienda. Los manifestantes se congregaron en la céntrica plaza del Rossio donde instalaron una gran acampada. Siguiendo el ejemplo de España y Francia reclaman la convocatoria de una huelga general en noviembre.










 


































Ver esta publicación en Instagram






































































 




Una publicación compartida por Acampada de Lisboa pela Habitação (@acampada.lisboa)













Albania




En un contexto de alta conflictividad desde antes de verano, el 13 de octubre entró en escena el movimiento estudiantil con movilizaciones multitudinarias que acabaron con fuertes choques con la policía. Los estudiantes protestan contra las malas condiciones de las universidades, el aumento del coste de los estudios, la falta de becas y de perspectivas económicas, la desigualdad y la corrupción. La brutal represión, con tanques de agua y gases lacrimógenos, hizo escalar las movilizaciones, que se convirtieron al día siguiente en una auténtica revuelta contra el Gobierno.




El 14 de octubre, decenas de miles de estudiantes salieron a las calles de Tirana. Los medios y los vídeos reportaron incendios parciales en el Ministerio de Educación, en oficinas gubernamentales y sucursales bancarias. Desde que el primer ministro Edi Rama ganó un cuarto mandato en mayo, se ha enfrentado a un creciente descontento por la corrupción en su gabinete y otros altos funcionarios. Las denuncias por el clientelismo, que limitan la posibilidad de conseguir trabajo en el país, y la dimensión que ha alcanzado el exilio económico —el 44% de los albaneses vive en el extranjero— ha acentuado el hartazgo entre los más jóvenes por la falta de oportunidades.







 Total chaos in Tirana on the second day of violent student protests. https://t.co/0M8fpUU2ku




— kos_data (@kos_data) 

October 14, 2026







Entre los ejemplos más llamativos de corrupción, el alcalde de Tirana, 

Erion Veliaj

, del mismo partido que el primer ministro, ha sido detenido por blanqueo de capitales y ocultación de patrimonio y gobierna desde la cárcel. Un avatar generado por IA anuncia sus medidas.




La oposición al Gobierno de Rama no es nueva. Arrastra un rechazo popular masivo a un complejo de lujo impulsado por Jared Kushner, yerno de Donald Trump, situado en la costa sur de Albania. Lo que comenzó como un conflicto ecologista local se transformó en una ola de protestas que ha sacudido el país y ha removido el sentimiento nacional. La llamada “

Revolución de los flamencos

” experimentó un punto de inflexión el pasado junio, cuando se difundió un vídeo de una paliza a un manifestante en el terreno del resort. Las protestas se convirtieron rápidamente en una ola de rechazo al Gobierno con lemas de “Rama dimisión”, un cántico que estos días vuelve a oírse con más fuerza. Este miércoles las protestas se extendieron a las universidades de Elbasan y Shkodra. El jueves, el movimiento estudiantil emitió un ultimátum: no pararán hasta que Rama dimita. Y el sábado 17 volvieron la protestas, con incendios en varios puntos de la ciudad, entre ellos la sede de la Corte Suprema y el Banco Central.







 | AHORA: Enormes protestas en Tirana, Albania. https://t.co/3T8KmN3YdU




— Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24) 

October 17, 2026







Países Bajos, Alemania, Irlanda y Grecia




El desahucio de Maricarmen y la reacción del movimiento de vivienda produjeron, además de en Portugal, una fuerte conmoción en Países Bajos, donde grupos activistas convocaron protestas y levantaron tiendas de campaña de forma puntual en Ámsterdam, Almere y La Haya.




Y no se trata solo de solidaridad. Los problemas de la vivienda en España se repiten en los Países Bajos: promesas incumplidas de construcción de nuevas viviendas públicas mientras los alquileres aumentan “vertiginosamente”, la oferta de vivienda asequible es “cada vez más escasa”, aumenta el número de personas sin hogar y se “culpa a los inmigrantes” de la crisis, según denuncia 

Woonopstand

 (Levantamiento por la Vivienda), una plataforma de organizaciones sociales. El 10 de octubre, una nutrida manifestación en Ámsterdam demandó en el Día de las Personas sin Hogar “viviendas para las personas, no para el negocio».




El 10 de octubre, unas 2.000 personas se manifestaron también en 

Potsdam

 (Alemania) contra los desalojos y los alquileres imposibles. Bajo el lema “¡Dennos los pisos! ¡Bajen los alquileres!”, los manifestantes, en su mayoría jóvenes, protestaban contra los promotores inmobiliarios que compran edificios de la ciudad para luego expulsar a sus vecinos: “Estamos furiosos de que la ciudad de Potsdam siga extendiendo la alfombra roja a estos tiburones inmobiliarios”. Hubo, además, movilizaciones de solidaridad con España en Londres, Dublín o Bruselas en los primeros días de octubre.




En Alemania, el 25 de septiembre, cerca de 45.000 jóvenes salieron a la calle en cien ciudades para rechazar la propuesta de reintroducir el servicio militar obligatorio




Las protestas por la educación, contra los recortes y la austeridad se ubican en un proceso de remilitarización de Europa, con un importante aumento del gasto militar y propuesta para la vuelta del servicio militar obligatorio en muchos países. En Alemania, el 25 de septiembre, 

cerca de 45.000 jóvenes

 salieron a la calle en cien ciudades para rechazar la reintroducción del servicio militar obligatorio. También para denunciar los recortes sociales y educativos mientras el país aumenta el gasto en armamento.




Las protestas por la vivienda también llegaron a Grecia. En la noche del 13 de octubre, integrantes de organizaciones estudiantiles de Atenas instalaron tiendas en la 

plaza Syntagma

 para protestar por las dificultades que tienen que enfrentar los jóvenes estudiantes para encontrar una vivienda digna en una lucha inspirada por las acampadas españolas y la revuelta juvenil en Francia. Con el lema “¿Estudiar o sobrevivir?”, los manifestantes contaron con el apoyo de la Juventud Comunista de Grecia (KNE) y Syriza. “Esto no puede continuar”, decían desde el podio improvisado con un discurso de hartazgo que parece replicarse en buena parte del subcontinente europeo.
