title: Jineolojî Academy: Jineolojî should be at the heart of social organization
content:
In a message sent to the European Jineolojî Conference, the Jineolojî Academy Board reflected on 11 years of accumulated experience in Jineolojî activities and highlighted the tasks and responsibilities of the new period.




Stating that Jineolojî is rooted in the historical experience of struggle of the Kurdish Women’s Freedom Movement, the board emphasized that its activities should be developed on the basis of building a democratic society and advancing women’s freedom.




Stating that Jineolojî should not be confined to a single committee, the board emphasized that all institutions within the women’s movement should incorporate this perspective into their activities.




“Every individual, institution, organization, and structure working towards social transformation and revolution can achieve their political objectives only through a sound sociological approach,” the message stated.










https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261016113503_2026-10-16-haelen-avrupa-jineoloji-konferansi-pajk-mesaji_1.mp4













‘Jineolojî should be organized under the umbrella of the Jineolojî Academy’




The message stressed the need for a new organizational model at the current stage of Jineolojî activities, highlighting the importance of transitioning from a committee structure to an academy model. It called for research, education, written studies, and academic activities to be organized under a common umbrella, urging the establishment of “a functional academy model worthy of its role as the science of the women’s revolution.”




The board emphasized the need to distinguish between integrating the Jineolojî perspective into all areas of work and the specific responsibilities of institutions specializing in Jineolojî. Highlighting the importance of coordination and joint planning among institutions, the message stressed the need to prevent confusion over duties and roles.




‘We must reach our own social base’




The message highlighted the significant international impact of Jineolojî activities in Europe, while identifying the failure to sufficiently strengthen ties with women from Kurdistan and the Middle East as one of the main shortcomings. “We must engage in self-criticism regarding our failure to reach and establish a meaningful presence within the social fabric of Kurdistan and the Middle East,” the board stated.




Drawing attention to the changing sociological realities of the Kurdish community living in Europe, the message emphasized that activities should move beyond an approach focused solely on supporting the struggle in Kurdistan. It highlighted the importance of organizing Jineolojî within its own social base and developing solutions to the problems faced by women and society.




‘Defending society must be a priority’




Addressing violence against women, the targeting of young people by prostitution and drug gangs, and the problems arising from nationalist and religious influences on society, the message stressed that Jineolojî activities must develop responses to these challenges.




The board pointed out that educational, research, and camp activities carried out within the framework of Jineolojî should strengthen social organization. “When determining the perspective, model, and planning of Jineolojî activities, the most important task must be to defend and organize society as a collective,” it said.




The message also warned against distorting the concept of Jineolojî by severing it from its historical roots. Emphasizing that Jineolojî is grounded in the experience of the struggle of the Kurdish Women’s Freedom Movement, the board called for the accumulated knowledge and experience to be brought together and further developed through a strategic perspective.

title: I giovani lo sanno.
content:
Oltre 40 città si sono mobilitate nella giornata di sciopero studentesco di venerdì 16 ottobre. Il tema è chiaro: contro la guerra e contro chi vuole mandarci in guerra. Una guerra che si traduce in crisi sociale e impoverimento a tutti i livelli, la scuola è uno di questi. 




Torino, Padova, Bologna, Roma, Cosenza, Campobasso sono solo alcune delle città che hanno visto decine di migliaia di studenti e studentesse manifestare insieme. La Polizia ha risposto con cariche a Bologna e con idranti e lacrimogeni a Torino nel tentativo di reprimere le proteste. Nei giorni scorsi si è scatenata un’ offensiva poliziesca contro le scuole in occupazione senza precedenti, con arresti e fermi all’interno degli istituti scolastici.




La chiarezza riguarda anche gli intenti: non ci potrà essere qualcun altro a decidere al posto dei giovani. Chi oggi è sceso in piazza, uscendo dalla propria scuola occupata, dai licei ai tecnici, ha vissuto passaggi epocali in questa fase storica. Prima una pandemia globale, poi la guerra sempre più vicina. Chiusura di prospettive e assenza di futuro, non solo dal punto di vista della valorizzazione delle proprie capacità ma di un futuro 

sostenibile

, nel più profondo senso del termine. Se va così è perché l’assenza di senso complessivo è totale, a partire dalle proprie aule scolastiche. A partire da ben prima dell’istruzione media superiore la perdita completa di un obiettivo comune, del perché si è lì ogni giorno su banchi sporchi e tra quattro mura scrostate, del motivo per il quale bisognerebbe stare a sentire qualcuno che a sua volta – molto spesso e non in tutti i casi – non sa perché si trovi lì, è un processo devastante. Non c’è nessun bisogno che qualcun altro, tendenzialmente adulto e incline a contribuire al fallimento generale, dica come è meglio fare. O come bisogna stare. 




Un mondo mediatizzato e ipercollegato permette di vedere che in Francia i ragazzi e le ragazze si sentono esattamente nello stesso modo. Permette un collegamento profondo tra chi si riconosce su delle istanze che hanno un significato politico intrinseco. Distruggere perché non c’è niente di riformabile. Ma anche riconquistare uno spazio in cui esserci, sentirsi collettività, imporsi, nella gioia e nella rabbia. 




Il ruolo del mediatico è evidentemente ambivalente e la narrazione dei giornali ha immediatamente assunto un piano banale e becero ossia la caccia “all’incappucciato” che non sarebbe studente (eppure giovane lo è) e che si infiltra nelle scuole o nei cortei per essere “violento”. Fioccano gli inviti di dirigenti (perché la scuola è un’azienda) a isolare i violenti, a tenere fuori gli esterni e a gestire gli infiltrati, il tutto con il supporto delle forze dell’ordine. Eppure, al di là dei titoli e di qualche video sensazionalistico, quel che si è visto oggi nelle piazze in tutta Italia è una gioventù che insieme ha partecipato a cortei con numeri e determinazione significativi. Si è visto la presenza di docenti e personale scolastico solidale. Si è visto che il rifiuto della divisione razzista portata dall’alto non passa tramite il buonismo moralista di sinistra ma dall’essere insieme con un sentire comune. 




Sarebbe inutile lanciarsi in immagini evocative che vogliono romanticizzare una realtà che invece porta con sé le sue contraddizioni. Ma la realtà è fatta di dati: una mobilitazione a macchia d’olio si sta diffondendo, scuole che mai avevano occupato prima d’ora oppure che lo avevano fatto per la prima volta con il Blocchiamo Tutto dell’autunno scorso lo hanno rifatto, l’insofferenza si traduce in moto collettivo. Non è poco in un tempo di frammentarietà e individualismo. Non è poco quando il governo italiano si trova a dover affrontare una crisi probabilmente recessiva nell’arco di pochi mesi, non è poco quando anche altri settori sociali decidono di mobilitarsi, come gli autotrasportatori e gli agricoltori. 




La coperta è corta e per capire che con i rapporti di forza è possibile anche vincere il passo è breve.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Chuck Schumer Hasn’t Said a Word About Trump’s Attempt to Deport Ilhan Omar
content:
Ethics lawyers say the raid violated the Hatch Act. The Democratic Senate minority leader has been silent.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Days after the Trump administration’s unprecedented raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minnesota) house just weeks before the midterm elections, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York) has not once publicly defended the progressive Democrat against the naked political prosecution.

The Democratic leader — one of the most powerful in the country — has not issued statements to the press or through his social media channels about the Homeland Security Investigations raid on Monday, nor has he done any media appearances to comment on the issue, which critics have described as a five alarm fire for the state of democracy in the U.S.

This is despite the fact that the Trump administration is waging an inter-agency effort to denaturalize and deport Omar, as reports have uncovered this week. The timing of the raid is also unprecedented, coming just 22 days before the midterm elections in which Omar is on the ballot; these elections should be of grave import to Schumer, since they’ll determine whether or not Democrats will have the power to follow through on their pledges to hold Donald Trump accountable for his escalating fascist authoritarianism.

Other top Democrats have spoken out in defense of Omar — but even those statements have been muted in relation to the magnitude of the attacks.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and other House Democratic leaders issued a short statement following the raid that called it “deeply disturbing” and said that it “raises serious questions” about the Trump administration’s “weaponization of the federal government.”

The only mention of consequences in the statement, however, is a promise that the Democrats “will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice.” There is no mention of what that “accountability” would entail.

Jeffries also addressed the issue in an interview on MS NOW about the elections. Throughout the 11-minute interview, Jeffries doesn’t bring up the attacks on Omar once — until he’s asked about them at the very end. In that answer, he simply says that the Department of Justice (DOJ) “is going to be held accountable” and rattles off a list of other people that Trump has tried to prosecute, including Republican Federal Reserve Governor Jerome Powell.

The Democratic Party has also been relatively mum. Chair Ken Martin’s statement about the raid was short, simply calling it a “new low for the Trump administration.”

By contrast, it was shorter than the post about the raid by far right former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, who said that she and Omar are “far apart” on beliefs but called the raid a distraction from real issues like gas and health insurance prices: “People are so sick and tired of the bullshit,” Greene said.

This is despite the fact that Democrats have many avenues to defend Omar. The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Trump administration officials had already tried to search Omar’s immigration records for evidence to take away her citizenship in 2019, but found insufficient evidence to mount a full investigation.

None of the top Democrats’ statements named Trump’s attacks on Omar as openly racist and Islamophobic, despite Trump having called Omar and other Somalis “garbage” for years. Meanwhile, a group of prominent ethics lawyers have said that they believe the actions of the DOJ and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) were actually illegal. The lawyers, including former counsels to the White House, said that the raid was a violation of the Hatch Act because of its timing in relation to the election.

“DOJ and DHS’s decision to instigate this raid at this very moment and for these alleged reasons is unexplainable — except for as a politically motivated use of power to influence the Minnesota congressional election in violation of the Hatch Act,” the lawyers wrote.

Critics say that Schumer’s silence may be explained by the simple fact that he does not ally himself with Omar, despite sharing a party with her. Omar is a vocal critic of Israel; Schumer is a vehement supporter of the genocidal state. In 2019, when Omar criticized the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC — one of the most powerful groups in Washington for decades — Schumer and then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-California) piled on to Omar, forcing her to apologize and smearing her as an antisemite.

“Schumer’s silence is hardly surprising,” wrote Jeet Heer for The Nation. “Because Omar has been outspoken in her criticism of Israel and the Israel lobby, establishment Democrats such as Schumer have often kept their distance from her.”

This and Omar’s other progressive viewpoints may also explain the relative media silence about the attacks. Media critic Adam Johnson compared legacy media’s coverage of the Omar raid to Trump’s raid on conservative John Bolton, which spawned an explosion of scathing columns and opinion pieces. By contrast, Johnson noted, the raid of Omar’s home has scarcely prompted any op-eds or columns in the legacy corporate media — only an Atlantic article that argued for both sides.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Chris Walker
title: HHS Demands Answers From Orgs Over Support for Youth Gender-Affirming Care
content:
Studies have demonstrated that gender-affirming care for transgender young people can be life-saving treatment.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) sent letters this week to multiple medical organizations, demanding they provide the department with a “clear, current statement” on their positions regarding gender-affirming care for transgender youth.

The organizations in question have expressed support for such care, with many noting that gender-affirming care is based on years of study and careful implementation.

Conversely, HHS framed the letters using non-medical terminology, asking the groups to “answer” for their support of so-called “sex-rejecting procedures for minors.”

The letters from HHS have been sent to the Endocrine Society, the American Psychiatric Association, the American Medical Association, the American Psychological Association, Columbia University trans health expert Asa Radix, and American Academy of Pediatrics CEO Mark Del Monte.

“HHS has asked these organizations for clear answers about their current positions, the evidence supporting their guidance, and whether they intend to change it,” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in announcing the letters.

In a press release explaining why the letters were sent out, HHS stated it also wants “identification of any planned revisions to their respective guidance, and a timeline for those changes.” The department is giving the organizations 10 business days to respond.

Past statements from some of these organizations note that health care for transgender individuals — including trans children and teenagers — is beneficial, and that denial of such care when it’s warranted is harmful.

“We recognize health as a basic human right for every person, regardless of gender identity or sexual orientation,” reads a statement from the American Psychiatric Association published in 2021. “For gender-diverse individuals, including children and adolescents, this means access to gender-affirming care that is part of comprehensive primary care.”

“Physicians must be able to practice medicine that is informed by their years of medical education, training, experience, and the available evidence, freely and without threat of punishment,” the organization added. “Patients and their physicians, not policymakers, should be the ones to make decisions together about what care is best for them.”

The American Medical Association made a similar statement that same year, writing that:

Physicians are guided by their ethical duty to act in the best interest of their patients and must tailor recommendations about specific interventions and the timing of those interventions to each patient’s unique circumstances. Such decisions must be sensitive to the child’s clinical situation, nurture the child’s short- and long-term development, and balance the need to preserve the child’s opportunity to make important life choices autonomously in the future.

Dozens of other medical organizations, beyond those that HHS sent letters to, have also affirmed the need to preserve gender-affirming care, including for young trans patients.

Gender-affirming care is life-saving for many transgender and/or nonbinary individuals, including for young people. An observational study from late 2025, examining hundreds of trans patients between the ages of 12 and 20 from 2017-2024, found that suicidality rates for these patients dropped by 67 percent after they were given treatments that affirmed their gender identity.

Despite overwhelming evidence demonstrating the benefits of gender-affirming care, dozens of states across the U.S. have banned such treatment options for trans youth and young adults, often using misinformation to justify doing so.

President Donald Trump has also used blatantly false anti-trans talking points in an attempt to scare or anger people into backing Republicans in this year’s midterm elections. Meanwhile, some Democrats have also tried to appeal to voters by claiming they are skeptical of transgender rights, supporting, for example, unfounded bans on trans athletes, disallowing them to participate on teams corresponding to their correct genders.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification
content:
from the 

CrimethInc.

 collective, 15/10/2026







A Report from Madrid and Barcelona




On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the 

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the 

Occupy

 movement in the United States.




Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.




Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.







Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.







The housing movement in Spain has a long and complex history. For any period that we might choose as a point of departure, there always exists a prior precedent that could serve just as well—so where we begin depends on how we wish to make sense of what is happening today, how we wish to narrate this story that is still being written in the streets. What follows, then, is an attempt, however insufficient and incomplete, to tell this story, in hopes that you can learn or be inspired by something from it and, in this way, become part of this story and build upon it wherever you live.




We could perhaps begin with the 

15-M movement

, which erupted a decade and a half ago as part of the sequence of uprisings that unfolded across the globe in 2011. Encampments spread across Spain much as they have today, full of people clamoring for “

real democracy

.”




Whereas elsewhere, repression often put these movements to an unresolved end, in Spain, this movement culminated with the formation of several far-left political parties, including Podemos, as well as strong municipalist movements in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities. Today, these parties lie in ruins, while the municipalists have largely lost whatever power they once held. Ultimately, much like 

Occupy Wall Street

 and the Arab Spring, the true legacy of this sequence remains ambiguous, contested, and open to interpretation. Perhaps the 15-M movement is not the beginning of the story we’re telling, but simply the ruins from which the current one is being told.




Riot police are covered in eggs and paint while attempting to evict a building in Barcelona, 2021.




The movement that is now swelling across Spain emerged as a result of strong and stable union-style organizations that operate apart from the official institutional structures that are otherwise so present and influential in political life here. These organizations were built to tackle the housing crisis using horizontal and grassroots power, while simultaneously driving widespread and popular mobilizations like those we are witnessing today. These unions are novel in that they don’t involve questions of work directly, but rather address the conditions in which we live. The movement’s most significant antecedents lie in the creation of organizations such as the PAH (Platform for People Affected by Mortgages), the first chapter of which was founded in Barcelona in 2009. Like the more recently created housing organizations, the PAH groups practice what we call “social unionism.”




The premise is simple: an individual problem like a person facing the threat of losing their home is transformed into a collective issue addressed through shared political action. A variety of union-style tactics soon began to emerge, leading to the halting of many imminent evictions.







A group of thirty or so people assembles in front of an apartment in the historic city center as the sun is rising. People cling to one another tightly, locked arm in arm, crowding in front of the door of the building’s entrance while several vans of riot police pull up and park nearby as scheduled. There’s an announcement from a police loudspeaker to the effect that people must disperse, but no one does. Eventually, the cops move in, struggling to pull each person away one by one, until finally everyone has been cleared. In the end, the eviction is successful, but it takes several dozen police and several hours, slowing the pace of evictions and making it ever more costly and difficult for the city to execute them.




Those who took part in the defense are members the neighborhood’s tenants’ union. Afterwards, they head their separate ways, but then see one another again soon at their next meeting, reflect upon how the defense went, and make plans for the next one. Occasionally, they hold public gatherings, putting out folding chairs in a circle in a plaza or street where people from the neighborhood are invited to take turns describing the problems that they experience with their landlords or reflecting on the broader challenges they face. These people are young and old. Some are radicals with a depth of experiences in various social movements; others simply live nearby and don’t want to see their neighbors kicked out of their homes.




Similar scenes are unfolding across Spain with increasing regularity. It is possible to come across eviction defense actions unexpectedly as one goes on a morning walk to buy bread. They are becoming a part of the fabric of everyday life.




Members of the Tenants’ Union block the front of an apartment building to halt an eviction.







The 2008 crisis shifted the terrain upon which housing organizations operated by drastically transforming the Spanish real estate market. While at first, housing disputes centered on those who had mortgage agreements, changes in legislation and property structures eventually caused struggles around rent to take center stage. Tenants’ unions were founded in Madrid and Catalonia in 2017, a period that also saw the emergence of numerous other housing groups and significant disputes between them. These unions developed new organizing strategies, such as the organization and mobilization of entire apartment buildings and neighborhoods; they focused on organic growth by inviting people to become formal members and attend regular meetings in radical social centers, bookstores, and public spaces. Eviction by eviction, dispute by dispute, block by block: the social explosion of recent weeks is, in reality, the result of this patient work that unfolded over years, addressing a social issue that was bound to erupt sooner or later.




The current housing mobilizations cannot be understood without recognizing the presence of these grassroots organizations, which are the product of a deliberate political strategy by social movement activists—particularly those who come from the autonomous, libertarian, and communist traditions that operate outside of the standard institutional frameworks, which are now widely considered a dead end. This most recent cycle of mobilizations arguably began with a massive demonstration on October 13, 2024 under the slogan “Enough is enough. Let’s lower rents!” The massive scale of that event took many by surprise, including the activists themselves. Since then, other major mobilizations and high-profile evictions have laid the groundwork for the recent social upheaval.




A housing protest takes place in Barcelona in 2024. Its scale surprised even the organizers.







Thousands upon thousands of people pour into the streets. Some carry large banners; others light smoke flares that illuminate the crowd in the evening light and cause them to cheer. Every so often, people take their keys out of their pockets and shake them above their heads, displaying what has come to be symbol of the movement while creating a discordant chorus of metal clanking upon metal. Small groups of people weave in and out of the march with flat pieces of cardboard and cans of spray paint in their hands, decorating the bus stops, bank windows, and walls of the city with messages against the financial “vultures” that prey upon the housing market.




People are awakening to the possibility that this could be something more, something bigger, something with force.




A protester holds up their apartment keys, the symbol of the movement, 2026.







In societies with relatively low economic productivity, such as ours, capital seeks to extract profit from financial markets such as the housing market. This is a systemic phenomenon; people across the globe feel the pressure of it in their daily lives. It takes various forms: neighborhoods rapidly changing, being forced to move because housing has become unaffordable, being compelled to allocate an ever-larger share of their wages to housing costs. One can see organizations similar to our local housing unions in many other countries, as conflict inevitably follows capital wherever it goes.




All of this is palpable in people’s everyday lives. There are other equally important issues, the causes of which can be traced back to capitalism but which may not be so clearly linked to people’s daily experiences—for instance, the rising food prices caused by wars taking place thousands of kilometers away. But being evicted from your home or seeing your neighbor evicted is something very palpable, as it has immediate and tangible consequences.




It is also easy to identify the culprits: everyone knows that they are the police who physically remove people from their homes, the companies or landlords who request such actions, the judges who issue the orders, and the politicians who have created the legal framework that enables this to happen. The key success lies in having framed this as a political and social issue, through housing organizations and the political networks in which they are embedded. A future challenge, though significant work has already been done in this regard, is to link the struggle for housing with other struggles and the various other problems that people face.




As the state recedes as a horizon of political possibility, the potential of another way from below becomes more legible—it can be felt as more attainable and real.




Members of the Tenants’ Union block the front of an apartment building to halt an eviction.







A squatted social center faces eviction under the socialist government in Barcelona, and there is a call to defend the space. It’s a cold January at the opening of the year 2025. Neighbors have used the space for several years as an autonomously organized gym, meeting space, and library, but because it is close to the tourist area of the city, the local politicians want to tear it down. The people who have been active in L’Antiga Massana, named after the art school which previously had its home there, call for a series of demonstrations aiming to halt the eviction, but the police arrive without warning one morning to seal the doors shut.




Large crowds mobilize in the evening in an attempt to take back the building, but armies of police block the way, and the gathering concludes with street fighting throughout the neighborhood with fireworks and flares, until everyone eventually feels like they must call it a night and disperse. Another squatted space is tragically lost, and the city is transformed an inch further into a place not for living, but for shopping and tourism—not for sharing, but for capital.




Protesters mobilize to defend the squatted social center L’Antiga Massana, 2025.







In these tumultuous times, our political landscape has changed completely. It has been a total U-turn, one we welcome with great joy and which gives us a new momentum to fight harder and more effectively. We were experiencing a period of relative paralysis, during which we watched helplessly as fascism gained ground in Spain and across Europe. Now, we see the emergence of a massive social force eager to change everything. Suddenly, we are preparing for a general strike, something this country hasn’t seen in over a decade.




This strike, however, is not taking place under the circumstances we had hoped for. Parliament has been dissolved after failing to pass housing relief, and elections will be held on November 29—elections that the progressive media and left-wing parties will seek to frame as a national referendum on housing. The right will try to take advantage of this situation, trying to present the encampments and the government as two sides of the same coin. The socialist PSOE party in power has played its cards well, as it is in a position to capitalize—at least in the eyes of part of the general public—on what was initially a strong wave of protests against the government’s housing policies.




The right and the far right may well win the upcoming elections, or the socialists may survive this moment once again, but all this has shown that regardless of what happens, they will face a mobilized opposition on the streets. An opposition mobilized notony against fascism and the failures of the state, but as an autonomous force intent on securing material improvements for our class.




The Tenants’ Union holds a public assembly to organize the neighborhood.







The tenants’ unions continue to develop and grow—organizing within each neighborhood and regularly calling for public meetings, developing forms of solidarity, and reflecting upon their evolving strategies and tactics. These unions draw people together from across the political spectrum, bringing together people from socialist youth groups, independentist political parties, anarchists, and people with less clear political affiliations.




Another flashpoint emerges in Barcelona around Casa Orsola, a large apartment building in the residential area of the city that is home to several families, as speculators attempt to evict it so that it can be converted into short-term rental units. Demonstrations are called in order to defend the space; this draws hundreds of neighbors onto the streets on the day the police are expected to arrive. People of all ages and backgrounds can be seen gathering. Grandparents stand alongside their children and grandchildren in front of the building’s doors, while masked figures dressed all in black stalk the rooftop, ready for whatever might come. After a standoff that lasts all morning, the local government halts the eviction and declares its intention to purchase the building and convert it into public housing.




The local government sides with the movement, for now, hoping thus to bring calm and redirect some of its energy back into institutional frameworks.




Neighbors gather to defend Casa Orsola, 2025.







As the general strike is organized, there are already several forces that seek to steer it in this or that direction. The CCOO (Comisiones Obreras) and UGT (Unión General de Trabajadores), unions that have historically functioned as state proxies and buffers to suppress social conflict, have already announced that they are supporting the general strike. As the largest unions, their backing was crucial for ensuring strong participation in the strike—though, to an extent, this support was wrested from them, as it is not their natural stance. At the same time, it is equally important to push beyond the pacifying role these unions have played. The CCOO and UGT will seek to channel the strike into forms of civic expression and frame it as “the people” closing ranks with the left wing of the state, a narrative which we must resist.




The encampment and any future mobilizations must struggle to maintain their original spirit of challenging the status quo by opposing the entire parliamentary system, while specifically highlighting the hypocrisy of the progressive government and opposing the housing business and all the capitalist interests that profit from it.




Protesters mobilize to defend the squatted social center L’Antiga Massana, 2025.







The encampments that have spread across the country continue to blossom, building community kitchens, establishing info points to inform people about upcoming events and demonstrations, holding regular meetings and skillshares throughout the day. Occasional threats from far-right fascist groups give rise to anti-fascist demonstrations that defend the camps. The number of tents grows, and grows, and grows.




Various organizations establish themselves in the encampments, but most only last a few days before withdrawing again, confirming the encampment’s autonomous and horizontal form. In Madrid, an eviction is successfully halted after people from the encampment drive the police away. Then, a series of incredibly large demonstrations take place across Spain to build upon the energy of the movement, filling the centers of most large cities. Chants such as “Here are the anti-fascists!” and “A, Anti, Anticapitalista!” and “Long live the struggle of the working class!” suggest a broader horizon than the tenants’ struggle. The demonstration in Barcelona ends in a confrontation with the police, leading to a street battle that involves the improvised assembly of flaming barricades and the liberation of nearby construction materials, which participants throw at riot police and their vans as they retreat.




In the aftermath, people look towards the general strike as a moment to expand the movement and sharpen its intensity. The various groups that had developed to capacity to regularly organize neighborhood meetings around eviction defense now put these skills to use again by holding regular meetings with neighbors to prepare for the strike.




People build barricades after riot police halt a housing demonstration in Barcelona, 2026.







Across Europe, there is new life in the streets. Across France, 

students are in revolt

 against a state that has abandoned them. Recently, this revolt has spread to Belgium, and there are early signs of it in Italy—now [Albania’s education ministry has caught fire], and it may go further still.




To break out of the pincer movement in which the progressive government and the CCOO and UGT have trapped us here in Spain, we must ensure that upcoming mobilizations, especially the general strike in November, do not turn out the way they want them to. The streets must not fall in line behind any government. Both our demands and our forms of action must outflank all of these actors from the left, placing them once again in an untenable position. We need to become unacceptable to the institutional left within the state apparatus once more. Otherwise, the window for mobilization that has opened up could close far too soon. The general strike must not become the end of this story, but only one additional chapter, one which we here must struggle to leap past and continue to push beyond.




People build barricades after riot police halt a housing demonstration in Barcelona, 2026.

On the current encampment movement:







The Destituent Question of the Encampments




And Suddenly, a Jolt: Notes on the Fly from the Puerta del Sol Encampment

 (in Spanish)







On tenants’ unions and rent strikes:







Picking Fights: Seventeen Years of Organizing in the Seattle Solidarity Network

author: Unknown
title: Women discuss Jineolojî experiences and the needs of the new period
content:
The European Jineolojî Conference, held in Haelen, the Netherlands, under the slogan “Bi Jineolojî ber bi avakirina jiyana komunal û azad” (With Jineolojî towards building a communal and free life), continued with its first session, titled “Jineolojî: The Science of Building Women’s Identity on the Basis of Freedom.” The session addressed the experiences, achievements, shortcomings, and perspectives for the new period of Jineolojî activities carried out across Europe.




Jineolojî experience in Europe evaluated




The session began with an extensive visual presentation featuring testimonies from women, photographs, short videos, and audio recordings documenting conferences, camps, educational programs, research initiatives, and committee activities organized or attended by European Jineolojî committees over the years.




The presentation, which traced the development of Jineolojî activities in Europe over the past 15 years, highlighted the considerable knowledge and experience accumulated through conferences, educational programs, research, and camps. It emphasized the need to transform these activities into lasting organizational structures, strengthen ties with local women, and make the knowledge produced accessible throughout society.




The visual presentation examined the development of Jineolojî activities in Europe, their achievements, and the challenges encountered. It highlighted how thousands of women living in different countries had come together through conferences, educational programs, research, and camps centered on Jineolojî, creating a shared experience and collective memory.




The presentation noted that the concept of Jineolojî was first introduced in 2008 through Abdullah Öcalan’s book 

Sociology of Freedom

. Jineolojî activities subsequently took shape as a committee in the guerrilla-held Medya Defense Zones in 2011 and began developing more systematically from 2013 onwards.




The first Jineolojî Conference, held in Kurdistan in 2015, was described as a significant turning point that helped clarify the direction of the activities. The second conference, held in 2018, was also highlighted as an important milestone in evaluating the accumulated knowledge and experience and identifying the needs of the new period.










https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261016155657_2026-10-16-haelen-jineoloji-konferasi-kadinlar-jineoloji-deneyimini-tartisti-1.mp4













Activities expanded across Europe




The presentation highlighted the important role played by the first European Jineolojî Conference, held in Cologne in 2014, in the development of Jineolojî activities across Europe. It noted that subsequent conferences in Paris and Stockholm created common platforms for discussion among women living in different countries.




The assessment stated that the conferences were followed by educational programs, seminars, reading groups, and local initiatives. Camps also developed into spaces where women experienced living, producing, making decisions, and learning together. These activities were described as strengthening the connection between knowledge and everyday life and contributing to experiences of communal living.




The visual presentation noted that Jineolojî committees and research groups began emerging in various European countries from 2019 onwards. Activities carried out in Switzerland, Germany, France, England, Italy, Sweden, Norway, Catalonia, the Basque Country, Ireland, and Scotland were said to have generated new experiences and marked significant progress in education, research, and organization.




The main areas of research included women’s history, witch hunts, the history of colonialism, migration experiences, women’s resistance movements, women’s archaeology, mythology, the relationship between women and nature, and local women’s collective memories. These studies aimed to bring renewed visibility to women’s experiences and traditions of resistance that had been rendered invisible throughout history.




Shortcomings and the needs of the new period




Jineolojî Committee members Sarah Marcha and Necîbe Qeredaxî used storytelling to describe the committees’ organizational structures and working methods, their shortcomings, and the needs of the new period.




Necîbe Qeredaxî greeted the delegates and the women who have contributed to Jineolojî activities in every sphere of life, recalling that the work began under difficult circumstances and gradually developed its own cadres.




Stating that Jineolojî activities had developed within a communal framework, free from hierarchy and based on the unity of theory and practice, she acknowledged that they had encountered obstacles arising from dogmatism at certain stages.




Responding to the moderator’s question, “Where do we begin?”, Necîbe Qeredaxî emphasized the importance of diversifying methods such as storytelling, oral history, art, theater, and music to reach a broader range of women.




Qeredaxî stated that Jineolojî had developed strong resistance to European positivism and brought a new dimension to relations between women and men, as well as within society. She noted that, during the initial stages of the work, Abdullah Öcalan, who developed the paradigm of women’s freedom, had not gained acceptance. However, she explained that sustained efforts to persuade others had made it easier today to share the arguments put forward by Jineolojî with different women’s organizations and movements.




Stating that Jineolojî had reached every women’s council, Necîbe Qeredaxî asked, “So where does the problem lie?” She pointed out that the conceptual language of Jineolojî could sometimes be challenging for women newly joining the activities and emphasized the need to make methods of communication and knowledge-sharing more accessible.




“Jineolojî is a river that determines its own course,” Necîbe Qeredaxî said, expressing confidence that the conference would achieve its objectives.




The need for lasting organization and broader social engagement




Sarah Marcha stated that Jineolojî is organized on the basis of democratic modernity. Emphasizing that Jineolojî is not merely about gathering knowledge, she explained that emotions and feelings, which are closely connected to knowledge, also form the foundations of this science. She provided information about the working methods and approaches of Jineolojî committees.




Marcha pointed out that although Jineolojî activities in Europe had generated considerable experience and accumulated knowledge, difficulties remained in transforming these achievements into lasting and sustainable organizational structures. She noted that it had not always been possible to translate the impact of conferences, educational programs, and camps into long-term activities.




Marcha explained that workloads, economic difficulties, care responsibilities, and family obligations made it challenging for women to participate in activities and maintain their involvement over time. These problems, she said, were compounded by the lack of clarity regarding the place of Jineolojî activities within the organizational system and the limited connections with local organizations.




Sarah Marcha stated that Jineolojî activities had often remained limited to initiatives aimed at international and external audiences, noting that local committees had sometimes developed independently of the work carried out by councils. Steps were taken in some countries to establish committees within local community structures, she added, emphasizing the need to expand these experiences to broader areas and ensure their continuity.




Marcha also stressed the importance of assessing the extent to which Jineolojî activities had become embedded in society, pointing out that participation remained limited, particularly among women working under demanding conditions.




Noting that research had contributed to a better understanding of local realities across Europe, Marcha acknowledged shortcomings in disseminating research findings to wider audiences and connecting them with organizational activities. She also emphasized the need to strengthen the relationship between local specificities and collective coordination.




Marcha stated that the European Jineolojî Conference would provide an important platform for collectively evaluating the experience accumulated so far, discussing shortcomings, and defining the tasks and responsibilities of the new period.




Women describe the transformation they experienced through Jineolojî




As the session continued, ten delegates from different countries, cultures, and walks of life took to the stage to briefly share what Jineolojî meant to them, how it had influenced their lives, and the transformations it had helped bring about.




The delegates stated that Jineolojî had enabled them to better understand how the colonial mindset shapes human thought, recognize organization as the most effective form of self-defense, and gain the strength to struggle against capitalism. They also expressed that Jineolojî had strengthened their belief in finding solutions to problems and brought them closer to Öcalan. The delegates thanked those who had contributed to Jineolojî activities.




Video messages sent from Abya Yala were then screened. The delegates welcomed the messages of solidarity with the slogan “Jin Jiyan Azadî” [Woman, Life, Freedom].




Following the conclusion of the first session, seven separate workshops will be held during the afternoon program of the conference under the theme “The role of Jineolojî in building democratic and communal life.” The workshops aim to facilitate discussions and reach collective decisions.

title: Bayındır: It is time to open the door wide to freedom, peace, and equality
content:
The Democratic Regions Party (DBP) met with civil society organizations and residents in the Tatvan district of Bitlis under the slogan “We are building dialogue for peace with the people.” DBP Co-Chair Keskin Bayındır attended the gatherings.




Speaking during a meeting with representatives of civil society organizations on Friday, Bayındır recalled previous peace processes that had failed to produce results and highlighted the importance of the current Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Stating that the cessation of conflict for the past two years was significant, Bayındır emphasized that resolving the Kurdish question was not simply a matter of laying down arms. He said the Kurdish people’s demands for constitutional recognition and status must also be addressed.




Bayındır described the commission established in parliament as part of the process and efforts to draft a framework law as important but insufficient. He called for the release of political prisoners and legal arrangements that would enable guerrilla fighters and members of the Kurdish diaspora living in Europe to return.




Emphasizing that the process could not advance through statements of goodwill alone, Bayındır said, “The rights and demands of the Kurdish people must be recognized. It is time to open the door wide to freedom, peace, and equality in these lands.”




Bayındır also addressed the economic crisis and social problems, calling for a united struggle for peace, freedom, and equality.




Speaking at a public gathering in the village of Avêtax in Tatvan, Bayındır argued that years of struggle had created the conditions for negotiations and a political resolution. “We are now a force for a resolution,” he said.




Residents who spoke at the gatherings expressed their trust in Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan who initiated the current process and called on the government to take the necessary steps for further progress. The DBP’s public gatherings are expected to continue in the villages of Şîrînşas and Siwar.

author: Unknown
title: Karabulut: Existing trade unions cannot even protect their own members
content:
Low wages, precarious employment conditions, and increasing obstacles to trade union organizing shape the working lives of millions of people in Turkey. According to the Ministry of Labor and Social Security, only 2.5 million of approximately 17.6 million registered workers are unionized. This means that around 86 percent of officially registered employees are not members of a trade union.




Özgür Karabulut, chair of the Revolutionary Construction and Road Workers’ Union (Dev-Yapı-İş), which is affiliated with the Confederation of Progressive Trade Unions of Turkey (DİSK), sees this as the result of policies that favor employers and systematically hinder workers’ ability to collectively assert their rights. Speaking to ANF, he also criticized traditional trade union structures, arguing that many are no longer capable of representing the interests of their own members.







‘Workers are at the mercy of employers’




Karabulut described working conditions in Turkey as increasingly precarious. He said millions of people were affected by unemployment, low wages, and a lack of social security. The fragmentation of employment into different working arrangements and contractual relationships further complicates efforts to organize collectively, he noted.




“Even the most fundamental right, the right to receive wages, is being violated. Under the pretext of the economic crisis, hundreds of workers are no longer even receiving their salaries regularly. Workers now have to fight not only for new rights but also simply to ensure that their wages are paid,” Karabulut stated.




Protests by workers whose wages have sometimes remained unpaid for months are now taking place in almost all industrial zones and at numerous construction sites. Those who resist these conditions or attempt to organize in trade unions face the threat of dismissal and repression. Karabulut also holds state institutions responsible for this situation. He argues that existing laws designed to protect workers are not consistently enforced, while companies that violate labor rights often face no effective consequences.




Traditional trade unions face criticism




Karabulut’s criticism also explicitly targets established trade unions. He argues that many have confined themselves to defending existing rights rather than securing new gains. Even this defensive strategy, he says, has increasingly failed.




“Traditional trade union structures are not even capable of protecting and advancing the rights and interests of their own members. They are even less capable of offering solutions to workers who are completely unorganized and left at the mercy of employers.”




Karabulut also traces the causes of this development to the history of Turkey’s trade union movement. “Following the military coup of September 12, 1980, hard-won workers’ rights were severely restricted, resilient trade unions were dismantled, and employer-friendly organizations were promoted. This created a trade union landscape focused more on controlling social conflicts than on securing collective rights.”




According to Karabulut, the consequences are still being felt today. “In many workplaces, there is now little difference in wages and working conditions between unionized and non-unionized workers. Just because a building bears a sign reading ‘Workers’ Union’ does not necessarily mean that the organization actually defends workers’ rights,” he said.




Karabulut added that some trade unions now operate more like corporate human resources departments than independent organizations representing workers’ interests.




New forms of labor struggle emerge




Despite the difficult circumstances, Karabulut sees signs of a new direction within the labor movement. Increasing attacks on wages and labor rights are prompting workers to seek new forms of organization rather than relying exclusively on established trade unions.




“When existing structures can no longer provide answers, workers will develop forms of struggle and organizational mechanisms that go beyond these structures,” he explained.




Karabulut emphasized the need for a fundamental democratization of trade unions. He argued that unions must abandon employer-friendly practices and once again become organizations that independently represent collective interests and actively engage in labor struggles.




He also opposed limiting trade union activities to collective bargaining and economic demands.




“A trade union must establish structures that not only address workers’ economic problems but also strengthen their democratic rights and contribute to solving social problems. That is what we are fighting for.”

title: TUHAY-DER in Mardin calls for the release of political prisoners in Turkey
content:
The Association for Solidarity and Cooperation with Families of Prisoners and Convicts (TUHAY-DER) staged a sit-in outside the courthouse in Mardin, calling for the release of political prisoners and concrete steps in the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Under the slogan “Freedom for Prisoners, Hope for Peace,” relatives of political prisoners, representatives of political parties and civil society organizations, and numerous other people gathered for the protest. A banner read: “No Extensions of Imprisonment – Freedom for Political Prisoners.”




Ayşe Bozan, co-chair of TUHAY-DER’s Mardin branch, particularly criticized the practice of keeping political prisoners behind bars even after they have served their sentences. She said that repeatedly denying their release prevented them from returning to a life of freedom. Many relatives, especially mothers, have long been waiting for the prison gates to finally open, she added.




Bozan pointed to the contradiction between the stated efforts to achieve a democratic and peaceful solution to the Kurdish question and the continued repression within the prison system. “While talks focus on strengthening democratic politics and establishing lasting social peace, practices that prevent equal participation in political and social life remain in place,” she noted.




Bozan emphasized that political prisoners must be given the opportunity to participate in the peace process under conditions of freedom. She called for the release of all political prisoners and an end to arbitrary extensions of imprisonment.




“The practices that cast a shadow over the process must be brought to an end, and concrete steps must be taken immediately to pave the way for peace,” Bozan stated.




The demonstration concluded with a sit-in and chants of “Bijî Berxwedana Zindana” (Long live the resistance in the prisons).

title: Muğla Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Ahmet Aras, CHP'den istifa etti
content:
Fotoğraf: Muğla Büyükşehir Belediyesi

Muğla Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Ahmet Aras, CHP üyeliğinden ayrılarak görevini bağımsız sürdürme kararı aldığını açıkladı. Aras, “Bir süredir şahsım üzerinden yürütülen siyasi tartışmaların, kentimiz için yaptığımız çalışmaların önüne geçtiğini görüyorum. Bu tartışmaların Muğla’ya ve hemşehrilerimize bir katkı sağlamadığına inanıyorum” dedi.

Bir süredir AKP'ye geçeceğine dair iddialar gündeme gelen Muğla Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Ahmet Aras en son bir hafta önce ODA TV'ye yaptığı açıklamada “Kesinlikle hayır. Ne AKP ne de başka bir parti. Bunu defalarca dile getirdim. Yolumuza CHP çatısı altında devam edeceğiz” demişti.

Ahmet Aras'ın açıklamasının tamamı şöyle:

“Sevgili hemşehrilerim, Muğla Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanlığı görevini Cumhuriyet Halk Partisi çatısı altında, sizlerin güveni ve desteğiyle üstlendim. Bu yolda benimle omuz omuza yürüyen, emek veren bütün yol arkadaşlarımın katkısını; birlikte verdiğimiz mücadelenin, kurduğumuz dostlukların ve ortak emeğimizin kıymetini her zaman saygıyla taşıyacağım. Bugün Muğla’mızın gündeminde çözüm bekleyen önemli meseleler, hayata geçirilmeyi bekleyen hizmetler ve geleceğimize yön verecek büyük sorumluluklar bulunuyor. Buna karşın bir süredir şahsım üzerinden yürütülen siyasi tartışmaların, kentimiz için yaptığımız çalışmaların önüne geçtiğini görüyorum. Bu tartışmaların Muğla’ya ve hemşehrilerimize bir katkı sağlamadığına inanıyorum. Bugün itibarıyla Cumhuriyet Halk Partisi üyeliğimden ayrılarak Muğla Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanlığı görevimi bağımsız olarak sürdürme kararı aldım. Kararımın temelinde, Muğla’ya karşı taşıdığım sorumluluğu halkımızın iradesi ve kentimizin ihtiyaçları doğrultusunda sürdürme anlayışı bulunmaktadır. Belediye başkanlığı, ayrım yapmadan herkesin belediye başkanı olmayı gerektirir. Bugüne kadar olduğu gibi bundan sonra da siyasi görüşü, yaşam biçimi veya yaşadığı yer ne olursa olsun her hemşehrimize aynı samimiyetle yaklaşmaya; Muğla’mızın bütün ilçelerine ve mahallelerine adaletle hizmet götürmeye devam edeceğim. Hizmet anlayışımızın ölçüsü değişmeyecek: Güçlü bir altyapı, güvenli ulaşım, korunan doğa, desteklenen üretici, dayanışmayla güçlenen bir toplum ve çocuklarımıza bırakacağımız yaşanabilir bir Muğla için çalışacağız. Merkezi yönetimle, kamu kurumlarıyla, siyasi partilerle, ilçe belediyelerimizle, meslek odalarıyla ve sivil toplum kuruluşlarıyla Muğla’nın yararına olan her konuda iş birliği içinde olacağız. Kentimizin menfaatine yönelik her samimi adıma açık olacak, çözüm üretmek isteyen herkesle ortak bir zeminde buluşacağız. Bu karar, geçmişimizi yok saymak değildir. Birlikte verilen emeğe, kurulan dostluklara ve paylaşılan mücadeleye duyduğum saygı daima devam edecektir. Aynı zamanda bu karar, Muğla’nın bugünü ve geleceği için taşıdığım sorumluluğun bir gereğidir. Bugün aldığım kararda olduğu gibi, yarın üstleneceğim sorumluluklarda da halkımızın güvenini ve rızasını esas alacağım. Muğlalı hemşehrilerimin takdiri ve kentimizin öncelikleri, yoluma yön verecektir. Benim tarafım Muğla’dır. Önceliğim hemşehrilerimizin huzuru, refahı ve kentimizin geleceğidir. Muğla için çalışmaya, halkımızla birlikte yürümeye aynı inanç ve kararlılıkla devam edeceğim. Sevgi ve saygılarımla.”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: New Nunavik rehabilitation service to begin with 46 patients
content:
A new service that will give Nunavimmiut access to specialized services that are typically difficult to access in the North is set to begin later this month with 46 patients.




It’s the product of a 

partnership

 between the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services, the Constance-Lethbridge Rehabilitation Centre and the Quebec Health Centre-West-of-Montreal University.




“Work on the initiative began in 2022 and involved several years of consultation, co-ordination and planning,” said Maude Parenteau, planning, programming and research officer at the health board, Thursday in an email.




The service, administered by a technologist, will provide help with orthotics, prosthetics and positioning equipment, such as braces, artificial limbs and specialized wheelchairs.




Patients who need this care currently must travel to Montreal.




The technologist plans to visit two communities on the Hudson Bay coast during the week of Oct. 25. Two c

ommunities on the Ungava Bay coast are set to get their initial visit the week of Dec. 7.




Parenteau declined to identify the villages that will receive the service first. She also did not say if the technologist would visit every village.
















First visits will focus on assessment, taking measurements and making moulds. Later visits will allow staff to deliver and fit the equipment and make any needed adjustments.




Several sources are funding the service, including Quebec’s health insurance board and the federal Non-Insured Health Benefits Program. Health centres and the regional health board will also cover costs.




Who pays for equipment and services will depend on the type of equipment needed and the patient’s eligibility for coverage.




Some patients with more complex needs may still have to travel to southern Quebec for assessments or procedures that cannot be done locally, Parenteau said.

author: Mada Masr
title: As Sisi vows to leave power by 2030, sources differ on whether he really means it
content:
Speaking at the 44th Cultural and Educational Symposium of the Egyptian Armed Forces on 

Wednesday

, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi 

said

 Egypt’s “Constitution would not be touched.”

 




His remarks came as part of a longer speech warning against a return to the demonstrations and protests that swept the country after 2011, alongside a series of other political messages, including a 

declaration

 that he 

would

 “never tire of protecting Egypt.”

 

He reiterated similar messages again on 

Thursday,

 during a speech at the Police Academy’s graduation ceremony, saying he would continue working “until the final day” of his presidential term in 2030.




With 

talk

 of lifting presidential term limits already a feature of political conversations in the leadup to the 2025 parliamentary election, a parliamentary source told Mada Masr at the time, Sisi’s comments sparked immediate queries about how long the president will remain in power.

 




Speaking on condition of anonymity, three parliamentary sources close to a sovereign security agency told Mada Masr that Sisi’s pledge not to touch the Constitution is inseparable from a broader plan to reshape the country’s political landscape, and is driven by his desire to avoid the mistakes of ousted President Hosny Mubarak, whose three decades in power fostered the widespread resentment that would lead to the 2011 revolution.




But his remarks were described differently by a judicial source and an opposition party source, who said the president’s remarks were a “political maneuver” intended to diffuse public anger while leaving his political future up to the public. They said the statement also leaves the door open for a peaceful transfer of power, or, the judicial source said, it could pave the way for a “popular call” for Sisi to remain in office on the grounds that no suitable successor is ready to take over. 




The three parliamentary sources and a government source agreed that the president’s pledge not to touch the Constitution was consistent with Sisi’s personal desire not to remain in power beyond 2030.




A parliamentarian with a military background recalled Sisi saying during closed sessions that he wouldn’t wait for the defense minister “to tell me to go to Sharm el-Sheikh,” alluding to Mubarak’s departure for the 

Red Sea

 resort in the midst of the January 25 revolution.

 In early February 2011, then-Vice President Omar Soliman announced Mubarak’s resignation after 30 years in power and said the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, headed by then-Defense Minister Mohamed Hussein Tantawy, would assume power. 




The same parliamentarian added that the remainder of Sisi’s presidency could see the government implement several of the constitutional provisions 

introduced

 in 2019, including the one that allows the president to appoint a vice president.

 He suggested that the president could make such an appointment to ensure a smoother transfer of power.




Article 150-bis of the Constitution allows the president to appoint one or more vice presidents, define their roles, delegate some of his powers to them, remove them from office and accept their resignations.




The judicial source told Mada Masr that Sisi’s remarks about not remaining in power beyond 2030 sent positive signals that could help ease public anger and discontent with the executive branch over the country’s economic and political conditions, and could  spark public debate about his successor.




The source also said that Sisi’s remarks do not rule out efforts to extend his presidency before his current term expires, suggesting that a reinterpretation of the constitution could be put forward, or that the president, or one-fifth of the House, could exercise their constitutional prerogative to propose amendments to its text.




The party source, who heads an opposition party represented in the House of Representatives, said it was too early to determine whether the Constitution would be amended. 




“Not before 2028,” the source said. The call for constitutional amendments cannot come from the president himself, he said, adding that, “others make the call, but not now.” He described the current political climate is not conducive to raising the issue, saying “there’s no rush.”




The source said Egyptians are going through a difficult period and needed someone to speak to them clearly about the state of the country and where it is headed, pointing to the deterioration of public services and political and economic conditions.




The party leader stressed that Sisi receives daily reports warning that public anger has reached dangerous levels. He said the president’s remarks about leaving the Constitution unchanged and ensuring the peaceful transfer of power could assuage public ire as they reinforce his earlier assurances to that effect.




Sisi’s latest remarks call to mind the 13-year pattern of public assurances that preceded the 2019 constitutional amendments. Despite his repeated promises not to amend the Constitution or exceed his original two-term limit, the 2019 amendments doubled his maximum legal tenure from eight to 16 years. 




In the summer of 

2013

, sources close to Sisi, who was defense minister at the time, said he had no intention of running for president and was resisting pressure from those around him following the “million man march mandate.”

 By January 

2014

, his tone had shifted. Speaking at an Armed Forces educational symposium, he responded to appeals from politicians and artists, saying he would only run for president if called upon by the public and given a mandate by the military. 

The matter was settled on March 26 that year, when he appeared in military uniform and 

announced

 his candidacy.




A year after taking office, Sisi began laying the groundwork for constitutional amendments. 

In September 

2015

, he said the Constitution was drafted with good intentions, but good intentions alone were not enough to build a country.




In a February 2016 interview with Paris-based magazine 

Jeune Afrique

, Sisi said the Egyptian people would not allow him to exceed his eight-year mandate because they “know very well how to choose,” pointing to the 30 million people he said had taken to the streets to reject former President Mohamed Morsi’s rule.

 

In the same interview, he described 

democratic

 transition as a lengthy process, saying Egypt would need 20-25 years to achieve it.

 




Between 

September

 and 

December

 2016, Sisi repeatedly said he could not remain in office for even a single day beyond his presidential term or serve more than two consecutive terms, pledging to uphold the Constitution.




In 2017, editors-in-chief of state-owned newspapers asked Sisi whether he intended to seek a second term. He 

replied

, “we’ll deal with that when the time comes.” In November that year, Sisi told 

CNBC

, “I am with preserving two four-year terms.” Egypt had a new Constitution, he said, and he wasn’t in favor of amending it. He insisted that no president could remain in office beyond the eight-year limit set by the Constitution.




In January 

2018

, Sisi announced his bid for a second term, insisting he could not remain against the will of the people.

 

That same month, former Armed Forces Chief of Staff Samy Anan declared his intention to run against Sisi and was 

arrested

 on the grounds that he was running in violation of military bylaws as he had not been discharged as a reserve officer.

 He was released nearly two years later.




Anan’s case followed that of retired Colonel 

Ahmed Qonsowa

, who was sentenced to six years in prison by a military court after announcing his intention to run for president.

 




In November 2018, Sisi 

said

 that “no one stays in power forever,” adding that the people would bring about change if they wanted it.




In 2019, Parliament passed the constitutional amendments following 

months

 of coordination within the political establishment. They extended Sisi’s second term, which was due to end in 2022, to 2024 and allowed him to serve a third term. 

His third term began in April 

2024

 and is scheduled to end in April 2030.

 




Sisi’s remarks at the 44th Cultural and Educational Symposium of the Egyptian Armed Forces on Wednesday sparked confusion in the press. At around 5 pm that day, several websites took down reports of his comments about preserving the Constitution. 




The reports carried headlines such as “President Sisi: No one will touch the Constitution.” 

At 7 p.m., the presidential 

spokesperson

 released the text of Sisi’s speech, around two hours before it was ultimately broadcast on television, after which the reports were 

republished

 by state-owned and affiliated outlets.

 




One of the parliamentary sources close to a sovereign security agency also noted that the confusion was evident in the delayed onset of the usual chorus of praise from state-aligned parties. 




It was several hours before members of the Nation’s Future 

Party 

and the 

Homeland Defenders

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Israel Badly Burns Young Girl and Kills Her Mother in Airstrike on Gaza Home
content:
A small child has been found sitting alone on a bed engulfed by smoke and flames moments after Israel destroyed her home in Gaza City, leaving her badly burned and killing her mother.




Dramatic footage captured by 

Palestinian journalist Ali al-Jaafrawi

 showed him racing to rescue the girl, later identified as Maryam Ahmed Ghanem, from the burning building. Her mother was 33-year-old Reem Asaad Awad.




“I went back to rescue others and to document what happened, but I suffocated and lost consciousness because of the thick smoke. I saw a woman on fire inside the apartment,” he told Al Jazeera Arabic.




Hospital photos of Maryam with extensive burns on her face have led to widespread condemnation of the attacks.




Children’s educator and YouTube star Ms Rachel, a vocal critic of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, questioned why Maryam’s story had not received greater media coverage. 




“The mainstream news is complicit in this genocide as well as everyone who witnesses it and stays silent,” she wrote on social media. 




The strikes killed four people and injured several others, 

the Anadolu Agency

 reported, citing a source from Al-Shifa Hospital. It is unclear if the girl had other relatives who were killed or injured. Her father was killed in a seperate attack at the start of the genocide, the New Arab reported. 




Israel says it was targeting a Hamas member but has not provided evidence to substantiate the claim.




The Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), a civil rights group, called on US lawmakers to condemn Israel for “burning a Palestinian mother alive while her daughter watched in Gaza.” 




Media reports about the attack have not confirmed the exact cause of the mother’s death. But throughout the genocide in Gaza, Israeli airstrikes have set thousands of buildings and tents alight, burning their inhabitants to death.




In June, an 

entire sleeping family of five

 burned to death in their Gaza City home. Last December, Israeli strikes killed five people inside their tents, including two children, in the al-Mawasi displacement camp, a “safe zone” west of Khan Younis. Medical sources at the nearby Kuwaiti Hospital said the bodies of the victims 

arrived badly charred

. 




Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldiers say the military routinely bombs homes knowing 

multiple civilians are inside

, while a UN report in June found that Israel 

deliberately 

kills and tortures Palestinian children. 




The IDF has repeatedly violated a so-called ceasefire agreement signed with Hamas in October 2025, killing at least 1,498 Palestinians and injuring more than 5,000, Gaza health ministry figures show.

title: AKOM'dan turuncu alarm: “Mecbur kalmadıkça dışarıya çıkmayın”
content:
İstanbul Büyükşehir Belediyesi (İBB) Başkanvekili Nuri Aslan, Afet Koordinasyon Merkezi’nde (AKOM) gelişmeler hakkında aldığı bilgileri paylaştığı bir açıklama yaptı.

Salı gününden itibaren teyakkuzda olduklarını ifade eden Aslan, “Dün bakanlarımızla toplantılar yaptık. Bugün de Çevre ve Şehircilik Bakanımız ve İçişleri Bakanımız ile beraber sabahın erken saatlerinden itibaren Ayazağa'daydık. Devletin bütün kurumları eş güdüm içinde çalışıyor. İstanbul Valiliğiyle ve AFAD ile koordineli çalışıyoruz. Bugün meteorolojik verilere göre maalesef yurt genelinde sarı ve turuncu kodlu alarm seviyeleri var. Kocaeli, Adapazarı, Yalova, Bursa civarlarında turuncu kod seviyesine geçildi. Yurdun bazı yerlerinde de sarı kodla önlemler alınmaya çalışılıyor. İstanbul'da cuma günü beklenen hafif sağanak yağışlar, akşam 18.00'den sonra yağışın birazcık daha şiddetlenmesini bekliyoruz. Ancak cumartesi öğlene doğru kuvvetlenme ihtimali çok yüksek. Dolayısıyla İstanbul'da da turuncu alarm seviyesindeyiz” dedi.

“Mecbur kalmadıkça dışarıya çıkmayın” uyarısı yapan Aslan, “Bu akşamdan itibaren, mecbur kalınmadıkça dışarıya çıkılmaması, mecbursanız da kendi aracınızla değil, toplu taşıma araçlarıyla trafiğe çıkmanızı öneriyoruz. İnşallah yaşadığımız bu büyük felaketi bir daha yaşamayız. Tek amacımız var: İstanbul'daki hemşerilerimizin herhangi bir felakette olumsuz etkilenmesini engellemek. Başka bir düşüncemiz yok. Bu tür afetlerde İstanbulluların göstermiş olduğu gayrete, yardımlaşmaya, dayanışmaya teşekkür ediyorum” ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Man Shot by ICE in NYC Last Week Yet to Receive Surgery for Bullet in His Neck
content:
Lawyers for Oscar Belgal have called for his immediate release, citing inadequate care.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Oscar Belgal, the 28-year-old Dominican man shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New York City last Thursday, has not received surgery to remove a bullet lodged in his neck for over a week.

Lawyers for Oscar Belgal have called for his immediate release, citing inadequate care.

On Wednesday, the Legal Aid Society, which is representing Belgal, filed a habeas corpus petition decrying ICE’s “flagrant abuses of authority and categorically lawless conduct.”

ICE agents attacked Belgal in Manhattan on October 8 around 4 PM, soon after he picked up his 5-year-old son from school. The Legal Aid Society’s petition describes ICE’s sudden attack, noting that “an anonymous, masked man stormed Oscar’s driverside window with his firearm drawn, followed closely behind by several other masked men also wielding firearms. The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way.” They were all wearing civilian clothing, the report added.

The petition goes on to describe the attack against Belgal, as an ICE agent shot into his car “while his son cowered in the back seat.” ICE agents then “pinned him to the ground” and left him semi-conscious, without aid. Only later, when he woke up in a hospital, did the agents identify themselves as ICE officers.

Days later, the petition explains, the bullet remains lodged in his neck, and Belgal has “experienced a loss of sensation in half of his face, as well as hearing loss in his left ear, and has not received surgery to remove the bullet from his neck.”

Lawyers from the Legal Aid Society said Thursday that ICE has held Belgal in solitary confinement, under 24-hour lockdown. Initially detained in New Jersey, he was moved on October 9 to the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn – the same jail where former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro is being held.

Legal Aid Society lawyers said Wednesday that this is “a facility notorious for medical neglect.”

“With a bullet still lodged in his neck and his serious medical needs unmet, every additional day in custody puts him at further risk. The Court must intervene and order his immediate release,” they added.

Belgal’s shooting last week spurred a renewal of protests against ICE in New York City. Protestors demanded an end to ICE’s presence in the city and called for the abolition of the agency. In addition, demonstrators have called for an end to ICE’s use of local parking lots – and for city police commissioner Jessica Tisch to resign. Activists who attended a Manhattan protest that erupted the night of the shooting reported seeing NYPD “helping the ICE vehicles whisk away our neighbors and come in and out of the hospital.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.
