They equate the form of struggle with its political content, and so avoid the central question, which is the question of power.

Three Things That Are Not the Same

Any analysis of a social protest has to distinguish at least three levels.

The first is the **social cause**. What objective contradictions produced the protest? In France the answer is clear: a crisis of public services, austerity policy, and educational inequality.

The second is the form of struggle . How is the protest organized, and what means does it use? Riot, occupation, destruction of property, street fighting, strike, blockade, or civil disobedience.

The third is the political direction . Whose interests does the protest ultimately serve, and what relations of power does it change?

The common mistake is to slide from one level to another. Because the cause of a protest is legitimate, we conclude that every form it takes is also legitimate and effective. Because the form is radical, we conclude that its direction must be emancipatory. To clear the ground, three propositions should be set side by side:

The legitimacy of a demand does not guarantee the legitimacy of every form of action.

The radicalism of a form of struggle does not guarantee the radicalism of its political content.

And perhaps most important: the political outcome of a movement is not necessarily what its first participants intended.

The last proposition lifts the problem out of the moral register of “good violence versus bad violence.” The question is no longer whether the protesters are right to be angry. It is what their action does within the real network of social forces.

No Form Is Inherently Left-Wing

By “form” I mean the repertoire of tools and methods of action: riot, occupation, destruction, street fighting, strike, blockade, and civil disobedience. The essential point is that none of these is inherently left or right.

In Marxist logic, the fact that a crowd occupies a street, fights the police or sets fire to a government building says nothing in itself about the class character or political direction of the movement. A riot can be anti-capitalist or anti-austerity. It can be the cry of the dispossessed against the state. It can also be a purely local, defensive reaction, or one with no definite class orientation, and under some conditions it can even strengthen the far right.

The same holds for the strike. A strike by workers in a private firm for higher wages can remain entirely within the framework of redistribution inside capitalism, while a riot can, in other circumstances, be part of the politicization of the subordinate classes. The distinction I want to draw is therefore not between “bad riots” and “good strikes.” It is between the radicalism of form and the radicalism of content. The radicalism of form concerns the apparent intensity of an action: how aggressive, how spectacular. The radicalism of content concerns the depth of the change an action can produce in relations of power. The two sometimes arrive together and sometimes come apart.

The great temptation here is to construct a linear formula: protest, then strike, then organization, then class alliance, then victory. The history of social movements offers no such straight line. France today shows that protest, organization, repression, solidarity and politicization can occur simultaneously and in back-and-forth patterns.

The question, then, is not whether every protest must pass from demonstration to strike and from strike to revolution. The question is whether the form of struggle that is chosen increases the capacity for organization, solidarity and collective power, or wears it down. A legitimate protest may build solidarity in one situation and destroy it in another. This depends not only on the intentions of the protesters but also on the response of the state, the media, the political forces on the scene, and the wider social conditions surrounding the movement.

If I had to reduce the issue to a single question, the serious Marxist question is not “Is this riot left-wing?” It is this: what kind of social power does this protest produce, and who will ultimately use it?

A riot may disrupt the state for a few days. But if it cannot build organization, class solidarity and durable power, it subsides, leaving little but the memory of flames and, often, the heavy burden of repression. A strike that looks calm, by contrast, can exert far greater pressure on capital if it disrupts production, transport, energy and public services.

Even so, the social power of subordinate classes should not be reduced to the ability to disrupt accumulation. That would be an economistic reading, and it is not even Luxemburg’s account of the mass strike. For her, the mass strike is not merely a tool for halting production. It is a political and social process of self-organization, of the spread of consciousness, and of linking economic struggle to political struggle. The social power of the subordinate classes comes not only from their capacity to cause disruption but from their capacity to organize, to widen solidarity, and to turn temporary disruption into collective and political power. Political radicalism should be measured by this capacity, not by the intensity of the pictures that travel from the street to the television screen.

Defenders of the logic of the riot may argue the following. People who have won no concessions through institutional channels have no choice but the language of revolt. The riot is, in some circumstances, the political expression of groups excluded from formal means of organization. And experience shows that states often retreat only under the pressure of visible disruption.

This argument contains part of the truth. Riots have at times drawn public attention to crises that had been ignored for months, and at times they have forced governments to negotiate. It does not follow that the riot is always a politically ineffective or backward form. E. P. Thompson’s work on the “moral economy of the crowd” showed that collective action without formal organization should not be dismissed as irrational or as lacking consciousness.

The issue, therefore, is not to strike the riot from the list of legitimate forms of struggle. It is whether the riot is embedded in a broader process of organization and class conflict, or takes its place; and whether it dissolves into a wider movement or overshadows it. Without this distinction, a critic from the left could easily say that we are repeating the liberal line: protest is fine until it turns violent. That is not my position. My position is that both the critique of repression and the critique of ineffective forms of action spring from a single concern: the power of the subordinate classes.

France Today: Evidence for the Distinction

France is instructive because it shows both sides of the problem at once. On the one hand, clashes, destruction and arson are part of the reality of the protests. On the other, what has given the movement greater weight and reach is not the intensity of the confrontations but its spread, both horizontal and vertical: students, university students, teachers, parents, and union organizations. This convergence is the product of a capacity that grew out of shared material demands, not out of the flames.

The French left is not uniform in its response. La France Insoumise has supported the protests, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, according to reports, has stood with the students and sharply criticized police conduct. There are also reports of disagreement among the students themselves over methods of action. This disagreement is not accidental. It shows that the question of form is alive within the movement itself.

Crisis, Image, and the Battle over Meaning

One of the most important things the left must take seriously is that a social crisis always unfolds in a political field, and in that field both the radical left and the far right try to convert discontent into political capital. The dangerous sequence can be described as follows: crisis, then images of violence, then social fear, then the elevation of security as the central issue, then a demand for order, and finally an opening for the far right. At every link in this chain, media and political representation play a decisive role. The phrase “urban violence,” which the government used from the first days, is itself part of this struggle over meaning. It is a name that conceals the social cause and reduces a structural crisis to a matter of policing.

The analysis by Stuart Hall and his colleagues in Policing the Crisis, though it belongs to a different historical and geographical setting, Britain in the 1970s, shows how a social crisis can be transformed through media and political representation into a question of “law and order.” It should not be taken as a direct explanation of France today. But it is a clear warning to the left: a society can explode, and the result may be not socialism but more authoritarianism, a more securitized politics, and a stronger far right. The issue is therefore not only the ethics of protest. It is the battle over what a protest means in public space.

The Second Trap: Accepting the State’s Frame

There is a trap on the other side as well. Suppose the state erodes public services, weakens education, and leaves a generation in insecurity, and then, when that generation protests, reduces the whole affair to “violence.” The left must not accept that frame. According to reports, the extensive use of police force, riot-control weapons and mass arrests has itself become an aggravating factor. Two propositions can therefore be true at once:

First, state repression and police violence must be criticized.

Second, not every violent act by protesters necessarily advances the social movement.

There is no contradiction between the two. The contradiction arises only if we assume that criticizing repression requires praising every form of resistance, or that criticizing one form of resistance requires agreeing with the state.

In the Marxist tradition, social discontent is not yet class consciousness; class consciousness is not yet class organization; class organization is not yet political power; and a riot, however intense, is not yet a revolution. A society can be deeply discontented without being organized. It can riot without producing power. It can weaken a government without weakening capitalism. It can even destabilize a political regime and open the space for a more reactionary force.

For this reason, the left’s final question about the French protests should not be “Is this riot radical enough?” It should be: can this protest move beyond a momentary explosion of discontent toward the lasting organization of the subordinate classes, toward a bond between the young generation, teachers and the working class, and toward collective forms of social power? There is no guarantee, and no predetermined path. But one can ask of each form of action whether it increases this capacity or wears it down.

Here a sharper criticism can be made of a particular tendency in the contemporary left: the substitution of the intensity of action for the politics of power. This is a left that turns “the street” into a value in itself, as though the more violent and unstable the street, the more left-wing the movement. The classical Marxist tradition, by contrast, is fundamentally about converting scattered discontent into the organized power of a class, not about glorifying disorder. This criticism does not mean silence in the face of state violence, nor does it condemn young protesters. It means taking them seriously enough to want their protest to become power rather than memory.

For the left, the question is not how fiercely the street has burned. It is what remains of the power of the subordinate classes after the fire has gone out.

Majid Maleki Meighani, (sometimes writing under the name Majid Maleki), is an Iranian political analyst, writer, and translator. He was imprisoned for his political activities. His work focuses on critical analysis of Iran’s labor movement, the political left, anti-imperialist critiques of geopolitics, and social movements in West Asia and the Global South. His analysis is grounded in direct fieldwork and interviews within local communities. He has translated into Persian Walter LaFeber’s Inevitable Revolutions: The United States in Central America and the collection Voices of the Arab Spring. He has been a contributor to ZNetwork, Tribune Zamane, and Akhbar-e Rooz. You can access his full body of work on his author page on ZNetwork.

author: Tahrir Hamdi
title: Palestine Resists: From Fanon and Kanafani to Armed Struggle and Return
content:
How does one resist dispossession and displacement, ongoing genocide, culturicide, scholasticide and epistemicide, and all forms of erasure of a people’s past, present and future? The answer: Resist by all available means—armed resistance, cultural resistance, and economic resistance; this is a legal right recognized under international law, but before that, it is morally legitimate, justified, and necessary. Israel is a brutal settler colony that was made possible by two main strategies: the expulsion of the Palestinian people from their indigenous land (historic Palestine) and ongoing genocide that is now 78 years old.

Armed resistance, as theorized by anti-colonial theorists such as Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Amílcar Cabral, Ghassan Kanafani, and Edward Said, is an essential part of the anti-colonial struggle for the liberation of colonized minds and lands. In his book The Wretched of the Earth (1963), Frantz Fanon, a psychiatrist by training, forcefully argued for anti-colonial armed resistance, stating precisely because colonization is such a violent and dehumanizing process, “decolonization is always a violent phenomenon” (35). For Fanon, colonization always dehumanizes the colonized; therefore, the colonized must use violence against the colonizer to allow for the rehumanization of the colonized because revolutionary violence is meant to end the oppression, colonization and dehumanization of the colonized population (94).

The revolutionary thinker Amilcar Cabral argued in his speech titled “The Weapon of Theory, (1966)”: “the only effective way of definitively fulfilling the aspirations of the peoples, that is to say of attaining national liberation, is by armed struggle.” In his essay titled “National Liberation and Culture,” Cabral argues that the colonizer seeks to physically destroy a significant proportion of the dominated or colonized population; accordingly, the colonizer, in addition to resorting to mass killing and genocide, will always target the culture of the colonized. It is precisely for this reason that the preservation and continuation of people’s culture and their knowledge systems are essential to national liberation. Thus, cultural resistance and armed resistance go hand in hand.

The revolutionary Palestinian theorist and activist (who also wrote intellectual and theoretical pieces for the Arab Nationalist Movement and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine), Ghassan Kanafani, like Fanon and Cabral, emphasized the absolute importance of cultural and armed resistance. Kanafani argued for a vibrant culture of resistance that would enable the armed struggle for liberation. This is why Kanafani wrote stories of Palestinian resistance. In a novella titled Returning to Haifa, Kanafani makes it clear, through his character Said, that any genuine return to Palestine required a successful armed struggle, a war. Kanafani also emphasized the absolute importance of the unity of armed resistance organizations. In his essay titled “Towards a Constructive Dialogue on Palestinian National Unity,” Kanafani writes: “Any setback to any active fida’i organization, whether militarily or fundamentally, cannot be limited to that organization, but rather is immediately reflected on all other organizations” (262). Kanafani was well aware that divisions do not just weaken one Palestinian organization, but the Palestinian struggle for liberation as a whole.

Echoing Kanafani’s and other anti-colonial theorists’ position on armed struggle, the Palestinian American intellectual Edward Said told Tim Sebastian on the BBC’s “Hardtalk” program in 2002 that he is “for any kind of violence that would resist occupation and apartheid […] occupation and apartheid have to be resisted by whatever means bring about their end.” Thus, Zionist settler colonialism must be resisted “by whatever means bring[s] about [its] end” or in the words of Fanon, by the “use of all means, and that of force first and foremost” (61). As Said was nearing the end of his life, he wrote about the absolute refusal to surrender, which he theorized in his book published posthumously, titled On Late Style (2006). The inevitable link between armed resistance and the culture of resistance is of great importance—it is this link that guarantees the continuation of resistance to oppression and brutal Zionist settler colonialism.

There has always been Palestinian resistance to colonization, which in the early 20th century began with popular uprisings led by Izzidin Al Qassam against the brutal rule of the British Mandate, a colonial authority in Palestine that (through the infamous Balfour Declaration in 1917) promised the Zionist British banker Lionel Walter Rothschild, a Jewish homeland in historic Palestine, the land of the Indigenous Palestinians. The Balfour Declaration set in motion the attempted physical destruction of a significant part of the Palestinian population, their culture and their continued displacement.

After the 1948 Nakba and ethnic cleansing of Palestine, which resulted in the expulsion of more than 750,000 Palestinians and the destruction of 536 (Abu- Lughod and Sa’di, 2007: 3) Palestinian towns and villages in addition to tens of massacres in different Palestinian villages, Palestinians found themselves as refugees both inside occupied Palestine—in Gaza and what is now erroneously termed the “West Bank,” which the Palestinian poet Mourid Barghouti calls verbicide, meant to erase history and memory by renaming, and across neighboring Arab countries—such as Lebanon, Jordan, Syria and other countries. As Ramzy Baroud points out in his article titled “Outsmarting the Sky,” Palestinian armed resistance began almost at the very point of rupture—immediately after the 1948 Nakba with Palestinian fida’iyeen (specifically the peasantry, the fellahin in Arabic) in Gaza that would cross the border into the newly established Zionist settler colony for fida’i operations against enemy army positions.

However, perhaps more organized armed resistance began with the official birth of armed Palestinian organizations; the first among them was the left-leaning Arab Nationalist Movement (ANM) in the early 1950s, which was founded by George Habash, Wadie Haddad, and others. The slogan raised by the ANM was “Unity, Liberation, Revenge, and the Recovery of Palestine” (Hamdi Matar). One of these young men was my late father, Khalil Hamdi, who spent his young adult life organizing for the ANM, gathering community support for the idea of Palestinian resistance and liberation in the Palestinian refugee camps in Jordan and traveling to Beirut for meetings with other members like Habash and Haddad, where future plans would be made.

Of course, these activities also included organizing armed fida’i groups and various fida’i operations. Under the influence of the political climate of the 1950s with the rise of the charismatic leader of Egypt, Gamal Abdel Nasser, it was the belief of the founding members of the ANM that Arab nations would unite against the expansionist, Zionist settler colony, and this would then lead to the liberation of Palestine. Unfortunately for the ANM and the Palestinian cause, the claws of colonialism in the Arab region were as deep then as they are now. All members of the ANM, including my own father, were imprisoned and tortured. Zionist settler colonialism and American and British imperialism, along with Arab reaction/reactionary regimes, united against the freedom aims of the nascent Arab Nationalist Movement that envisioned Arab unity, social and political reform, and a free, liberated Palestine.

After the devastating Arab defeat in 1967 and the loss of more Arab land to “Israel,” George Habash along with Wadie Haddad, Abu Ali Mustapha and others from the ANM went on to form the Marxist-Leninist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which, as we learned from Ramzy Baroud’s above mentioned article, found tremendous support amongst the young fida’i movement in Gaza at that time. Of course, Yasser Arafat’s secular Palestine Liberation Organization had already been formed a few years earlier in 1964. Palestinian armed resistance continues to this day, however, with a more Islamic (but still very Palestinian nationalist minded) framework; the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) was formed in 1981 by Fathi Shaqaqi, inspired by the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979 and a few years later, Hamas, under the leadership of Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, was formed in 1987.

As can be readily observed from the different Palestinian armed resistance movements over the decades, Palestinian resistance has had radically different ideological visions—ranging from secular, to leftist, Marxist-Leninist to Islamic, but all have one goal: the liberation of historic Palestine and social and political reform by means of anti-colonial struggle—whether this resistance is armed, cultural or economic—freedom, dignity, the liberation and return to Palestine is the aim that unites all Palestinians in their different cultures of exile. Until there is a free Palestine, and in the words of the Palestinian poet Mahmoud Darwish from his long poem “Mural,”—the “return of the wandering soul as if nothing had happened,” the resistance will continue. Perhaps the most fitting description of Palestinian resilience is best expressed by Darwish himself in his tribute to Gaza in a poem titled “Silence for Gaza” (1973):

What is beautiful about Gaza is that our voices do not reach it. Nothing distracts it; nothing takes its fist away from the enemy’s face. Not the forms of the Palestinian state we will establish whether on the eastern side of the moon, or the western side of Mars when it is explored. Gaza is devoted to rejection… hunger and rejection, thirst and rejection, displacement and rejection, torture and rejection, siege and rejection, death and rejection. (…)

(Enemies) might implant tanks on the insides of its children and women. They might throw it into the sea, sand, or blood.

But it will not repeat lies and say “Yes” to invaders.

It is neither death, nor suicide. It is Gaza’s way of declaring that it deserves to live. It will continue to explode.

Abu-Lughod, Lila and Sa’di, Ahmad. (2007). Nakba: Palestine, 1948 and the Claims of Memory. New York: Columbia University Press.

Barghouti, Mourid. (2003). “Verbicide.” New Internationalist.

Baroud, Ramzy. (2026). “Outsmarting the Sky: The Secret History of Gaza’s Subterranean Resistance.”

Cabral, Amilcar. (1966) “The Weapon of Theory.” https://www.marxists.org/subject/africa/cabral/1966/weapon-theory.htm

Cabral, Amilcar. (1970). “National Liberation and Culture.” https://www.marxists.org/subject/africa/cabral/1970/cabral-nat-lib-culture.htm

Darwish, Mahmoud. (2003) “Mural.” In Unfortunately, It Was Paradise. Antoon, Sinan and El-Zein, Amira (eds.). Akash, Munir and Forche, Carolyn (trans.). Berkeley, CA: University of California.

Darwish, Mahmoud. (1973, 2012) “Silence for Gaza.” Mondoweiss. https://mondoweiss.net/2012/11/mahmoud-darwish-silence-for-gaza/

Fanon, Frantz. (1963). The Wretched of the Earth. Farrington, Constance (trans.) New York: Grove Press.

Kanafani, Ghassan. (2000). Palestine’s Children: Returning to Haifa and Other Stories.

Kanafani, Ghassan. (2024). Ghassan Kanafani: Selected Political Writings. Brehony, Louis and Hamdi, Tahrir (eds.). London: Pluto Press.

Matar, Hamdi. Palestine Remembered. https://www.palestineremembered.com/Jerusalem/Qalunya/Story9138.html

Said, Edward. On Late Style: Music and Literature Against the Grain. (2006). New York: Vintage.

Tahrir Hamdi is a professor of postcolonial literature at Arab Open University in Jordan. Her work explores resistance literature, anticolonial theory, geography, exile and Palestinian national identity.

author: Marcelo Oliveira
title: Meta bloqueia conteúdos políticos pró-Lula e contra Flávio acusando terrorismo e nudez
content:
Investigamos o que importa para os brasileiros além do que passa na campanha eleitoral. Leia mais reportagens como essa clicando 

aqui

.













Imagine de uma noite para a outra você ficar sem o seu WhatsApp, Instagram e sem seu número de telefone? Foi o que aconteceu com a arquiteta e urbanista Carolina Martins, 43 anos, moradora de Brasília. Ela coordena uma comunidade no WhatsApp de mobilização para “virar voto” em prol da candidatura de Lula.

 A comunidade tem um grupo de bate-papo e ambos foram suspensos pela Meta (dona do WhatsApp, Instagram e Facebook) sob a alegação de “atividade relacionada a organizações terroristas”. 




A suspensão ocorreu no último dia 8 de outubro e o grupo ficou paralisado por pelo menos três dias. 

Martins adoeceu. Teve uma crise de fibromialgia e ficou acamada boa parte do tempo. Até agora ela conta que está sem seu número, que foi bloqueado, e só está conseguindo voltar aos aplicativos e à gestão do grupo pois adquiriu outro chip de telefone. 




“Eu tenho fibromialgia, então assim, fiquei tão estressada, sem andar. Para além das outras coisas, dos atentados à soberania, nossa liberdade de reunião e de expressão, teve toda essa parte da minha saúde emocional”, contou a arquiteta à 

Agência Pùblica

.

 
















Comunidade e grupo de bate-papo pró-Lula foram suspensos por atividade relacionada a organizações terroristas




Martins já está com o Instagram ativo novamente e com a comunidade, que tem agora 895 participantes. Antes do bloqueio, a comunidade tinha atingido o limite de mil membros. Por intermédio de uma amiga ela conseguiu contato com a Meta e apurou que o bloqueio teria se dado por uma suposta “falha de tradução” de um monitoramento da comunidade que apontou “disruptive behaviour” (comportamento perturbador), o que teria sido interpretado como terrorismo. 







Meta bloqueia vídeo crítico a Flávio por “nudez infantil” 




Já o professor e artesão Karl Hadzic Júnior, 47 anos, morador de São Paulo, republicou em sua timeline o vídeo viral “como mãe de menina, meu voto jamais será dessa família”, postado originalmente pela professora paraense Vanessa Silva, no dia 7 de outubro, e que teve quase 45 mil compartilhamentos e 115 mil curtidas. 

O vídeo foi bloqueado pela Meta também no dia 8 de outubro, sob a acusação de ter ferido padrões de comunidade sobre nudez infantil. 




O vídeo começa com uma foto de Silva abraçada com a filha, sem expor nenhuma região sensível da garota. A publicação utiliza um vídeo de Flávio Bolsonaro que ficou conhecido em 2023 no qual ele aparece sem camisa, supostamente imitando o irmão Jair Renan, dizendo: “sou filho do presidente, quer me dar?”. 







 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

View this post on Instagram

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 




Vídeo que viralizou no Instagram e foi marcado pela Meta como conteúdo sensível




O vídeo de Silva segue no ar, mas foi sinalizado com um filtro do Instagram que aparece antes da reprodução, informando sobre “conteúdo sensível”.

 A professora contou à 

Pública

 que várias pessoas que publicaram o vídeo nos stories disseram a ela que a publicação foi suspensa ou até mesmo tiveram as contas bloqueadas. 




A 

Pública

 procurou a Meta para ouvir a companhia sobre casos relatados nessa reportagem, mas não houve resposta.
















Professor compartilhou vídeo crítico a Flávio Bolsonaro, mas foi bloqueado pela Meta por nudez infantil







MPF pede esclarecimentos à Meta após levantamento indicar parcialidade nos bloqueios




Tanto o caso de Marins, quanto de Júnior foram compilados pela organização social brasileira Ctrl+Z, voltada ao enfrentamento dos abusos e do modelo de operação das grandes empresas de tecnologia, que reuniu mais de mil denúncias de usuários de produtos da Meta e do X que relatam casos de bloqueio ou suspensão de contas e postagens relacionados às eleições.




A 

Pública

 

mostrou

 como esse levantamento indica que a Meta tem barrado mais conteúdos pró-Lula e progressistas que pró-Flávio. 

Reportagem

 da Folha mostrou que funcionários da Meta admitiram em mensagens internas que a “conta de Lula estava ‘limitada’ em comparação à de Flávio, e que isso seria negativo pela “alta chance” de haver ação jurídica”.




O levantamento da Ctrl+Z ganhou apoio das organizações de direitos humanos Conectas, Artigo 19 e Sleeping Giants Brasil e transformou-se em uma representação à 

Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão do Ministério Público Federal (MPF) que abriu uma investigação no último dia 13 e pediu, no dia seguinte, uma série de esclarecimentos à Meta. 




A reportagem da 

Pública

 teve acesso ao ofício do MPF, à representação e a um anexo contendo 74 relatos de casos envolvendo suspensões e bloqueios de posts e perfis de usuários do Instagram e do WhatsApp. Dos 74 relatos, recolhidos entre 25 de setembro e 9 de outubro, 33 (44,5%) aconteceram no dia 8 de outubro. 




O levantamento foi iniciado pela CTRL+Z em 25 de setembro, dois dias após a Meta ter suspendido o perfil no Instagram do 

projeto Revelando Brasil

, que postou no YouTube o vídeo viral sobre as ligações entre a igreja Batista da Lagoinha e o escândalo do Banco Master. Devido à repercussão do caso, a Meta liberou o perfil novamente. 







Meta é investigada por violação da liberdade de expressão




A Procuradoria Federal dos Direitos do Cidadão (PFDC) apura na investigação a regularidade e a legalidade das práticas de moderação de conteúdo adotadas pelo X e pela Meta, e verifica se a companhia está violando a liberdade de expressão dos usuários. 




Segundo as organizações, os atingidos formam um conjunto heterogêneo de perfis orgânicos, sem vínculo direto com candidaturas, partidos, federações ou coligações. A denúncia narra que a maioria dos afetados são cidadãos comuns, mas há dezenas de influenciadores, comunicadores, pesquisadores e movimentos estudantis e sociais. 




“Ao que tudo indica, há falhas graves na moderação e aplicação irregular da lei, com conteúdos políticos classificados erroneamente como exploração sexual infantil ou terrorismo”, afirmam os autores da denúncia ao MPF.




O procedimento da PFDC apura como se dá a moderação automatizada de conteúdo e restrições desproporcionais ou injustificadas aplicadas a perfis, publicações e funcionalidades de cidadãos, jornalistas, veículos independentes de imprensa, entidades estudantis e movimentos sociais nas plataformas controladas pela Meta. 




A PFDC remeteu cópia integral do procedimento ao coordenador-Geral de fiscalização da ANPD, Fabrício Madruga, pois as organizações autoras da denúncia relatam a aplicação de sanções recorrentes por sistemas automatizados/algorítmicos sem notificação adequada, a ausência de motivação individualizada e a falta de canais efetivos de revisão aos donos dos perfis, o que fere deveres de transparência das plataformas digitais e a forma como tratam os dados dos clientes. 




À Meta e ao X, o MPF indaga se as medidas de moderação noticiadas foram promovidas, indicando a conta ou publicação atingida, as plataformas em que foram aplicadas, a data e o horário de sua adoção e sua duração; a natureza exata da medida adotada e seus fundamentos fáticos e jurídicos; se a medida permanece em vigor ou foi revertida, indicando, neste último caso, a data da reversão e as suas razões; os procedimentos adotados para garantir a notificação prévia, a motivação individualizada e o canal de recurso ao usuário e se há mecanismos internos de auditoria e correção de erros de moderação em massa. 




O MPF deu cinco dias para a Meta e para o X responderem ao ofício e quer uma explicação para cada medida de moderação tomada contra cada perfil listado na representação feita pelas ONGs. Esse prazo vence no início da última semana antes da votação do segundo turno.




Ainda em relação a cada uma dessas medidas, devem ser esclarecidos seus fundamentos jurídicos ou contratuais. Deve ser informado, para cada caso, se a medida de moderação foi adotada espontaneamente pela empresa, se foi a Meta quem identificou a irregularidade ou se houve denúncia, notificação ou reclamação apresentada por terceiros ou se a Meta cumpria ordem judicial.




A reportagem questionou a Meta sobre as denúncias e o procedimento do MPF, que ainda não respondeu.
















Ministério Público Federal deu prazo para Meta e X responderem sobre critérios de moderação de contas durante o período eleitoral







Bloqueios em série de perfis progressistas




Em conjunto, os casos compilados pela CTRL+Z descrevem restrições à liberdade de expressão no ambiente digital em diferentes níveis: perda do perfil inteiro, retirada de uma publicação, bloqueio apenas para quem acessa do Brasil, restrição de mensagens e dificuldade de publicar ou republicar conteúdo.

 Em alguns relatos, houve recuperação posterior; em outros, o acesso continuava indisponível na data da manifestação. Vários denunciantes relataram não ter recebido explicação individualizada ou não ter conseguido recorrer.




Uma categoria importante de contas que sofreram restrições são aquelas vinculadas a coletivos ou organizações. Por exemplo, a União Paranaense dos Estudantes — UPE Paraná (@upeparana) relatou a derrubada de seu antigo perfil quando este se aproximava de 600 mil visualizações.




O coordenador do Diretório Acadêmico Alfredo Balena, da UFMG, informou que a conta da entidade foi apagada um dia depois de uma postagem de apoio a um dos candidatos à Presidência da República e a candidaturas em Minas Gerais. Houve restrição também ao perfil do DCE da UFMG, cuja suspensão ocorreu durante uma mobilização estudantil.




O perfil do Movimento Sem Terra no Pará teria sido desativado desde a noite de 2 de outubro, mesmo após o setor de comunicação ter realizado os procedimentos de autenticação solicitados pela plataforma.




A representação também relata o bloqueio de perfis de jornalistas como 

Eduardo Moreira

, dono do ICL, de postagens da Mídia Ninja, Folha de S. Paulo e Amado Mundo.

content:

L’appuntamento si inserisce in settimane di inizio autunno che hanno visto cortei di massa per la Palestina il 10 ottobre, occupazioni nelle scuole con la mobilitazione studentesca di oggi 16 ottobre, blocchi degli autotrasportatori al Sud e, in prospettiva, vedranno altri cortei sui temi della guerra e del riarmo oltre allo sciopero del 30 ottobre.

Da questo incontro è emersa chiaramente l’intenzione di muoversi insieme agli agricoltori del sud Italia, ma anche ad altri cittadini e cittadine per opporsi all’aumento dei costi di produzione, al caro energia e al carovita. CONTRO IL CAROVITA: MANIFESTAZIONE A BRESCIA SABATO 17 OTTOBRE




Sabato 17 ottobre anche a Brescia è organizzata la manifestazione “Italia in Piazza” con numerose rivendicazioni: contro il carovita, per il lavoro sicuro, contro gli stipendi da fame, per aumentare i finanziamenti alla sanità pubblica, alle scuole e all’università.




Il “nodo” bresciano di questa manifestazione si dà appuntamento in Largo Formentone a partire dalle ore 14. Una manifestazione che viene organizzata prevalentemente attraverso whatsapp e i social network (qui il link al profilo 

Instagram

)




Noi abbiamo intervistato due delle organizzatrici, Sara Marini e Giulia Benedetti










MANIFESTO

 




In questo documento sono racchiuse le motivazioni e i fini della manifestazione  “Italia in Piazza”.  




“Italia in piazza” è una manifestazione apartitica. Essa vuole essere una riunione  pacifica di cittadini, diritto sancito dall’articolo 17 della Costituzione Italiana, con lo  scopo di mettere il focus sulle problematiche che affrontiamo ogni giorno. Il  sistema in cui viviamo, che spesso ci sembra inalterabile, è in realtà  estremamente fragile: solo lasciandoci dietro divisioni e pregiudizi possiamo  veramente essere uniti per pretendere di vivere, e non solo di sopravvivere. 

Non  importa chi siamo, in cosa ci identifichiamo, quale sia il nostro orientamento  sessuale o quali divinità preghiamo

: a unirci è il fatto che non lasceremo che ci  rubino ciò che ci spetta di diritto. 




“Italia in piazza” nasce per unire i cittadini per la stessa causa, i cui punti principali  sono: 




Lavoro sicuro, futuro sicuro: basta morti sul lavoro e giovani in  fuga. 




I lavoratori italiani sono costretti ad accettare condizioni lavorative inadeguate o a  fuggire all’estero: quello che resta è un mercato del lavoro caratterizzato da nero  dilagante, abuso di forme contrattuali precarie (tirocini, contratti a termine),  retribuzioni da barzelletta e condizioni di sicurezza che mietono morti ogni  giorno1. 




Basta stipendi da fame incapaci di coprire il costante aumento  del costo della vita. 




Carburanti, energia e beni alimentari di prima necessità costano sempre di più a  causa delle scelte egoistiche di potenti di cui il nostro Paese è succube: i nostri  soldi vengono spesi in armi e soldati mentre le famiglie ne hanno sempre meno  per vivere. I partiti che di volta in volta governano si affannano a farci credere che  vada tutto bene, ma la realtà è sempre più uno sfacelo: guerra dopo guerra, una  crisi dopo l’altra, il costo di qualunque cosa è in continuo aumento mentre gli  stipendi italiani sono gli stessi da 30 anni. 




La sanità non può continuare a diventare sempre più un lusso. 




Per la sanità pubblica si spende sempre meno e una porzione sempre maggiore  di quella spesa è fatta di acquisti di prestazioni e materiali da aziende private che,  ciliegina sulla torta, beneficiano anche di sgravi fiscali sempre più corposi. La  realtà del Sistema Sanitario Nazionale è totalmente inadeguata rispetto alle reali  necessità della popolazione, tra liste d’attesa infinite e ospedali svuotati di  personale e attrezzature. Mentre la sanità pubblica soffre, lo Stato rinuncia a  milioni di euro di tasse regalando esenzioni fiscali al settore sanitario privato. A  pagare il conto sono periferie e classi sociali più deboli e marginalizzate: 

nel 2026,  5,8 milioni di italiani rinunciano a visite ed esami 

e i governi festeggiano  insieme a chi si arricchisce sulla nostra salute.  




Scuole senza strutture. Università senza futuro. 




L’istruzione pubblica, il pilastro portante del nostro futuro (e, farebbe bene  ricordarci, anche del nostro presente), vede tra scuola e università due scenari  raccapriccianti: 




La scuola è fatta di strutture fatiscenti o abbandonate, personale docente e  tecnico sfruttato che vive di contratti precari e mobili per decine di anni di  carriera e una programmazione didattica sempre più svuotata da  qualunque insegnamento che non serva a diventare un ingranaggio della  macchina produttiva.  




L’università ha perso più della metà del personale di ricerca (che eroga fino  al 30% dei corsi universitari) nell’ultimo anno. I progetti di ricerca sono  sempre più nelle mani delle aziende private che li finanziano per i loro fini  produttivi, e una percentuale sempre maggiore ha scopi bellici.  




Nel frattempo, le misure di sostegno economico per gli studenti sono sempre più  striminzite, e le loro necessità abitative diventano speculazione edilizia e  incremento degli affitti nelle città. 




Le case sono fatte per essere abitate, non per farci soldi. 




Nelle nostre città non mancano case: manca la possibilità di abitarle per chi in  quelle città ci vive, ci studia e ci lavora. 




Una parte enorme del patrimonio abitativo è chiusa, usata di rado o convertita in  alloggio turistico, e non esiste un singolo censimento pubblico che ci dia un  quadro della situazione sulla proprietà degli alloggi lasciati vuoti. Il tutto mentre  migliaia di persone dormono per strada, i veri abitanti delle città vengono  allontanati dai centri storici e gli studenti diventano la carne da macello di  speculatori privati a cui sono stati persino dati i fondi pubblici e del PNRR per la  costruzione di residenze universitarie, usati invece per centri polifunzionali di  lusso con scritto “Campus”. Sono gli effetti di un sistema che interpreta la casa  non come un diritto ma come una commodity da sfruttare economicamente a  scapito di chi non la possiede. 




Strade sicure. Ma per davvero. 




Mentre vengono pompate le finanze di eserciti e polizia armata, si continuano a  trascurare le vere radici economiche, politiche e culturali della crescente  sensazione di insicurezza che si prova ovunque. Tra i fenomeni di incuria sociale,  la marginalizzazione sistemica di chi è povero economicamente e umanamente e  il dirottamento degli sforzi delle forze dell’ordine verso materie lontane dalla vita  dei cittadini, sempre più persone sentono che la propria sicurezza non è più una  priorità per lo Stato che sostengono con il loro lavoro e le loro tasse. 




Chiarimenti 




Questa manifestazione è apolitica? 




No, la manifestazione non è apolitica: si stanno trattando temi profondamente politici.  Tuttavia, è apartitica: non è organizzata da nessun partito politico, sindacato o  organizzazione militante. 




Ma quindi è una manifestazione di destra o di sinistra? 




Vogliamo che questa piattaforma di protesta superi le divisioni politiche, ma niente è più  politico di proporre una soluzione. La nostra proposta è di parlarne insieme, tutti, come  popolo unito che affronta gli stessi problemi. La soluzione politica che proponiamo è la  liberazione da tutte le forme di limitazione del potere popolare. Chi ci rappresenta non  vive i nostri problemi6 e finché la politica rimarrà un’attività che deleghiamo ad altri ci  saranno persone che la renderanno il proprio privilegio e faranno di tutto pur di  conservarlo. Vogliamo che ogni decisione presa per conto del popolo sia presa da e per il  popolo. Vogliamo che i potenti ci diano indietro il potere di decidere per noi stessi. Sei  d’accordo con le rivendicazioni della manifestazione? Questo sistema ti fa schifo e vuoi  cambiarlo? Allora scendi in piazza con noi! 




Ci saranno bandiere alla manifestazione? 




Full disclosure: ci avete rotto il cazzo <3 




Scherzi a parte: 

non possiamo dirvi cosa portare o non portare. 




Ci sono persone che non vogliono vedere solo bandiere italiane, persone che non vogliono  bandiere di partito, persone che non vogliono bandiere della Palestina: fate come vi pare.  Da organizzatori, visto che la cosa che ci accomuna tutti è la condizione in cui versa il  posto in cui viviamo, pensiamo sarebbe carino se ognuno portasse una bandiera italiana  (che sia croce o delizia) con disegnato o scritto quello che preferisce. 




La cosa che riteniamo fondamentale è che, se portate una bandiera, crediate nell’idea  che rappresenta. 




Se credete in PD, Lega o qualunque partito che abbia governato negli ultimi 30 anni,  portate quelle, non sappiamo che dirvi. 




Ma per favore, basta chiedercelo.

author: Randi Beers
title: Judge puts Mary River Mine’s future in hands of neutral decision-makers
content:
Final say over the future of the Mary River iron mine is in the hands of two neutral, court-appointed parties, an Ontario judge has ordered.




Justice Jana Steele’s decision on Oct. 14 comes as Baffinland Iron Mines Corp. 

enters

 a sale and investment solicitation process, an effort to keep the mine operational after the company 

announced

 in May that it 

could not repay

 roughly $1.2 billion to various lenders.




The mine contributes roughly 25 per cent of Nunavut’s gross domestic product.




“At this time, the alternative to a transaction is a liquidation, which would have a devastating impact … including the loss of over 1,200 jobs,” said Steele, a superior court judge.




Export Development Canada and the company’s other lenders proposed that a court appointed monitor and neutral chief restructuring officer should have final say over any potential deal. Baffinland wanted a committee of shareholder representatives in that role.




“While the distinction may appear academic at first blush, the ultimate decision-maker in the [sale process] will have the authority to make critical decisions, including waiving bidding criteria, selecting the successful bid, and finalizing any resulting transaction,” Steele said in her decision, before concluding an independent decision-maker is the “best path forward” for the company.




While the process could end in the sale of Baffinland’s assets or the mine itself, the aim is to solicit bids for a “broad range of transaction alternatives.”
















Baffinland will work with all parties to support a “successful outcome,” said company spokesperson Peter Akman Friday in an email.




“The court’s decision provides a clear path forward,” he said.




Work to solicit bids is already underway, Steele noted in her decision. “Select” potentially interested parties have non-disclosure agreements and have arranged site visits.




A sale process, she said, “needs to get going — and soon.”

title: Sportswashing the Racing Circuit: Rwanda and Formula One
content:
Tyrants and demagogues love sports and the governing bodies that preside over them. Despite strictures, injunctions and warnings about dealing with unsavoury regimes, a sporting body or organisation can always be relied on to ignore the fine print of their charters and make a dash for the revenue till. While the candidates for such a list are long – the International Olympic Committee and the world footballing body FIFA figure with amoral sprightliness in that regard – Formula One (F1) has shown itself to be most promiscuous.

In its October 13 statement, FI glows with the announcement that motor racing will “return to Africa for the first time since 1993.” Then, the apartheid government of South Africa, one nearing expiration, still offered their good services to F1 to run the tournament as part of a controversial tradition. (The South African Grand Prix had been something of a fixture since the 1960s, barring the interrupting hiccup in the latter 1980s.) In a ten-year agreement with the Rwandan government, the Formula 1 African Grand Prix will become a part of the racing calendar in the early 2030s, beginning its first race at the still to be completed Bugesera circuit. “The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure, and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board.”

The language of the announcement resembles the best traditions of sporting colonialism on the hunt for willing consumers. “Africa represents one of the most exciting growth opportunities for the sport, with more than 100 million fans already following F1 across the continent, and almost 60% of fans in key Sub-Saharan African Markets under the age of 35.” The project is celebrated as beneficial with its promise of creating “a legacy of supporting tourism, attracting investment, developing local talent and creating new opportunities for communities and businesses.”

F1 also praises Rwanda for its appeal “as one of Africa’s leading destinations for international events, successfully hosting major sport and global gatherings”. These include, amongst others, the UCI Road World Championships, the ICC Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 FIFA Congress and the Basketball Africa League.

The Rwandan President, Paul Kagame, heaped praise on the project. As is a tendency befalling many African leaders, the decision of one country is treated as having been made for the benefit of an entire, neglected continent. “Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world’s premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement.”

What, then is there not to like? The answer: much and more besides. For one thing, the motorsport body, despite stipulating the need to respect “internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally” in its own charter, has decided to overlook the distinct unpleasantness of the Kagame regime, one not above using arbitrary detention, torture and stomping on free speech. In its 2026 accounting of the country’s human rights record, Human Rights Watch (HRW) notes continued attacks on freedom of expression and association, including the arrest of Victore Ingabire in June of the unregistered opposition party Development and Liberty for All (DALFA-Umurinzi). Among the charges she faces are forming a criminal group and planning activities with the purpose of inciting public disorder. HRW also notes a lack of progress in investigating the “suspicious deaths of disappearance of critics, journalists, and opposition activists.” Kigali’s spotty record on protecting refugee and migrant rights is reiterated. In terms of foreign policies, a stern eye is trained on the ongoing support for the notorious M23 armed group in eastern Congo, responsible for “mass summary executions, arbitrary detention, torture, forced labor, forced recruitment including child recruitment, forced deportations, sexual violence, and intimidation of journalists and activists.”

In June, the Democratic Republic of Congo filed a case against Rwanda in the International Court of Justice concerning “abuses attributable to Rwanda over a period extending from 1996 to the present day”. These were perpetrated “as part of a campaign of genocide and serious, widespread human rights violations waged by the Rwandan authorities in eastern Zaire, and subsequently in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo” most directed at “Hutus present on Zairean, and subsequently Congolese, territory following the genocide against the Tutsi in 1994.” Other ethnic groups, including the Nyindu, Bembe, the Lega, the Nande, the Hunde and the Bashi, are also alleged to have been targets.

In its response to the Formula 1 African Grand Prix agreement, Amnesty International was particularly vocal, with its UK Head of Campaigns, Felix Jakens, adamant that Rwanda was “buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record” at home, and its deplorable military policy in eastern Congo, including ongoing support for the M23 armed group.

Kagame’s Rwanda, however, is relentlessly ambitious when it comes to cultivating the international sporting market. The F1 announcement is in keeping with a broader strategy, one that is doing wonders to burnish Kigali’s image as a responsible investor and reliable international citizen. The English Premier League, for instance, has shown itself most enthusiastic about that state’s forays into the competition, notably through its £20 million-a-year Aston Villa-Visit Rwanda sponsorship deal involving merchandise, tourism and the provision of coffee. This more than happily replaced the previous sponsorship arrangements with Arsenal Football Club, which concluded an eight-season partnership in June this year worth £10 million a year. In a media release, the Club praised the agreement in gushing terms as exceeding “the original goals” in “promoting conservation and sustainable tourism, inspiring millions of supporters to discover the country, and creating a lasting foundation for tourism growth.”

On the European continent, Rwandan sponsorship has also left its mark on Germany’s premier football club, Bayern Munich, and France’s Paris Saint-Germain (PSG). The former ended its commercial ties with Visit Rwanda in August 2025 preferring to focus on expanding its youth academy in Kigali but Visit Rwanda, according to its own website, remains “a Premium Partner” of PSG at least till 2028. Clearly, the by Congo’s persistent Foreign Minister Therese Kayikwamba Wagner to end “blood-stained” sponsorships between such clubs and Kigali have yielded patchy results.

Hearteningly, the fans at these clubs have not remained silent. At Arsenal, a fanbase group calling themselves Gunners for Peace thought differently from their administrative grandees, having campaigned for an end to a deal that funded “a brutal militia committing atrocities against thousands of innocent victims in Eastern Congo.” In the sharpest of barbs featuring their rivals of old, the group even began a “Visit Tottenham campaign to highlight just how wrong Visit Rwanda is.”

Wrong, and yet, for those in F1 more than just right. As Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) president Mohammed Ben Sulayem told BBC Sport Africa, “When people cannot get what they want, they always blame it on sportswashing.” With bemoaning critics boxed and dismissed, motor racing’s top poohbah expressed a sneering sentiment shared by sporting governors the world over: “I honestly don’t care about what they say.”

Binoy Kampmark was a Commonwealth Scholar at Selwyn College, Cambridge. He lectures at RMIT University, Melbourne.

author: Ramzy Baroud
title: What Does the Green Party’s Historic Anti-Zionist Motion Mean for Palestine?
content:
The Green Party has put the conversation back on track: the problem is not the lack of creative solutions to the Israeli occupation of Palestine. The problem is Zionism itself.

To appreciate the significance of Motion A105, adopted by the Green Party of England and Wales on October 4, consider its basic tenets.

The party is now formally anti-Zionist. It endorses the Palestinian right of return, supports one democratic state throughout historic Palestine, reaffirms its commitment to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, distinguishes anti-Zionism from antisemitism, and calls for a full arms embargo against Israel.

Though the decision may seem revolutionary within British politics, it is hardly revolutionary when examined against the history of Palestinian dispossession, beginning long before the Nakba of 1948.

Indeed, the Greens were not the first to equate Zionism with racism. That history owes much to Africa’s anti-colonial movements and their struggle against apartheid.

In 1975, the Organization of African Unity, meeting in Kampala, Uganda, drew explicit parallels between the racial systems governing South Africa, Rhodesia and occupied Palestine, identifying their common imperialist origins.

This position helped lay the groundwork for UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, adopted on November 10, 1975, which determined that Zionism was a form of racism and racial discrimination.

Under intense American and Israeli diplomatic pressure, the UN eventually reversed that determination on December 16, 1991.

Israel, however, was not required to dismantle the discriminatory structures that had prompted the original condemnation. The revocation changed the UN’s position, not the realities confronting Palestinians.

Those who yielded to American pressure in 1991 must therefore confront a troubling question of moral responsibility: did their decision help legitimize the very political structures that have sustained Palestinian dispossession, occupation and settler colonialism?

The Greens have now reopened that historical debate. But they have also done something more consequential.

By adopting the motion with 1,022 votes against 813, party members demonstrated that ideas once dismissed as radical are increasingly challenging the boundaries of mainstream British politics.

Yet within this achievement lie important fault lines, revealing the nature of the struggle ahead.

Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the resolution. More tellingly, Sandy Ruthven, chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust, resigned his Green Party membership altogether.

In explaining his decision, Ruthven accused the party of seeking to court the hard-left vote while failing to confront prejudice within its own ranks.

His resignation exposes a contradiction worth examining, particularly given his association with an organization that has already documented Israeli apartheid against Palestinians.

In February 2022, Amnesty International published a landmark report concluding that Israel maintained an institutionalized system of oppression and domination over Palestinians amounting to apartheid.

That recognition was belated, but critically important. Apartheid, however, does not emerge in an ideological vacuum. It is sustained by political assumptions about belonging, sovereignty, demographic control and the unequal distribution of rights.

The question, therefore, is not merely whether Israeli apartheid exists, but what political principles have made its establishment and perpetuation possible.

The Zionist movement emerged in late nineteenth-century Europe as a nationalist project seeking a Jewish homeland, eventually pursuing Jewish statehood in Palestine. Its implementation ultimately led to the mass displacement of Palestinians in 1948.

The connection between that foundational project and the discriminatory structures documented by Amnesty itself is impossible to ignore. How, then, can the likes of Ruthven condemn apartheid without confronting the ideology that underpins it? And if that ideology is not Zionism, what is it?

The larger issue, however, is not a lack of historical knowledge among Britain’s political and intellectual elites.

Rather, these elites have long positioned themselves as guardians of the permissible discourse on Israel and Palestine – a narrative that accommodates occasional criticism, sometimes even harsh condemnation, but rarely permits a fundamental challenge to the political structures themselves.

The Green Party’s grassroots have now challenged that conventional wisdom. They have crossed the boundary separating what may be criticized from what must remain politically untouchable.

Due to the ongoing Israeli genocide in Gaza, the Greens have effectively declared that the time for carefully managed criticism has passed.

In doing so, they have opened a political space that others may eventually occupy, including within the Labour Party, historically divided between its progressive grassroots and an increasingly centrist leadership whose policies, particularly on Palestine, have become virtually indistinguishable from those of the political right.

The vote could also encourage similar debates across Europe, challenging political parties to confront the relationship between Zionism, antisemitism, Palestinian rights and the future of historic Palestine.

But perhaps the Greens’ most consequential contribution is that they have challenged the very premise of the debate. For decades, international diplomacy has focused overwhelmingly on finding solutions while leaving the ideological foundations of the existing political order largely unexamined.

The Greens have reversed that approach, essentially declaring that no political solution in Palestine, however idealistic or supposedly pragmatic, can coexist with Zionism.

The backlash against the Greens was, of course, expected. But so, too, is the growing determination of British voters to challenge the boundaries of permissible debate across the political spectrum.

Ramzy Baroud is a US-Palestinian journalist, media consultant, an author, internationally-syndicated columnist, Editor of Palestine Chronicle (1999-present), former Managing Editor of London-based Middle East Eye, former Editor-in-Chief of The Brunei Times and former Deputy Managing Editor of Al Jazeera online. Baroud’s work has been published in hundreds of newspapers and journals worldwide, and is the author of six books and a contributor to many others. Baroud is also a regular guest on many television and radio programs including RT, Al Jazeera, CNN International, BBC, ABC Australia, National Public Radio, Press TV, TRT, and many other stations. Baroud was inducted as an Honorary Member into the Pi Sigma Alpha National Political Science Honor Society, NU OMEGA Chapter of Oakland University, Feb 18, 2020.

author: Jake Johnson
title: Trump Profited From His Giveaway to Big Pharma While Jacking Up Drug Costs
content:
An analysis estimates Trump increased his stock holdings from $1.7 million in 2024 to up to $56.2 million last year.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

An analysis released Friday by Democrats on the congressional Joint Economic Committee details how US President Donald Trump loaded up on shares of major pharmaceutical companies last year as his administration and Republican allies enacted policies that benefited the industry — at the expense seniors and other patients.

The JEC analysis estimates that Trump increased his stock holdings in the pharmaceutical sector from $1.7 million in 2024 to as much as $56.2 million last year. The committee notes that Trump, who has repeatedly promised to cut drug prices while implementing policies that raised them, “held as much as $39.1 million in stock in the same Big Pharma companies that directly benefited” from a budget package that the president signed into law last summer.

“Trump and congressional Republicans intentionally force seniors to pay more for cancer treatment so that Big Pharma can rake in more money that Trump can personally profit from,” said Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the JEC’s ranking member. “It’s outrageous and yet typical from this president, who makes the American people foot the bill again and again for his own gains.”

Tucked in the Trump-GOP budget law was a provision exempting some widely used, high-priced prescription drugs from Medicare price negotiations. Merck’s cancer medication Keytruda was one of the drugs temporarily shielded by the provision; Merck appears more than 60 times in the president’s 2025 financial disclosure.

The JEC analysis notes that “in 2025, Merck reported $18.8 billion in US revenues for Keytruda, which helped the company net $22.5 billion in profits that year, a 16% increase compared to 2024.”

The president also made big purchases of stock in Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Pfizer, and Amgen last year. The JEC found that each of those companies “had at least one drug that benefited from the carveouts” in the Trump-GOP budget law.

Additionally, the Trump administration has entered friendly agreements with pharmaceutical companies in which the president is invested, including Pfizer and Eli Lilly.

“Trump’s drug pricing deals are a mirage, designed to convince Americans that he’s taken significant action on drug pricing while creating minimal if any downside for Big Pharma,” Peter Maybarduk, access to medicines director for the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, said last month after his organization obtained heavily redacted texts of the agreements.

“The texts show Trump handing out favors to Big Pharma, undercutting his own models to lower prices, and throwing the support of the US government behind corporate decisions to deny medicines entirely to other countries,” said Maybarduk.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Progressive International
title: When the Bargain Breaks
content:
On 23 September, Spanish police evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for 71 years. After buying her flat, property company Urbagestión had sought to increase Abascal’s rent to more than her monthly pension. Neighbours had prevented three previous attempts to evict her. The fourth succeeded. Abascal was carried out of her home on a stretcher and taken to hospital. The eviction was lawful.

Tens of thousands marched through Madrid in outrage. Protesters occupied Puerta del Sol, erecting more than 1,200 tents, complete with named streets and a makeshift medical centre. They demanded rent controls, protection against eviction and an end to housing speculation. Parliament rejected two emergency housing decrees, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November. On 7 October, Abascal died in hospital, one day before she was due to sign an agreement allowing her to return home.

Across the Pyrenees, a protest that began at a secondary school in a Paris suburb has become a national uprising. Lycée Saint-Exupéry was missing 13 teachers, a deputy head and essential support staff. Students and teachers walked out. Within days, blockades and other disruptions had spread to more than 1,000 schools. At Lycée Paul-Éluard in Saint-Denis, students described rats in the corridors, collapsing ceilings, windows sealed for fear they would fall on pupils, and one nurse for 2,000 students.

On 6 October, over 250,000 people marched across France, as teachers, parents, trade unions and university students joined the school children. Police used tear gas and made hundreds of arrests. The government promised 3,000 substitute teachers, but the protests continued. As one student put it: “We ask for teachers, they send us police.”

On the Indian subcontinent, 6,000 kilometres away, the capital city of Delhi is under siege by its own government. The Modi regime deployed nearly 35000 police to lockdown the city against student protests. More than 2.2 million students sat the national medical entrance examination in May, competing for far fewer places. When questions were found to have circulated in advance, the examination was cancelled. Students who had spent years preparing, and families who had spent their savings supporting them, erupted in anger.

These unemployed graduates and disenchanted youth called themselves the Cockroach Janta Party, reclaiming a disparaging remark from the Chief Justice about unemployed youth as a badge of pride. What began as an Instagram joke with an AI-generated cockroach logo became a mass movement. In July, the protests forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. By October, the movement had joined the struggle against the removal of some 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, which critics accuse the Election Commission of manipulating to benefit Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

On 10 and 11 October, police and paramilitary forces sealed roads, closed metro stations and detained protesters demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Denied access to Jantar Mantar, Delhi’s designated protest site, demonstrators regrouped at markets, intersections and flyovers across the capital.

In Albania, that fire was sparked from a stretch of barbed wire. This May, developers fenced off access to the coast at Zvërnec, where a luxury resort backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner threatens the protected Vjosa-Narta wetlands. Villagers produced property deeds and a 2013 court ruling recognising their claim to the land. When residents and environmental activists confronted the development, private security guards dragged them away.

The injustice struck a nerve. The capital, Tirana, has repeatedly been brought to a standstill by protestors carrying inflatable flamingos, the birds whose habitat the development threatens, declaring that “Albania is not for sale”. The protests grew into a revolt against corruption and the grip of oligarchs on the country’s economy and political system. This week, tens of thousands of students protesting over education and living costs have joined the movement, with clashes leaving dozens injured and arrested. Footage is circulating on social media of citizens being abducted into unmarked vans. Prime Minister Edi Rama refuses to resign.

The historian E. P. Thompson described the moral economy of the eighteenth-century English crowd: shared expectations of legitimate conduct whose violation could turn hardship into rebellion. A fair examination, a functioning school, security in old age, access to public land: in each country, a particular injustice exposed years of accumulated grievances.

The protests have brought down an Indian minister, forced France to promise thousands of additional teachers, removed the fences at Zvërnec and helped precipitate a general election in Spain. But the institutions that produced the grievances — from India’s electoral systems to the power of property in Spain and Albania — remain intact. The forces united against a particular injustice may have very different ideas about what should come next.

How can these new rebellions acquire the organised power to change the conditions that produced them?

In Spain, the tenants’ movement is already joining forces with the labour movement. At the tenants’ unions’ initiative, Spain’s two largest labour confederations, UGT and CCOO, are backing a 24-hour general strike on 11 November — the first in fourteen years with their joint support. The Madrid Sindicato de Inquilinas has demanded a Decreto Maricarmen to protect tenants against eviction and rent increases, while their allies in Congress have now called for the expropriation of hundreds of thousands of homes held by investment funds for conversion into social housing. General elections in Spain are set for 29 November.

In India, the Cockroach Janta Party is forging links with the organised left and workers’ movements. At a joint press conference in Delhi on Thursday, founder Abhijeet Dipke appeared alongside leaders of three Left student organisations — AISA, SFI and AISF — as well as PI Cabinet member Nikhil Dey of the workers’ and farmers’ organisation MKSS, and Shaik Salauddin of the Telangana Gig and Platform Workers Union, both of whom are also PI Members. Together, they demanded the resignation of the chief election commissioner and an end to the repression of protesters. Opposition parties in the INDIA bloc are pursuing a parallel campaign against the electoral roll revision.

In France, the Union Syndicale Lycéenne has coordinated blockades and demanded €10 billion in emergency education funding. Its president, Ryad Rani, has called on students to join Saturday’s Gilets Jaunes mobilisation against the cost of living. Meanwhile, La France Insoumise has challenged police violence against the students in the streets and in parliament and is taking their demands for investment and an end to university selection into the 2027 presidential election.

In Albania, Progressive International’s member Lëvizja Bashkë is building on years of organising among workers, tenants and students to challenge the country’s oligarchic order. After winning its first parliamentary seat in 2025, the party has stood alongside the protesters defending the coast, contesting both the luxury development and demanding the repeal of the 2024 legislation that opened protected areas to construction. Many of its members have been beaten and arrested in the protests.

These are the forces that the Progressive International is working to support and connect. Tenant organisations bringing trade unions into a housing struggle. Student movements joining wider coalitions for democratic rights. Political parties emerging from years of workplace and community organising, developing programmes and contesting elections.

Popular anger can spread across a country in days. Building organisations that can confront entrenched interests, withstand repression and win control over political and economic decisions takes years.

Maricarmen Abascal’s neighbours stopped three evictions. On the fourth attempt, the property company prevailed with the police enforcing its claim. The task now is to build the power to resist the next abuse, change the laws that enforce them and the ownership they defend.

The Progressive International Secretariat
