author: Gabby Birenbaum
title: Elon Musk Is Bankrolling Massive Push for Ken Paxton in Texas
content:
Musk’s PAC has also boosted Republican candidates in the five most competitive US House races in the state.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

After months of being outspent by Democrat James Talarico on the airwaves, Republicans launched a massive rescue mission for Ken Paxton in September, dropping over $200 million to boost their U.S. Senate candidate in Texas.

New campaign finance filings revealed that much of the advertising flurry was funded by one highly motivated donor: Elon Musk, the world’s wealthiest man.

Musk, who lives near the SpaceX Starbase facility in South Texas, appears to have poured nearly $190 million into the U.S. Senate race in his adopted home state. His role in financing Paxton’s air support was disclosed in reports filed Thursday to the Federal Election Commission by Senate Leadership Fund, the Senate GOP’s main super PAC and the biggest spender in Texas’ Senate contest.

On Sept. 9, the first day of the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Musk gave $75 million to SLF. The next day, SLF put $75 million into a new entity called Texas PAC. By the weekend after the convention, the new super PAC was up on the air with a positive spot about Paxton’s work on sex trafficking and a negative ad attacking Talarico as being for “they/them, not you.”

Two weeks after cutting his first check, Musk gave an additional $83 million to SLF, according to the group’s filing. Sure enough, SLF deposited $83 million into Texas PAC’s coffers the following day.

Musk’s donations armed Senate Republicans to take over the airwaves in Texas. Using Texas PAC as the vessel to book airtime, SLF has thus far spent over $159 million on TV, radio and digital advertising, double the outlay from Talarico’s campaign, according to media tracking firm AdImpact.

SLF backed Sen. John Cornyn in the primary, estimating that a Paxton candidacy would require $150 million to $200 million to retain the seat — money that could come at the expense of other states. While the prediction proved prescient, Musk’s investment has changed the calculus.

“Thanks to some generous investors who have dedicated money to an affiliate, Texas PAC, we’ve been able to go in and support Ken Paxton,” SLF executive director Alex Latcham told Bloomberg TV Wednesday. “We’ll spend nearly $200 million in that race. But again, thanks to Leader John Thune and the Republican caucus and our fundraising, we haven’t had to subtract resources from other states to do so.”

The Tesla and SpaceX founder got involved in the race after his political team reached out to Senate Leadership Fund, the Senate GOP’s main outside campaign group, to voice Musk’s concerns about Paxton’s standing in the race, according to a person familiar with the conversations. That led to an agreement between Musk’s orbit and SLF — Musk would provide $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, the main outside group boosting Paxton, if SLF gave $5 million and the PAC raised an additional $5 million. The details of the conversation were first reported by Axios.

That windfall was badly needed. Lone Star Liberty PAC had only $35,000 in the bank at the end of June, having drained its coffers on Paxton’s hard-fought primary win over Cornyn. Talarico, meanwhile, was continuing his torrid fundraising pace and was poised to keep dominating the political ad spending battle if help did not arrive for Paxton.

Talarico posted another record quarter amid Paxton’s SLF-powered ad surge, hauling in $64 million between July and September — a third-quarter record among all U.S. Senate candidates. The Austin Democrat has maintained a polling lead for months in averages of nonpartisan public surveys, an alarming sight for a Republican Party whose unbeaten streak in Texas statewide races spans more than three decades.

With Musk’s donation and the matching funds, Lone Star Liberty PAC spent $17.5 million on broadcast TV advertising in early September, by far the most significant pro-Paxton ad buy of the general election. By the end of the month, a handful of outside groups led by SLF had dropped over $217 million on ads in the Texas Senate race.

Paxton has not commented publicly about Musk’s support.

In the past, the attorney general has praised Musk for backing Republicans in 2024. He spent hours at Musk’s home two days before that year’s election hearing Musk recount all his efforts to boost GOP candidates, Paxton said at Turning Point USA’s AmericaFest in 2024.

“Aren’t you all glad he’s on our side?” Paxton said to cheers. “I am convinced that whatever he did, whatever rocket science thing he did, made a huge difference in this election.”

Paxton has also aligned himself with Musk through his role as Texas attorney general — and largely skirted scrutinizing Musk’s companies as his office has increasingly taken on Big Tech.

In 2022, as Musk sought to buy Twitter, Paxton opened an investigation into the social media company for how it reported the number of accounts on the platform that were fake or bots — inspecting whether the service was inflating the number of its actual users to boost its value for revenue. At the time, Musk was raising similar questions. He ultimately bought Twitter and renamed it X.

In 2024, Paxton opened an investigation into World Federation of Advertisers, an organization that represents marketers, to assess whether its members were conspiring to boycott specific social media services. TechCrunch reported Musk’s X, which had filed an antitrust suit against the group, was likely among the social media platforms.

Meanwhile, Paxton has taken on tech giants including Netflix, WhatsApp, Discord, and Meta — probes he has touted on the campaign trail.

“As attorney general, I’ve sued some of the largest companies in the world … for taking advantage of our kids by exposing them to dangerous, addictive material,” Paxton said after defeating Cornyn in May. “In Washington, I will not stop fighting to protect Texas children from Big Tech.”

But Paxton has taken arrows from critics who’ve accused him of turning a blind eye to X and Musk. In January, a group of Democratic state representatives demanded the attorney general investigate the platform’s artificial intelligence agent, Grok, and its creation of exploitative content about children and women. Paxton did not respond to the letter publicly.

The same month, a group of attorneys general from across the country sent Musk’s company a letter demanding that it address its AI agent’s creation of child sex abuse content. Paxton was not among the signatories.

Musk’s political operation is also deeply involved in the Republican ground game in Texas, from canvassing to mailers, across several key races. America PAC, which he seeded with nearly $90 million last quarter, had pumped $18.8 million into the Senate race through Tuesday, per FEC filings, which capture efforts like text messaging, mailers and ads but not in-person canvassing such as block-walking and phone-banking. Over 80% of that money has gone to anti-Talarico messaging.

The tech mogul has significant business interests in the Lone Star State. Musk has moved the state of incorporation for many of his companies to Texas in recent years. Boring Company and X are headquartered in Bastrop, SpaceX is near Brownsville and Tesla’s corporate headquarters is now in Austin.

And it’s not just the Senate race. Musk’s PAC has spent about $800,000 boosting Republican candidates in the five most competitive U.S. House races in Texas. The biggest share has gone to the 35th Congressional District, a San Antonio-area seat Republicans redrew last summer with the intention of flipping, but which has proven highly competitive.

Musk spent hundreds of millions in 2024 to boost Republicans, including Donald Trump’s presidential bid. Trump rewarded Musk by tapping him to lead the controversial Department of Government Efficiency initiative. The two had a public falling out later that year, when Musk disparaged the president’s signature legislative effort and alleged Trump was in the Jeffrey Epstein files.

The dustup did not appear to sap Musk’s appetite for bankrolling Republicans’ political spending. The world’s wealthiest man has already surpassed his 2024 political spending this cycle, with Texas the largest focus of his operation.

Other GOP groups are fundraising off of Musk’s Texas spending bonanza as well.

“Elon Musk understands what it’s like to live under far left Democrats,” reads one National Republican Senatorial Committee fundraising email, which notes that Musk has spent $276 million in the midterms and directs readers to a WinRed fundraising page. “He fled an oppressive regime in California that crippled the state with a radical agenda before finding a new home in Texas. But now, the same Far Left Democrats that ran California into the ground are coming to SEIZE Elon’s new home!”

While far from reaching Musk’s investment levels, some prominent Texas GOP donors also came off the sidelines for Paxton in recent months, new filings show.

West Texas oil billionaire Farris Wilks, who has supported Paxton in his state campaigns and directed millions to hardline Republicans, donated $250,000 to one of Paxton’s joint fundraising committees in mid-August, his first federal expenditure of the cycle.

Amarillo billionaire Alex Fairly, meanwhile, had maxed out to Paxton’s direct campaign account with a $7,000 donation in the spring; in late August, he gave $274,300 to Paxton’s joint fundraising committee.

Paxton also received large sums this quarter from the Dallas Cowboys brass. Team president Stephen Jones and chief sales and marketing officer Jerry Jones Jr. gave $122,000 and $100,000, respectively. Their father, Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, donated a six-figure sum in the second quarter.

The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan media organization that informs Texans — and engages with them — about public policy, politics, government and statewide issues.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Laís Gouveia
title: Meta Discovers New Tool to Sabotage Lula’s Campaign
content:
It is no secret that Lula’s campaign is facing a David versus Goliath battle. As many people have put it, this is “the toughest and most decisive campaign of our lives.” When we look at how much big tech is investing in efforts to boost Brazil’s far right, we begin to understand just how much is at stake in this election. The direction Brazil takes over the next few years will have profound consequences for a world increasingly dominated by groups that hold the machinery to grind ordinary people into the dirt.

Last week, I wrote that a confidential source working at Meta Brazil had told me that the company, controlled by Donald Trump’s close friend Mark Zuckerberg, had carried out mass layoffs of its content moderators. It replaced a significant portion of its staff with machines and artificial intelligence systems that now decide what can and cannot be published in Brazil. The change came precisely during the election campaign. No, your algorithm did not suddenly go haywire by sheer coincidence. There are external commands and interventions at work.

Now another cobra strike by the all powerful tech giant has come to light: sabotage through WhatsApp.

Instagram’s algorithms have turned the platform into a collection of isolated bubbles, with appalling engagement for the progressive camp. Meanwhile, far right figures such as Nikolas Ferreira are achieving engagement levels comparable to Beyoncé’s on their videos, despite having vastly fewer followers. The world is remarkably generous to those on the far right. That leaves WhatsApp as the only viable alternative, and one that had been working extremely well.

Of course, we have countless contacts there. Everyone from the evangelical aunt we see once a year to Adalberto, the plumber who still hasn’t decided who to vote for. It is fertile ground for reaching voters, but the chief saboteur already has it in its sights.

First came Supreme Court Justice Kássio “Orgyman” Nunes who went completely off the rails with two individual rulings and ordered the WhatsApp group Exército de Lula, or Lula’s Army, shut down. He did so without establishing that the group had spread any fake news that could justify such a move.

Now Meta has joined in, sabotaging WhatsApp’s AI in a far subtler move than that of the pro Bolsonaro Supreme Court justice. A report by Thais Bilenky of UOL indicates that “Meta’s artificial intelligence tool on WhatsApp treats Lula (Workers’ Party/PT) and Flávio Bolsonaro (Liberal Party/PL) differently when generating digital campaign material. When given identical requests to generate a Brazilian flag in green and yellow bearing the words Lula 13 and Flávio 22, the system only generates the image of the Bolsonaro candidate. Likewise, Meta refuses to generate an image of Lula on Paulista Avenue bearing the number 13, while fulfilling the same request for Flávio.”

This is blatant sabotage, without even bothering to disguise it. An outright spit in our faces. And I believe things will get much worse, especially when it comes to Status, those little green circles that are essential for promoting the president’s campaign. I predict loading failures and videos disappearing out of nowhere.

Big tech companies stand to gain enormously from the president’s defeat. Flávio is the leading activist against social media regulation. In reality, it is his so called hate machine that stands to benefit enormously from the lawless environment that has taken hold online. It helps elect his allies to Congress through folkloric displays of outrage and a steady stream of lies. The foundation of Bolsonarismo is an unrestricted, unregulated social media environment where fake news can be blasted out at will. In other words, this sinister partnership between Flávio and Zuckerberg has never been more profitable.

This article originally appeared in Brasil 247, was translated by Panamerican Dispatch with express consent of the editor-in-chief, and can be read in its original Portuguese here.

Laís Gouveia has been a reporter at Brasil 247 since 2018. Before that, she was educational policy director at the National Student Union (União Nacional dos Estudantes/UNE) and an editor at Portal Vermelho.

author: Unknown
title: Ephéméride des luttes : 16 octobre
content:
L'éphéméride des luttes du 16 octobre lève le poing et les barricades contre la répression et l'émergence de nouvelles forces en tous points opposés à nous. Mais nous ne sommes pas en reste, et le combat pour la liberté continue sous de nombreuses formes.




1793 :

 Marie-Antoinette est guillotinée à Paris.




1859 :

 En Virginie occidentale, le leader abolitionniste John Brown et ses partisans attaquent le dépot de munitions de Harper's Ferry.




1902 :

 Première utilisation de la comparaison des empreintes digitales à des fins d'identification.




1906 :

 Clôture du Congrès d'Amiens de la CGT, à l'époque très influencée par les anarchistes. L'une des phrases de la charte dit notamment "

La C.G.T regroupe, en dehors de toute école politique, tous les travailleurs conscients de la lutte à mener pour la disparition du salariat et du patronat

", ce qui est une position politique radicalement différente de celle que ce syndicat porte aujourd'hui.




1919 :

 - Aux USA, la loi sur la déportation des anarchistes est adoptée et appliquée le jour même.




 Le même jour, Hitler donne son premier meeting dans une brasserie de Munich, devant 300 personnes.




1936 :

 En Espagne, de durs combats opposent le groupe international de la Colonne de Fer anarchiste de Durruti et les franquistes : 

Plusieurs dizaines de volontaires étrangers dont des militants français sont tués : Louis BERTHOMIEU qui se fait sauter à la dynamite plutôt que de tomber aux mains des fascistes. Ancien capitaine de l'armée française, vivant à Barcelone, il était avec Charles RIDEL (Louis Mercier Vega), et François-Charles CARPENTIER, le fondateur du Groupe international.Au moins trois femmes qui s'occupaient de l'infirmerie et de la cantine trouveront la mort :




 Georgette Kokoczinscki (dite "Mimosa")

 Augusta Marx (miliante socialiste Allemande)

 Madeleine Gierth (militante allemande)


Mort également : GIRAL (ou GIRALT) anarcho-syndicaliste de la C.G.T- S.R, déjà blessé lors de la prise de Sietamo ; BIUDEAUX, etc.




Repris de l'éphéméride anarchiste.




1949 :

 Fin de la guerre civile en Grèce après que le Parti Communiste annonce un cessez-le-feu.




1968 :

 Les athlètes afro-américains Tommy Smith et John Carlos sont exclus de l'équipe olympique pour avoir brandi leur point ganté de noir, symbole des Black Panthers et de la lutte contre l'oppression raciste, lors de leur victoire aux Jeux Olympiques.




1971 :

 A Derry, l'IRA abat un soldat de l'armée britannique d'occupation de l'Irlande du Nord.




1972 :

 Dans le comté Tyrone en Irlande du Nord, deux membres de l'IRA 'Officielle' (OIRA) sont abattus par l'armée.




1976 :

 - En Irlande, l'IRA fait sauter une bombe contre la police, tuant une agent.




 A Belfast, trois membres de l'IRA meurent dans l'explosion d'une bombe qu'ils préparaient.




1993 :

 A Welling dans le Kent aux Etats-Unis, des militant-e-s anti-nazis affrontent la police qui protège les quartiers généraux du parti nazi local, alors qu'une manifestation se déroule contre eux.




1998 :

 A Londres, arrestation d'Augusto Pinochet sur ordre d'un juge Espagnol.




2000 :

 A Séville, ETA abat le colonel de l'armée de l'air Antonio Muñoz Cariñanos. Les deux membres du groupes, Jon Igor Solana Matarranz et Harriet Iragi Gurrutxaga, sont capturés après une fusillade.




2012 :

 Sur la ZAD de Notre-Dame-des-Landes, près de Nantes, c'est le début de l'opération policière 'César' qui vise à expulser (à l'aide de 1200 policiers) les occupants de la zone pour permettre la construction d'un nouvel aéroport. La résistance sera farouche et de durs affrontements auront lieu pendant trois semaines, repoussant finalement les assauts policiers. En réponse, de nombreuses permanences du Parti Socialiste sont attaquées dans toute la France, mais aussi les locaux de Vinci ou encore une voiture d'Eiffage.




 

 

 

 




2018 :

 A Nantes, un camion de Spie Batignolles est incendié par "

un enragé contre l'Etat et ses larbins

" dans la nuit contre le rôle de l'entreprise dans le développement de l'industrie carcérale




Voir 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 16 octobre.

author: Yohannes Woldemariam
title: From Haile Selassie to Abiy Ahmed: the Human Cost of Imperial Nostalgia
content:
The irony is difficult to escape. Haile Selassie became a symbol of resistance to foreign aggression while denying Eritreans the right to self-determination. Abiy Ahmed was rewarded for accepting Eritrea’s internationally recognized border, yet within a few years his government began advancing claims to sovereign access to the Red Sea. The very territorial settlement that helped earn him the Nobel Peace Prize now stands in tension with his maritime ambitions.

Both men benefited enormously from international recognition. Their reputations gave them prestige and influence, but those reputations have too often overshadowed the suffering of the people under their rule. Haile Selassie’s imperial government suppressed resistance in Tigray and annexed Eritrea. Under Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopia has endured devastating wars, while his government’s Red Sea rhetoric has renewed Eritrean fears of territorial aggression.

I have written about the dangers of romanticizing Ethiopia’s imperial past, most recently in Imperial Nostalgia: History, Sovereignty, and the Unfinished Work of Decolonization in the Horn of Africa. What concerns me today is that this nostalgia is no longer confined to history books or monuments. It has returned to contemporary politics, and the consequences could be catastrophic for another generation of Ethiopians and Eritreans.

Haile Selassie’s reputation rests heavily on his resistance to Italian fascism. His appearance before the League of Nations in 1936 became one of the defining moments of his international career. But the familiar account gives the emperor far more prominence than the people who actually fought the occupation.

Haile Selassie left Ethiopia in 1936 and spent the following years in Britain. Meanwhile, Ethiopian patriots remained behind, fighting a brutal occupation. They lived in the mountains, organized resistance, endured enormous hardship and risked their lives. The emperor became the international face of their struggle, but he was not the one carrying its daily burden.

Consider Belay Zeleke, one of the patriots who fought the Italians. After the emperor returned to power, Belay came into conflict with the imperial government. In January 1945, he was executed alongside his brother and other associates. Think about the irony. A man who had fought foreign occupation was hanged under the authority of an emperor celebrated around the world for resisting that same occupation.

The emperor’s record in Tigray reveals another contradiction. In 1943, when people in Tigray rose against imperial authority during the first Woyane uprising, Haile Selassie turned to Britain for military assistance. British Royal Air Force aircraft bombed Mekelle and other locations. As Human Rights Watch documented, British air power helped suppress resistance to the imperial government.

Here was an emperor celebrated for standing against European aggression using European aircraft against people resisting his own rule. How does that fit the image of a champion of freedom?

Haile Selassie’s reputation as a Pan-Africanist also deserves scrutiny. His role in establishing the Organization of African Unity in Addis Ababa in 1963 was important. But diplomatic achievement should not be confused with a consistent commitment to African freedom.

Haile Selassie and his foreign minister, Ketema Yifru, worked to establish Ethiopia as a center of African diplomacy. Hosting the OAU gave the emperor enormous prestige. Yet the same government was denying Eritreans the right to determine their future.

Eritrea’s federal autonomy had been systematically dismantled before Haile Selassie annexed the territory in 1962. While the emperor was celebrated as a defender of African independence, Eritreans were beginning a liberation struggle that would last thirty years.

The OAU largely treated Eritrea as an internal Ethiopian matter. Its silence is especially striking when compared with Western Sahara. The organization admitted the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic despite Morocco’s fierce opposition. It was prepared to confront one African government over self-determination but failed to extend comparable recognition to Eritreans struggling against Ethiopian rule.

The romanticization of Haile Selassie reached extraordinary heights through the Rastafari movement. Emerging from racial oppression in Jamaica, the movement invested in the Ethiopian emperor with immense spiritual and political significance. For some Rastafarians, he became a divine figure.

I understand the longing for African dignity that helped produce this reverence. But the status bestowed on Haile Selassie was profoundly misplaced. The emperor imagined as a symbol of Black liberation presided over an authoritarian state that denied freedom to many of the people under its control.

There is another irony. The Shah of Iran and Mobutu Sese Seko are widely remembered for their repression. Haile Selassie has been treated differently. In 2019, the African Union unveiled a statue in his honor at its Addis Ababa headquarters.

What does such a monument tell Eritreans whose independence he denied? What does it tell Tigrayans whose communities were bombed under his government, or the families of patriots executed after fighting Italian occupation?

In 1972, Haile Selassie celebrated his eightieth birthday with imperial extravagance. Hunger and deprivation were already part of life in the countryside, and the famine that devastated Wollo and Tigray in the following years exposed the extraordinary distance between the imperial court and the people it governed.

The images of starving Ethiopians became inseparable from those of imperial luxury. They revealed a political order in which the grandeur of the ruler could coexist with the desperation of his subjects.

More than half a century later, Tigrayans have again endured hunger, displacement and the destruction of their livelihoods. The war that began in 2020 devastated agriculture, markets, health services and entire communities. The Pretoria Agreement was supposed to bring peace and recovery, yet its implementation remained deeply contested, and renewed fighting has placed civilians under further pressure.

At the same time, Abiy Ahmed has pursued monumental construction projects, including the enormous Chaka palace development. Reporting on the project has described its extraordinary scale.

Abiy presents these projects as evidence of national renewal. But what kind of renewal is meaningful to a family struggling to find food? What does the magnificence of a palace mean to people who have lost their homes, farms and children to war?

The comparison is not simply between Haile Selassie’s birthday celebration and Abiy’s construction projects. It concerns the priorities of rulers who seek grandeur while ordinary people struggle to survive.

Ethiopia’s successive conflicts have consumed the lives of young people, many from impoverished rural communities. Reports of coercive recruitment raise grave questions about how the state obtains manpower for its wars. Critics have described mass infantry assaults as human wave tactics, exposing large numbers of soldiers to devastating casualties.

These young people are not abstractions. They have parents, brothers, sisters and children. Many have little influence over the decisions that send them to the battlefield. Rulers speak of greatness and destiny. Poor families bury their children.

In important respects, Haile Selassie and Abiy Ahmed have fought variations of the same wars. Both periods have been marked by violent struggles over centralized authority and the political rights of peoples within Ethiopia. Both have involved devastating military campaigns in Tigray. And both bring us back to Ethiopian ambitions toward Eritrea.

The historical circumstances are different. Haile Selassie denied Eritreans self-determination. Abiy governs a country that must recognize Eritrea as an independent state. But the political temptation is familiar: presenting the ambitions of rulers as the necessities of the nation.

Eritrea paid an extraordinary price for independence. While many African countries achieved independence through negotiated transfers of power, Eritreans endured thirty years of armed struggle from 1961 to 1991. Algeria, Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, Zimbabwe and Namibia also experienced prolonged liberation wars, but Eritrea’s experience was especially bitter because much of independent Africa failed to recognize its claim.

Generations of Eritrea’s finest young people sacrificed their education, professions, families and lives. Some never had the opportunity to build the futures they imagined. Others survived only to carry the memories of those who did not.

Their sacrifice is the foundation of Eritrea’s sovereignty.

Ethiopia’s inland geography creates economic challenges, but it does not confer a right to annex Eritrean ports or coastline. Commercial access can be negotiated between sovereign countries. Territorial sovereignty is an entirely different matter.

The language of sea access must not obscure that distinction. Eritreans hear echoes of the imperial claims against which their parents and grandparents fought.

For nearly three years, since Abiy began publicly advancing Ethiopia’s demand for sovereign access to the Red Sea in 2023, Ethiopian officials have repeatedly invoked geography, population, history and economic necessity. What is presented internationally as a question of access has increasingly raised the prospect of territorial control.

This is the deeper threat that international diplomacy must confront, rather than treating the present crisis as though it appeared overnight.

On October 5, the European Union warned of escalating violence and called for restraint and respect for sovereignty. On October 14, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Abiy Ahmed about de-escalation, territorial integrity and avoiding cross-border incursions.

These principles are necessary. But appeals directed equally at both countries risk obscuring the political origins of the confrontation. There is a difference between advancing a claim to another country’s coastline and defending an internationally recognized border. Diplomacy should not erase that distinction.

The contradiction became especially apparent when Ethiopia accused Eritrea of an invasion in a letter to the United Nations Security Council. Eritrea rejected the accusation and, arguing that Ethiopia’s campaign for sovereign access to the Red Sea had created the danger.

The competing allegations about military movements deserve independent examination. But Ethiopia’s diplomatic accusation should not make the preceding three years disappear. International attention can quickly shift to the latest claim of victimhood while overlooking the rhetoric that helped produce the confrontation.

This is how political framing reshapes the public understanding of a conflict. A government advancing territorial ambitions presents itself as the threatened party, and the historical origins of the dispute are pushed aside.

The African Union has its own responsibility. It honors Haile Selassie while failing to confront the historical denial of Eritrean self-determination. Its mediation of the Pretoria Agreement has also been followed by renewed fighting and continuing humanitarian suffering. The United States and Europe cannot limit their response to warnings while overlooking the territorial ambitions that have contributed to the crisis.

Nor should criticism of Ethiopian rulers excuse the conduct of Eritrea’s government. Eritreans paid a terrible price during the 2020 to 2022 war. Defending Eritrean sovereignty does not require defending Isaias Afwerki’s decisions or accepting the sacrifice of Eritrean lives in wars that need not have been fought.

Haile Selassie’s Pan-African credentials could not justify the denial of Eritrean independence. Abiy Ahmed’s Nobel Peace Prize, palaces and promises of national greatness cannot justify another generation of suffering.

History repeats itself when old claims of domination return in new language, when human suffering becomes the price of national greatness, and when international institutions fail to distinguish the rights of peoples from the ambitions of rulers.

Africa does not need another emperor, another seventh king or another generation sacrificed to imperial nostalgia. It needs governments that respect their peoples and the sovereignty of their neighbors.

The measure of a leader should not be the size of his palace, the grandeur of his monument or the wars fought in his name. It should be whether ordinary people can live in peace, feed their families and build futures without being asked to die for someone else’s ambitions.

author: Marcelle Edenlord
title: California Takes Action to Address Housing Barriers for Survivors
content:
More than one in three women and one in six men in the United States have experienced sexual violence, physical violence and/or stalking by an intimate partner in their lifetime. For survivors trying to leave abusive relationships, finding safe, stable housing can be a major obstacle.

The Violence Against Women Act (VAWA), first enacted in 1994, established federal resources to address domestic violence and sexual assault. In the decades since, advocates and policymakers have worked to expand protections and services for survivors. However, access to these resources remains uneven, and recent reductions in federal funding have placed additional pressure on organizations that provide critical support.

From 2020 to 2024, violent crimes involving domestic relationships have increased by 1.9%, disrupting the consecutive decline in violence we saw in previous years. One factor we can attribute this to is the dramatic decline of the federal Victims of Crime Fund. This fund ensures countless crisis centers across the country serve their communities. In its depletion, the numbers speak for themselves.

So what are states doing about it?

On September 27th, California enacted Assembly Bill 1573, known as the Unseen and Unheard Housing Act. This law ensures future housing plans in the state will accommodate and plan for the housing needs of survivors of violence, sexual assault, and human trafficking. ⁠This is monumental, as housing is a huge barrier victims face when attempting to leave their abusers, as it’s common for abusive partners to control their partners’ lives through financial resources, such as keeping assets and in their name.

Housing can be a massive barrier to freedom and safety, especially in a state like California, which has one of the highest costs of living, where rent can exceed thousands of dollars in metro areas. This is evident as one in five unhoused women in California left their most recent residence to escape domestic violence.

In metro areas, these numbers can be significantly higher; in Los Angeles, almost half of unhoused women are domestic violence survivors and approximately a quarter of these women attribute becoming houseless to the violence they experienced. Additionally, 17% of unhoused women report experiencing domestic violence within six months before being homeless, showing the clear connections between the two.

When housing is available, it’s often unable to meet survivors’ full needs. In California alone, almost 75,000 survivors are unhoused, but there are only approximately 100 units that are designed to meet their needs.

Additionally, the majority of domestic violence shelters that offer emergency housing can only accommodate one to three month stays. Realities like these make it clear that legislation like AB 1573 are life-saving to reduce barriers to escaping domestic abuse and create pathways towards freedom for survivors.

The violence inflicted on survivors of domestic violence should not define the trajectory of their life and their ability to obtain safe long-term housing. California is paving the way by taking violence against women seriously and creating long-term state-level solutions in light of federal funding shortfalls. As federal dollars for crucial services continue to be cut, it’s on state legislatures to support and provide for their communities.

author: Phil Wilson
title: Wisconsin Gubernatorial Candidate, Carlos LeMar Dixon, Joins the Class Struggle in Northampton, Massachusetts
content:
Northampton, Massachusetts masquerades as one of the most progressive cities in America – a place where police raided a homeless encampment and took away warm clothes on a cold, rainy “Columbus Day” weekend two years ago. In Northampton we manufacture armaments to reduce Gaza to rubble. We underfund our schools, attempt to build gaudy renewal projects to attract gentrification, but the city council convenes beneath an austere portrait of Frederick Douglas. We are a cauldron of pretense, indifference, hope and confusion – as American as apple pie. My wife, Shelly, and I have lived here among wonderful neighbors and friends for more than three decades, but like everywhere else we are cleaved into irreconcilable segments – rich and poor, working class and managerial class, college professors and tent city residents.

At 11PM on a Wednesday night I am walking fast down Prospect Street in Northampton, Massachusetts with our house guest, Carlos LeMar Dixon – a write-in candidate for Governor of Wisconsin. It’s a long story. Our pace might be brisk, but our discussion floats leisurely, expansively encompassing an array of topics from war and ecology to NBA basketball. We undoubtedly get a few double-takes from the occasional late night driver passing by – me: old, weathered and white, Carlos: long, lean and Black, almost a foot taller and young enough to be unnoticed if he stepped off of a pro basketball team bus.

The two of us, unlikely comrades at a glance, quickly discover that we share compatible visions of radical political possibility – our discussions seamlessly turn into plans. We talk about a visit tomorrow to a Northampton “homeless” encampment (I prefer the rejected designation, “homeless,” to the fashionable, “unhoused,” because the former seems to describe an existential condition, the latter a mere matter of circumstance, but this is a semantic trifle). Carlos has been homeless much of his adult life and I formerly worked as an outreach worker with a small number of clients who camped in the woods – thus, I defer to him. In fact, Carlos launched his Wisconsin gubernatorial candidacy from a Milwaukee shelter.

“We make maybe 50 peanut-butter sandwiches,” he says, “stuff some fruit and water bottles into a bag, and just listen. It’s not about us and what we want. It’s about them.” I nod. Carlos often talks about the “non-profit industrial complex” – the institutional shadow that moves with, breathes with, and shapes the institution of poverty. He warns me that a homeless encampment will be a battleground for control between politicians, police and various representatives of the agencies that oversee the industry of poverty. Our goal, if I understand Carlos accurately, is to find the unfiltered voices of the people living in the tent city adjacent to Texas Road by the Mill River.

Carlos and former Northampton City Councilmember, Quaverly Rothenberg, struck up a friendship on Instagram. Shelly and I don’t think twice when Quaverly asks us to host Carlos. Quaverly, too is a force, passionate and fast on her feet – a classically trained cellist and born iconoclast. The members of the entrenched, local political establishment regard Quaverly with the uneasy, frozen sort of contemplation that vampires reserve for baskets of garlic.

I have written a number of pieces arguing that the leftwing in the US is sorely lacking the input and leadership of poor and disenfranchised people. Carlos’ story fits almost too perfectly into my somewhat abstract political narrative. He remembers pointing (for a court investigator) at the spot where his grandmother struck him – he had just turned three. He recently considered suing his grandmother, until he realized that she had worked her whole adult life in the US Postal Service, and, despite becoming a supervisor, was still poor. “I just couldn’t do it,” he says.

He began his odyssey across the landscape of temporary foster placements at the age of twelve – nine different ones in a single year, followed by group homes and large institutions. I know the story, sort of. I lived in a foster home as an eleven year old myself, but my months of benign neglect taught me little about the larger system of trauma and abandonment. However, I also worked for three years in a group home in Hayward, California. I have seen my share of wounded kids passing through a makeshift system of overmatched bureaucrats and overwhelmed staff. Underpaid workers in the foster care system enter the lives of emotionally starved children and leave like passing mirages in the desert.

Carlos hears Shelly deftly improvising at the piano and asks her if she can write the piece out. No, she says, I have no idea how to. He records the piece on his laptop and then sits down and writes it on a music notepad with exquisitely fine notation, his musical script resembles calligraphy. He runs the piece through various apps and changes the orchestration, the rhythm. We ask him if he had music lessons as a child and he tells us about once visiting a friend of his grandmother who owned a piano. He sat down and played a perfect a minor chord but his grandmother scolded him, “Carlos, leave that piano alone.” The friend intervened and told him to play all he wanted, but the story ends right there. He had no musical training growing up. I try to imagine McCoy Tyner growing up in foster care, shuffled from one pianoless placement to another. As far as I can tell, Carlos’ childhood was bereft of opportunity, with little encouragement, and a completely undiscovered cache of remarkable potential. Shelly calls him a renaissance man.

Now Carlos will spend almost the entire day inventing dense chord progressions as a sort of search for meditative inner peace. He sings accompanying lines in both a deep bass and a lifting falsetto. The talent hits you over the head, but he plays shyly, privately.

Carlos calls himself a “manufactured revolutionary.”

“The reason that some Black parents beat their kids comes from colonialism. The personal is political. Slavery taught us about the usefulness of violence.”

“Zionists have passed on the holocaust to the Palestinians,” Carlos expands. “Colonized people have to look inside themselves,” he says, “otherwise the process of extraction goes on and on. I have to watch myself, not to take too much.” It is a striking thought from a man whose worldly belongings fit into a single back pack.

We pass out sandwiches downtown to anyone who appears to need one. Homeless people define downtown scenes – the town square collects the weary bodies of those with no other place to rest. Homelessness in its vast, complex and unsettled ways sways back and forth between background and foreground, between invisible suffering and public inventory. In Spain, the eviction of an 87 year old woman mobilizes the ire of a country, an entire planet, perhaps. In downtown Northampton, Carlos and I talk with a couple (perhaps) in their late thirties holding a docile pit-bull on a rope. They tell us that six or seven cops came to their encampment to complain that too many tents occupy a small area, but they also tell us that trespassing citations have been served to people whose tents were set back into the woods. “Are we packed too tightly or spread out too much?” asks the woman.

Poverty spits out a succession of impossible questions. Do I pay my utility bills or my rent? Do I put my aunt on the street to avoid eviction for violating my lease, even though she provides childcare while I work? Poor people are simultaneously invisible, and intensely scrutinized.

While Carlos and I talk to people and hand out food in front of Northampton’s Pulaski Park, we notice a medical truck parked right in front of us with the word’s “Tapestry Health” on the rear door. This is an organization that I had always sent my clients to for any issue related to women’s health care, reproductive health or harm reduction. But, in larger letters above the “Tapestry Health” logo we note the name, “Robert Kraft,” and a smaller message informing us, “brought to you by the generosity of the Robert Kraft family.” Carlos points and says, “that’s the motherfucker who kicked Macklemore off of Ed Sheeran’s tour.”

He elaborates: “when you get into the trenches you find yourself in bed with the nonprofit industrial complex, funded by arch-Zionist, Robert Kraft.”

We walk a mile to two local encampments, one called “tent city” and another adjacent one called “Texas Road” – named for a nearby street. Carlos talks with a young Hispanic couple – he asks them whether they would be willing to speak at the next City Council meeting. Yes, they tell us. We give them our phone numbers but the man tells us he has no phone. Another man standing nearby shows us the shattered screen of his own I-Phone, as if to illustrate that phonelessness is a theme not an anomaly. A broken phone might just be the symbolic endpoint of civilization – the place where the nexus binding all of humanity drops off of a cliff, and life simply floats into the void. On the other hand, this tent city may just be the most tightly connected community in Northampton – as many as a hundred people share a wooded area no bigger than a large backyard. When people shyly take one sandwich Carlos exhorts them to take more. “As many as you need.”

Carlos explains the systemic basis of homelessness. “For every ‘unhoused’ person (our discussions feature the cautious language rift of uncertain words) there are hundreds more working jobs they hate because nervousness about losing the roof over your head drives the system. People work for long hours and low pay doing boring shit ‘cuz the idea of sleeping on the sidewalk crawls into their brain.”

As we walk back to my car, Carlos suddenly stops – startled by a sudden thought – “These council people can’t be trusted.” he says, “The police already have their eyes on these encampments, and they might react to their public statements by busting them up,” he says.

In 1964 a former Northampton next-door neighbor of ours went to Mississippi to help register Black voters. Three volunteers in his group were murdered by the Klan in one of the most infamous events of the civil rights era. The analogy does not fit our task at all. We are not battling bravely against external oppression and violence – we, at little personal risk, search for an agonizingly subtle way to create trust, while taking no direct role. We do not ask people to vote, or to accept our leadership. Carlos has described the task to me (which I explain in my own words) – we enter a community that has absolutely no reason to expect that a hostile system can be transformed. We do this in order to activate the idea that this community already has significant, if unrealized, power. Once we push our ideas onto members of an oppressed community, the magic of their own agency evaporates.

It strikes me that organizing a tent encampment involving people struggling (many of them) with addiction and mental health issues, ought to be seen as a laudable example of resilience and agency. One might blithely see a tent city as an object of shame, but if one thinks a little deeper, the tent city becomes a small triumph – people with nothing, resented and reviled, holding on to one another for dear life.

If the methods Carlos describes are ephemeral, mysterious and just a hair beyond our conceptual grasp, the needs could not be clearer. In our last town election 57% of voters stayed home. We have tried, with limited success as yet, to connect with the local DSA around our efforts to develop an alliance with Northampton’s poorest residents. The River Valley DSA ran two losing candidates for city council. A third candidate from the CPUSA also lost. The largely affluent Northampton voting base rejected a progressive agenda. To me, it is folly to focus only on convincing reluctant people to move to the left while neglecting the biggest local constituency – poor non-voters.

While Carlos and I have focused initially on the tent cities, the issues in Northampton are classic matters of wealth, power and social class. The school population is much poorer than the voting population, and the schools have been so poorly funded that Northampton’s neoliberal austerity is already being undone with a spate of lawsuits for violating the IEPs of many children. While the schools cut teachers and support staff, the town politicians plow forward with a gaudy downtown redevelopment project called “Picture Main Street,” with plans to build a life-sized chess board, decorative manhole covers and other sorts of glittery facade aimed at attracting affluent residents for newly planned development. The price tag for the whole thing is estimated at over 43 million dollars, with advocates asserting that the money will come from state sources that can’t be redirected to, say, low income housing. Carlos hears this and pauses to smile and shake his head before letting out a long, resonant, “bullshittttt!

Carlos and I sometimes lapse into the most extreme fantasies in our late night walks through Northampton’s bucolic streets, past manicured lawns and ornate Victorian homes. I tell him that I imagine a society of complete financial equality in which no one gets a dime more than anyone else. Carlos, more rooted in practical ideas of the “here and now,” pictures the members of the tent encampments as forming a workers’ cooperative with all sharing in the decisions and wealth. “You know, that is not an impossible thought,” he says softly, as if only to himself. I mention that the cumulative wealth of all US residents living in America would, if divided with absolute fairness, give every person almost a half a million dollars. It is an abstraction – and I lack the economic knowledge to explain the complexities of how capitalist accumulation might manifest in its redistributed form. I also observe that our housing infrastructure, with mansions and trailer parks, has been constructed to sustain the contours of capital. How do we undo that?

We also talk about how economic segregation works against any sort of solidarity. Shelly and I lived in the working class Berkeley flats when we got married 43 years ago. There, people of all sorts lived together – doctors, lawyers, postal employees and preschool teachers, all races and backgrounds in one block. Carlos has worked as an Uber Driver and a classroom aid, but he also holds a real estate license and consults his phone to discover that our former Berkeley property now is appraised at well over a million dollars. Our former diverse neighborhood has been gentrified into extinction. Carlos does the math. Since 1984 our national minimum wage has doubled, but our Berkeley house has appreciated by a factor of fourteen.

Carlos tells me how he came under the wing of an elderly member of The Black Panther Party, but he has taken that knowledge and reapplied it to be more inclusive. He took the slogan, “power to the people,” and tweaked it – “all power to all people,” or APTAP, his Instagram handle. “I don’t like any hierarchy at all,” he says.

Carlos has amassed tens of thousands of followers in a short time with a series of charismatic Instagram videos. He describes himself as a teacher rather than a leader – true to his philosophy of unequivocal equality. “I don’t try to monetize my platform,” Carlos says

These videos are quite brilliant, hard hitting and performed with an improvisational air. “I am reading from my script” he tells me, but it all appears to be spontaneously composed on the spot. “I am a rapper and that background helps me a lot.”

The videos have a manic edge, but Carlos talks to people at the encampment with the soft humility of a student rather than a teacher. No outsider would be able to enter this community with the sincerity that Carlos softly projects. Even after decades of working with poor people as a community mental health therapist, I am unable to comfortably belong to these communities. Political organization cannot be initiated with either ideological jargon, or even using well intentioned, heartfelt sentiments. The real work must be enacted from within the community. Carlos simply belongs to any community of poor people in a way that I do not. There is no solidarity with poor communities without radicalized people who have lived their pain.

We sit in our kitchen and Carlos tells us how he came to tentatively enter the Wisconsin gubernatorial contest while living in a Milwaukee shelter. After declaring his candidacy he attended a political rally for Francesca Hong where a man had questioned her about a now notorious “gaff” that she had made regarding a protester’s display of a red-paint soaked Israeli flag during a 2023 event staged against the Gazan genocide. (Carlos said that he hoped he could support Hong and possibly drop out of the race.) Hong had called police to report an anti-Semitic “incident,” and while she had subsequently apologized for (in Carlos’ words) conflating anti-Israeli free speech with anti-Semitism, she appeared to “tap-dance” around the issue. Carlos then asked Hong how she would respond to pressure from mainstream Democrats, and he viewed her response as more “tap-dancing.” He had already been uneasy about Hong’s inability to get an endorsement from Bernie Sanders, and added that he was later stupefied by how immediately she conceded to (Democratic primary opponent) David Crowley before the final votes had even been counted. The next day, Carlos told us, Hong endorsed Crowley with no demands to embrace any part of the Democratic Socialist agenda. Carlos describes David Crowley as a corporate, status quo Democrat with deep ties to local lobbyists.

After the Francesca Hong rally Carlos intensified his campaign efforts. He used a Facebook dating site as a front for campaigning and famously pilfered Hong and Crowley lawn signs as a method of guerilla-theater. But candidacy offered Carlos an opportunity to see the class structure beneath the veneer of US politics. He would be able to gather signatures (to be officially named as a candidate on official ballots) but lacked the money and legal backing to fight the challenges to those names, and “Act Blue,” refused platform access (for fund raising) because there was already “a glut of progressive candidates.” Out of seven declared candidates, only he was denied Act Blue platform access, he tells me. In theory, Carlos states, Act Blue can platform any progressive candidate including independents. Act Blue officials had every opportunity to explore and support Carlos’ radical agenda, but chose not to, he claims.

Carlos learns while with us in Northampton that he has gained the Wisconsin Green Party endorsement for his campaign and says, “Oh snap, now I got to give these motherfuckers $12 to join their party.”

I ask Carlos if he worries that his candidacy might result in a razor thin margin in favor of Republican, Tom Tiffany – a candidate who Carlos calls a “MAGA Warrior” who will siphon money from public schools and support AI data centers. Carlos’ voters, he tells me, have no role in this election. “People who vote for me are people who won’t vote for either Crowley or Tiffany. My support comes from non-voters who see me as being their voice. If anything, I might get one or two Republican votes.”

That brings me to Carlos’ part in the struggle to enfranchise the poorest people in Northampton. While Carlos “walks” for office in Wisconsin, he is physically present and deeply involved with our community. Carlos named several tasks: 1) Reaching out to the non-participants in our city (overwhelmingly comprised of our poorest citizens), like the residents living in the hundreds of Northampton Housing Authority’s low income and subsidized units. In some of Northampton’s many “affordable” developments barely 10% of eligible voters turn out. We aspire to greatly enlarge the voting base and also to involve more people in policy decisions and resistance. 2) Increase the numbers of people involved in the critical effort to fully fund the collapsing Northampton School System. 3) Be in a position (via an expanded voting base) to elect at least six radical candidates to the city council along with a progressive mayor. 4) Block the “Picture Main Street” project from sucking up resources that might be critically applied toward education and homelessness. 4) Prioritize a solution to aid our homeless population. This will involve town owned land and properties as well as possibly funding the building of small, prefab units. 5) Mobilize the public and town authorities to resist the continued operation of war industry icon, L3Harris. 6) Coordinate the fragmented assortment of radical organizations to support one another and to be involved in our movement to enfranchise poor residents.

We have a growing coalition of Northampton residents, including many residents of low income housing who have mobilized around unsafe housing conditions in the low income developments. A handicapped resident of one building posted a video of herself on social media edging painfully down a steep staircase after the elevator failed.

As I try to complete this piece, Quaverly and Carlos are frantically preparing home cooked meals for those in the tent encampments. Carlos tells me that the two of them plan to pressure the Northampton Tenant’s Union to include all members of the unhoused community in their organizational plans. Last night Carlos and I revealed our larger project aspirations to members of Demilitarize Western Mass – a local anti-war organization. Carlos imagines residents at the encampments joining us at our weekly L3Harris protests. “They know that money for housing is going to pay the police to stand around while we blast bullhorns outside the factory. All of these issues are connected,” he says.

I am absolutely convinced that poor people are a latent base for socialism. The people who live below or near the poverty line have every reason to see housing as a human right, and to believe that health care ought to be available to everyone. The fact that Trump and his billionaire stooges have become obsessed with limiting voting tells you everything you need to know about the political potential of poor people.

Bernie Sanders knows that most Americans live paycheck to paycheck, but millions have no paycheck at all. People live doubled up as couch surfers, waiting for years to acquire a housing subsidy. There is an enormous, unacknowledged sea of discontentment waiting to be ignited from within, to find their voices inside of their own communities.

I don’t know if we can succeed in Northampton, but we have ripe conditions – a legacy of activism, a history of tolerance and diversity, and an untapped community of poor people. We have city council elections coming in 2027 and a short period of time to gather momentum. Voting may seem to be the low hanging fruit, but the real work involves an internal shift in poor communities, a sense of agency. We encounter a widespread antipathy toward the idea of voter mobilization. Now is the time to build coalitions and trust. We have a plan and charismatic people with a vision. We are hoping to convince Carlos LeMar Dixon to relocate from Milwaukee. Every step will be hard. Northampton has been asleep for decades.

This article was originally produced by Nobody’s Voice.

Phil Wilson is a retired mental health worker and union member. His writing has been published in ZNetwork.org, Current Affairs, Counterpunch, Resilience, Mother Pelican, Common Dreams, The Hampshire Gazette, The Common Ground Review, The Future Fire and other publications. title: ΟΧΙ ΑΛΛΗ ΒΙΟΛΑΝΤΑ -Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στα Δικαστήρια Θεσσαλονίκης
content:
ΟΧΙ ΑΛΛΗ ΒΙΟΛΑΝΤΑ -Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στα Δικαστήρια Θεσσαλονίκης.




Σχετικά με τη σύλληψη μέλους μας στη Θεσσαλονίκη.




Συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης Δευτέρα 19 Οκτωβρίου, 12:00 στα Δικαστήρια Θεσσαλονίκης




Στις 14 του μήνα μέλη του Ρουβίκωνα πραγματοποίησαν παρέμβαση στην κατασκευαστική εταιρεία Intelligent Entertainment στα Διαβατά. Την επόμενη μέρα, η αστυνομία συνέλαβε μέλος μας με βαρύτατες κατηγορίες σχετικά με την υπόθεση, ενώ η κοινωνική κουζίνα της οργάνωσης πραγματοποιούσε το εβδομαδιαίο μοίρασμα φαγητού.




Η συγκεκριμένη εταιρεία λειτουργεί χρόνια τώρα με πολύ σοβαρές παραλείψεις σε μέτρα ασφαλείας και ατομικής προστασίας των εργαζομένων στον χώρο της. Το τελευταίο χρονικό διάστημα, έχουν σημειωθεί τουλάχιστον τρία εργατικά ατυχήματα τα οποία έχουν περίτεχνα συγκαλυφθεί από την εργοδοσία και για τα οποία, παρά τις καταγγελίες των εργαζομένων, η Επιθεώρηση Εργασίας δεν έκανε τίποτα. Χάρη στις διασυνδέσεις της εργοδοσίας, οι υποθέσεις μπήκανε στο συρτάρι και οι αρμόδιοι έκριναν πως δεν υπάρχει κανένα ζήτημα.




Παρά τη μήνυση της εταιρείας προς το μέλος μας, είναι αξιοσημείωτο πως εντός 24ώρου κλήθηκαν από την εταιρεία συνεργεία ηλεκτρολόγων στον χώρο και κινήθηκαν διαδικασίες για τη λήψη μέτρων ασφαλείας και την επισκευή διαφόρων προβλημάτων στις εγκαταστάσεις. Το γεγονός αυτό επιβεβαιώνει φυσικά τις καταγγελίες των εργαζομένων και νομιμοποιεί ουσιαστικά την κίνηση της οργάνωσης.




Παρ’ όλα αυτά, η αστική δικαιοσύνη αποφάσισε να ξεκινήσει δίωξη κατά της οργάνωσης, η οποία το μόνο που απαίτησε ήταν να τηρηθούν τα απολύτως νόμιμα και πολύ βασικά πρωτόκολλα ασφαλείας σε έναν τέτοιο χώρο εργασίας, ενδεχομένως αποτρέποντας μελλοντικά ατυχήματα ή και χειρότερα. Η υπόθεση αυτή μας θυμίζει πολύ αυτή της Βιολάντας, όπου οι αρμόδιες αρχές αδιαφορούσαν για τις συνθήκες που επικρατούσαν και παράλληλα παραβλέπαν τις καταγγελίες των εργαζομένων, με αποτέλεσμα να πεθάνουν πέντε εργαζόμενες.




Αν οι δικαστικές αρχές, οι οποίες όλον αυτό το καιρό δεν έκαναν καμία κίνηση για τη παράνομη λειτουργία της Intelligent Entertainment, δεν απαλλάξουν τον σύντροφό μας από τις κατηγορίες στην επερχόμενη δίκη, επί της ουσίας θα κλείνουν το μάτι και θα είναι συνένοχες στο μελλοντικό ενδεχόμενο εργατικού ατυχήματος ή και θανάτου στη συγκεκριμένη εταιρεία αλλά και σε άλλες.




Όλα αυτά μάλιστα συμβαίνουν τη στιγμή που στο κάτεργο της Motor Oil συνεχίζουμε να μετράμε νεκρούς και τσακισμένους εργάτες τον έναν μετά τον άλλον.




Οι βρώμικες προσπάθειες κύκλων εξουσίας να αποδώσουν κακουργηματικού χαρακτήρα κατηγορίες σε βάρος μελών μας, αλλά και μανιωδώς να καταδικάσουν τον Ρουβίκωνα ως εγκληματική οργάνωση επειδή κάνει τα αυτονόητα, θα πέσουν στο κενό.




Κάτω τα χέρια από τους αγωνιστές και τις αγωνίστριες.




Ο συλληφθείς σύντροφός μας θα περάσει από ανακριτή τη Δευτέρα, 19 Οκτωβρίου, στα δικαστήρια Θεσσαλονίκης.




ΟΥΤΕ ΒΗΜΑ ΠΙΣΩ




Ρουβίκωνας

author: Chris Walker
title: New Bill Seeks to Expose What Major Banks Knew Regarding Epstein’s Spending
content:
“We need to know what financial institutions and their executives knew about Epstein,” Rep. Robert Garcia said.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Several members of Congress have submitted new legislation that would require financial regulators and private banking institutions to disclose thus far unreleased transactions made by disgraced financier and accused child sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.

The Epstein Wall Street Records Act would require federal banking regulators — including the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), the Federal Reserve, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Comptroller of the Currency — to make public any files relating to how Epstein spent his money. The legislation is needed, sponsors of the bill say, because it’s unclear whether banking institutions were aware of his crimes and may have helped facilitate them.

In addition to Epstein, the bill would require disclosures for “any entity owned or controlled” by Epstein, as well as financial holdings and transactions made by Ghislaine Maxwell, his former girlfriend and accomplice, or associates of the two.

Large private financial entities that could be affected by the bill include Barclays, Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan Chase, Bank of America, and others.

The proposed legislation is sponsored by every Democratic member of the House Oversight Committee, including ranking Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California). Joining in sponsorship of the bill are Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), and Ron Wyden (D-Oregon). Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) is the only Republican signed onto the bill so far.

Garcia explained the justification for the bill by stating:

Jeffrey Epstein used his immense wealth to abuse women and girls for decades. Meanwhile, banks and financial institutions enriched him and themselves by servicing his accounts and helping him move money around. We need to know what financial institutions and their executives knew about Epstein, whether they complied with relevant law, and what regulatory agencies learned.

Warren similarly expressed the need for the bill’s passage.

“The bipartisan Epstein Wall Street Records Act will ensure overdue accountability for the wealthy and well-connected on Wall Street who put profits over people,” she said.

“The Epstein Files Transparency Act forced the Attorney General to release DOJ, FBI, and U.S. Attorney’s Offices’ files,” Massie said, referring to a bill that was passed into law last year. “This bill does the same for bank regulators. Justice for the survivors means following the money.”

During the 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump pledged to release files relating to investigations of Epstein, despite the two of them formerly having a very close friendship. After taking office in January 2025, however, Trump balked at disclosing the records, and harshly criticized anyone pointing out that he was breaking his campaign promise, calling those pushing for the release of the files part of a “hoax” against him.

Only after months of pressure did Trump finally acquiesce, signing into law the Epstein Files Transparency Act. Still, after signing the bill, Trump continued to deride the issue as a “Democrat Hoax.”

After the bill’s passage there continued to be delays in the release of the files, which included many mentioning Trump’s connections to Epstein and sexual allegations against the president. Millions of documents relating to Epstein remain unpublished, with many of those that have been made public featuring heavy redactions, in spite of the law’s demand for greater transparency.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: David Swanson
title: Trump’s Threats to Annihilate Iran
content:
Asia, Endangerment, Immorality, North America, World

By Ivana Nikolić Hughes and Peter Kuznick, World BEYOND War, October 16, 2026

It is not possible to excuse, justify, or condone this kind of rhetoric. The only question is what to do about it.

Of all of the things that Donald Trump has said publicly since returning to the White House, his threats to annihilate Iran are arguably the worst. This is not only because the repeated statements are deeply immoral and illegal–deliberate killing of civilians is a war crime–but because they represent the kind of irresponsible rhetoric that will lead us into a global apocalypse and collapse of not just the Persian nation but human civilization as a whole. It is not possible to excuse, justify, or condone this kind of rhetoric. The only question is what to do about it.

As much as some well-meaning people might want to see nuclear weapons as instruments that ended World War II and have kept the peace ever since, the exact opposite has actually been true. Nuclear weapons brutally murdered a couple of hundred thousand civilians in Hiroshima and Nagasaki and injured and sentenced to years and decades of illness and suffering many hundreds of thousands more. As we have written before, multiple alternatives existed to end the war in 1945. In many ways, the false narrative of the atomic bombings averting an invasion and saving lives has enabled the perpetuation of nuclear weapons, bringing the risks to humanity’s survival to levels previously unimaginable. Turning a brutally violent beginning of the nuclear age into something positive has managed to complicate and obfuscate an issue that should never have been complicated. Nuclear weapons are and have always been immoral. Their possession should be illegal.

Although the end of World War II coincided with the advent of nuclear weapons, and we have technically not fought another world war since, this is merely a correlation. Other significant changes in our world, including the founding of the United Nations, technological and scientific progress, and globalized trade, took place over that same time period. In addition, one has to wonder, whose peace we are talking about. Since 1945, over 20 million people have died in armed conflicts around the world, with up to 50 million more indirect deaths stemming from those conflicts. Today, there are nearly 100 armed conflicts across the planet according to the Geneva Academy, and 25 international armed conflicts involving more than one nation state.

All along, in addition to the deaths and suffering in war zones across the planet and the horrific toll exacted by poverty and inequality, humanity has been waiting almost helplessly for another nuclear weapon to explode by accident, miscalculation, or intention, likely triggering a full-blown nuclear war in which tens or even thousands of nuclear weapons are used. The past eight decades have witnessed numerous incidents in which human wisdom and decency or just plain luck interrupted a course of events that seemed inexorably leading to nuclear war. Nuclear weapons have not brought the peace. Quite the opposite – they threaten what little of it we have each and every day.

And yet, for all of his threats on Truth Social and most recently in the halls of the United Nations, Trump has also stated that nuclear weapons “could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over,” calling for “denuclearization.” In fact, two days after his unacceptable statement to “drive [Iran] into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness” at the UN General Assembly in September, Trump suggested to President Xi in DC that there be a nuclear summit between China, Russia, and the United States.

Trump did so knowing full well that Xi’s government’s participation in arms control negotiations is contingent upon China achieving rough parity with the nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia. This should be pursued not by China continuing to expand its arsenal to the gargantuan size of the U.S. and Russian arsenals, but by the U.S. and Russia reducing theirs to the size of China’s, and adopting China’s demand for an across-the-board no-first-use policy.

Since his latest threat, delivered in the world’s premier diplomatic space unlike his earlier Truth Social rants, including the one on April 7 that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again,” Trump actually seemed to welcome Iranian destruction of Los Angeles and San Diego at an election rally. Even if he now unconvincingly claims that the original clips, which suggested that such destruction was a small price to pay, were taken out of context and the small price to pay was about the price of gas, it is not reassuring to have the US President talking about nuclear bombs exploding over American cities. Never mind that Iran neither has the nuclear weapons nor the ability to send missiles toward US soil. Nuclear Armageddon seems to be on Trump’s mind.

Is the real estate developer who seemed to understand that a lot of effort, capital, and human ingenuity, not to mention time, go into building modern cities gone? What happened to the businessman who in 1986 “summoned Dr. Bernard Lown of the International Physicians for Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW) to the Trump Tower for a meeting?” Trump sought advice from Dr. Lown on negotiating nuclear arms agreements with Mikhail Gorbachev just after IPPNW had won the Nobel Peace Prize a year earlier. Is that person no longer here or do his “denuclearization” comments offer some hope?

Among those refusing to be passive in all of this is Pope Leo XIV who has not only deplored war and called for nuclear disarmament but who recently decried leaders, presumably including Trump, who are “beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive,” and urged leaders to “come together, sit down, engage in dialogue.” The Holy See was one of the original parties to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons and remains a strong supporter of nuclear abolition. It is time for Pope Leo XIV, speaking for the planet, to use his unique moral authority to demand an emergency summit of, at a minimum, Trump, Xi, and Putin to get us off this path of war and potential nuclear annihilation.

In addition to insisting on such actions from others, each of us needs to think long and hard about what we can do to address the insanity of Trump’s threats and the insanity of nuclear weapons.

Get rid of nuclear weapons, get rid of Donald Trump, and work towards complete multilateral world disarmament. Reply Yes. We have to get rid of all kinds of weapons and we absolutely can. I just want to say that like I said before, I learned that even if a full-on nuclear war broke out, there’d still be a few billion survivors who’d be able to survive and rebuild. Still, we have to prevent a nuclear war from ever happening and we can achieve that great and peaceful and loving future for everyone I’m always dreaming of. Reply

I just want to say that like I said before, I learned that even if a full-on nuclear war broke out, there’d still be a few billion survivors who’d be able to survive and rebuild. Still, we have to prevent a nuclear war from ever happening and we can achieve that great and peaceful and loving future for everyone I’m always dreaming of.

title: Osman Kavala: AİHM kararına rağmen yeniden yargılamanın reddi yargıya zarar veriyor
content:
Gezi davasında ağırlaştırılmış müebbet hapis cezası verilen ve 1 Kasım 2017’den bu yana cezaevinde tutulan sivil toplum ve insan hakları savunucusu Osman Kavala, AİHM kararının uygulanmamasına ilişkin açıklama yaptı.




Kavala, İstanbul 13. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi’nin “yargının itibarına zarar verdiğini” belirterek şunları söyledi:




“25 Ağustos tarihli AİHM kararında maruz kaldığım yargısal işlemler, adaletin inkârı olarak nitelendirilmişti. Bunun ana nedeni suç işlemiş olduğuma dair bir bulgu olmadan ve olmadığının bilinmesine rağmen hukukun özünü zedeleyen işlemlerle özgürlüğümün kısıtlanmasının sürdürülmesi oldu.




13. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi’nin vahim bir insan hakları ihlaline son vermek yerine AİHM’e bireysel başvuru hakkı ve CMK maddelerini keyfi biçimde yorumlayarak yeniden yargılamayı reddetmesi yargının itibarına da zarar veriyor.”




AİHM Büyük Dairesi, 25 Ağustos’taki kararında Kavala’nın özgürlük ve güvenlik, adil yargılanma, ifade ve barışçıl toplanma özgürlüğü haklarının ihlal edildiğine hükmetmişti. Mahkeme, Kavala’nın mümkün olan en kısa sürede serbest bırakılması ve mahkumiyetinin bütün sonuçlarının ortadan kaldırılmasına karar vermişti.




İstanbul 13. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi ise AİHM’e başvuru öncesinde iç hukuk yollarının tüketilmesi gerektiğini savunarak yeniden yargılama talebini reddetti. Mahkeme, AİHM’nin bir temyiz mahkemesi olmadığını ve delillerin değerlendirilmesinin ulusal mahkemelerin yetkisinde bulunduğunu ileri sürdü.



















Mahkeme bir kez daha AİHM’nin Osman Kavala kararını tanımadı




13 Ekim 2026













Osman Kavala'nın hapsi




Sivil toplum ve insan hakları savunucusu Osman Kavala, 2013'teki Gezi Parkı protestolarını organize ve finanse ettiği iddiasıyla yürütülen soruşturma kapsamında 18 Ekim 2017'de gözaltına alındı, 1 Kasım 2017'de tutuklandı.




Avrupa İnsan Hakları Mahkemesi (AİHM), 10 Aralık 2019'da Kavala'nın tutuklanması için makul şüphe bulunmadığına ve tutukluluğunun kendisini insan hakları savunucusu olarak susturma amacı taşıdığına hükmederek serbest bırakılmasını istedi.




İstanbul 30. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi, 18 Şubat 2020'de Gezi davasında Kavala'nın beraatine ve tahliyesine karar verdi. Ancak Kavala, cezaevinden çıkamadan yeniden gözaltına alındı ve farklı suçlamalarla tutuklandı. Beraat kararı daha sonra istinaf mahkemesince bozuldu.




Yeniden görülen Gezi davasında İstanbul 13. Ağır Ceza Mahkemesi, 25 Nisan 2022'de Kavala'yı "hükümeti ortadan kaldırmaya teşebbüs" suçundan ağırlaştırılmış müebbet hapis cezasına çarptırdı. Karar, 28 Eylül 2023'te Yargıtay tarafından onandı.




Türkiye'nin 2019 tarihli AİHM kararını uygulamaması üzerine Avrupa Konseyi Bakanlar Komitesi ihlal prosedürü başlattı. AİHM, 11 Temmuz 2022'de Türkiye'nin söz konusu karara uyma yükümlülüğünü ihlal ettiğine hükmetti.




AİHM Büyük Dairesi, 25 Ağustos 2026'da verdiği yeni kararda da Kavala'nın özgürlük ve güvenlik, adil yargılanma, ifade ve barışçıl toplanma özgürlüğü haklarının ihlal edildiğine karar verdi.
