title: Gök yarılırken cepheye sürülür gibi: İstanbul’un altında kalanlar
content:
Valilik “zorunlu olmadıkça dışarı çıkmayın” dedi. Fabrikada, tersanede, sokakta, hastanede çalışanlar için o zorunluluğu yine patronlar belirledi.

19 yaşındaki Mazlum Gürbüz, 29 Eylül'de Eyüpsultan Kemerburgaz'daki bir şantiyede yağmur hafifler hafiflemez tabela montajı için sahaya geri çağrıldı. Elindeki metal çıta yüksek gerilim hattına değdi, bir haftalık yaşam mücadelesinin ardından 5 Ekim'de hayatını kaybetti. Çocukluk arkadaşı Levent Çelik, o gün neden işi bırakamadıklarını şöyle anlatmıştı: “İşten çıkarılma korkusuyla mecbur kaldık, çalıştık.”

Aradan iki hafta geçmeden İstanbul ve çevresi çok daha büyük bir sağanakla boğuştu. Valilik okulları tatil etti, kamuda yalnızca belli gruplara idari izin verdi, motokuryeleri trafikten çekti ve halka “zorunlu olmadıkça dışarı çıkmayın” çağrısı yaptı. Özel sektörde çalışan milyonlar için ise tek bir düzenleme çıkmadı.

Kocaeli Başiskele'de Hayat Kimya ve Özka Lastik fabrikalarını su bastı, işçi servisleri tekerlek hizasına kadar suya gömüldü. Arslanbey OSB'de işçiler fabrikaya suların içinden geçerek ulaştı. Ford Otosan'da su basan bölümlerde işçiler sırılsıklam çalıştı. Tuzla ve Yalova tersanelerinde üretim bir an bile aksamadı, vinçlerin yalnızca “kontrollü” kullanılması istendi.

Bunlar ulaşabildiklerimiz. Ulaşamadığımız nice işyerinde de afet koşullarında bile kâr hesabı işçinin canının önüne kondu. Bu koşullarda çalıştırılan her işçi, kapıda bekleyen yeni bir Mazlum Gürbüz demek.

PTT'de taşeron olarak çalışan üç çocuk babası bir dağıtımcı, paketleri sokak sokak yürüyerek dağıtıyor. Çarşamba 165 paketle çıktı, ancak 135'ini teslim edebildi. Dün yine sokaktaydı: “Valilik 'zorunlu olmadıkça çıkmayın' demiş ama bize kimse 'bugün çalışmayın' demedi. Bu sabah da 130 paketle çıktım, bu en az 15 kilometre yol demek. Bizim gibi insanlar için zorunluluk bu.”

Dağıtımcıları yağmurda sokağa iten prim sistemi. 60 paketin üzerine çıkınca prim devreye giriyor: “Üstüne bir 60 daha koyarsam bir yevmiye daha almış gibi oluyorum. Böyle çalışmasam yetiremem. Böyle de yetmiyor gerçi.” Yetmediği için PTT'den sonra Maslak'ta servis şoförlüğü yapıyor, dün eve ancak 23.30'da girebildi: “İnsan işi değil ama başka yolu yok. PTT'den aldığım para ancak çocukların okuluna, beslenmesine gidiyor. Kirayı, faturayı kim ödeyecek?”

Uber Eats'te çalışan bir kurye, sabah birkaç paket teslim edip eve dönmüş ama çalışmayı sürdüren arkadaşlarına kızamıyor: “Hepimiz borçla yaşıyoruz. Ben çalışmadım çünkü bir dayanağım var. Dayanağı olmayan adam mecbur çalışacak, hem de bu havada daha çok çalışacak.” Sokakta kurye azalınca kişi başına düşen paket artıyor, sağanak birçok kurye için bir “fırsata” dönüşüyor. Boynuna kadar suya gömülmüş kurye görüntüsü için şunları söylüyor: “O insanı zincirle sürüsen suya sokamazsın. Ama bizi kendilerine köle ettiler, sıcak evimizden kendi ayağımızla çıkıp suyun içine giriyoruz.”

Motokurye yasağı ise sabit ücreti olmayan kurye için gelirsiz gün demek: “Millet ne yiyecek diye düşünmek yasağı koyanların görevi değil mi? Bunu ücretli izne dönüştürmek çok mu zor? Şirket paketini düşünüyor, devlet gelişigüzel yasak koyuyor, kurye ne yapacak? Beni düşünmediğin yasak önlem değil.”

Bakırköy Belediyesi'nin süpürge işçileri yağmurun bıraktıklarını temizlemek için sahaya sürüldü. Daha önce de haberlerimize konu olan soyunma kulübeleri artık kullanılamaz durumda: “Sivil kıyafetlerimizi koyacak yerimiz bile yok. Dün mesai bitiminde üstümü değiştirmeye girdiğimde kıyafetlerimi su içinde buldum. Herkes evine kaçmanın yolunu ararken kenti temizleyen işçilere reva gördükleri soyunma yeri bu mu?” İşçiler insani dinlenme alanı talebini yılın başında, sözleşme sürecinde dile getirmişti: “Kulak arkası ettiler. Şimdi damı akan, çamur içindeki kulübelerde üstümüzü değiştiriyoruz.”

Park bahçeler ve fen işleri müdürlüğündeki işçi sayısı ise eski başkan Kerimoğlu döneminde 95'ken işten çıkarmalar ve emekliliklerle 35'e düşmüş. Bir işçi anlatıyor: “Dün koca Bakırköy'ün felaketini 5 işçi 24 saat çalışarak toparlamaya çalıştı. 20'nin üzerinde ağaç devrilmiş, onlarca evi, dükkânı su basmış. Hepsine yetişmeye çalışıyoruz.”

Okmeydanı Perpa'da özel bir şirkette çalışan bir emekçi, dün 16.00'da izin alıp çıktı. 40 dakika otobüs bekledi, Sünnet Köprüsü'nde trafik kilitlenince yağmurun altında Alibeyköy metrosuna yürüdü: “Yanımızda kadın, erkek, genç, yaşlı vardı. Hasta bir teyzenin koluna girip oraya kadar getirdik.” Metrodan sonra Gazi'nin girişine kadar yine yürüdü, eve 19.50'de varabildi. Evi uzak iş arkadaşları gece 01.30'a kadar eve giremedi. “Her yer betonlaştı, altyapıya yatırım yapılmadı” diyor: “Yolda İstanbul'da deprem olsa ne olur diye düşündüm.”

Okullar 15 ve 16 Ekim'de tatil edildi, idari izin ise sınırlı sayıda kamu çalışanını kapsadı. Özel sektörde çalışan ya da izin dışında tutulan anneler için bu, çocuğu bırakacak yer bulamamak demek. Kreş yok, yasakları koyanlar çocukları düşünmemiş.

İstanbul Eğitim ve Araştırma Hastanesi'nde bugün birçok hemşire çocuğunu işe getirdi. Bir sağlık emekçisi, arkadaşının çocuğunun, “Okullar tatil, ne güzel evdeyiz” diyen bir arkadaşına verdiği yanıtı aktarıyor: “Benim annem babam çalışıyor. O yüzden iş yerine gitmek zorundayım.” Kadın sağlık emekçileri pandemiyi hatırlatıyor: “Ailelerimiz uzakta. Pandemide çocukları ailelerin yanına gönderdik. Biz niye yeniden buna maruz kalıyoruz?”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: US Reportedly Considering Dropping “Mother of All Bombs” on Iran
content:
The US has only ever dropped a MOAB once before — on Afghanistan in 2017.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Pentagon has reportedly drawn up plans to attack Iran with the “Mother of All Bombs” (MOAB), the largest conventional weapon ever developed by weight, after being ordered by President Donald Trump to develop strike plans for targets that include “a lot of energy infrastructure.”

Energy infrastructure is largely considered to be civilian in nature and thus protected under international law.

The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, is the U.S.’s largest non-nuclear bomb. It is designed to explode a few feet before hitting the ground, creating a massive blast and shooting out plumes of fire, destroying everything within a 0.6 mile radius and causing damage within one mile. It is not an effective weapon against targets like Iran’s highly fortified nuclear infrastructure, experts said, because it does not penetrate deep below ground.

Legal experts have previously raised concerns about disproportionate harm to civilians in the U.S.’s use of 2,000-pound bombs on Iran. The MOAB, by contrast, weighs 21,000 pounds, and has a much larger blast radius.

The MOAB options were first reported by CNN and confirmed by CBS. The MOAB was first tested in 2003, as the George W. Bush administration developed its strategy of “shock and awe” in Iraq; as CNN notes, at the time, the Pentagon said it hoped that the mere existence of the MOAB was enough to cause “psychological” damage to the enemy.

The bomb has only been used once before in combat, by Trump. In 2017, the U.S. dropped a MOAB east of Kabul, in Nangarhar, Afghanistan, a province with a population of 1.5 million people. The Pentagon claimed that more than 94 ISIS members were killed in the attack. No civilian deaths were reported; some reports said that the area had long been evacuated. But some local reports suggested that civilians were harmed, and critics afterward noted that the U.S. had previously never considered using the bomb in Iraq because of civilian damage concerns. It caused a mushroom cloud visible from 20 miles away.

.@USFOR_A releases GBU-43 #MOAB strike video against #ISIS-K cave complex, #Nangarhar, #Afghanistan #DefeatDaeshhttps://t.co/MuhU7JXuNn pic.twitter.com/qBqptpuzbE

It is unclear what the timing of such an attack on Iran would be. Trump has said that he won’t relaunch strikes against Iran before the midterms, but reports have also said that his administration has drawn up plans to do just that. CNN said advisers privately wonder if Trump’s pledges are definitive.

CNN additionally found that the Trump administration and military planners have spent recent weeks looking for “an off-ramp that gives Trump a ‘symbolic’ win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.” This includes plans that could amount to strikes for a “fireworks show,” after which Trump would declare victory.

“The Trump administration’s threats to commit war crimes in Iran cannot be normalized,” said Ryan Costello, policy director for the National Iranian American Council, in response to the MOAB report. “President Trump acts on many of his threats, necessitating more urgent action to bring this illegal war of choice to a definitive end.”

The Trump administration has already been under fire for killing civilians in Iran, with several attacks having been described as war crimes by UN experts. This includes the February 28 strike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran, which killed 160 people, including 123 children.

Pentagon officials said in May that their report on the Minab attack, which is the single worst strike on civilians by the U.S. in the 21st century, was nearing conclusion. But Bloomberg reported on Thursday that the Pentagon is planning to withhold the report at least until after the midterm elections next month, and potentially even longer.

The attempt to withhold information about the U.S.’s conduct in the deeply unpopular war has incensed critics.

Defense Secretary Pete “Hegseth eliminated staff who prevent civilian casualties, called the rules of engagement safeguarding civilians ‘stupid,’ & now he’s covering up the report on the Minab school strike that killed over 120 children,” said Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland). “He needs to be removed from office & we need accountability NOW.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: TELE1 çalışanları hakkını alamadı, Halk TV'de belirsizlik sürüyor: Kayyım baskısı gazetecilerin çalışma alanını da daraltıyor
content:
Son iki yılda aralarında Flash Haber, EkoTürk, Habertürk TV, Show TV, Bloomberg HT, HT Spor, Show Türk, Show Max, TELE1 ve Halk TV’nin bulunduğu 10 televizyon kanalına kayyım atandı. Farklı gerekçelerle yürütülen süreçlerde televizyonların yönetimleri Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu’na (TMSF) devredilirken, TELE1 ve Halk TV’ye yönelik müdahaleler, iktidar çizgisi dışında yayın yapan az sayıdaki televizyon kanalının yönetimlerinin değiştirilmesi açısından diğer kayyım süreçlerinden ayrıldı. Bu kanallarda çalışanların ve işten çıkarılanların yaşadıkları ise basın özgürlüğü ile çalışma hakkının aynı süreçte nasıl kesiştiğini ortaya koydu.

TELE1’e 24 Ekim 2025’te kayyım atanmasının ardından kanalın başına getirilen İbrahim Paşalı, 14 Ekim 2026’da Halk TV’ye de kayyım olarak atandı. Yeni Şafak’ta köşe yazarlığı yapan Paşalı, daha önce Flash Haber, Habertürk, Show TV ve Bloomberg HT’nin de aralarında bulunduğu medya kuruluşlarında kayyım olarak görev almıştı.

TELE1’de kayyım atandıktan sonra istifa eden bir gazeteci kayyım atamasının ardından yaşanan süreci anlattı. Kanalın kayyım yönetimine geçtiğinde 140 kişilik bir çalışan kadrosuna sahip olduğunu belirten gazeteci, önce Ankara bürosunun kapatıldığını, kanalın İstanbul’dan yürütüleceğinin söylendiğini, ardından İstanbul bürosunda da işten çıkarmaların devam ettiğini söyledi.

“140 kişilik ekibimizden 130 kişiyi işten attılar” diyen gazeteci, işten çıkarılan bazı arkadaşlarının Koza TV, İlke TV ve son olarak Halk TV’ye geçtiğini anlattı.

Ancak medya sektöründeki kayyım ve baskı süreçleri nedeniyle gazetecilerin çalışabileceği alanların zaten daraldığını belirten gazeteci, Halk TV’ye de kayyım atanmasının ardından bu alanın daha da küçüldüğünü söyledi. TELE1’de kayyım tarafından işten çıkarılanların önemli bölümünün halen işsiz olduğunu belirten gazeteci, bazı çalışanların ücret ve kıdem tazminatlarını da alamadığını söyledi. “Bu insanlar aylardır işsiz, hakları olan ücretleri alamadı, “bu sadece halkın haber alma hürriyetine kayyım atanması değil, bu gazetecilerin çalışamaması sonucu basının da işlevsiz bırakılmasıdır” dedi.

TELE1’de kayyım sonrasında işten çıkarılan başka bir gazeteci ise tazminat ve diğer alacakların ödenmediğini belirterek, işsizliğin sektördeki daralmayla birlikte ağırlaştığını söyledi.

“24 Ekim 2025’te TELE1’e kayyım atanmasının ardından aslında yıllardır süregelen kayyım uygulamasının mağdurları arasına eklendik” diyen gazeteci, bazı çalışanların ayrılmayı, bazılarının ise ekonomik zorluklara rağmen bir süre çalışmayı tercih ettiğini anlattı.

“Sonuç olarak hepimiz işten çıkarıldık. Aradan geçen zamana rağmen ödenmesi gereken, bilgi mesajıyla iletilen tazminatlarımız hala ödenmedi” dedi.

İşini kaybetmenin yarattığı ekonomik sıkıntıya hak edilen alacakların ödenmemesinin de eklendiğini belirten gazeteci, “Bir günde işten çıkarıldık, hala iş bulamayan basın emekçileri var” diye konuştu.

Gazeteci, bugün işini kaybetmenin yalnızca yeni bir iş aramak anlamına gelmediğini belirterek, “Giderek daralan çalışma alanlarında yeniden iş bulmaya çalışmak, geçinebilmek, kira ve faturaları ödemek, geleceğe dair belirsizlikle mücadele etmek anlamına geliyor” dedi.

TELE1’de işten çıkarılan çalışanların bir bölümünün daha sonra Halk TV’ye geçtiğini anlatan TELE1 çalışanının sözleri, Halk TV’de kayyım sonrası oluşan belirsizlikle de kesişiyor.

Halk TV reji ekibinden bir işçi, kayyım atanmasının ardından çalışanlar ve yöneticiler açısından ciddi bir belirsizlik oluştuğunu söyledi. Kayyım yönetimiyle yapılan görüşme sonrasında Halk TV yöneticileri, “Biz onlara yardımcı olmayacağız. Onlar burayı devam ettirmek istiyorlarmış. Kimseye ‘şunu yapın’ demiyoruz, karar sizin” denildiğini aktardı.

Kayyım yönetiminin kanalı sürdürmek istediğini söylediğini belirten işçi, “Buranın mali durumu iyi. Biz burayı döndürmek, devam ettirmek istiyoruz” ifadelerinin kullanıldığını söyledi.

Çalışanların öncelikle ne sunulacağını görmesi gerektiğini belirten işçi, teknik ekipteki çalışma arkadaşlarına da ani karar vermemeleri çağrısı yaptığını anlattı:

“Burada insanlar ev geçindiriyor, çoluğu çocuğu olan, faturası olan var. Hiç fevri bir karar vermektense önce bir dinleyelim, bize ne sunacaklar bir görelim. Ardından sendikayla da görüşelim, hep beraber bir karar alalım.”

İşçi, çalışanların özellikle kıdem ve ihbar tazminatlarının ne olacağı konusunda belirsizlik yaşadığını belirtti. Yaklaşık bir buçuk-iki yıldır “TGS’yi işyerine sokmaya çalıştıklarını anlatan işçi, sendika temsilcisiyle kayyım sürecinin hemen ardından görüştüklerini söyledi.

Sendikanın çalışanları bazı hakların verilmeyebileceği konusunda uyardığını aktaran işçi, “Size kıdem tazminatınızı vermeyebilir, size doğrudan haklı fesih hakkınızı vermeyebilir” denildiğini söyledi.

Kayyım yönetiminin çalışanlarla ilgili tutumunun haber merkezinde daha fazla kaygı yarattığını belirten işçi, teknik ekip ile haber merkezinin durumunun farklılaşabileceğini söyledi.

“Teknik iş yapan insanları, tutmak isteyebilirler ama haber merkezindeki insanları tutmak istemeyebilirler. Haber politikasını veya haber çizgisini değiştirecekleri için onların durumu biraz daha kritik” diyen işçi, haber merkezinde “Şimdi ne olacak, nasıl ilerleyeceğiz?” belirsizliğinin daha yoğun yaşandığını belirtti.

Halk TV’de daha önce başka kanallarda çalışmış ve işsizlik yaşamış çalışanların da bulunduğunu söyleyen işçi, “Tele 1’den gelen arkadaşlar var. Uzun süre işsiz kalmış, hakkını alamamış, süreçten sonra gidecek bir yer bulamamış ve bize gelmiş arkadaşlar var” dedi.

Medya sektöründe iş bulmanın kolay olmadığını belirten işçi, Halk TV çalışanlarının kayyım yönetimine karşı tutum alması durumunda önlerinde sınırlı sayıda seçenek bulunduğunu söyledi.

“Buradan şimdi bu ilkeli duruşu veya tırnak içinde söylüyorum, bu kayyıma boyun eğmemeyi gösterdiğiniz noktada da gidebileceğiniz yer sayısı bir, Sözcü. Sözcü’de de küçülme var, işten çıkarma var, Halk TV1’de çalışan200 kişi var bu insanların tamamına ne olacak” diye konuştu.

Teknik ekip açısından başka kanallara geçmenin çalışma koşulları ve ücretler bakımından gerileme anlamına gelebileceğini belirten işçi, “Özellikle teknik ekip açısından hem standardın düşmesi hem de ücretinin düşmesi demek oluyor” dedi.

Haber merkezi çalışanlarının ise başka kanallara geçmesi halinde yaptıkları haberlerin değişebileceğini belirten işçi, “CNN’e gittiklerinde burada yazdıkları haberi yazamayacaklar. TV100’e gittiklerinde burada yazdıkları haberi yazamayacaklar. Kayyımla çalışmaya devam ederlerse özgür şekilde haber yazamayacaklar” ifadelerini kullandı.

Çalışanların işten ayrılma kararlarının ekonomik koşullardan bağımsız değerlendirilemeyeceğini belirten işçi, “İnsanların kira, fatura, evli olan, çocuğu olan, borcu olanlar var” dedi.

Medya sektöründeki işsizlik nedeniyle çalışanların mevcut işyerlerinde kalmak zorunda kaldığını ifade eden işçi, “Buradaki insanların işten ayrılmamasının sebebi, Cafer Mahiroğlu gibi korkunç bir patrona rağmen burada bu kötü şartlarda çalışmasının sebebi de bu kıskaç. Ne gidebileceğiniz bir alan var ne de üç aşağı beş yukarı patrondan kaçabileceğimiz bir yer var” diye konuştu.

Halk TV’de kalmayı ya da ayrılmayı tercih eden çalışanların birbirini suçlamaması gerektiğini söyleyen işçi, “Burada kalan da giden de, kovulan da atılan da burada hepimiz iş yapıyoruz ve bu iş karşılığında hayatımızı geçindirmeye çalışıyoruz. Aynı çarkın altında biz de eziliyoruz” dedi.

“Buradan giden onurlu olacak, burada kalan arkadaşlarını satmış olacak diye bir şey yok. Hepimiz başımıza geleni yaşıyoruz. Elimizde olmayan koşulların, elimizde olmayan süreçlerin ve elimizde olmayan bir ekonomik tablonun sorununu yaşıyoruz” ifadelerini kullandı.

On yılı aşkın kanalda çalışan Muhabirinden editörüne bütün çalışanların bir anda karar vererek işten ayrılmasının kolay olmadığını anlatan işçi, sabahın 04.00-05.00’inde kalkıp kanala gelerek sabah bültenini hazırlayan bir editörü örnek verdi. “Yeni bir eve çıktı, şimdi ayrılmadı diye kötü bir insan mı oldu? Yıllardır verdiği emeği terk etmiş mi oldu?” diye sordu. Yıllardır kanalda çalışanların bir anda tazminatını, geleceğini ve geçmişini bırakarak gitmesinin kolay olmadığını belirten işçi, “Hiçbirimiz sırça köşklerde yaşamıyoruz. Hepimiz bir emeğin parçasıyız.” dedi.

DİSK Basın-İş Genel Başkanı Turgut Dedeoğlu, Halk TV’ye kayyım atanmasının basın özgürlüğüne ilişkin anayasal hükümler açısından değerlendirilmesi gerektiğini söyledi.

Anayasa’nın 29. maddesinin süreli veya süresiz yayınların önceden izin ya da mali teminata bağlanamayacağını, haber, düşünce ve kanaatlerin serbestçe yayımlanmasını engelleyen veya zorlaştıran şartlar konulamayacağını düzenlediğini hatırlatan Dedeoğlu, 30. maddenin de kanuna uygun şekilde kurulmuş basın işletmelerinin matbaa ve basın araçlarının suç aleti olduğu gerekçesiyle zapt edilmesini veya işletilmekten alıkonulmasını yasakladığını belirtti.

“Bu hükümler, basın kuruluşlarının faaliyetlerini sürdürebilmesinin anayasal güvence altında olduğunu ortaya koymaktadır” diyen Dedeoğlu, Halk TV’ye yönelik müdahalede bu hükümlerin ihlal edildiğini söyledi.

Dedeoğlu, “Siz bir kuruma el koysanız bile, yani o kurumun sahibinin mal varlığına el koysanız veya onunla ilgili bir hukuki süreç başlatsanız bile, kanunen kurulmuş ve herhangi bir sıkıntısı olmayan yayın kuruluşunun yayınını bu şekilde durduramazsınız” dedi.

Halk TV ve TELE1’e yönelik müdahalelerin anayasal hükümler uygulanmış olsaydı yaşanmayacağını belirten Dedeoğlu, TMSF’ye devredilen kuruluşların bünyesinde çok sayıda televizyon, radyo, internet sitesi ve gazetenin bulunduğunu söyledi.

Bu sürecin geçmişteki örneklerine de dikkat çeken Dedeoğlu, Hayat TV ve İMC TV’ye yönelik müdahaleleri hatırlattı. Hayat TV’nin herhangi bir hukuki süreç işletilmeden yayın platformundan çıkarıldığını belirten Dedeoğlu, “Hayat TV’yi, İMC TV’yi sarı öküzü vermek olarak görsek, onlar için mücadele etseydik bugünleri görmeyecektik” dedi.

Kayyım ve yayın durdurma uygulamalarının basın çalışanlarının çalışma koşullarını doğrudan etkilediğini belirten Dedeoğlu, yayın yapılamamasının gazetecilerin emek sürecini de ortadan kaldırdığını söyledi.

“Yayının durdurulmasıyla yalnızca ekran kararmıyor. Muhabirler haber üretemiyor, editörler içerik hazırlayamıyor, kameramanlar çekim yapamıyor. Reji ve teknik ekiplerin yayını sürdürme olanağı kalmıyor” dedi.

Sansür ile çalışanların emek süreçleri arasında doğrudan bağ bulunduğunu belirten Dedeoğlu, “Gazetenin haber yapma olanağını kaybetmesi, aynı zamanda çalışma olanağını da kaybetmesi demek. Haber yapamıyorsanız çalışamıyorsunuz. Çalışamıyorsanız da para kazanamıyorsunuz.” ifadelerini kullandı.

Dedeoğlu, “Aslında tümüyle bir mesleği yok etmeye çalışan bir mekanizma sansür” dedi.

Sansürün yanı sıra otosansürün de gazetecilerin çalışma koşullarını etkilediğini belirten Dedeoğlu, gazetelerin bazı haberleri yayımlamaktan kaçındığını, bunun nedenleri arasında kurumun kapatılması, gazetecinin işinden olması veya cezaevine girme korkusunun bulunduğunu söyledi.

Türkiye’de basın mesleğinin giderek daha fazla baskı altında olduğunu belirten Dedeoğlu, “İktidarın benim izin verdiğim, benim hoşuma giden, haberleri yaptığın sürece yayın yapabilirsin. Ama beni eleştiren, benim yaptığım sıkıntılı durumları, fon yolsuzluğu gibi haberleştirirsen ben senin kanalını kapatırım, senin sesini kısarım” anlayışının olduğunu söyledi.

Basın ve ifade özgürlüğünün yeniden kazanılmasının sendikal ve mesleki mücadeleden geçtiğini belirten Dedeoğlu, “Bunu ancak sendikal mücadelelerle, meslek örgütlerinin mücadelesiyle, basın özgürlüğünü ve ifade özgürlüğünü tekrar elde etmek mümkün” dedi.

Basın meslek örgütleri ve sendikaların daha somut bir mücadele yürütmesi gerektiğini söyleyen Dedeoğlu, sosyal medya üzerinden yapılan kınamaların yeterli olmadığını belirterek, “Twitter’dan ‘kınıyorum, çok kınıyorum, daha şiddetli kınıyorum’ gibi açıklamalar bu siyasi iktidar için yeterli olmuyor. Sokağa çıkarak sesimizi duyurmamız gerekiyor” diye konuştu.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Ünlüce'yi tebrik eden CHP Sözcüsü Sarı'dan "muhalefetin ortak iradesi" vurgusu
content:
CHP Sözcüsü Müslim Sarı, Türkiye Belediyeler Birliği (TBB) Başkan Vekilliğine seçilen Eskişehir Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Ayşe Ünlüce’yi tebrik etti. Sarı, sonucun muhalefetin ortak iradesiyle elde edildiği vurgusunu yaptı.

Sarı, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı paylaşımda, "Türkiye Belediyeler Birliği Başkanvekilliğine, partimizin desteğiyle seçilen Eskişehir Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Sayın Ayşe Ünlüce’yi tebrik ediyorum. Muhalefetin ortak iradesiyle elde edilen bu sonuç, yerel yönetimler açısından önemli bir kazanımdır" ifadesini kullandı.

TBB Başkan Vekilliği seçiminde Yeni Parti, Ayşe Ünlüce'yi aday olarak göstermiş, CHP de aday çıkarmayarak Ünlüce'yi destekleyeceğini duyurmuştu.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Sally Ncube
title: Child marriage laws in Africa need more funding to protect girls
content:
15th October 2026










Child marriage laws in Africa need more funding to protect girls
















12 min read



















News and Insights




End child marriage




Africa


























































With global funding to end child marriage falling yearly since 2019, African governments must take action to strengthen budgeting and implementation of child marriage laws.  




By 

Sally Ncube,

 Equality Now, and 

Fatou Gueye Ndir,

 Senior Regional Engagement and Advocacy Officer, Girls Not Brides




Although numerous African governments have strengthened laws against child marriage, legal protections remain widely underfunded and ineffectively enforced. Many countries have no clearly outlined, dedicated national budget line for ending child marriage. Instead, allocated money is incorporated into broader gender or social protection budgets, where funds are often difficult or impossible for auditors to trace or civil society to access. 




Funding to end child marriage is falling 




The joint report, ‘

International Funding to End Child Marriage: Reviewing a Decade of Investment

,’ by 

Girls Not Brides

 and 

Girls First Fund

, with input from 

Publish What You Fund

, found that funding to end child marriage accounts for only a tiny fraction of Official Development Assistance (ODA), while local frontline organisations working directly with girls and communities receive only a sliver of available budgets.  




Between 2015 and 2023, just 0.025 per cent of all ODA globally was directed to projects whose primary objective was to end child marriage. A further 0.081 per cent went to broader projects in which addressing child marriage was one of several objectives, rather than the primary purpose, and it was not possible to determine how much of this secondary funding was specifically spent on child marriage interventions. 




Investment to end child marriage peaked in 2019. Since then, it has fallen every year, dropping from US$76 million to US$51 million by 2023, and this deterioration accelerated with 

2025’s historic decline in global aid

. With several major donors scaling back investment in gender equality, ODA faces mounting pressure.




Over the next five years, more than 70 million girls worldwide are expected to be at risk of child marriage. Yet current levels of international funding dedicated to ending this form of violence against children amount to less than US$1 per girl at risk each year globally. At a time when conflict, climate change, anti-rights movements and shrinking civic space are all exacerbating the dangers girls face, declining investment threatens to further undermine child protection in Africa.




Ending child marriage is also an economic imperative: 

girls who marry later stay in school longer, earn more, and raise healthier families

, with gains that impact entire communities. 




Legal loopholes and poor enforcement of laws leave girls vulnerable to child marriage 




Passing laws is only the first step. Governments must back them with dedicated funding, strengthening relevant institutions and duty bearers, for effective enforcement, oversight, and clear accountability. A dedicated budget line is not a bureaucratic technicality; it is the difference between turning legal promises and human rights obligations and commitments to end child marriage on paper into meaningful real-world protection for girls.




Most African Union Member States have ratified the 

African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child

, which requires countries to prohibit child marriage. The Charter has established a strong regional legal framework and contributed to many countries enacting laws to prevent child marriage. What is now needed is a concerted effort to improve implementation of existing laws and remove remaining gaps in legal protections. 




According to the African Union’s 2026 report, 

Ending Child Marriage in Africa

, 18 countries in Africa have a minimum marriage age of 18 or above, with no exceptions. The continent’s remaining 37 countries do not meet this standard. Some set a minimum age below 18 for one or both sexes, while others have raised the age of marriage to 18 but permit exemptions, such as allowing judicial, parental or other legal authorisation for a child to marry.




The African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC), in its 2026 

Thematic Report on Harmful Practices Affecting Children in Africa

, stated that despite decades of advocacy and progress in strengthening legal frameworks, child marriage remains widespread and deeply entrenched across much of Africa. 




ACERWC noted that progress has been persistently hindered by weak and inconsistent enforcement of laws, legal loopholes and customary law exceptions, inadequate funding, and inadequate coordination between relevant authorities. It also highlighted limited collection and analysis of reliable data to guide action and measure progress, weak monitoring and accountability mechanisms, and barriers to accessing justice for children affected by harmful practices. 




A report by Women and Law in Southern Africa and Equality Now illustrates why stronger laws must be backed by stronger systems. They found that although 

18 is the minimum legal age of marriage with no exceptions

 in 

Zimbabwe, child marriage remains widespread

 and survivors continue to struggle to access justice, healthcare and education. 




How to end child marriage in Africa




Things need to change.




The ACERWC should call on every State Party to include a dedicated financing section in its periodic submissions, showing budget allocations by ministry and year. 

It should also set a firm 2027 deadline for governments to establish trackable national budget lines, with progress reviewed at the Committee’s

 

48th Ordinary Session

.




Girls should sit at the centre of accountability frameworks built in their name: not as recipients of decisions made by others, but as rights-holders who can inform policy and push governments to turn commitments into action.




Without well-funded laws, child marriage will continue in Africa




Parliaments, audit institutions, human rights bodies, and civil society already know what needs to be done. With the right laws enacted and properly resourced, we can achieve the positive change needed.




Governments must create clear, public budget lines for child marriage prevention, and rely less on donor funding by raising more of their own resources. 




Ministries should have clear accountability systems to prevent responsibility from being shifted between people

. And the

 

African Union Accountability Framework on the Elimination of Harmful Practices

 should move beyond its six pioneer states to cover every AU member.




We call on donors and development partners to increase and ringfence funding, as well as incorporate child marriage prevention into health, education, and humanitarian budgets. In addition, at least half of all primary funding should go directly to local and national civil society organisations who work closest and most directly with girls and their communities.




Budget transparency is integral to child protection. Governments cannot enforce what they do not fund, and cannot be held effectively accountable for commitments they are never required to report on.




This article was first published by the Times Group.




END




Notes to editors:




For media enquiries, contact Sphiwe Dlamini, Communications Officer, Equality Now, 

sdlamini@equalitynow.org

, T. +27 (0)711429179  (available on WhatsApp).

  




Note: Child marriage, also refferred to as “Child, early, and forced marriages and unions (CEFMU)” are formal marriages or informal unions in which at least one party is under 18 years of age, and/or in which one or both parties do not give full, free and informed consent due to coercion, duress, social or family pressure, or inability to leave the union. Child marriage is considered a form of forced marriage because children under 18 cannot give valid consent.




About the authors:




Sally Ncube

 is Equality Now’s

 Regional Representative for Southern Africa. She leads and supports Equality Now 

regional legal advocacy and movement-building initiatives that promote legal equality, reform rape, family and nationality laws, strengthen access to justice, and address gender-based violence, including ending child marriage, female genital mutilation, sexual exploitation and sex trafficking through strategic engagement with governments, regional institutions, and civil society.

 




Fatou Gueye Ndir

 is Girls Not Brides Senior Regional Engagement and Advocacy Officer within the Africa Team. Fatou is responsible for regional advocacy, including supporting members for greater visibility at the regional and continental level. She is based in Senegal and provides critical support to strengthen Girls Not Brides National Partnerships, coalitions and other networks and alliances at the national level.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Cancels Livestream of Firing Squad Execution After Fierce Backlash
content:
Polling released before the announcement found only 18 percent of Americans support the livestreaming idea.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump has cancelled a plan to livestream the firing squad execution of former soldier Nidal Malik Hasan after widespread backlash from the public, politicians, military members, and faith leaders.

Trump made the announcement on Truth Social.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” he said. Studies have repeatedly found no evidence that the death penalty acts as a deterrent to crime.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!”

On Thursday, shortly before Trump announced his decision, polling by The Washington Post, ABC News, and Ipsos found that the idea of livestreaming an execution is extremely unpopular among the public. According to the poll, 80 percent of Americans say they oppose it, while only 18 percent said they are in support. The idea is even overwhelmingly unpopular among the respondents who said they overall support the firing squad execution of Hasan, with 69 percent opposition to and 30 percent approval of the livestream among that group.

The only group that saw majority support of the livestream was among MAGA Republican men, among whom 57 percent backed the idea.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who often speaks of violence as a virtue, initially announced the livestream last week during an interview with far right commentator Jack Posobiec.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it’s public. Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.

But the idea was faced with immediate opposition, and in recent days, Trump had reportedly been gathering opinions from allies as to whether he should make the killing publicly watchable.

After Hegseth’s announcement, both Democrats and Republicans in Congress condemned the livestream idea. Vice President J.D. Vance, perhaps seeing the backlash, said that he would not personally watch it. The military’s archbishop put out a statement disapproving of the idea, saying that it would harm the reputation of the U.S. military.

Many other religious leaders condemned the idea. Pope Leo put out a statement, meanwhile, calling for the abolition of the death penalty altogether.

“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” said the pope. “The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) introduced a bill on Thursday that seeks to ban the public broadcasting of any military executions.

The Trump administration has reveled in imagery of state-perpetrated violence. Pentagon officials have repeatedly published footage of its deadly strikes on boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean, which have been likened to snuff films. His administration has gone produced propaganda videos with video game footage spliced between clips of alleged war crimes, making light of killing.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: GEO Files Unfair Labor Practice Charge Against the University of Michigan (GEO 3550)
content:
A post shared by Graduate Employees’ Organization 3550 (University of Michigan) (@geo_3550)

ANN ARBOR, MI — On Wednesday October 14th, the Graduate Employees’ Organization (GEO) filed an Unfair Labor Practice (ULP) charge against the University of Michigan for issuing two politically motivated felony charges against GEO president, Hiab Teshome. Hiab was charged with embezzlement and false pretenses charges concerning purchases made by a student group she was a co-signer of. This pretextual and unprecedented legal assault was the University’s latest attempt to interfere with protected Union activities and the collective bargaining process.

In June 2026, so-called “progressive” Washtenaw County Prosecutor and Michigan Attorney General candidate Eli Savit took up the University of Michigan Police Department’s (UMPD) request for felony charges against Hiab. The UMPD have historically violently repressed labor and the Palestine solidarity movement. The arrest warrant and charges were brought forth through a collaboration between Savit, UMPD’s Sergeant Ryan Cavanaugh, and the Center for Campus Involvement (CCI), particularly CCI director Nick Smith. Cavanaugh and UMPD have directly harassed and attempted to intimidate Hiab, including an attempt to visit her prior address. On August 6th, all charges were dismissed by Judge Cedric Simpson.

In addition, UMPD unilaterally usurped the prosecutor’s office and filed to the magistrate judge requests for additional bond conditions against Hiab including attempting to ban her from campus and successfully banning her from the Ruthven Building due to it being the location of the Regent’s offices. The Regents set major University policy and have targeted individuals in the labor and pro-Palestine movement.

The University’s decision to involve law enforcement over alleged misconduct in a student organization is unprecedented and directly contradicts the University’s student organization accountability processes, which explicitly deem criminalization inappropriate. The Central Student Government (CGS), which typically oversees student organizations, released a statement affirming the inappropriate use of the legal system against individuals in their capacity as members of a student organization. The University never engaged in their own internal process and never contacted Hiab until she was being investigated by Cavanaugh and still have not contacted her.

The University of Michigan initiated legal processes against its own policies in an attempt to interfere, restrain, and coerce the elected president of GEO from her rights as a public employee and to deprive the Union of the right to select its own bargaining agents. As such, GEO maintains that the University has violated the Public Employment Relations Act and we are demanding accountability.

It is abundantly clear that, if not for Hiab’s protected union activity, the University of Michigan would never have sought the issuance of such meritless charges. These charges were an attempt to limit Hiab from appearing as a bargaining representative and to restrict her rights as a public employee.

The University used the threat of criminal proceedings to try to silence and intimidate not just a Union member, but our entire Union. GEO will not stand for any attempts by the University of Michigan and its collaborators in the legal system to repress Palestine solidarity or labor organizing. We affirm our commitment to workers at the University of Michigan and will continue to fight for just labor conditions for all workers.

Representatives are available for interviews with the press to talk about the Unfair Labor Practice and GEO’s ongoing contract negotiations with U-M.

author: Lisa Femia
title: Our Lawsuit Against the Trump Administration’s Social Media Surveillance Moves Forward. Here’s What the Court Said.
content:
No one should have to choose between speaking freely and protecting their immigration status. Yet that’s precisely the choice the Trump administration’s mass surveillance of online speech forces on noncitizens living in the U.S. 

  




Last fall, we 

sued

 on behalf of three major labor unions to stop this surveillance program. And just this month, we won our first major ruling: A federal district court 

denied

 the government’s motion to dismiss our lawsuit. This means the case can move forward—a win for free speech and a critical step in protecting our First Amendment rights online. We’ve already explained why this is a 

big deal

 for our clients, so let's take a closer look at the court’s reasoning.

  




Our Lawsuit

 




 Since taking power, the Trump administration has used AI and other automated tools to 

broadly surveil

 the social media and online speech of visa and green card holders, with the goal of identifying and punishing people who express views it opposes. The government is targeting a broad range of views, including 

criticism of the

 

Trump administration

; 

support for Palestine

 or 

criticism of Israel

; 

“rationalizing or making light of”

 Charlie Kirk’s murder; and anything nebulously 

“hostile”

 to American culture, 

founding principles

, 

“traditional American views,”

 or 

“our way of life.”

 

 




It has paired that surveillance with a public intimidation campaign. High-ranking officials have explicitly 

threatened

 to punish noncitizens for their online speech, then followed through with a series of terrifying viewpoint-driven enforcement actions. 

This has led to a significant chilling effect on speech, not just for noncitizens, but also for their families, coworkers, and friends.

 




In response, three major labor unions—the United Auto Workers (UAW), the Communications Workers of America (CWA), and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT)—

sued

 the Departments of State and Homeland Security alleging that this viewpoint-based surveillance program violates the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).  

The unions are represented by EFF, Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA).

 




The government moved to dismiss our lawsuit, arguing first that federal immigration law prevents federal district courts from hearing the case, and second, that the unions don’t have “standing” to sue. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York rejected both arguments and allowed the case to proceed. At this stage in the litigation, the court accepted all of the facts in our complaint as true and analyzed the law based on those facts. We will now prove these facts as the case proceeds.

 




Federal Immigration Law Doesn’t Block Our Lawsuit

 




 The government first argued that the court had no power to hear our case at all. It pointed to three provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) that restrict when federal courts can review immigration matters. The district court disagreed and rejected each provision in turn.

 




The first provision, 

8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9)

, is often called the “zipper clause.” It bars federal courts from hearing challenges that arise from efforts to deport someone, except through review of an individual’s final removal order. The government 

claimed

 the zipper clause applies here because our lawsuit is really an effort to stop it from initiating adverse immigration actions.

 




 The district court wholly rejected this argument. Relying on the Second Circuit’s decision in 

Ozturk v. Hyde

, it held that the zipper clause bars only challenges to a particular individual’s removal proceedings, not a lawsuit like ours that challenges the constitutionality of the surveillance program itself. That the surveillance program might affect someone’s immigration proceeding down the line doesn’t turn our lawsuit into a removal challenge.

 




 The court similarly rejected the government’s argument that 

§ 1252(g)

 and 

§ 1252(f)(1)

 prevent federal courts from hearing this case. Our suit, the court explained, “challenges the constitutionality of a government policy that is collateral to any active removal proceedings,” so § 1252(g) doesn’t apply. And § 1252(f)(1) only limits what kind of relief a court can give. So while the court may not be able to stop a particular person’s removal proceedings, it can still block “an unlawful surveillance program that suppresses free speech.”

 




 

The Unions Have Standing to Sue

 




 To sue in federal court, a plaintiff must show that it has “standing” to bring its claims. This requires a plaintiff to show an “

injury in fact

” that is, among other things, “concrete.” That’s often a high bar in surveillance cases, where plaintiffs can’t easily see what the government is doing behind the scenes. And the Supreme Court 

has

 

held

 that a person’s mere subjective fear of surveillance is too speculative to confer standing.

  




Even so, our plaintiffs cleared the bar. The court held that the unions alleged concrete injuries, including a chill on members’ speech that is objectively reasonable, not just subjectively felt. It found that the unions had established standing in two ways: 

“organizational standing,” based on the unions’ own injuries, and “associational standing,” based on injuries the unions’ members have suffered.

 




Organizational Standing

 




The court first held that our plaintiffs had successfully alleged an injury to the unions themselves (injury was the only aspect of organizational standing the government disputed). The surveillance program has harmed the unions’ ability to carry out their core responsibilities, including “organizing their members and advocating for the unions’ goals.” The court made two key points:

 




1. Unions Are Injured When Members Go Silent 




As we explained in our 

complaint

, the surveillance program has caused members to step back from union leadership roles; stop participating in union activities online and in person; remove their names from union webpages; and avoid filling out bargaining surveys. Members who might otherwise spread the unions’ message and raise awareness of union issues are staying quiet, hampering the unions’ ability to organize. The court said this amounts to a concrete injury for purposes of standing.

 




2. Surveillance Doesn’t Need to Target Pro-Union Speech 

 




 The court also rejected the government’s claim that members’ retreat from union activities was “essentially an overreaction,” because the surveillance doesn't target pro-union views. The court said this misunderstands the issue: “the question is whether the Government’s conduct would deter a person of ordinary firmness from engaging in protected activity, not whether the specific expression a member forgoes is itself among the viewpoints the Government disfavors.”

 




Here, the surveillance program monitors noncitizens’ online activity indiscriminately, and members “cannot reliably predict which of their activities will be captured” and attributed to a disfavored viewpoint. What’s more, the court noted, the unions’ organizing often happens alongside the very advocacy the government is alleged to target, “including pro-Palestine and anti-ICE activism on college campuses.” That makes members’ retreat from union activity a foreseeable consequence of the program.

 




Associational Standing 

 




 The court also held that the unions established associational standing to sue on behalf of their members. Of the three requirements for associational standing, the government challenged only two. It argued that members lacked sufficiently concrete injuries to sue in their own right, and that the claims aren’t “germane” to the unions’ purpose.

 




The court disagreed and found associational standing for every claim but one: members’ right to receive information. That claim survives anyway, because the unions’ organizational standing covers it. Along the way, the court made several important rulings.

 




 1. The Ongoing Surveillance Is a Present Injury 




 As a threshold matter, the government argued that our case is a “pre-enforcement challenge,” meaning we sued before the government actually punished anyone. That would trigger a different test, and the government argued we failed it because we hadn’t alleged a sufficiently imminent threat of prosecution.

 




The court disagreed, explaining that “Plaintiffs’ allegations are of an ongoing surveillance program that is actively chilling the speech of their members and otherwise causing harm.” That chilling effect is a First Amendment injury even if there isn’t a direct prohibition on speech. And when government conduct is actively chilling speech right now, a challenge to it isn’t pre-enforcement.

 




 2. Surveillance + Public Threats Reasonably Chills Speech 




 The court rejected the government’s argument that we alleged only a generalized, subjective, speculative fear of surveillance, explaining that “the chilling effect” of the program can “itself be an injury when the plaintiffs are surveilled.” Here, plaintiffs have alleged that their members are under active surveillance, which has had objective chilling effects on their speech. And the government is targeting certain disfavored viewpoints, making it “viewpoint discrimination” that is “presumptively unconstitutional.”

 




The chill is also objectively reasonable, the court held, because the government has extensively publicized the surveillance program through public statements and social media posts, making clear that noncitizens who post disfavored views will be targeted for removal. Notably, the court agreed with us that the “threat of adverse immigration consequences, under a government whose harsh immigration crackdowns has been heavily publicized and reported on, is certainly enough to deter a person of ordinary firmness from the exercise of First Amendment rights.” 

This is a concrete injury sufficient for standing.

 




3. 

Demanding Social Media Handles Also Causes Harm

 




Under the surveillance program, applicants for certain immigration benefits must 

disclose

 all social media handles they have used during the preceding five years and, in some instances, maintain 

public social media accounts

. The district court held that this too amounts to a First Amendment injury, undermining the rights to anonymity and freedom of association. 

 




The judge pointed to one CWA member we identified, a lawful permanent resident with a pending naturalization application who is subject to the five-year disclosure requirement. The member has deleted one social media account, set another to private, and removed past posts expressing disfavored views. These allegations, the court said, show an actual and objectively reasonable injury due to the government’s surveillance program.




4. General, Public Threats Can Still Be Coercive

 




We also argued that the Trump administration is waging a campaign of coercive threats to suppress disfavored speech, which the First Amendment prohibits. The court agreed that this campaign can be an actionable injury of its own.

 




Notably, the court held that it didn’t matter that the government’s statements were not specifically targeted at certain individuals, and were instead made on social media or to the public. In this case, the court explained, “the number, severity, and high-profile examples of action upon those threats are such that a reasonable person would perceive the communication as coercive.”

 




That means it’s reasonable that the unions’ members “would, and did, limit their public speech on disfavored viewpoints” in response. That the threats were made to the general public “does not diminish this injury,” as the very purpose of the challenged surveillance program is to intimidate noncitizens into silence.

  




5. Free Speech is Central to Union Functioning

 




The court also found that the unions met the second prong of associational standing. It held that the unions’ interests in protecting their members’ rights to speak freely, organize, and advocate, are “germane” to the unions’ missions. 

The court put it plainly: 




The freedom of Plaintiffs’ members to speak, associate, and appear publicly is not incidental to union work, but rather is the mechanism through which unions recruit, organize, communicate, and bargain. A program alleged to silence members and drive them from the unions’ rolls therefore strikes at the unions’ representational function itself.







Next Steps

 




When the government surveils what people post online and threatens to punish them for their viewpoints, the result is exactly what our clients have experienced. Members have deleted their accounts, scrubbed posts, and withdrawn from union activities. 




The government must now answer our complaint and we will move forward with the discovery process, in which we anticipate getting more information from the government about its surveillance program. We look forward to continuing to prove our case.

author: Chris Walker
title: ICE Is Fast-Tracking a Nationwide Domestic Spy Program Across Dozens of Cities
content:
The agency plans to contract with around 142 agents to take part in domestic spying operations.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is reportedly fast-tracking a program designed to expand its domestic surveillance capabilities in dozens of cities across the United States.

Details of the new spy program, entitled the Enforcement and Removal Operations Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, or ERO ONE, were published on a federal website in September. The American Prospect reported on ERO ONE earlier this week.

Around $100 million is expected to be allocated from the Department of Homeland Security to the program, which intends to contract 142 intelligence agents who will be placed in at least two dozen cities throughout the country. Those agents would coordinate with nearby ICE offices, as well as with a central hub located in Washington, D.C.

The published plan doesn’t specify what these agents will do while in the field, but it does indicate that they will analyze classified and nonclassified information to create “network, link, and relationship” analyses. Such research examines not only a specific person, but also their connections — including members of their household, extended family members, friends, and even acquaintances.

The government’s explainer of the program states that agents will “provide research, analysis, evaluation, reporting, coordination, and related intelligence support to ERO ONE headquarters and designated field locations.”

The document places some restrictions on ERO ONE agents, who will not be allowed to engage in actions such as “arrest, detention, search, seizure, interrogation, inspection, investigative, or other law enforcement authorities.” However, given that ICE agents have repeatedly overreached their own enforcement powers or blatantly lied to residents during enforcement operations, it’s not unreasonable to believe these restrictions could be ignored.

ICE has already expanded its domestic spying capabilities through facial recognition and mobile phone location data software, as well as artificial intelligence (AI) technologies as part of its mass deportation efforts. ICE has also used “zero-click” technology that allows the agency to access encrypted data on an individual’s phone by sending a link to the user that doesn’t require them to click it at all.

Critics warn the new program is not only set to target immigrants in the country, but could be the precipice of a new domestic surveillance paradigm.

“It looks dangerously like the construction of an internal spying agency,” Jay Stanley, senior policy analyst with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, explained to The American Prospect. “It’s a nightmare in the making.”

This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.
