author: David Swanson
title: We Will Miss Denis J. Halliday
content:
Chapters, Culture of Peace, Europe, Ireland Chapter, Videos

By World BEYOND War, October 14, 2026

Here is a video of a WBW webinar with Denis Halliday:

Notice of death from this website:

Denis J. Halliday, son of the late Stanley and Kathleen of Terenure, Dublin 6 and Errislannan, Co. Galway, brother of the late Leo, died peacefully in the presence of his family on 11th October 2026.

Deeply loved and treasured by Fransisca, Keaton and Lena, Leo and Eileen, Orla, Niamh and Vincent, Paul, Aiden, Jasmine and Nichole.

Lovingly cherished by his extended family and friends, colleagues, his fellow Friends and many more around the world.

Remembered always for the courage of his convictions, his integrity and kindness. A sane voice in an insane world, and one needed now more than ever. A rare man who stood for what was right, even at personal cost.

With Denis’s departure, our consciences are quietened, yet awakened. May we keep a part of his voice alive in our own by speaking out when others stay silent.

Denis began a life of service as a Friends (Quaker) volunteer in Kenya, followed by 34 years with the United Nations, where he rose to Assistant Secretary-General and served as Humanitarian Coordinator in Iraq. His resignation in 1998, in protest of the Iraqi sanctions, marked not an end but a new chapter. Denis continued to devote himself to peace and human rights. His work was recognised with the Gandhi International Peace Award in 2003.

Denis was not only a voice for peace but an active participant, he sailed in 2010 on the MV Rachel Corrie, the Irish aid ship that sought to break the blockade of Gaza.

At home in Ireland Denis was a steadfast advocate of Irish neutrality, opposing the use of Shannon Airport by US military aircraft. He lent his voice to countless other causes, and through it all, his commitment to humanity and accountability never wavered.

Denis will be remembered at Churchtown Friend’s Meeting House, Religious Society of Friends, Dublin 14, D14 F620 on Tuesday (20th October) from 10.30am to 11.30am followed by private burial.

Family flowers only please. Donations, if desired, to Barnardos or the NSPCA.

Due to limited parking in the area, public transport is recommended to reach the Meeting House. Luas stop, Windy Arbour, located 200 metres away.

If you select to make a recurring contribution of at least $15 per month, you may select a thank-you gift. We thank our recurring donors on our website.

author: Eliel Peterson
title: Death as liberation
content:
Death as liberation is hardly a comfortable political proposition to digest. In a world where Black death is often the common condition, there is a well-established insistence on our living. So what do we make of two of Africa’s greatest filmmakers, Ousmane Sembène and Souleymane Cissé, whose earliest cinematic visions, expressed through their respective debut features 

Black Girl

 (1966) and 

Den Muso

 (1975), center on the suffering, alienation, and eventual deaths of Black women?

Sembène’s 

Black Girl

 is preoccupied with racial violence and the economic exploitation that continues to structure relations between Senegal and France. The film follows Diouana, a young Senegalese woman who accepts employment with a white French family and travels to Antibes believing she is embarking on a new life. While Cissé’s 

Den Muso

, turns inward, examining interpersonal violence and the ways patriarchal power consumes family life and communities, weakening the broader social fabric of a nation. The film follows Tenin, a mute young woman who becomes pregnant after being raped, exposing the brutal underbelly of the patriarchal violence imposed upon her. Despite the differences in their circumstances, both films position death as a troubling possibility of liberation for their central characters.

Tenin (Dounamba Dany Coulibaly) in a still from Souleymane Cissé’s 

Den Muso

 (1975).

The history of Black resistance has not solely been confined to the preservation of life. From enslaved Africans who leapt from ships during the Middle Passage, to those who faced death in the fight against their oppression, 

It is true

 that to rather die than to endure is not a popular or digestible form of liberation. Although these acts are not equivalent, nor do they carry the same weight as the deaths of these fictional characters, Sembène and Cissé, raise an uncomfortable question: what does life mean for a person stripped of agency, recognition, and self-determination?

For Diouana and Tenin, freedom remains out of reach because of the structures governing their everyday lives that continually deny these women full humanity: Tenin’s father and her rapist, Diouana’s white employers. This sustained stripping of humanity produces what I would argue is already a death, albeit a social one, that precedes their physical endings. Sembène and Cissé challenge audiences by asking what is living for the dehumanized. Diouana travels to France only to find her livelihood replaced by isolation and unpaid, alienated labor, while Tenin’s body becomes a site upon which familial and communal shame, punishment, and control are dumped. Death, therefore, is at the core of both films from the outset, existing not only as a shocking culminating event, but as a condition of violence. By the end of each film, Sembène and Cissé are not arguing over whether death is a worthy or noble choice for self-liberation; rather, they position the act of self-annihilation as the only remaining form of control available to their characters, and as an indictment of a society in which death is the only option. 

It is understandable to recoil at the self-inflicted violence that ultimately claims both Diouana and Tenin. One might ask why their rage is not directed solely towards those who harmed them. Why does Tenin’s retaliation extend beyond her rapist? Why doesn’t Diouana exact revenge on her employers and flee France? These questions linger because death feels like an unsatisfying conclusion, one that denies us, as audiences, the catharsis of resistance. We want these women to fight back and survive. We want their suffering to lead somewhere other than death. Yet perhaps the more daunting question is not why these women die, but whether we find their deaths more difficult to accept than the suffering that precedes them. What is ultimately more uncomfortable to confront: their deaths, or the conditions that made life itself unbearable?

Neither film offers an uncomplicated answer. To read Diouana’s and Tenin’s deaths as acts of liberation is not to suggest that their deaths resolve the violence they endure, or that self-annihilation is freedom in any complete sense. Their deaths do not dismantle the structures that dehumanized them. What death offers these women, perhaps then, is not freedom but a final assertion of agency within those systems. This is what makes their endings so devastating: the possibility of control emerges only when the possibility of living on their own terms has been all but extinguished.

Decades later, 

Black Girl

 and 

Den Muso

 remain essential viewing, not only for their place in the landscape of African cinema, but for their boldness in confronting the most uncomfortable, divisive, and difficult questions surrounding post-independent life. Both films position death as a troubling yet legible response to systems that make life itself untenable, refusing a comforting resolution. Sembène and Cissé began their careers with audacious visions and hard questions, a truth that held throughout their working lives.

Long live the giants of African cinema, and may their audacious clarity continue to shape how we see, think, and imagine our world.

author: Chris Walker
title: Supreme Court to Hear Trump Arguments to Keep Musk’s DOGE Records Secret
content:
Elon Musk has spent over $360 million in support of Trump’s MAGA allies for this year’s midterm elections.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

On Tuesday, the United States Supreme Court agreed to hear an appeal from the Trump administration challenging a lawsuit that seeks access to records stemming from Elon Musk’s time leading the so-called “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE).

DOGE was responsible for ripping through the budgets of several federal agencies last year, ostensibly in the name of cutting wasteful spending but oftentimes targeting spending priorities opposed by President Donald Trump and Musk. The initiative operated without congressional oversight.

The U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), which ran foreign aid projects around the world, faced the largest cuts. A former leading USAID administrator estimated over 700,000 deaths could be attributable to cuts made by DOGE from its beginning through July 2026.

Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), a nonprofit watchdog group, filed a lawsuit to access records relating to DOGE’s work, arguing that the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) applied to DOGE. A federal judge agreed, and an appellate court confirmed the ruling. However, in June 2025, the Supreme Court intervened and sent the lawsuit back to the lower court to narrow the scope of open records requests.

After the lawsuit began to advance again, the Trump administration appealed to the Supreme Court to block it, arguing that the lower court decision “intrudes into the autonomy and confidentiality of presidential advisers and augurs time-consuming and burdensome discovery litigation.” The high court agreed to review the decision and to hear the case during this term, likely at the start of next year.

The Trump administration’s effort to keep information about DOGE hidden from the public is yet another example contradicting the president’s claims that he is “the most transparent” chief executive in U.S. history.

In a recent interview with The Economist, Musk said that he “got a little too involved in politics, got carried away, frankly.”

However, he appears to be back in the game: Musk has spent around $366 million in this year’s midterm election cycle in support of Republican candidates backing Trump’s MAGA agenda. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has also brought him on board a three-person panel that will examine the future of technology for the U.S. military – a tremendous conflict of interest, given that Musk regularly seeks (and is often granted) billion-dollar contracts with the government.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Burnham Rules Out Coalition With the Green Party
content:
Andy Burnham has ruled out a coalition deal with the Greens over the party’s recently-passed conference motion on Zionism, calling it “antisemitic”. 




In the Commons on Wednesday, the prime minister responded to a question from Tory MP Dame Harriett Baldwin by saying he “unequivocally condemns” the ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion, which 

passed by 1,022 votes to 813

 at the Greens’ biggest ever conference in Brighton earlier this month. 




Burnham said: “It is wrong. It is antisemitic. This side of the House will have nothing to do with it”, adding that “we cannot support a partnership with a party that holds the position that has recently been adopted”. 




Burnham’s rejection of a future deal with the Greens over a conference motion stands in contrast to the position of Green party leader Zack Polanski, who said it would be “silly” to rule out a coalition with Labour at the next general election. 




He told Channel 4 News at the party conference: “If a Labour government were ready to make the serious change that we needed, then of course my door would be open.”




Polling currently suggests there will be a hung parliament at the next general election. While Labour is expected to be the largest party, according to 

predictions from Electoral Calculus

 as of 30 September, it’s predicted to fall 13 seats short of the 326 needed for a majority, meaning it would need to do a deal with another party to rule. 




Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch has also ruled out a deal – in this case with Reform –

 telling the BBC earlier this month

 that Reform is “neck deep in scandal” and joining forces with them would “just be one problem after another”.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: ‘Unacceptable’ for officer who killed Clyde River man to avoid inquest: Coroner
content:
A public inquest into an RCMP officer’s 

fatal shooting

 of a Clyde River man in 2020 has been adjourned because the officer who fired the fatal shot in the incident has not confirmed he will participate.




Jerry Natanine wants the officer who killed his son Abraham Natatine to answer questions about the May 2020 incident that led to Abraham’s death. (Photo courtesy of Clara Noah)




Abraham Natanine was 31 when he died on May 6, 2020, after Cpl. Bryan Vaughan, shot him. The shooting happened after officers responded to a disturbance at a home at around 11 p.m. the evening prior.




In 2021, Ottawa police investigated and 

concluded

 there were no grounds for charges. The police investigation also concluded Vaughan fired the fatal shot, said Andrew Morrison, the lawyer representing the Natanine family.




Nunavut law requires a public inquest into deaths involving an on-duty police officer. The inquest into Natanine’s death was scheduled to start on Oct. 5 and end on Oct. 9.




“I take their investigation at face value, but I still want to ask questions to the officer that was involved in the shooting,” said Jerry Natanine, Abraham’s father, in an interview.




Morrison asked a judge on Sept. 28 to adjourn the inquest after Nunavut Chief Coroner Marianna Cervantes informed him it would go ahead despite Vaughan’s presence being unconfirmed.
















A judge granted that adjournment on Sept. 29.




The purpose of the inquest is to shine a light on what happened that night, which Morrison said can’t happen without each officer’s participation.




Cervantes declined to comment on the reason, when reached by Nunatsiaq News.




The Nunavut Coroner’s Act gives the chief coroner power to summon witnesses for inquests.




“The RCMP officer that was involved in the shooting hasn’t been summoned,” said Jerry Natanine.




“Summoning RCMP officers that are involved in shootings, that’s the norm. That’s normal for coroners inquests. It’s been done before in Nunavut.”
















Natanine’s family wants to question Vaughan over discrepancies about what occurred on the day Abraham Natanine was killed, including Abraham’s words and conduct, the alleged weapon and the number of shots fired.




“Questions also remain about the officers’ actions after the shooting,” says the request for adjournment Morrison filed with the court.




The two other officers who were present when Natanine was shot had confirmed their attendance as of Sept. 18, according to court documents.




Nunatsiaq News reached out to Matthew Scott, the lawyer representing the involved RCMP officers. He declined to comment, redirecting requests for comment to RCMP.




Nunavut RCMP will participate in the inquest if called upon to provide evidence, said Sgt. George Henrie, spokesperson for Nunavut RCMP, although he said he had no information he could share about the participation of officers involved.
















“Our family is not seeking to prevent the inquest from occurring,” Jerry Natanine said in an affidavit. “We seek a short adjournment so that reasonable steps can be taken to secure the meaningful participation of a witness whom the chief coroner has already described as central.”




Court documents also note RCMP’s reasons for Vaughan to not attend, which include concerns about his mental health and prior threats from community members. Vaughan is no longer employed with the RCMP, so he cannot be compelled by RCMP to attend, say the court documents.




“It is not acceptable for Cpl. Vaughan to avoid taking part in the inquest,” Cervantes noted in a Sept. 18 letter to RCMP’s counsel.




“Unless the RCMP provide adequate reasoning and evidence that Cpl. Vaughan cannot attend, initiating contempt proceedings is available under sec. 46 of the Coroner’s Act.”




Cervantes has offered various accommodations, such as a single-day attendance, a support person, and an advance hearing to set ground rules.




Natanine’s father also said does not believe enough evidence was brought forward to assess the validity of Vaughan’s mental health concerns, and suggested the inquest could be good for Vaughan, too.




“This can be a good closure, for the family, for all of us, and for the RCMP officer himself too,” he said. “If the officer is having issues psychologically, I would imagine he would want closure from this as well.”

author: newsroom
title: Παρέμβαση Γιάννη Μάγγου: «Αμετανόητοι οι κατηγορούμενοι»
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης: 

Παρέμβαση Γιάννη Μάγγου: «Αμετανόητοι οι κατηγορούμενοι»




Ο Γιάννης Μάγγος, πατέρας του Βασίλειου Μάγγου, μετά την ολοκλήρωση των απολογιών 

των κατηγορουμένων αστυνομικών για τον βασανισμό του γιού του

 στο Μικτό Ορκωτό Δικαστήριο της Καρδίτσας, παρεμβαίνει με δημόσια ανάρτησή του στην οποία θέτει ερωτήματα και προς τον υπουργό Μιχάλη Χρυσοχοΐδη.




Υπενθυμίζεται ότι το δικαστήριο δεν έχει επιτρέψει την παράσταση προς υποστήριξη της κατηγορίας για την οικογένεια του Β. Μάγγου.




Ολόκληρο το κείμενο της παρέμβασης που δημοσίευσε ο Γιάννης Μάγγος:







Αμετανόητοι οι κατηγορούμενοι




Ολοκληρώθηκαν στις 12.10.2026 οι απολογίες των έξι κατηγορούμενων αστυνομικών, βασανιστών του Βασίλειου Μάγγου. Όσον αφορά για το συνολικό περιστατικό, παραδέχτηκαν ότι «έγινε σωρεία λαθών και παραλείψεων» για τα οποία ευθύνονται και οι ίδιοι. «Έπραξα λάθος» είπαν.




Κανένας τους όμως δεν ζήτησε συγγνώμη από εμάς τους γονείς του για την προσβλητική, κακοποιητική και ανάρμοστη συμπεριφορά τους.




Είναι αδίστακτοι και αμετανόητοι.







Στην ερώτηση για την κινητικότητά του, απάντησαν πως, όταν κατέβηκε από το αυτοκίνητο, περπάτησε κανονικά, ανέβηκε τις σκάλες και έφτασε στον πρώτο όροφο της Υποδιεύθυνσης Ασφάλειας Βόλου χωρίς δυσκολία.







Ακριβώς! Επειδή τα πιο σφοδρά χτυπήματα και η πιο βάναυση συμπεριφορά επακολούθησαν κατόπιν μέσα στην Ασφάλεια.







Και σε άλλη ερώτηση του δικαστηρίου, πώς δικαιολογούνται τα έξι σπασμένα πλευρά και η θλάση στο ήπαρ, η απάντηση όλων των κατηγορούμενων ήταν ότι αυτοί μέσα στην Υ/Α δεν έκαναν τίποτα, ότι ο Βασίλειος Μάγγος δεν είχε τίποτα, δεν παραπονέθηκε για τίποτα…













– Και γιατί ο Μάγγος δεν πονούσε μόνο κατά το διάστημα από 4 μέχρι 5 μ.μ. που τον είχαν στην Ασφάλεια;




– …













Οι μάρτυρες που τον βρήκαν κατέθεσαν ότι πονούσε φρικτά και δεν μπορούσε να σηκωθεί να περπατήσει. Όλα αυτά επιβεβαιώθηκαν από τις καταθέσεις των γιατρών και την αξονική τομογραφία. Και γιατί δεν τον πήγαν στο νοσοκομείο; «Δεν το ζήτησε»…










Ούτε τους ζήτησε νερό: «Αν ζητούσε κάτι, μέχρι και ελικόπτερο θα κατεβάζαμε για να του το δώσουμε»… Κανένας όμως δεν είπε ότι του έδωσαν, έστω, ένα ποτήρι νερό.







Όπως κατήγγειλε ο ίδιος, τον παρέπεμψαν να πιει νερό από ένα χαλασμένο ψύκτη, σύρθηκε μέχρι εκεί και προσπάθησε να πάρει λίγες σταγόνες νερού στο στόμα του για να ανακουφίσει το σωματικό και ψυχικό του μαρτύριο. Και αυτοί τον χλεύαζαν και γελούσαν εις βάρος του για την προσπάθεια που κατέβαλλε. Αυτό του κόστισε ανυπολόγιστα, ακύρωσε την ύπαρξή του, όπως διαπιστώσαμε κι εμείς οι γονείς του.




– Και σαν προσαχθείς, σε ποιον ήταν χρεωμένος;




– …




Και ενώ δεν επρόκειτο παρά για μία «απλή προσαγωγή» κι ο Βασίλειος Μάγγος ήταν «ήσυχος και ήρεμος» (όπως είπαν), γιατί απαιτούνταν η συνδρομή έξι αστυνομικών; Τέσσερις της ΟΠΚΕ και δύο της Υ/Α Βόλου;




Πάλι απάντησαν ανεύθυνα, λέγοντας ψέμματα ότι δεν παρείχαν συνδρομή. Στην προανάκριση όμως άλλα κατέθεσαν. 




Π.χ. κατηγορούμενος της ΟΠΚΕ: «..προσήλθαν και όλοι οι υπόλοιποι μηνυόμενοι. Παρείχαμε επιτήρηση στον Μάγγο Β.» (έγγραφα 1,2,6).



















Κάποιος, σε σχετική ερώτηση του δικαστηρίου, γιατί άλλα έλεγαν πριν και άλλα τώρα, είχε την αφέλεια να απαντήσει ότι «άλλαξε η υπερασπιστική γραμμή»… Παρατήρηση του δικαστηρίου: «η αλήθεια δεν αλλάζει».




Όπως ακριβώς με την ιατροδικαστή και τους γιατρούς τους. Οι τρεις γνωμάτευσαν ότι τα πλευρά τα είχε σπασμένα, πριν τον χτυπήσουν μπροστά στα δικαστήρια και ο τέταρτος υποστήριξε ότι του τα έσπασαν μπροστά στα δικαστήρια.




Και τί ώρα αποχώρησαν από την υπηρεσία τους;




Οι αστυνομικοί της ΟΠΚΕ απάντησαν ότι αποχώρησαν πριν τις 5 μ.μ. Όμως στον Πίνακα Διάταξης της Υπηρεσίας και σε δεύτερο έγγραφο αναφέρεται ότι η υπηρεσία τους ήταν από 10π.μ. έως 6 μ.μ. (έγγραφα 3, 4, 5). Και ο σκοπός πύλης κατηγορηματικά κατέθεσε ότι τους είδε να αποχωρούν στις 6μ.μ.



















Και ποιοι αποχώρησαν πρώτοι; Όλοι ισχυρίστηκαν ότι οι κατηγορούμενοι της ΟΠΚΕ αποχώρησαν πρώτοι. Όμως στην προδικασία ένας κατηγορούμενος ισχυρίστηκε το αντίθετο (έγγραφο 6 – βλ. παραπάνω).




Αντιφάσεις, αντιφάσεις και ψέμματα…







Γιατί τον κράτησαν σχεδόν δύο ώρες και τον άφησαν αβοήθητο, ενώ ήταν ήδη χτυπημένος;







Του έκαναν σωματική έρευνα, (δεν του βρήκαν τίποτα) αλλά δεν αντιλήφθηκαν να πάσχει από κάτι: «Ηταν μια χαρά!».




Έκθεση σωματικής έρευνας, όμως, δεν συνέταξαν.

 Ούτε ενημέρωσαν τον εισαγγελέα. Κι ενώ έπρεπε, όπως ισχυρίστηκαν, να τον συλλάβουν για τα υποτιθέμενα αδικήματα αντίστασης κατά της αρχής και απόπειρα απελευθέρωσης κρατουμένου, παρ΄όλα αυτά δεν το έκαναν, ούτε σχημάτισαν δικογραφία εις βάρος του…




Όμως «αυτοί δεν ευθύνονται για τίποτα», οι ανώτεροί τους φταίνε που έδωσαν προφορικές εντολές να μη σχηματιστεί δικογραφία και να τον ελευθερώσουν.




«Φταίει ο διοικητής της Υ/Α»… «Ήταν εντολή άνωθεν να μη γίνει σύλληψη και δικογραφία»… «Ο διοικητής της Υ/Α δεν ενημέρωσε τον εισαγγελέα και βρισκόμαστε εμείς στο εδώλιο», κραύγαζαν αγανακτισμένοι! 




Όμως δεν ζήτησαν εξηγήσεις, γιατί «κανένας ανώτερος δεν θα δώσει λόγο σε κατώτερο ποτέ»! Και γι αυτό «πάντα την πληρώνουν οι χαμηλόβαθμοι»…




Και στην ερώτηση, 

γιατί δεν ήρθε ο διοικητής να καταθέσει

, «

Δεν ξέρω, είναι και εν ενεργεία

», απάντησαν.




Όμως, παρά την εμπειρία τους και την «εντιμότητά» τους, δεν αντέδρασαν, ούτε έκαναν αυτό που όφειλαν να πράξουν, να απαιτήσουν δηλαδή τη σύλληψή του και το σχηματισμό δικογραφίας, όπως οι ίδιοι διατείνονταν ότι έπρεπε να γίνει.




Στην προανάκριση όμως δεν ανέφεραν τίποτα από όλα αυτά!




Παρατηρούμε εδώ μία προσπάθεια να μεταφερθούν ευθύνες στην Αστυνομική Διεύθυνση ή στην Υ/Α Βόλου. Θα είχε μεγάλο ενδιαφέρον να ακούγαμε τις εξηγήσεις των ανωτέρων τους στις «μομφές» των κατηγορουμένων.




Ο διοικητής της Υ/Α Βόλου πάντως, παρότι ήταν μάρτυρας, 

δεν εμφανίστηκε στο δικαστήριο

…




Το πιο σημαντικό όμως που συνδέεται άμεσα με την προστασία του πολίτη είναι 

αν πράγματι η Αστυνομική Διεύθυνση Μαγνησίας και η Υ/Α Βόλου λειτουργούν κατ αυτόν τον παράτυπο, ανεξέλεγκτο τρόπο. Χωρίς δηλαδή να εφαρμόζεται ο νόμος, αλλά οι αποφάσεις παίρνονται από τους ανώτερους και εκτελούνται με προφορικές εντολές από τους υφισταμένους τους

, σύμφωνα με τις απολογίες των κατηγορούμενων…




Κάτι που αν ισχύει, πρέπει να απασχολήσει σοβαρά τον υπουργό Προστασίας του Πολίτη.




Κύριε Χρυσοχοΐδη, στη συγκεκριμένη περίπτωση, ο Βασίλειος Μάγγος οδηγήθηκε στο θάνατο εξ αιτίας όσων υπέστη μέσα στην Υ/Α Βόλου και οι κατηγορούμενοι πετάνε το μπαλάκι στους ανώτερους. Μήπως αυτά είναι δικαιολογίες και προφάσεις των κατηγορουμένων να ενεργούν κατ’ αυτόν τον τρόπο, γνωρίζοντας ότι θα έχουν το ατιμώρητο; Τι πραγματικά συμβαίνει;




Επίσης υποστήριξαν ότι είναι έμπειροι αστυνομικοί, ότι έχουν κάνει χιλιάδες συλλήψεις, όμως εκείνη την ημέρα όλα πήγαν στραβά, τίποτα δεν λειτούργησε σωστά, υπήρξε «σωρεία λαθών και παραλείψεων».




Καταμετρήσαμε και 21(!) παρεμβάσεις των συνηγόρων υπεράσπισης στις απολογίες των κατηγορουμένων καθώς και στις ερωτήσεις του δικαστηρίου. Τέλος, επικαλούμενοι τα θρησκευτικά τους αισθήματα, χρησιμοποίησαν επιχειρήματα που μόνο ως ύβρεις μπορούν να εκληφθούν.




Και όλοι τους δήλωσαν πως είναι περήφανοι που είναι οικογενειάρχες, που έχουν παιδιά και τα μεγαλώνουν.




Αυτό όμως δεν στάθηκε εμπόδιο στις 14 Ιουνίου 2020 να χτυπήσουν ανελέητα, να βασανίσουν ένα άλλο παιδί τον Βασίλειο Μάγγο και να τον στείλουν στο θάνατο.




[Από το Facebook του Γ. Μάγγου]




Παρέμβαση Γιάννη Μάγγου: «Αμετανόητοι οι κατηγορούμενοι»

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit crosswalk lights temporarily shut down
content:
Iqaluit’s only controlled 

crosswalk

 

is disabled following a two-vehicle collision last week.




The lighted crossing is adjacent to the intersection of Niaqungusiariaq Road and Queen Elizabeth Way.




One of the crosswalk’s two light poles 

fell Oct. 8

 after the incident, which halted

 early afternoon traffic for 90 minutes. No injuries were reported.




Residents should exercise caution while using the crosswalk, said acting city spokesperson Donna Keenainak in a public service announcement issued Wednesday morning.




Drivers are also asked to be cautious when approaching the intersection.




The busy intersection sits between the Qikiqtani General Hospital clinic entrance and the Sailijaaqvik Boarding Home, which sits at the southeast corner of the intersection. 




The city’s public works department did not immediately provide a timeline for repairs.
















The crosswalk was installed in 2024.

author: Jai Dulani
title: The Tech Oligarchs Have Captured Washington — Now They’re Pivoting to the States
content:
AI and crypto firms have spent record amounts on the 2026 midterms.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Late last month, the wealthiest tech executives on the planet smiled next to President Donald Trump after essentially pinky-swearing they would voluntarily adopt safety policies around AI. While Trump described the agreement as “morally binding,” legal liability or enforcement measures were not explicit parts of the accord. The key takeaway from this handshake deal is that the people with the most amount of political power sit in Silicon Valley, not in Washington, D.C.

With the midterm elections just weeks away, it’s a good time to reflect on what Big Tech’s actions during this election season have revealed about its agenda and the larger context of the industry’s political influence. From CNN to The New York Times to NPR, there has been extensive news coverage of the hundreds of millions of dollars Big Tech has spent on the midterm elections. Months before Election Day, corporate spending this election cycle had already exceeded total disclosed corporate spending in the 2024 presidential election by 12 percent. The top two industries setting this record — with over half a billion dollars spent and counting — are crypto and AI. This unprecedented corporate spending on midterm elections is key to the tech industry’s plan to rig every level of government to work for the industry, from state legislatures to Congress.

The crypto industry is the largest political spender this election cycle, having spent over $200 million so far. The race it spent the most on was Felix Barry Moore’s campaign for U.S. Senate in Alabama. Crypto super PACs spent over $12 million supporting Moore, who has a pro-crypto track record; as the U.S. representative for Alabama’s 1st district, Moore co-sponsored a bill that prohibits the Federal Reserve from developing or issuing a central bank digital currency for U.S. monetary policy. This leaves digital assets under private control, away from federal scrutiny, which is what the industry wants.

In Illinois, crypto-related PACs spent over $10 million against former Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, who is running for a seat in the U.S. Senate. Stratton has been vocal against the crypto industry. Politico reported that Stratton is endorsed by two prominent industry critics: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Pritzker signed a digital assets law last year establishing regulatory oversight and protections for consumers against scams and fraud. In 2025, the FBI reported over $11 billion in losses related to cryptocurrency fraud in its Internet Crime Report.

Crypto corporations were also the dominant corporate political spenders in 2024 and gave $18 million to Trump’s 2025 inauguration. These contributions have paid off many times over the course of Trump’s second term. Trump removed Biden-era regulators and replaced them with crypto industry business partners or former industry insiders. In April 2025, the Trump administration shuttered the Department of Justice’s crypto enforcement team. Trump pardoned several crypto companies and billionaires that were under investigation for criminal money laundering and fraud, often after receiving investments in his own crypto empire. In June of this year, it was revealed that the Trump family has made at least $2.3 billion from crypto-related ventures during Trump’s second term.

Unprecedented corporate spending on midterm elections is key to the tech industry’s plan to rig every level of government to work for the industry.

This election season, Trump and the crypto industry were pushing for Congress to pass the Clarity Act, a bill essentially written by the crypto industry that locks in deregulation. From 2025 through August 2026, crypto companies Coinbase and Ripple spent a combined $18 million on lobbying Congress. Crypto donors gave Trump’s primary super PAC, MAGA Inc., over $88 million, more than any other industry. On September 15, the Clarity Act failed to advance through the Senate by a vote of 49-50. However, the attempt shed light on what the industry is seeking in terms of legislation: exemption from robust oversight, weak consumer and investor protections, and no prevention of conflicts of interest for self-enrichment and corruption.

One doesn’t need to be invested in crypto to be harmed by the industry. Crypto is increasingly making its way into banks, retirement plans, and payment systems. As economic expert Tonantzin Carmona has noted, when it comes to crypto, “Fundamental public interest questions remain underexplored in current policy discussions. … From financial instability to investor fraud to environmental and public safety risks, the potential consequences are real and growing.” Indeed, Black and Latino communities are disproportionately harmed by the volatility and predatory targeting of the crypto industry. Chastity Murphy, a former economic policy adviser to Rep. Rashida Tlaib, said the fight around regulation is “about who controls money, and whether digital infrastructure serves the public or entrenches private power.”

Crypto’s political spending is about entrenching private power and extracting wealth, leaving everyday people vulnerable to a destabilized financial system with no recourse when scammed.

As Alex Hanna and Emily M. Bender describe in their book, The AI Con, there are two camps in the AI world: AI doomers and AI boosters. Each camp is part of the same AI hype machine, in which, as scientists and advocate Timnit Gebru states, “the utopia and doom is still a marketing ploy.” Over the course of the AI industry’s massive spending leading up to the midterms, the two forces that have embodied this debate are OpenAI and Anthropic. The Leading the Future super PAC network, often referred to as OpenAI’s super PAC, and the Public First Action super PAC network, backed by Anthropic, have been framed as pro-innovation and pro-safety respectively.

A look at super PAC spending in North Carolina exemplifies the difference between the two super PAC networks, as well as how they ultimately advance the same outcome. Anthropic’s super PAC spent over $1.6 million on ads backing Rep. Valerie Foushee in the primary for North Carolina’s 4th congressional district. Foushee is one of three co-chairs of the House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy, to which she was appointed in December 2025. Foushee has supported regulation such as a requirement to label when content is made by generative AI. Also in North Carolina, Leading the Future spent over $500,000 on ads promoting Republican Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina’s 1st district Republican primary. Buckhout has promised to maintain “American dominance in AI.” While the “innovation” camp tends to spend more on Republicans and the “safety” camp on Democrats, these two sides are fundamentally the same; focusing on future hypothetical hype or doom leads to the public ignoring the current harms of AI: surveillance, data centers, labor exploitation, pollution, and discrimination.

David Sacks, former AI and crypto czar for the Trump administration, has described Anthropic as running a “sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering.” In many ways, Sacks is right. As Lina Khan, who served as chair of the Federal Trade Commission from 2021 to 2025, has pointed out, “Much of the commentary from the executives suggests they currently operate in a legal vacuum, as if AI has wiped clean the regulatory map. In fact, their business practices — including how they develop and deploy their technologies — are already subject to longstanding laws.” As Big Tech and corporate media set false terms of debate — innovation vs. regulation — we must remember, there are plenty of laws on the books to tackle the harms of AI. What we’re lacking is enforcement.

Last year, Trump and the AI industry pushed for federal preemption, proposing to block states from regulating AI for a decade. Crypto exchange Coinbase also asked the Department of Justice to submit a “views letter” to Congress arguing that any new federal crypto legislation should include strong preemption provisions, meaning that when federal law is explicit, it overrides conflicting state crypto regulations. The tech industry didn’t win preemption. Now, in response to the growing wins in the grassroots movement to resist data centers, the industry has pivoted to political spending in state and local races.

The industry is running the same playbook at the state level that it ran federally: game the system to ensure there is little to no meaningful regulation.

California has been a major battleground of this pivot. Just this past year, nearly 30 AI-related measures have been enacted in the state, with Gov. Gavin Newsom having recently signed 11 AI regulatory bills into law. Crypto and AI corporations have poured money into lobbying efforts as well as California state PACs. Meta launched its own California PAC, Mobilizing Economic Transformation Across (Meta) California, pouring in $20 million solely for local elections in the state. The result has largely been watered-down bills and some vetoes, with some notable exceptions. Workers were able to claim victory as bills were passed that protect workers against surveillance and the ability to be fired by an algorithm. Overall, the industry is running the same playbook at the state level that it ran federally: game the system to ensure there is little to no meaningful regulation.

Research reveals that the policies Meta and Google opposed via super PAC spending include AI safety laws like California’s Senate Bill 53 (S.B. 53), which would require companies to disclose how various safety issues are approached, how “catastrophic” risks are inspected, and how “critical safety incidents” are responded to. S.B. 53 would also make it easier for members of the public and company whistleblowers to report potential safety risks.

Another law Meta and Google opposed via super PAC spending is California’s Assembly Bill 2013 (A.B. 2013), also known as the Generative AI Training Data Transparency Act. The law requires AI developers to clearly explain which dataset sources were used to train models and if personal information or synthetic data was used to train the model.

Crypto billionaires Chris Larsen and Tim Draper also funded the Grow California PAC, which focused on electing corporate-friendly candidates as a “counterforce” to the state’s labor movement. In District 67 (Los Angeles and Orange County), Grow California spent nearly $1.5 million opposing UNITE HERE Co-President Ada Briceño. This was the highest spending in any state assembly race in California. The tech billionaires outspent organized labor almost 7 to 1. Briceño lost in the primary. Big Tech is not just protecting its industry; it is also funding opposition to worker organizing.

Big Tech is also funding broader attacks on democracy. Larsen is funding a ballot measure in San Francisco that would make it harder to advance public proposals via petitions. Proposition D would increase the number of signatures required to qualify ballot initiatives from 2 percent to 8 percent of the city’s registered votes, or roughly 10,000 to 42,000. Previously, Larson has also personally spent over $9 million expanding police surveillance in San Francisco through a fleet of drones and 2,700 private cameras that cops can watch in real time.

What has been revealed this election cycle is that, in the age of crypto and the AI boom, Silicon Valley has carried out a near-total capture of our federal government. Meanwhile, Big Tech has pivoted to state elections in an attempt to undermine the levels of government where our organizing still has leverage. Our best tool is to continue organizing people — fighting data centers, fighting flock cameras, fighting the tech companies that are destroying our lives. It is only through this grassroots power that we can show politicians and political parties that they need to be more afraid of organized people than they are of upsetting tech donors.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Sally Rooney’s Books Can No Longer Be Sold in the UK
content:
Bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney has announced that her books can no longer be sold in the UK due to the British government’s ban on Palestine Action. 




In a statement on Wednesday, the award-winning Normal People author said that due to her publicly-stated intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, including with 

royalties from her work

, “the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence”. 




Rooney added: “After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”




Palestine Action became the first direct action group in British history to be proscribed as a terror organisation under Keir Starmer’s Labour government last summer. 




Palestine Action is not proscribed or otherwise banned in the Republic of Ireland, where Rooney lives. 




Rooney’s 

outspoken support for Palestine Action

 has previously disrupted her work in Britain. In September 2025, she was forced 

to cancel a trip to the UK

 to receive the Sky Arts award for her latest novel, 2024’s Intermezzo, due to the risk she would be arrested under the Terrorism Act. 




She also submitted a statement to the High Court in support of the legal challenge to Palestine Action’s proscription in November 2025, arguing that the ban impeded free expression, including cultural and artistic expression, and warning that her works could disappear from UK booksellers altogether. 




Faber, Rooney’s UK and Ireland publisher, said: “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.




“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”




Since the ban on Palestine Action came into force, more than 3,700 people have been arrested for opposing the proscription, the vast majority for holding paper signs that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”




According to the Home Office’s own data, terror-related arrests have risen by 1,553% in the last year, with 94% of them linked to support for Palestine Action. 




Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori is challenging the proscription in the Supreme Court, beginning on 4 November.

title: Newcomers to Trail Hunting Week: A Very Awkward Recruitment Drive.
content:
After last year’s embarrassing 

Farcical Friday

, the pro-blood sports lobby group, the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA), has somehow managed to surpass itself in the ridiculousness stakes – and it’s not even 

Smokescreen Saturday

 yet!




By now, you might have thought the hunting fraternity would have learned to exercise a little more care when selecting which hunts to showcase in its desperate attempt to maintain the smokescreen of trail hunting.




But no, you actually couldn’t make this up if you tried.




Erm, awkward. Trail Hunting is banned in Scotland.




Just days after a 

Lauderdale Hunt huntswoman

 was convicted of illegally hunting a fox with hounds, the Lauderdale is advertising an event encouraging newcomers to discover the joys of ‘trail hunting’. The event poster was uploaded onto the Lauderdale Hunt’s social media and quickly spotted by Glasgow Hunt Saboteurs.




In Scotland. Where trail hunting is banned.




The Lauderdale’s joint meet with the Berwickshire Hounds is seemingly delighted to support 

Newcomers to Trail Hunting Week

 in Wedderlie, Gordon, on Saturday 17 October.




Saturday also happens to be the annual smokescreen performance day, when a carefully selected (or perhaps a not-so carefully selected) handful of hunts are wheeled out to put on a display for Tory MP’s and other indignitaries. If they are lucky, GBeebies and the Torygraph might even dispatch a tea-boy masquerading as a journalist to cover the spectacle.




The since-deleted poster promises a warm-welcome courtesy of the Tilson family, a chance to meet the hounds and follow on horseback or foot. No previous experience is necessary.




Clearly, no previous knowledge of Scottish hunting legislation is needed either.




So-called trail hunting has been banned in Scotland since 2023.  Under the Hunting with Dogs (Scotland) Act 2023, following an animal-based scent laid for hounds is prohibited.




As if that weren’t awkward enough, the Lauderdale Hunt was in the news recently for illegal hunting. 




On 05 October 2026, Claire Bellamy, former master and huntswoman of the Lauderdale Hunt, was convicted in Paisley Sheriff Court of deliberately hunting a fox with dogs outside the area permitted by a NatureScot licence.




In fact, it was reported that she wasn’t even named on the NatureScot licence in any case!




Convicted huntswoman Claire Bellamy wasn’t even named on the licence.

 Image: Glasgow Hunt Saboteurs




The poster invites the public to “Come and discover more about trail hunting and our community”.




Perhaps they first ought to discover what the law says.




The poster forms part of the wider campaign organised and promoted by the Countryside Alliance’s propaganda wing, 

Future for Hunting

 and the British Hound Sports Association (BHSA) – itself a rebrand of the disgraced Hunting Office.




As if that wasn’t farcical enough, another participating hunt has managed to make this public relations disaster even more awkward.




Three Counties Hunt Saboteurs reported this week that The Worcestershire Hunt – one of the four hunts selected to put on a trail demo on Saturday – was filmed by a member of the West Midlands Badger group in an incident involving a fox and a badger sett.




The incident was said to have occurred in the Wilmcote/Aston Cantlow area of Warwickshire. Sabs say that an officer from the Badger Group who had been in the area in relation to a swan rescue, witnessed the hunted fox run past them near a canal.




She noticed two men in the corner of a nearby wood and approached them telling them that police were on their way. The men scarpered and the large badger sett where they had been was discovered to have freshly blocked entrances.




One of the two men by the freshly blocked badger sett at the Worcestershire Hunt meet.




After last year’s Farcical Friday, you might have expected the BHSA to be a little more selective, but then again, finding a hunt that actually lays a trail must certainly be quite a challenge for hunting’s propaganda unit.




A HSA spokesperson said




“It is no surprise to see this poster advertising what is essentially an illegal activity, made even worse by the Launderdale’s recent conviction. Sometimes they drop the ball and tell us exactly who they are, whereas other times they put up the smokescreen and invite pro-hunt MP’s and media to report on it once a year.




No one is fooled.




The government needs to get on with the job now and ban it properly”. 
















The post 

Newcomers to Trail Hunting Week: A Very Awkward Recruitment Drive.

 appeared first on 

Hunt Saboteurs Association

.

author: Redação
title: Big Problema
content:
O 

Big Problema

 é uma conversa sobre o impacto das escolhas de quem está com a caneta na mão. Esse podcast narrativo foi idealizado pela primeira turma de 

trainees da

 Agência Pública

 e procura entender como grandes empreendimentos têm impactado a cultura local das cidades brasileiras. Sabe quando bate um desespero porque a solução dos problemas ao seu redor não parece estar sob seu controle? Então, esse é um Big Problema.




A cada episódio, uma reportagem em áudio parte da vivência de um dos trainees para abordar como nossa relação com o espaço tem sido transformada com a chegada de gigantes da tecnologia e mais. Olhando as particularidades de cada cidade, esperamos mostrar que a distância não deve nos enganar: no fim, um problema local também é um problema coletivo. O nosso questionamento é: em nome dos interesses de poucos, o que temos deixado de fazer?

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” – 

Ivorian activist







The fourth regional 

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.




Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.




The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.




As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.







“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 – 

DRC activist-participant







Turning shared struggles into collective power




From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.




Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.




Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:







The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  




Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.




Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.




Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.




Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?




Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.




Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.







The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The 

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.




The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.




It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.




Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises




Africa contributes relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces disproportionate climate impacts. Women in rural, coastal and forest communities frequently bear the burden of climate-related losses while also confronting the effects of land grabs, pollution, displacement and the expansion of extractive industries.




The WCA challenged approaches to climate action that reproduce these injustices or treat African communities as passive recipients of false solutions.




Climate reparations must mean more than promises of future assistance. They must include substantial and accessible resources to address loss and damage, support adaptation, restore ecosystems, and strengthen community-led alternatives. They must also confront the historical and ongoing responsibility of wealthy, high-emitting countries and corporations for the climate crisis.




African women demand accountability, not charity; justice, not debt; and development that puts the wellbeing of people and the planet above corporate profit.







“

African women are strongly connected to the climate. We are the ones doing agriculture. We are connected to our environment. Decisions cannot be taken without women.

” – 

Cordelia Ndagha, Ministry of Women’s Empowerment and the Family, Cameroon







From Yaoundé to the world: the work continues




The Assembly’s significance extends beyond the four days spent together in Yaoundé. It lies in the relationships and solidarities strengthened; the experiences, knowledge and skills shared; the collective analysis and perspectives deepened; and the foundations laid for sustained action across communities and countries.




At the heart of the WCA is a call for climate reparations as key to climate justice for Africa. This call will continue to shape the advancement of an ecofeminist Pan African permanent assembly that recognises that climate solutions cannot be imposed from “above.” Women and communities whose lives, territories, and futures are at stake must shape them.







“Beyond celebrating the success of hosting this event, we are excited to transform this momentum into a permanent space driven by concrete actions on the ground at our different national levels.”

 – 

Véronique Mbole, Cameroon







Building on the inaugural 

African Women’s Climate Justice Day

 held this April, the conclusion of the 2026 Women’s Climate Assembly marks the beginning of the next phase of movement building. The country delegations agreed to undertake solidarity actions, linking local community struggles to national, regional and international advocacy and collective actions at strategic moments.




ENDS




For media enquiries contact:




Veronique Mbole

 – Green Development Advocates | Cell: +237 79392311




Connie Nagiah

 – WoMin African Alliance | Cell: +27 0827300653

title: Diyarbakır City Hospital workers demand their rights
content:
Construction workers at the Diyarbakır (Amed) City Hospital construction site, where work began in November 2021, have been subjected to systematic pressure for years. The workers previously staged two protests over unpaid wages and difficult working conditions. Most recently, they launched another protest against dismissals linked to their union membership. The protest, organised by 75 members of the Construction and Road Workers' Union (Yapı Yol-Sen) demanding improved working conditions and the recognition of their employment rights, has continued for 14 days.







 







The workers have continued their protest with traditional halay dances, demanding an end to unfair wage deductions, the underpayment of Social Security Institution (SGK) contributions based on wages lower than their actual earnings, unpaid overtime and Sunday work, and problems concerning travel allowances and workplace safety. They said they faced pressure, threats and the risk of dismissal for exercising their trade union rights and vowed to continue their struggle until their demands were met.




‘We faced workplace bullying because of our union membership’




Yapı Yol-Sen member Mehmet Yariç said that all workers at the construction site, not only union members, were under pressure and that working conditions were deteriorating by the day.




Yariç said: “We were constantly under pressure at work. Three months ago, we faced another issue involving dismissals. We called in our union, an agreement was reached, and we continued working. However, from that day onwards, the pressure on us increased even further because of our union membership. We were subjected to serious workplace bullying.”




Yariç said union members were consistently assigned the most dangerous and exhausting tasks and added: “We were doing 90 per cent of the work, while the employer's own workers were given easier tasks. We were constantly under pressure because we belonged to a union. Every day, we were threatened with dismissal. Even arriving two or three minutes late was enough for them to threaten to sack us.”




‘Our wages were cut for going to lunch two minutes early’




Yariç stated that even their lunch breaks had become a source of conflict and said: “Most recently, half a day's wages were deducted because we went to lunch one, two or three minutes early. Most of us, in fact all of us, had deductions made from our wages. We objected and made it clear that we would not accept them. The main contractor was Gürbağ, and the subcontractor was Hermet. The supervisor responsible for us, whom I believe was Ali Ülküsever, deducted wages from all of us. We refused to accept wage deductions simply because we had gone to lunch two or three minutes early. They then told us, ‘Anyone who doesn't want to accept it can see where the door is. Go and sign your resignation and leave.’”




‘Workers face pressure in every sector’




Yariç said they rejected these demands and were pressured to resign and leave without receiving any payment because they had stood up for their rights.




Yariç also said: “We refused to accept this, called our union and began protesting the following day. Unionised workers in Turkey face pressure and threats. Workers are denied their rights, and their rights are not respected even in cases of workplace deaths. Workers must no longer be looked down upon, isolated or treated as though they are ignorant. How much longer will this injustice continue? How much longer will we have to resist? Why must we constantly struggle just to obtain what is rightfully ours? We want someone to intervene and put an end to this situation.”




‘We will stay here until we secure our rights’




Yariç called on workers to organise and appealed to the people of Diyarbakır for solidarity and said:“Everyone working here has children, parents and spouses. We are all trying to support our families through our work. Every one of us has mouths to feed and a family to take care of. We have legal rights recognised by the state, yet we are being prevented from exercising them. How much longer will this oppression continue? We want what is happening to stop immediately. The people of this city and its civil society organisations must support us. We will not leave until we secure our rights.”

title: Release of two prisoners postponed again
content:
The release of Zeliha Ustabaş, who is held at Sincan Women’s Closed Prison, has been blocked for the fifth time by a decision of the Prison Administration and Observation Board.




Ustabaş’s release, which has been postponed four times since 18 July 2024, has now been delayed by a further nine months.




It was reported that Ustabaş’s current sentence period is due to end on 24 July 2027, and that 8 July 2027 has been set as the date for a reassessment of her case.




The release of Orhan Yakışır, who is held at Sincan No. 1 High-Security Prison, has also been postponed, for the third time.




Yakışır’s release was previously postponed by three months on the first occasion and eight months on the second. His release has now been delayed by a further 11 months.




It was stated that the board’s next review of Yakışır’s case will take place on 7 September 2027.

title: Gülsüm Elvan: Peace requires justice and women's struggle
content:
Eighty women from the women's movement, politics, academia, culture and the arts came together on 21 September under the appeal “Side by Side, Talking About the Future”, declaring that resolving the Kurdish question through democratic politics and negotiations would mark a new era for democracy in Turkey.




Gülsüm Elvan, the mother of Berkin Elvan, who was struck by a police-fired tear gas canister during the Gezi Resistance and died at the age of 15 after spending nine months in a coma, spoke to ANF about why she signed the appeal and what peace means for women.




‘Let no more mothers weep, let no more children be killed’




Gülsüm Elvan explained her reasons for signing the appeal, stressing her pursuit of justice and her determination to prevent other families from experiencing the same suffering. Elvan said: “The reason I signed this appeal is clear. I am a mother whose heart has been broken, whose child was taken from her, who has sought justice but has never been able to find it. At the same time, throughout my struggle for justice, whenever I speak about Berkin, I have always said, ‘Let no more mothers weep, let no more children be killed.’”




‘We will bring peace through struggle, women are rising up’




Elvan said that, as a mother who had lost her child, she believed genuine peace meant defending life. She drew attention to femicides and the deepening cycle of violence.




Elvan said: “A woman is killed every day. We are not safe on the streets. Just as marriage is natural, so is divorce by mutual agreement. Yet women are treated like property and murdered even for this reason. Women are being murdered, our nature is being destroyed, and journalists who report on these crimes are being killed. They killed Hakan Tosun. Even children are now killing one another in schools. Our struggle is for life, not death. Peace must be on the side of life.”




Elvan stressed that women must have an active say in the process and said: We will bring peace through struggle because women are rising up now. Real peace means living side by side democratically and in solidarity, in workplaces, on the streets and at home, producing and working together.”




‘We can see the future only by confronting the past’




Gülsüm Elvan stressed that confronting the past was essential to achieving lasting peace and that justice must be served. Elvan said, “If we confront who did what to whom and at what time, if the crimes committed are acknowledged and justice is served, only then can something genuine emerge. We will be able to see the future only when we confront the past.”




‘Prisoners are on hunger strike, trustees remain in place’




Gülsüm Elvan pointed to political prisoners, saying that practices contradicting the spirit of the peace process were still continuing. She said, “There are still government-appointed trustees. Many people, including my lawyers, are in prison. University student Taceddin Erol Şahin is being held in a pit-type cell simply for commemorating Berkin, and he is on the 163rd day of his hunger strike.”




Women to gather in Ankara on 31 October–1 November




The women-led struggle for peace and justice aims to bring fresh momentum to discussions on democracy in Turkey. The “Side by Side, Talking About the Future” appeal will be followed by a two-day conference scheduled to take place in Ankara on 31 October and 1 November, where possible paths towards a solution will be discussed in detail.

title: Iranian mountaineer and musician Ali-Sina Mustafavi executed
content:
According to Mizan News Agency, affiliated with Iran’s judiciary, Ali-Sina Mustafavi, a 38-year-old from Kerman, was executed on Wednesday. Human rights organisations had warned a day before the execution that it could be imminent after Mustafavi was placed in solitary confinement. Prison authorities were reportedly in contact with his family and had summoned them for a final visit.




Human Rights for Sports, an organisation that advocates for athletes’ rights, had also included Mustafavi, a mountaineer and musician, on its list of athletes at risk of execution. Human rights organisations said that Mustafavi had been forced to confess.




Mizan News Agency accused Mustafavi of carrying out armed attacks in Kerman in which civilians were injured. The report alleged that the attacks were carried out in support of Iran’s Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi and Israel.




Mizan also claimed that Mustafavi had filmed areas that were struck during the war. However, the agency provided no details about the trial proceedings or the evidence presented in court.




Iranian authorities systematically and arbitrarily use charges such as espionage, crimes against national security, armed rebellion, “enmity against God” and “corruption on earth” to prosecute dissidents and protesters. Human rights organisations say these charges are used to portray opponents as security threats and to justify death sentences.




Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and United Nations experts have documented cases in which some death sentences handed down on the basis of such charges were carried out following proceedings involving serious violations of the right to a fair trial. In these cases, defendants were reportedly denied adequate access to lawyers, and confessions allegedly obtained under torture were used as the basis for verdicts.




Human rights organisations warn that many death sentences handed down under these circumstances may be arbitrary and politically motivated. They stress that the charges brought by Iranian authorities should not be accepted as independently verified facts.

title: Xebat Kobanê: A war veteran devoted to music and song
content:
Every war veteran who has sacrificed part of their body to protect their land and people in North and East Syria has a different story. Xebat Kobanê is one of them.




Xebat grew up in a patriotic family. One of his brothers was martyred, while one of his sisters joined the ranks of the revolution.







 







Xebat joined the People's Protection Units (YPG) with great enthusiasm and hope. He stood on the front lines of resistance in many areas against treacherous attacks targeting his land and people.




Xebat knew that martyrdom and injury were possibilities on this honourable path. Alongside his military training, he also developed himself ideologically. Conscious of following in the footsteps of Arîn and Rêvan, he took on all aspects of revolutionary work with great dedication.




Xebat Kobanê was wounded during a period of intense fighting, leaving both his legs paralysed. However, he has never regarded his injury as an obstacle. He follows Abdullah Öcalan's perspectives on war veterans and acts on the principle that “veterans are defenders of the revolution”.




Xebat has been interested in music for many years and plays the saz, a traditional long-necked string instrument, with remarkable skill. He also has a beautiful singing voice.




War veteran Xebat Kobanê takes his saz wherever he goes. He plays and sings songs for his fellow war veterans.
