title: Ecological destruction in the Zilan Valley continues
content:
Construction work on an irrigation canal in the Zilan Valley (Geliyê Zîlan), near the district of Erciş in Van province, is causing increasing damage to the region’s ecosystem. Since September 23, heavy construction machinery has been operating in the canyon as part of the so-called Pay Irrigation Canal Project. Excavation and construction work in the streambed and surrounding areas have altered the natural flow of water. Water levels have dropped significantly, and some sections of the stream have already dried up.




These developments threaten not only to have serious consequences for local wildlife and vegetation but also to exacerbate water supply problems in the region. Environmental activists have initiated legal proceedings against the project and requested a suspension of construction work. A court decision is still pending, while machinery continues operating in the valley.




Trees felled and riverside vegetation destroyed




The areas along the streambanks have been particularly severely affected. Trees have been felled and large sections of natural vegetation cleared within the valley. The grasses, shrubs, and trees growing in the area perform essential functions in maintaining the ecological balance: they stabilize the soil, prevent erosion, regulate water levels, and provide habitats for numerous animal species.




With the destruction of this vegetation, the streambanks are losing their natural protection. At the same time, wildlife habitats used for shelter, feeding, and reproduction are being destroyed. These interventions threaten the interconnected relationship between water, soil, and vegetation, which is crucial to the valley’s ecological stability.




The alterations to the streambed also have far-reaching consequences. Together with its banks, the stream forms a continuous habitat for fish, aquatic invertebrates, amphibians, birds, and other wildlife. Falling water levels and drying sections of the stream can destroy these habitats, reduce moisture in the surrounding soil, and make it more difficult for animals to access water.




Legal action against construction work




Environmental activists have filed an application with the Administrative Court in Van seeking a suspension of the project’s implementation. They have also filed a criminal complaint with the public prosecutor’s office in Erciş. No decision has yet been issued on the urgent application. Construction work continues despite the ongoing legal proceedings.




The controversial irrigation canal project dates back to 1993, when the Turkish State Hydraulic Works (DSI) initiated the project and issued a positive environmental impact assessment decision. After the project remained unimplemented for many years, it was put out to tender in 2016 and awarded to the company Günsay.




Zilan Valley threatened by large-scale projects for years




The irrigation project is not the only intervention threatening the natural environment of the Zilan Valley. For years, the region has been increasingly affected by state-backed energy and infrastructure projects. Particularly controversial is the development of geothermal resources, which has been pursued since 2020 and now threatens the livelihoods of several villages.




In Şorik, Karakilise, and Çaxirbeg, drilling and development activities are encroaching on agricultural land and residential areas. Residents now even fear that their villages may be evacuated. Environmental groups have also warned about the potential discharge of thermal waters contaminated with heavy metals into the region’s irrigation systems and waterways. However, publicly documented measurements are not yet available to allow a definitive assessment of the contamination levels.




The scale of the planned development is reflected in tenders issued in 2024, which offered licenses for the exploration and exploitation of geothermal resources covering approximately 8,860 hectares in total. The ongoing construction work on the Pay Irrigation Canal represents yet another intervention in an ecosystem already under pressure from energy projects.

title: Sağlık Bakanlığı: Eşitsizlikleri devam ettirmekte kararlıyız!
content:
Sağlık Bakanlığı İstatistik Yıllığı (SBİY) 2025 Haber Bülteni, 30 Eylül 2025, çarşamba günü, saat 17:00’de 

(!)

 yayımlandı. İlki 12 yıl önce, 2014 yılında yine eylül ayının son günü SBİY 2013 Haber Bülteni olarak yayımlanmıştı. Bülten, istatistik yıllığından yaklaşık üç, dört ay önce daha az sayıdaki veri grubunu kapsayacak şekilde yayımlanıyor. Bununla birlikte, ölümlülük, aşılama ve hizmet kullanımıyla ilgili bir önceki yılın verilerine 9-10 ay sonra da olsa ulaşabilmiş oluyoruz. Ve Türkiye’nin dokuz ilinin bulunduğu coğrafyada yaşayanların, AKP’li yılların bundan önceki 16 yılında olduğu gibi, 17nci yılında da değişmeyen bir biçimde sağlık ve sosyoekonomik eşitsizlere mahkûm edilmiş olduğunu görüyoruz. Bu haftaki yazıda söz konusu durumu ve AKP’li Sağlık Bakanlığı’nın verileri kendine saklamak gibi bir özelliğini kendilerinin sunduğu kaynaklar üzerinden ele alacağım.



















ERİŞ BİLALOĞLU YAZDI




Yeni Bir Sıfırlama Çabası mı: Türkiye’de Bebek Ölüm Hızı




29 Ocak 2015










AKP’li bakanlık verileri kendine saklıyor




AKP tarafından 2002 yılında kurulan 58. Hükümet’e kadar sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili veriler yıllardır istatistik yıllıklarıyla düzenli olarak kamuoyuyla paylaşılıyordu. Ancak 

58. Hükümet ve o kabinenin Sağlık Bakanı Recep Akdağ ile birlikte, sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili veriler kamuoyundan 2011 yılına kadar saklandı, 

paylaşılmadı. Dünya Sağlık Örgütü başta olmak üzere, Türkiye’nin üyesi olduğu uluslararası kuruluşların talebi üzerine, bir AKP Hükümeti ve Sağlık Bakanı olarak ilk defa 2011 yılında, 2008 yılına ait veriler “Sağlık Bakanlığı Sağlık İstatistikleri Yıllığı 2008” başlığında Bakan Akdağ’ın önsözüyle yayımlandı. O nedenle Türkiye’nin 2003-2007 yıllarına ait sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili verileri diğer yıllar gibi düzenli bir biçimde bugüne kadar paylaşılmadı.




Sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleriyle ilgili istatistikler, 2011 yılından sonra, Sağlık Bakanlığı ve Türkiye İstatistik Kurumu (TÜİK) tarafından düzenli olarak yayımlanıyor. TÜİK, özelikle doğurganlık ve ölümlülükle ilgili verileri Merkezi Nüfus İdaresi Sistemi (MERNİS) üzerinden iller düzeyinde, sağlık harcamalarıyla ilgili verileri Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı ile Sosyal Güvenlik Kurumu (SGK) ve yerel yönetimlerden ve “Hanehalkı Bütçe Anketi” çalışması üzerinden, hastalıklarla ilgili verileri de “Türkiye Sağlık Araştırması” üzerinden sağlıyor. Sağlık Bakanlığı da bu verileri kullanıp yaptığı hesaplamaları ve sağlık kurumları, sağlık emekçileri, ilaç, sağlık hizmetleri kullanımı vb. verileri Türkiye’nin makro düzeyde ekonomik ve sosyo-ekonomik yapıya göre gruplandığı 12 bölge, İstatistiki Bölge Bilgileri Sınıflaması-1 (İBBS-1), üzerinden paylaşıyor. Bununla birlikte, 

Sağlık Bakanlığı kaynakları üzerinden 81 ilden herhangi birinin sağlık ve sağlık hizmetleri verilerini, durumunu öğrenebilmek mümkün olamıyor. 

Çünkü Sağlık Bakanlığı illerin verilerini yayımlamayı uzun zamandır tercih etmiyor.










Tabip Odası Bebek Ölümlerine Önlem Paketini Açıkladı




25 Eylül 2008










Bebek ölüm hızı önemli bir toplumsal sağlık düzeyi göstergesidir




Toplumların sağlık düzeyinin değerlendirilmesi ve izlenebilmesi amacıyla “bebek ölüm hızı”, “beş yaş altı ölüm hızı” ve “doğumda beklenen yaşam süresi” uluslararası alanda sıklıkla kullanılan, kabul görmüş üç değişkendir. Bunlar aynı zamanda, ülkelerin gelişmişlik düzeyi göstergeleri arasında da yer almaktadır. Çünkü, bu üç gösterge bir ülkede, bölgede, ilde vb. öncelikle beslenme, barınma, alt yapı ve eğitim başta olmak üzere, sosyoekonomik koşulların durumu ve sağlık hizmetlerinin ulaşılabilir olup olmamasıyla sağlık hizmetlerinin niteliğinden doğrudan etkilenmektedir.




Gebeliğin herhangi bir döneminde, canlı doğan bebeğin, birinci doğum gününü göremeden ölmesi, nüfus bilim (demografi) ve tıp alanında bebek ölümü olarak kabul edilmekte, tanımlanmaktadır. Bir ilde, bölgede ve/veya ülkede yıl içinde canlı doğan her bin bebekten kaçının birinci doğum gününü göremeden öldüğü de bebek ölüm hızı olarak tanımlanmaktadır. Bebek ölümlerinden doğumdan sonraki 

ilk ay içinde gerçekleşen

ler neonatal ölüm, birinci aydan sonra gerçekleşenler de postneonatal ölüm olarak adlandırılmaktadır. Neonatal 

ölümler genellikle anne adayının sağlık, beslenme ve eğitim durumuyla doğum öncesi izlemlerin yapılıp yapılmaması ve doğum koşullarıyla ilişkilidir.

 

Postneonatal ölümler

in de 

bebeğin aşılama başta olmak üzere, sağlık hizmetlerine ulaşıp ulaşamaması vb. ile beslenme, barınma vb. ailesinin sosyoekonomik düzeyi, yaşam koşullarıyla doğrudan ilişkili

 olduğu bilimsel araştırmalarla gösterilmiştir.




Türkiye’de ve OECD ülkelerinde bebek ölüm hızları




SBİY 2025 Haber Bülteni’ndeki verilere göre, Türkiye’de 2025 yılında gerçekleşen bin canlı doğumdan 5,0’i doğumdan sonraki birinci ay içinde, 2,7’si de birinci ay ile 12. ay arasında yaşamını kaybetmiştir. Toplamda da bin canlı doğumdan 7,7’si birinci doğum gününü göremeden ölmüştür. Başka bir ifadeyle, Sağlık Bakanlığı tarafından Türkiye geneli için 2025 yılı bebek ölüm hızı binde 7,7; neonatal ölüm hızı binde 5,0 ve postneonatal ölüm hızı da binde 2,7 olarak bildirilmiştir.




Türkiye, yayımlanmış son verilere göre, üyesi olduğu Ekonomik Kalkınma ve İşbirliği Örgütü’ne (OECD) üye 38 ülke arasında, 2024 yılında BÖH en yüksek Meksika (binde 12,5) ve Kosta Rika’nın (binde 10,2) ardından binde 8,9 ile üçüncü sırada yer alıyor. Türkiye, benzer gelir, “kalkınmışlık” düzeyindeki ülkeler arasında toplumsal sağlık düzeyi en kötü olanlar arasında yer almakta ve bu durum yıllardır değişmemektedir.




AKP Hükümeti iddialı: Türkiye’de eşitsizliklerin en derin yaşandığı coğrafya yine değişmedi




TÜİK ve Sağlık Bakanlığı başta olmak üzere, İBBS-1’i kullanan kurumların gruplamasına göre, 

Adıyaman, Batman, Diyarbakır, Gaziantep, Kilis, Mardin, Siirt, Şanlıurfa ve Şırnak

 olmak üzere 

dokuz il

in bulunduğu coğrafya 

Güneydoğu Anadolu 

bölgesi olarak tanımlanıyor. Türkiye’de 

anadili Kürtçe ve Arapça

 

olan yurttaşların en yoğun olarak yaşadığı iller

den oluşan Güneydoğu Anadolu, AKP’nin düzenli olarak verileri yayımlamakta olduğu ve iktidarının son 17 yılı boyunca her yıl bebek ölüm hızının en yüksek olduğu coğrafya olma özelliği taşıyor.




İBBS-1’de yer alan bölgeleri, bebek ölüm hızının en düşük (en iyi) olduğu bölgeden en yüksek (en kötü) olduğu bölgeye doğru sıralandığında, ilk sırada en iyi durumda olan Batı Marmara’da 5,6; ikinci sıradaki İstanbul’da 5,7; Batı Anadolu’da 6,0; Doğu Marmara’da 6,1; beşinci sırada yer alan Doğu Karadeniz’de 6,2; Batı Karadeniz’de 6,4; Ege’de 6,9; sekizinci sıradaki Orta Anadolu’da 7,5; Kuzeydoğu Anadolu’da 7,8; onuncu sıradaki Akdeniz’de 8,2; Ortadoğu Anadolu’da 9,6 ve son sırada yer alan Güneydoğu Anadolu’da 11,5’dir.




Sayılarla eşitsizlikler




2025 yılında canlı doğan bin bebekten Batı Marmara’da 5,6’sı, Güneydoğu Anadolu’da ise 11,5’i birinci doğum gününü göremeden hayatını kaybetmiştir. Aralarındaki fark iki katından daha fazladır (

Hız oranı

=2,04). Bu durum, 2025 yılında bebek ölüm hızının en iyi/düşük olduğu Batı Marmara’da ölen her bir bebeğe karşılık, bebek ölüm hızının en kötü/yüksek olduğu Güneydoğu Anadolu’da iki bebeğin birinci doğum gününü göremeden öldüğünü göstermektedir.




Güneydoğu Anadolu, 2025 yılında Türkiye’de binde 11,5 ile bebek ölüm hızının yanı sıra, binde 7,2 ile neonatal ve binde 4,3 ile de postneonatal ölüm hızlarının en yüksek olduğu bölge konumundadır. Hız oranı 

neonatal ölüm hızı için 2,0

; 

postneonatal ölüm hızı için

 de 

2,4 

olarak hesaplanmıştır. Sağlık Bakanlığı’nın verileriyle yapılan hesaplamalara göre, her üç toplumsal sağlık düzeyi göstergesi açısından Türkiye’nin en kötü durumda olan bölgesi; İBBS-1 sınıflamasında Güneydoğu Anadolu olarak adlandırılan ve esas olarak anadili Kürtçe ve Arapça olan yurttaşların en yoğun olarak yaşadığı illerin bir araya getirilmesiyle tanımlanmış olan coğrafyadır.




Başka bir ifadeyle, bu coğrafya diğer bölgelere göre bebek ölüm hızının en yüksek olmasına neden olduğu bilinen beslenme, barınma, alt yapı ve eğitim başta olmak üzere, sosyoekonomik koşulların durumu ve sağlık hizmetlerinin ulaşılabilirliğiyle sağlık hizmetlerinin niteliği alanlarında da diğer bölgelere göre en kötü, eşitsizliklerin en fazla olduğu bölge durumundadır.




Sağlık eşitsizlikleri önlenemez değil




Türkiye’de sağlıktaki eşitsizlikler de gelir dağılımında, işsizlikte, eğitimde olduğu gibi uçuruma dönüştü. AKP iktidarının yarattığı sağlık alanındaki bu utanç tablosunun ancak toplumsal eşitsizlikler ortadan kaldırılarak yok edilebileceği biliniyor. Bunun için de 

sınıfsal dayanışma ve mücadele gerekiyor

. “Barış ve Demokratik Toplum” süreci tamamlanıp, silahlı çatışmaların sonlanması kalıcılaşıp, 

normalleşme aşaması başladığında

 ittifakların, ortak mücadelelerin ve dayanışmanın önü daha da açılacak. Umudumuz, toplumsal muhalefetin amasız, fakatsız açık desteğiyle bu aşamanın bir an önce başlayabilmesi ve 

eşitlikçi, barış içinde bir toplumsal yaşantı için “gerekenlerin” hep birlikte hayata geçirilebilmesi

.

author: Chris Walker
title: Report: Trump Is Having Second Thoughts About Livestreaming Military Execution
content:
Trump isn’t “particularly enthusiastic” about Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream a military execution in December.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump is reportedly asking advisors if he should go through with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream a military execution later this year.

Trump has publicly indicated that he’ll make a final decision on the matter soon.

“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it,” Trump said. “Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did.”

“I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision,” Trump added.

But according to reporting from Axios, Trump is questioning whether the execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan should be televised, asking his advisers for their views on the matter.

Hasan was convicted of killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009. He was shot during the rampage, and is now a paraplegic, paralyzed from the waist down. Hasan is set to be executed by a firing squad in December.

The president “didn’t sound particularly enthusiastic” about a live, national showing of the execution, a source close to Trump said to the publication, adding that “he’s calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think.”

The livestream event “might not happen,” another source confirmed.

Trump’s public statements about the death penalty reveal that he has errant views about capital punishment. Multiple studies have shown that there is no evidence supporting the idea that the death penalty can act as a deterrent, or that the threat of capital punishment somehow lessens violent crime. Indeed, several years of data demonstrate that the homicide rates in states with capital punishment are higher than in states without the death penalty.

Trump is also wrong about what “the military would like to do.” While there isn’t widespread data to demonstrate most servicemembers’ views one way or another, some officers have spoken out against the planned livestreaming of Hasan’s execution.

“It takes away everything America stands for when we do public executions,” one Army officer said in an anonymous comment to CNN. “The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable.”

Several religious leaders, including Pope Leo, and a bipartisan cadre of lawmakers, have also spoken out against livestreaming the execution.

Despite Trump’s reticence about this specific event, he has been an outspoken proponent of expanding the death penalty, including for non-lethal crimes such as drug dealing. In his first week in office, he signed an executive order peddling the the false claim that the death penalty is “an essential tool for deterring” crimes, calling for the attorney general to seek the death penalty for crimes involving the killing of law enforcement officers, or when the defendant being charged is an undocumented immigrant.

In an op-ed published last week, Truthout’s board of directors president Maya Schenwar decried the death penalty in all of its forms, describing the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee as an act of torture and Hegseth’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution as part of a larger “pro-death penalty fervor.”

“The brutality is the point. The torture is the point. The murder, not only state-sanctioned but state-celebrated, is the very point,” Schenwar wrote.

A cohesive life-affirming agenda rejects not only executions, but also the inherent violence of incarceration, policing, deportation, imperial wars, and military aid to genocidal forces. It makes no excuses — let alone expansions — that prop up or prolong the existence of these institutions in ‘kinder, gentler’ forms.

“Let’s not allow ourselves to give in to the inertia of our brutal present, in which death by hanging is a mercy. Let’s envision the cohesive, life-affirming agenda that embraces a future for all of us, a world in which the torture of Christa Pike — or anyone — is unthinkable,” Schenwar concluded.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

content:

Nairobi, Kenya, October 13, 2026: For 42 years, Kenya has committed to ensuring women’s equality in marriage and family life. In 1984, the country ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), and Article 2(6) of the Constitution makes the treaty part of Kenyan law. Yet in reality, this promise remains unrealised. Women in Kenya can still lose their homes when their husbands die, struggle to claim property they helped build, and face barriers to leaving marriages marked by violence. Kenya’s record on women’s rights is currently under scrutiny as the CEDAW Committee reviews the country’s implementation of the Convention during the Committee’s 93rd session at the United Nations in Geneva. The Global Campaign for Equality in Family Law, Equality Now and Kenyan partners, including Come Together Widows and Orphans Organization (CTWOO), have submitted a shadow report providing a civil society account of what happens on the ground in Kenya in relation to Article 16 of the CEDAW Convention. What CEDAW Article 16 means for women in Kenya Article 16 of CEDAW protects equality inside the family. This includes equal rights when spouses marry, during marriage and when it ends, with equal say over parenting, property and decisions about children. It protects the right to belong in a family, to be safe in it and to prosper in it, from marriage through widowhood. The Committee’s guidance on violence against women extends that protection to safety at home. That commitment is tested at every stage of family life. When a couple registers a marriage, when unpaid care counts towards family wealth, when a woman seeks a divorce, when a widow tries to keep her home and when a woman needs protection from violence. These are not separate failures but different ways in which equality can exist on paper and be denied in practice. Kenya has made real progress. Article 27 of the Constitution guarantees equality, and Article 45(3) applies that guarantee to spouses at every stage of marriage. The Marriage Act of 2014 brought many marriage laws into one statute, and the Matrimonial Property Act of 2013 recognised non-financial contribution to family wealth, reforms that the Federation of Women Lawyers in Kenya and other women’s organisations helped advance through strategic litigation, legislative proposals and community education. Marriage registration and women’s property rights in Kenya Equality in family life starts with being able to prove a marriage exists. The Marriage Act requires registration, yet it costs Kenya shillings 3,900, and both spouses must appear before the registrar. Only 19.3 per cent of married women aged 15 to 49 had registered their marriage in the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey, while the shadow report finds no fee waiver for poor households and no county registration drives to help make it easier for couples to register their marriages locally. For a family living on the World Bank’s international poverty line of US$3 a day, the fee equals ten days of income. Many families pass land down the husband’s line, so a wife who cannot prove her marriage can struggle to claim the family home and land after a divorce or a death, and courts have been inconsistent about the consequences of non-registration. Free registration for poor households and mobile registration teams in every county would remove the barrier. Kenya recognises unpaid contribution in property division, but no formula says how to value it, and in 2023 the Supreme Court held that Article 45(3) does not give spouses an automatic half share. Women must still establish their contribution to matrimonial property over the years, including non-monetary contributions such as childcare and housework. A presumption of equal sharing, supported by judicial guidelines on valuing unpaid work, would help turn the constitutional promise of equal rights into equal outcomes. Divorce, access to justice and women’s safety The question is not only whether Kenya has laws protecting women’s rights, but whether women can use them. Fees, distance from courts and lengthy proceedings stand between many women and justice, and Kenya’s divorce law is largely fault-based, so a petitioner must prove a ground such as adultery, cruelty or desertion. In 2022, the Court of Appeal ruled that the three-year wait to seek a divorce in a civil marriage is unconstitutional when a divorce is justified sooner, yet Parliament has not amended the Marriage Act. Chiefs, elders and clergy can also pressure women to reconcile, even where violence is present, but mediation cannot replace a court for a woman who fears for her safety. Widows’ rights in Kenya: more than a succession issue Kenyan law treats widowhood mainly as a succession issue, yet being widowed also determines who keeps property, dignity and safety. CTWOO’s August 2025 widowhood survey found that approximately one third of respondents faced eviction from their home or land after a spouse died and around a third were excluded from inheritance decisions. CTWOO recorded 139 cases involving widows in May 2026 alone. The Law of Succession Act ends a widow’s life interest in her husband’s estate if she remarries, a rule that does not apply to widowers. The High Court declared it unconstitutional in the Ripples International case in September 2022, but the provision remains in the text of the statute. The Widowed Persons Protection Bill, 2026, tabled in Parliament in May and drafted with input from CTWOO and Equality Now, would bring protections now scattered across succession, family and criminal law into one framework. Muslim women and equal protection under Kenya’s Constitution Here, the Constitution’s guarantee of equality meets a constitutional limitation. Article 24(4) allows that guarantee to be qualified “to the extent strictly necessary” for Muslim law in the Kadhis’ courts, covering marriage, divorce and inheritance, and the Law of Succession Act does not apply to the estates of deceased Muslims. In practice, Muslim daughters can receive half their brothers’ inheritance share, while Muslim wives have fewer routes to divorce than their husbands. Kenya’s Supreme Court has found that any departure from equality under Article 24(4) must be strictly necessary and proportionate. Equality Now and its partners therefore call for Article 24(4) to be repealed so that the constitutional equality guarantee applies equally to all women. Gender-based violence, reproductive rights and the risk of rollback The Africa Data Hub has documented the killings of at least 1,069 women in Kenya between 2016 and 2025. Section 43(5) of the Sexual Offences Act excludes lawfully married people from the section that defines unlawful sexual acts, creating a marital rape exemption. Usikimye’s accountability audit also notes that Kenyan law does not define femicide. Harmful practices persist, including child marriage, where data remain scarce, and female genital mutilation (FGM). A review of 68 prosecutions under the Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation Act by the American Bar Association Center for Human Rights found that 76 of the 137 identifiable accused people were survivors themselves, including 11 girls under 18, and only eight were cutters. The Act also has a gap. In 2021, the High Court found in Kamau v Attorney General, a case in which Equality Now was an interested party, that the Act leaves out Type IV practices such as pricking and piercing, and directed the Attorney General to propose amendments. Article 16 also covers decisions about the number and spacing of children. Article 26(4) of the Constitution allows abortion in defined circumstances, yet the Penal Code criminalises it. In April 2026, the Court of Appeal held that abortion is not a fundamental right and acknowledged the absence of a clear regulatory framework. Kenya’s reservation to the abortion provision of the Maputo Protocol, Africa’s treaty on women’s rights, also contradicts the Constitution. The shadow report finds that, since the Committee’s last review in 2017, most of CEDAW’s recommendations remain unimplemented, while the Linda Jamii constitutional amendment proposal and the National Policy on Family Promotion and Protection have raised concerns about rolling back protections for women, as Equality Now has documented. The pushback has also included the Family Protection Bill of 2023, which seeks to criminalise same-sex conduct, and calls for Kenya to adopt the regressive Draft African Charter on Family, Sovereignty and Values. Yet Article 45 recognises the family as the natural and fundamental unit of society while giving spouses equal rights. Protecting the family and protecting the equality of each member are therefore part of the same constitutional duty. Commitments Kenya should make after the CEDAW review Align the law. Kenya should amend provisions that conflict with the Constitution, CEDAW and the Maputo Protocol. The Widowed Persons Protection Bill 2026 should be enacted, and a stand-alone law on femicide introduced. The Protection Against Domestic Violence Act needs to be fully operationalised, and the Sexual Offences Act must be amended to remove the exemption for marital rape. Article 24(4) in Kenya’s Constitution that exempts Muslim women from constitutional protection also needs to be reformed. The government should also lift reservations on Article 14(2)(c) of the Maputo Protocol, which protects women’s access to medical abortion in specified circumstances, and align the country’s laws and policies with the Constitution’s protections for women’s reproductive health and rights. Implement existing decisions. Court rulings on widows’ inheritance, divorce and FGM, and the recommendations of the government’s Technical Working Group on gender-based violence should change the statute book and practice, so that women are not forced to litigate the same rights repeatedly. Make rights accessible and protect the gains. Fee waivers, marriage registration drives, legal aid and community education would lower the financial, geographic and procedural barriers, because discrimination rooted in culture and religion outlasts a new law. Kenya should also keep its constitutional and treaty guarantees intact against rollback. Equality in marriage and family life benefits every family in Kenya Equality in marriage is not only a women’s issue; sons, fathers, grandparents and children all bear the cost when a family loses its home, its land or its safety. Kenya has the Constitution, the court rulings and a Bill before Parliament to build on. Today’s review offers a chance to turn 42 years of legal promises into equality that families can feel at home. END Notes to editors For media enquiries, contact Millicent Kwambai, Associate Communications Manager, Equality Now mkwambai@equalitynow.org, T. +254 706 142 804 (available on WhatsApp) Deborah Nyokabi is Associate Manager, Economic Justice and Family Law, at Equality Now, a global human rights organisation dedicated to ending discrimination against all women and girls. She is based in Nairobi, Kenya. About: Equality Now is a worldwide human rights organisation dedicated to securing the legal and systemic change needed to end discrimination against all women and girls. Since its inception in 1992, it has played a role in reforming 140 discriminatory laws globally, positively impacting the lives of hundreds of millions of women and girls, their communities and nations, both now and for generations to come. Working with partners at national, regional and global levels, Equality Now draws on deep legal expertise and a diverse range of social, political and cultural perspectives to continue to lead the way in steering, shaping and driving the change needed to achieve enduring gender equality, to the benefit of all. For more information about child marriage in the United States, please review our factsheet and reporting toolkit. For more details about Equality Now, go to www.equalitynow.org ; LinkedIn Equality Now Africa.

Nairobi, Kenya, October 13, 2026: For 42 years, Kenya has committed to ensuring women’s equality in marriage and family life. In 1984, the country ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW), and Article 2(6) of the Constitution makes the treaty part of Kenyan law. Yet in reality, this promise remains unrealised. Women in Kenya can still lose their homes when their husbands die, struggle to claim property they helped build, and face barriers to leaving marriages marked by violence.

Kenya’s record on women’s rights is currently under scrutiny as the CEDAW Committee reviews the country’s implementation of the Convention during the Committee’s 93rd session at the United Nations in Geneva.

The Global Campaign for Equality in Family Law, Equality Now and Kenyan partners, including Come Together Widows and Orphans Organization (CTWOO), have submitted a shadow report providing a civil society account of what happens on the ground in Kenya in relation to Article 16 of the CEDAW Convention.

Article 16 of CEDAW protects equality inside the family. This includes equal rights when spouses marry, during marriage and when it ends, with equal say over parenting, property and decisions about children. It protects the right to belong in a family, to be safe in it and to prosper in it, from marriage through widowhood. The Committee’s guidance on violence against women extends that protection to safety at home.

That commitment is tested at every stage of family life. When a couple registers a marriage, when unpaid care counts towards family wealth, when a woman seeks a divorce, when a widow tries to keep her home and when a woman needs protection from violence. These are not separate failures but different ways in which equality can exist on paper and be denied in practice.

Kenya has made real progress. Article 27 of the Constitution guarantees equality, and Article 45(3) applies that guarantee to spouses at every stage of marriage. The Marriage Act of 2014 brought many marriage laws into one statute, and the Matrimonial Property Act of 2013 recognised non-financial contribution to family wealth, reforms that the Federation of Women Lawyers in Kenya and other women’s organisations helped advance through strategic litigation, legislative proposals and community education.

Equality in family life starts with being able to prove a marriage exists. The Marriage Act requires registration, yet it costs Kenya shillings 3,900, and both spouses must appear before the registrar. Only 19.3 per cent of married women aged 15 to 49 had registered their marriage in the 2022 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey, while the shadow report finds no fee waiver for poor households and no county registration drives to help make it easier for couples to register their marriages locally.

For a family living on the World Bank’s international poverty line of US$3 a day, the fee equals ten days of income. Many families pass land down the husband’s line, so a wife who cannot prove her marriage can struggle to claim the family home and land after a divorce or a death, and courts have been inconsistent about the consequences of non-registration. Free registration for poor households and mobile registration teams in every county would remove the barrier.

Kenya recognises unpaid contribution in property division, but no formula says how to value it, and in 2023 the Supreme Court held that Article 45(3) does not give spouses an automatic half share. Women must still establish their contribution to matrimonial property over the years, including non-monetary contributions such as childcare and housework. A presumption of equal sharing, supported by judicial guidelines on valuing unpaid work, would help turn the constitutional promise of equal rights into equal outcomes.

The question is not only whether Kenya has laws protecting women’s rights, but whether women can use them. Fees, distance from courts and lengthy proceedings stand between many women and justice, and Kenya’s divorce law is largely fault-based, so a petitioner must prove a ground such as adultery, cruelty or desertion.

In 2022, the Court of Appeal ruled that the three-year wait to seek a divorce in a civil marriage is unconstitutional when a divorce is justified sooner, yet Parliament has not amended the Marriage Act. Chiefs, elders and clergy can also pressure women to reconcile, even where violence is present, but mediation cannot replace a court for a woman who fears for her safety.

Kenyan law treats widowhood mainly as a succession issue, yet being widowed also determines who keeps property, dignity and safety. CTWOO’s August 2025 widowhood survey found that approximately one third of respondents faced eviction from their home or land after a spouse died and around a third were excluded from inheritance decisions. CTWOO recorded 139 cases involving widows in May 2026 alone.

The Law of Succession Act ends a widow’s life interest in her husband’s estate if she remarries, a rule that does not apply to widowers. The High Court declared it unconstitutional in the Ripples International case in September 2022, but the provision remains in the text of the statute.

The Widowed Persons Protection Bill, 2026, tabled in Parliament in May and drafted with input from CTWOO and Equality Now, would bring protections now scattered across succession, family and criminal law into one framework.

Here, the Constitution’s guarantee of equality meets a constitutional limitation. Article 24(4) allows that guarantee to be qualified “to the extent strictly necessary” for Muslim law in the Kadhis’ courts, covering marriage, divorce and inheritance, and the Law of Succession Act does not apply to the estates of deceased Muslims.

In practice, Muslim daughters can receive half their brothers’ inheritance share, while Muslim wives have fewer routes to divorce than their husbands. Kenya’s Supreme Court has found that any departure from equality under Article 24(4) must be strictly necessary and proportionate. Equality Now and its partners therefore call for Article 24(4) to be repealed so that the constitutional equality guarantee applies equally to all women.

The Africa Data Hub has documented the killings of at least 1,069 women in Kenya between 2016 and 2025. Section 43(5) of the Sexual Offences Act excludes lawfully married people from the section that defines unlawful sexual acts, creating a marital rape exemption. Usikimye’s accountability audit also notes that Kenyan law does not define femicide.

Harmful practices persist, including child marriage, where data remain scarce, and female genital mutilation (FGM). A review of 68 prosecutions under the Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation Act by the American Bar Association Center for Human Rights found that 76 of the 137 identifiable accused people were survivors themselves, including 11 girls under 18, and only eight were cutters.

The Act also has a gap. In 2021, the High Court found in Kamau v Attorney General, a case in which Equality Now was an interested party, that the Act leaves out Type IV practices such as pricking and piercing, and directed the Attorney General to propose amendments.

Article 16 also covers decisions about the number and spacing of children. Article 26(4) of the Constitution allows abortion in defined circumstances, yet the Penal Code criminalises it. In April 2026, the Court of Appeal held that abortion is not a fundamental right and acknowledged the absence of a clear regulatory framework. Kenya’s reservation to the abortion provision of the Maputo Protocol, Africa’s treaty on women’s rights, also contradicts the Constitution.

The shadow report finds that, since the Committee’s last review in 2017, most of CEDAW’s recommendations remain unimplemented, while the Linda Jamii constitutional amendment proposal and the National Policy on Family Promotion and Protection have raised concerns about rolling back protections for women, as Equality Now has documented.

The pushback has also included the Family Protection Bill of 2023, which seeks to criminalise same-sex conduct, and calls for Kenya to adopt the regressive Draft African Charter on Family, Sovereignty and Values.

Yet Article 45 recognises the family as the natural and fundamental unit of society while giving spouses equal rights. Protecting the family and protecting the equality of each member are therefore part of the same constitutional duty.

Align the law. Kenya should amend provisions that conflict with the Constitution, CEDAW and the Maputo Protocol. The Widowed Persons Protection Bill 2026 should be enacted, and a stand-alone law on femicide introduced. The Protection Against Domestic Violence Act needs to be fully operationalised, and the Sexual Offences Act must be amended to remove the exemption for marital rape.

Article 24(4) in Kenya’s Constitution that exempts Muslim women from constitutional protection also needs to be reformed. The government should also lift reservations on Article 14(2)(c) of the Maputo Protocol, which protects women’s access to medical abortion in specified circumstances, and align the country’s laws and policies with the Constitution’s protections for women’s reproductive health and rights.

Implement existing decisions. Court rulings on widows’ inheritance, divorce and FGM, and the recommendations of the government’s Technical Working Group on gender-based violence should change the statute book and practice, so that women are not forced to litigate the same rights repeatedly.

Make rights accessible and protect the gains. Fee waivers, marriage registration drives, legal aid and community education would lower the financial, geographic and procedural barriers, because discrimination rooted in culture and religion outlasts a new law. Kenya should also keep its constitutional and treaty guarantees intact against rollback.

Equality in marriage is not only a women’s issue; sons, fathers, grandparents and children all bear the cost when a family loses its home, its land or its safety.

Kenya has the Constitution, the court rulings and a Bill before Parliament to build on. Today’s review offers a chance to turn 42 years of legal promises into equality that families can feel at home.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Admin Is Reportedly Offering Children as Young as 5 $3,000 to Self-Deport
content:
The offers are meant to “coerce” the children into giving up on their immigration cases, an immigrant advocate said.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

ICE is offering children as young as 5 years old $3,000 “incentives” to voluntarily depart the country, legal advocates have reported, as the Trump administration works to separate immigrant families under the hammer of their mass deportation machine.

Bloomberg Law first reported on the offers, citing attorneys and immigrant advocacy groups who say that the offers are sometimes given to children who lack legal representation. The offers, they say, are a method of forcing children to take a deal so that they drop their legal challenges before they have gone through their time in the court system.

Shaina Aber, executive director for the Acacia Center for Justice, told Bloomberg Law that the tactic is “part of a larger pattern of really trying to coerce children, bully children, intensify pressure on children so that they abandon their cases.”

“It’s part of this deport-at-all-costs policy that seems to be in particular targeting children,” Aber went on.

The offer is being made by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) attorneys as well as immigration judges. In some cases, judges are telling children that it is a one-time offer and giving them no time to consider it, forcing them to make a decision “on the spot” even though “they might not understand what the longer term consequences are down the line,” Aber said.

Another group, the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said that it and similar groups have received the emails from ICE’s Office of the Principal Legal Advisor offering a “$3,000 incentive” for children. Michael Lukens, head of Amica, told Bloomberg Law that the latest offer came to his office this week for an 11-year-old.

The reporting shows that the Trump administration’s policies toward child deportations are even more extreme than previously thought. Last year, NBC reported that the Trump administration was offering children aged 14 and older $2,500 to self-deport or voluntarily leave the country, according to a Department of Health and Human Services memo.

Indeed, reports have since found that the Trump administration is carrying out this policy even in cases where the children were living with their families, in cases likened to President Donald Trump’s family separation policies from his first term.

The Department of Homeland Security didn’t confirm or deny the payments, saying that the administration is supposedly working to reunite children who come to the U.S. unaccompanied with their families.

According to a tracker maintained by the Marshall Project, as of August, the federal government has deported over 22,500 children since January 1, 2025. ICE arrests of children have only continued to escalate throughout Trump’s second term, with over 8,500 children having been arrested thus far — including 562 children and babies under 4.

author: Stephen Prager
title: Air Force Major Who Called for Trump’s Impeachment Held in Solitary Confinement
content:
Some legal experts say Jason Watson’s confinement for 24 hours a day could amount to illegal pretrial punishment.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Air Force Maj. Jason Watson was arrested July 1 on the steps of the US Capitol after calling for the impeachment of President Donald Trump. According to his lawyer, he’s now being held in solitary confinement 24 hours a day in what some legal experts say could amount to illegal pretrial punishment.

The Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ) contains provisions barring officers from engaging in public political activities that are typically protected for civilians, including criticizing the president and other elected officials.

Prosecutors have charged Watson with violating them when he participated in a news conference calling for Trump to be removed from office over his launching of military actions against Iran, Cuba, and Venezuela without congressional authorization.

After the speech, Watson stood on the Capitol steps holding a sign that read “Impeach, Convict, Remove” and was arrested after he refused to move.

Before he was charged, Watson gave a CNN interview on August 17 in which he continued to criticize Trump, accusing him of “flagrantly violating the Constitution” and “breaking the law.”

He acknowledged that he could face severe consequences as a result of his speech: “We just have to be willing to accept that we can change what is happening in our country if we are just willing to pay a price for it,” he said.

One day later, he was arrested while on duty and taken into pretrial confinement. He now faces a general court-martial, the military’s most severe trial, which is capable of imposing lengthy prison sentences.

“Cruel and unusual form of punishment.” U.S. Air Force Maj. Jason Watson is headed to the most severe form of military trial — a general court-martial — after calling for President Trump’s impeachment while in uniform at the U.S. Capitol. His attorney reveals that Maj. Watson… pic.twitter.com/7izEA47Gh2

On Friday, Watson’s lawyer, Christopher Mutimer, told CNN that after nearly two months, Watson is “still in solitary confinement 24 hours a day,” which he said amounted to “cruel and unusual” punishment.

“Even if he gets an hour to eat or to exercise, he is alone,” Mutimer said. “He is literally by himself, with his thoughts, in a room where the light never turns off all day.”

In an essay published Sunday by writer Monte Mader, Watson himself acknowledged spending his days in isolation, revealing that his Bible had only recently been returned to him and that he had little access to news.

Watson described the conditions of his confinement as the reality one must accept when choosing to engage in nonviolent resistance.

“Walking this path,” he said, “means exposing oneself to violence while refusing to retaliate against it.”

Major Jason Watson is NOT a Democrat. His protest was NOT about party politics. It was about what he believes his oath requires of him—and the price he’s willing to pay for speaking out. Everyone has seen the arrest. Now hear the courageous powerful speech that came first: pic.twitter.com/MMRoiYPV7K

After his July 1 protest, Watson had been restricted to Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling in Washington. Though the base reportedly has a confinement facility, following his detention, he was instead moved to a county jail in Maryland.

During Watson’s September 18 preliminary hearing, Maj. Joshua Wendell, the hearing officer, said Watson could not be confined with civilians and was therefore kept in solitary confinement.

“He was placed in confinement because of the law, which puts him in solitary confinement,” Wendell said, according to Stars and Stripes.

Article 13 of the UCMJ “forbids punishing a service member before trial and forbids pretrial restraint more rigorous than the circumstances require.”

Mutimer has pointed out that solitary confinement is “usually reserved for individuals who are disobeying or are violent, and injuring other people,” and usually only for “a day or two, or a week.” Watson, he said, has “been in there for months now.”

Rachel VanLandingham, a former Air Force judge advocate and professor of law at Southwestern Law School, told Common Dreams that this “seems to be a blatant case of illegal pretrial punishment given that the nature of his pretrial restraint does not seem necessary to either ensure his presence at trial or to prevent foreseeable serious criminal misconduct.”

“Solitary confinement is rare, and must be justified,” she said. “What, is the administration so afraid of this major’s words that he cannot talk to anyone?”

Military defense attorney Cody Harnish, who attended Watson’s preliminary hearing, has raised concerns that his detention could be unlawful and that his especially harsh treatment was political in nature.

“I represent people at court-martial in the military, who are accused of doing some very bad things,” he said during an interview this weekend with Meidas Defense. “They are not in pretrial confinement.”

Harnish noted other abnormal aspects of Watson’s preliminary hearing: He was denied the ability to wear his uniform and instead arrived handcuffed, unshaven, and wearing an undershirt, which pointed to the possibility that he was facing degrading treatment.

He also pointed out that Watson had submitted a request to resign his commission in exchange for avoiding a court-martial, but that the request was denied in 24 hours.

“Nothing gets processed in the military that fast,” he said, suggesting that this could indicate influence from senior Pentagon officials.

During his second term, Trump has used members of the military for political purposes in ways that have challenged longstanding norms of political neutrality. This has included hosting overtly political rallies before uniformed troops, screening them for ideology, and purging senior military officers deemed disloyal.

Harnish suggested that the Trump administration was seeking to make an example out of Watson for speaking out against the president.

“When someone speaks out against this administration in the military,” he said, “they’re going to crush him to silence anyone else in the ranks from ever thinking about it.”

title: Παρουσίαση δίσκου – ηχητικό ντοκουμέντο συναυλίας του Νίκου Παπάζογλου, Τετάρτη 14/10 στην Κάτω Τούμπα
content:
Στη «Μικρή Σκηνή», στις εγκαταστάσεις του πάλαι ποτέ στούντιο «Αγροτικόν» στην Κάτω Τούμπα, την Τετάρτη 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026, στις 21:30, θα παρουσιαστεί στους δημοσιογράφους, σε φίλους/ες ο διπλός δίσκος του Νίκου Παπάζογλου «Επιτόπια ηχογράφηση, Θέατρο Δάσους, 18 Αυγούστου 1986».




Πρόκειται για το ηχητικό ντοκουμέντο της συναυλίας που έδωσε ο Νίκος Παπάζογλου πριν 40 χρόνια, μπροστά σε περισσότερα από 4.000 άτομα εντός του χώρου του Θεάτρου Δάσους, και με άλλα τόσα τριγύρω στον δασικό «εξώστη». Ο Νίκος Παπάζογλου ερμήνευσε εκείνο το βράδυ τραγούδια της «Εκδίκησης της Γυφτιάς» (1978) και των «Δήθεν» (1979) με διαφορετικές ενορχηστρώσεις, τραγούδια από το πρώτο προσωπικό του «Χαράτσι» (1984), και παρουσίασε για πρώτη φορά κομμάτια από τον επερχόμενο δίσκο του «Μέσω νεφών» (1986), που ηχογραφούνταν την ίδια περίοδο, στο νέο «Αγροτικόν», στην 

Επταλόφου 14

, στην Κάτω Τούμπα.




Για την ενέργεια και την ιστορία πίσω από τον δίσκο, που κυκλοφορεί 15 χρόνια μετά τον θάνατο του Νίκου, σε παραγωγή «στρόγγυλοι δίσκοι», καθώς και για το μοναδικό και αυθεντικό αποτύπωμα του καλλιτέχνη στην εθνική και παγκόσμια μουσική σκηνή θα μιλήσουν:
