title: The people of Shengal must decide their own future
content:
More than 6,000 people were abducted during the attack on Shengal by ISIS mercenaries on 3 August 2014, and around 2,500 remain missing. The Yazidis refer to the attack, in which thousands of people were massacred and abducted, as the 74th Ferman in their history.




Shengal was liberated from ISIS in 2015. In the aftermath of the Ferman (Shengal genocide), the Yazidis established their own administrative and defence mechanisms, forming a People's Council and defence forces such as the Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Shengal Women's Units (YJŞ). The autonomous administration, which has operated in practice in Shengal ever since, continues to exist as an expression of the people's determination to govern and defend themselves.




Turkey-Iraq trade-off in New York




Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi met in New York on 23 September 2026 while attending the United Nations (UN) General Assembly. The joint statement issued after the meeting highlighted two main points: the full restoration of state authority in Shengal and the elimination of forces described in the statement as “prohibited foreign armed elements”, and the gradual transfer of the Turkish army's Bashiqa (Zilkan) base to the Iraqi federal government. The transfer process was made conditional on security measures to be taken by Iraq and a timetable to be agreed upon by both sides. However, no timetable has yet been announced.




The Turkish army established a presence at the Bashiqa base, approximately 30 kilometres northeast of Mosul, in December 2015. Around 600 Turkish soldiers are stationed at the base. Turkey's military presence in Iraq consists of five main bases, more than 2,000 soldiers and nearly 100 military positions. The transfer of the Bashiqa base, which accommodates fewer than a third of Turkey's total troops in Iraq, does not mean an end to Turkey's military presence in the country. Its other bases and military positions remain operational.




The agreement was interpreted in the Turkish press as an arrangement under which the Turkish army would end its presence at Bashiqa in exchange for the establishment of Iraqi state authority in Shengal. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also said at a press conference that these steps would be taken “after the terrorist group's presence in Shengal has been eliminated”.




Through this agreement, the Turkish state is seeking to position itself as a direct party to the Shengal issue. However, the administration and defence of a strategically important region such as Shengal have become a bargaining issue, traded against another state's military base in talks that excluded representatives of the people living there.




‘The solution lies in the constitution’




A meeting concerning the Yazidis was held in Baghdad on 1 September on the instructions of Ali Zeydi. All those attending the meeting on Shengal, which the Iraqi government held without Yazidi representatives, were military and security officials. Not a single Yazidi representative was invited. The appointment of a military district governor to Shengal was subsequently raised. However, the people of Shengal rejected the decision, stating that it had been made without their consent.




Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi later met with representatives of the YBŞ and the Yazidi community on 11 September. Sources familiar with the meeting reported that the Iraqi side had raised no serious objections to the Shengal delegation's demand to preserve its self-defence force, while the details of integration were left to a joint committee. The Iraqi Chief of General Staff visited Shengal with a military delegation on 22 September. The outcome of the visit was not disclosed, and the New York agreement was announced the following day.




This series of meetings demonstrates that Ankara was subsequently brought into the direct dialogue that Baghdad had established with Shengal. Baghdad has not ruled out the possibility of Shengal's self-defence forces continuing to operate within the Iraqi army under a recognised status. Keeping this possibility open, however, depends on continuing negotiations directly with Shengal.




Shengal's autonomy is, of course, another central issue in these discussions. Articles 122 and 123 of the Iraqi Constitution allow for extensive local autonomy without the establishment of a federal region. The constitution already provides for a degree of autonomy that would enable cultural and religious communities to preserve their existence, yet this fundamental right has not been recognised for the Yazidi community or Shengal. This demonstrates that Shengal's demands can be met within the framework of Iraq's existing constitution.




The women's dimension of the debate over self-defence in Shengal must not be overlooked. For women, this issue represents far more than a security arrangement. Leaving the YJŞ without recognised status carries the risk of returning women to the defencelessness they faced in 2014.




‘The future of Shengal and Rojava is being discussed at tables where they have no representation’




The process of military integration is also progressing in Rojava, but issues concerning mother-tongue education, local government institutions and the status of the Women's Protection Units (YPJ) remain unresolved. This experience demonstrates that integration involving the handover of weapons without recognition of local democracy would leave society without guarantees.




The Turkish state is also known to be seeking a say in the integration process and holding various talks with other countries on the issue. It appears that efforts are being made to determine the future of Shengal and Rojava at negotiating tables where their peoples have no representation.




‘The vacuum created by the lack of unity in Başûr’




Parliamentary elections in the Kurdistan Region were held on 20 October 2024. The Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), which together hold approximately two-thirds of the parliamentary seats, failed to reach an agreement on the distribution of government positions. As a result, no government has been formed despite the passage of nearly two years. Delegations from the two parties held at least 31 meetings during this period.




The mission of the International Coalition Against ISIS in Iraq ended on 30 September 2026, including its air defence systems in the Kurdistan Region. More than 1,000 drone and missile attacks have targeted Başûr since the war between the US, Israel and Iran began on 28 February 2026. Iran continued its attacks against Rojhilat parties in the Kurdistan Region even after the coalition's withdrawal.




In the wake of these developments, Peshmerga forces affiliated with the KDP and PUK were brought under a single ministry at a ceremony held in Erbil (Hewlêr) on 21 September. However, although the defence structure has been unified on paper, the forces remain under the control of the two parties on the ground.




‘Unity based on local democracy’




Abdullah Öcalan's proposal for Başûr has remained consistent for more than a year. At a meeting on Imrali in June 2025, Öcalan called on KDP President Masoud Barzani to take the lead in convening a National Congress. He also proposed to PUK President Bafel Talabani that the protocol agreed with Jalal Talabani in 1993 be renewed on the basis of democratic unity.




In a letter sent to the DEM Party Local Governments Conference held in Diyarbakır (Amed) on 8 June 2026, Öcalan also identified local democracy as the formula for a solution. He stressed that this approach should not be limited to Turkey but should serve as a formula for overcoming crises throughout the Middle East, particularly in Iraq and Syria, pointing to the need to establish a common political will and defence mechanism.




‘The will of the people of Shengal must be recognised’




Any unity that excludes Shengal cannot heal one of the deepest wounds within Başûr itself. Baghdad must therefore continue the talks it initiated on 11 September with the Shengal People's Council and the Autonomous Administration, without conditions imposed by a third state. The Shengal Resistance Units (YBŞ) and Shengal Women's Units (YJŞ) must be recognised within the Iraqi army under a status that allows them to remain in Shengal. The KDP and PUK must establish a unity government based on local democracy. The Turkish state, for its part, must withdraw not only from Bashiqa but also from its other military bases in Iraq.




The validity of any agreement concerning Shengal must depend on the consent and signature of the people of Shengal.

author: Unknown
title: PACE delegation meets with the DEM Party in Ankara, discusses the peace process
content:
Petra Bayr, President of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), held talks with the DEM Party during her official visit to Turkey on Monday. Accompanied by her delegation, she met with Co-Chair Tülay Hatimoğulları, Deputy Parliamentary Group Chair Sezai Temelli, and MP Sevilay Çelenk, who is a member of the Turkish delegation to PACE, at the Turkish Parliament.




The discussions focused on the role of Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan in the Peace and Democratic Society Process. Reference was made to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerning the so-called “right to hope.” DEM Party representatives emphasized that Öcalan must be provided with living and working conditions that would allow him to participate freely in the peace process.




The discussions also addressed the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) rulings concerning imprisoned politicians Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, as well as human rights activist and cultural philanthropist Osman Kavala, which have yet to be implemented. The Council of Europe delegation expressed its concern regarding these issues. Further meetings with political representatives in Turkey are scheduled as part of the official visit.

author: Battlescarred
title: The Founding Congress of the International Workers Association
content:
An account of the founding of the IWA in 1922

The founding of the International Workers Association at its constitutive congress in Berlin in 1922 was a long wished for goal of revolutionary syndicalists and anarchists around the world. The First International had been wound up at the congress in Philadelphia in 1875, and definitively dissolved in July of the following year. The end of the First International due to the clash between Marx and his followers and those who opposed him, including the grouping around Bakunin, Belgian socialists and British trade unionists, was a severe setback for the international workers’ movement. The so-called Anti-Authoritarian International founded at St Imier in Switzerland in 1872 had also foundered by 1877. Many revolutionary syndicalists felt the need for a new International, especially as the social-democratic parties had created their own international, the Second International, in 1889. This had been followed by the reformist trade unions creating their own international, The International Secretariat of National Trade Union Centres (ISNTUC) in 1901. When this collapsed because of the First World War, the reformist unions created the International Federation of Trade Unions (IFTU) at a congress in Amsterdam in July 1919. This united unions from United States, Belgium, Denmark, Germany, France, Great Britain, Holland, Luxemburg, Norway, Austria, Sweden, Switzerland, Spain, and Czechoslovakia. It represented 17.7 million workers and had a social-democratic orientation.

The first mass revolutionary syndicalist, anarchosyndicalist and industrial unionist unions had emerged at the end of the 19th century and beginning of the 20th century and included the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) founded 1905, and the Federación Obrera Regional Argentina (Workers Regional Federation of Argentina-FORA) the Confédération Générale du Travail (General Confederation of Labour-CGT) founded in France in 1895, the Italian Unione Sindacale Italiana (USI), the Swedish Sveriges Arbetares Centralorganisation (SAC) founded in 1910 and the Dutch industrial federations, The Spanish CNT founded in 1910.

The International Syndicalist Congress of 1913

The first attempt to create a new international from these various unions took place in London in 1913. This, the International Syndicalist Congress, took place at Holborn Town Hall between September 27th to October 2nd, at the initiative of the Dutch Nationaal Arbeids-Secretariaat (National Labour Secretariat –NAS) and the British Industrial Syndicalist Education League (ISEL). Solidaridad Obrera (Workers Solidarity) in Catalonia, a precursor of the CNT, supported the move. However, the French CGT opposed the convening of such a congress. It was still within the ISNTUC and feared internal ructions as its reformist wing was strengthening at the expense of the anarchist and revolutionary syndicalist wing.

Thirty eight delegates representing sixty five organisations met and passed the following resolution:

The first International Syndicalist Congress recognises that the working class of all countries suffers the same repression by the State and the capitalist system. For this reason, it declares itself in favour of class struggle, international solidarity and independent organisation of the working class on the basis of the federative union. This tends to the immediate material and moral elevation of the working class until the total destruction of capitalism and the State. This declares, furthermore, that the class struggle is a necessary consequence of the private possession of the means of production and distribution, and that, therefore, this Congress tends to the socialisation of these means. In this sense, the constitution and development of trade union organisations should be oriented, since they are in the best conditions to ensure the production and distribution of products for the benefit of society as a whole. Verifying that the international unions cannot successfully carry out the class struggle if the workers continue to be divided by political and religious differences, the Congress declares that the class struggle, as such, can only have an economic character, for which the workers' organisations should not seek the stated goal through collaboration with the government or with its allies, and that they should rely solely on the power of the organisations and their direct action. As a consequence of this declaration, the Congress calls on the workers of all countries to unite in independent, federal, industrial organisations, on the basis of international solidarity, in order to liberate themselves completely from the oppression exerted by the state and capitalism.

Thus, the principles of revolutionary syndicalism, affirmation of class struggle, international solidarity, socialisation of property and the abolition of capitalism and the State, rejection of parliamentary activity, and struggle on the economic level through direct action, were adopted by the congress. It was decided to follow this up with another congress the following year. Unfortunately, the outbreak of the First World War scuppered this. The NAS then sent out a circular calling for a new congress at the end of the war. Attempts to hold such a congress were foiled at every attempt, by the Dutch, Swedish and Danish governments. The First World War brought many problems to the international syndicalist movement, with the French CGT supporting the War, apart from a small revolutionary minority around Pierre Monatte and Alphonse Merrheim, the heavy repression unleashed against the IWW in the United States, and the ructions within the USI over support for the war, culminating in the move towards a clear anarchist and internationalist position and the departure of the pro-war faction.

Other problems were caused by the repercussions of the Russian revolution.

The Red Trade Union International

The accession to power of the Bolsheviks in 1917 led on to the founding of the Third International, known under the Russian abbreviation of the Comintern, in 1919, uniting various Communist Parties under the control of Moscow. Alongside this was the founding of the Red International of Labour Unions (RILU), also known under the Russian abbreviation Profintern in July 1921. The Soviet leadership sought to unite those trade unions worldwide that were opposed to the so-called Amsterdam international, the IFTU. They worked towards an alliance of Communist controlled labour organisations, revolutionary syndicalist and anarcho-syndicalist unions, and the revolutionary opposition within Amsterdam unions, as well as anti-colonial movements around the world. They thus sought to establish hegemony over these diverse groupings and to recruit to the Communist Parties. At first the USI, the CNT, some French unions and currents within the FORA supported the RILU. For example, the CNT at its second congress in Madrid in December 1919 passed the following motion in relation to the Third International:

The National Confederation of Labour declares itself a firm defender of the principles that inform the First International, supported by Bakunin. It declares that it adheres, and provisionally, to the Third International, due to the revolutionary character that presides over it, while the International Congress is being organised and held in Spain, which will lay the foundations by which the true International of workers will be governed.

The CNT decided to send delegates to Moscow on a fact-finding mission. Only one of them managed to get there. This was Angel Pestaña, who attended the Second Congress of the Third International, in the summer of 1920. Pestaña began to have doubts about the overbearing attitude of the Bolsheviks. The Bolshevik trade union leader Solomon Lozovski insisted that revolutionaries not leave the reformist trade unions. This was objected to by Pestaña and the German anarcho-syndicalist Augustin Souchy. Further objections came over the subordination of revolutionary syndicalist organisations to the various Communist Parties.

Revolutionary syndicalist bodies were accused of being minority organisations. A hasty convened first congress of international trade unionists and syndicalists then took place on July 15th. Further experiences convinced Pestaña and the USI delegate, the anarchist Armando Borghi, that the differences between the syndicalists and the Bolsheviks were profound and hastened their departure from Russia in late August-early September. In October Pestaña met with German syndicalists for lengthy discussions in Berlin and then moved on to Italy. However, here he was detained and deported to Spain two months later. He was immediately arrested in Barcelona and spent the whole of 1921 in jail. This deprived the CNT of his views of the Bolshevik government. As a result, the CNT held a conference where it was decided to send further delegates to the Third Congress of the Third International in June 1921. These included Andreu Nin, Joaquín Maurín, Jesús Ibáñez, Hilario Arlandis and Gaston Leval. These participated in the first congress of the RILU. This conference confirmed the dominance of the Bolsheviks. Concerns about anarchist prisoners on hunger strike in the Taganka prison were raised, and led the Bolsheviks into being forced to agree to their deportation. Tensions rose as both Trotsky and Bukharin denounced Russian anarchists as “petty bourgeois” and “counter-revolutionary”. Alexander Schapiro was not allowed the podium to defend Russian anarchist syndicalists. The pro- and anti-Bolshevik currents within the CNT took part in heated debates. Both the anarchists and the “pure” syndicalists, who objected to any political activity, objected to the stance of Maurín, Nin, Ibáñez, and Arlandis, who they accused of being too accommodating to the Communists. As a result, the anarchist character of the CNT was strengthened and in the following period Maurín and Nin became founders of the Partido Obrero de Unificación Marxista (Workers’ Party of Marxist Unification, POUM). The fierce polemic led on to moves by the CNT to disaffiliate from the RILU, and this was reinforced by the reports of Pestaña when he finally emerged from prison in 1922. In June of that year, the CNT held a conference in Zaragoza where Pestaña’s testimony and Gaston Leval’s criticisms of his co-delegates led to the CNT turning against the Third International and the RILU. A large majority agreed that whilst the CNT had supported the Russian Revolution, this did not mean that it supported Bolshevik practice and theory.

However, as support for the Comintern had been agreed on at the congress of 1919, the CNT conference could not overturn the original decision. As a result, it was decided to suspend relations with RILU and continue to discuss within the different unions of the Confederation. The CNT was now looking towards helping create a new international, hooking up with the German syndicalists. The move by syndicalists in France and Italy to convene a conference in Paris seemed to provide a springboard for this.

Earlier, German anarchist syndicalists in the Freie Arbeiter Union Deutschlands- (German Free Workers Union FAUD)-meeting in Dusseldorf in October made efforts to unite opposition to Moscow within the revolutionary syndicalist unions. The meeting was also attended by delegates from the NAS, the SAC, and the IWW, and called for the convoking of an international syndicalist conference in Berlin, caused by the failure of the RILU to establish an international free from political influence. This was endorsed by telegram by the USI. The CGT in France had been much compromised by its support for the world war and its leadership under Léon Jouhaux had accepted posts on various government committees during the war. After the war it had pronounced reformists positions and was hostile to the Russian Revolution. As a result, the revolutionary minority within the CGT organised, after the Lyon congress of 1919, the Comités syndicalistes révolutionnaires (CSR) which grouped together anarchists, pure syndicalists and those now favourable to the Comintern. The CSR were the main force behind the split within the CGT which led to the appearance of the CGTU (“U” for Unitaire, Unified) which had its first conference in late June 1922. At first the anarchists were dominant within the CGTU. The happenings at the RILU congress exacerbated the differences within the CGTU. It was decided to send delegates to the Berlin congress proposed by the FAUD in June 1922. Similarly, the FORA was also dismayed by the RILU congress and enthusiastically endorsed the Berlin congress, whilst openly severely criticising Tom Barker, who had taken the FORA mandate to the RILU Congress. The IWW also decided by the end of 1921 that it could not consider membership of the RILU.

The CGTU, SAC, NAS, FAUD. USI, CNT were all represented at the Berlin conference of June 16th -18th, as well as the Norsk Syndikalist Federation (NSF) of Norway and claimed to represent a total of 1,400,000 workers. The conference also recognised a delegation of Russian anarchist syndicalists in the shape of Alexander Schapiro and Mark Mrachnyi, who had left Russia for Germany. The conference had also invited the All-Russian Confederation of Trade Unions to attend. Andreyev, a representative of this Communist controlled body duly appeared on the second day of the conference and clashed with Mrachnyi, defending Red terror and the dictatorship of the proletariat, and demanding that Mrachnyi’s remarks be ruled inadmissible by conference. For some delegates wavering over what relationship they should have with the RILU, this was the last straw. The June conference was hardly a complete success. The CGTU delegation stated that it could not vote on any deliberations as its congress would be held in St. Etienne in two weeks and it thus had no mandate. The original libertarian dominance within the CGTU was being challenged by an increasingly belligerent Communist minority and by the syndicalists around Monatte, who were the target of a campaign by the RILU to win them over. Thus, it was unsure what the result of the St Etienne congress would be. Before Andreyev left the conference, he warned that “the RILU will go over the heads of the present leaders of the CGTU and the USI in order to organise the French and Italian workers’ movements according to its own directives”. As to taking a stand on the persecution of Russian anarchists, this was fudged by the conference. Louis Lecoin and Henri Toti, speaking for the French delegation, were concerned that the CGTU was close to being captured by the Communists and were sure that the Russians would send a representative to the St Etienne Congress. They appealed to the other delegates not to put a motion forward on the persecutions, which the latter reluctantly agreed to. More positively, conference agreed to a ten point declaration on syndicalism drafted by Rudolf Rocker of the FAUD and to the setting up of an International Bureau. Rocker concluded that “an existence in common with Moscow will become insufferable even for those filled with false hopes. In the meantime we will lose time and pessimism will infiltrate our ranks”. As a result, the creation of a revolutionary syndicalist international independent of Moscow was inevitable. Lozovski of the RILU denounced the forthcoming congress, accusing the syndicalists of sectarianism. The RILU executive broke off all correspondence with the International Syndicalist Bureau.

Over thirty delegates attended the illegal congress in Berlin from December 25th 1922 to January 2nd, 1923. They represented the USI, the FAUD, the SAC, the NAS, the NSF, and the Syndikalistik Propagandaforbund of Denmark, the FORA, and the CGT of Mexico. The Portuguese CGT sent its consent to the founding of the IWA as did the IWW of Chile, whose delegate only arrived after end of the congress. The delegates of the Spanish CNT were arrested in Paris before they reached Berlin. A delegate from the Federacion Obrera Regional Uruguaya (FORU) of Uruguay similarly arrived too late to take part. A number of consultative votes were given to the councilist union Allgemeine Arbeiter-Union Einheitsorganisation (AAUE), the Russian syndicalists in the form of Schapiro and Yarchuk, and the Czechoslovak Freie Arbeiter-Union. As to the French, the St Etienne Congress had led to the accession of the Communists in alliance with the syndicalists around Monatte and Monmousseau. As a result, the anarchist Pierre Besnard founded the Comité de Défense Syndicaliste- Committee of Syndicalist Defence (CDS) to organise those opposed to affiliation to the RILU. Besnard and Claudine Lemoine represented the CDS at Berlin but were in a delicate position. Whilst most of the delegations represented organisations that had rejected the RILU, the CDS was an organised minority within the CGTU which was negotiating with the RILU. The CDS grouping hoped to eventually win the day within the CGTU and were reluctant to force a split (there had been a split with the parent CGT only a year before) and called for unity of workers’ organisations nationally and internationally. Besnard and Lemoine were thus reluctant to create a new revolutionary syndicalist international. Lemoine and Dissel of the NAS delegation called for further negotiation with the RILU. Delegate after delegate rose to argue against this, stating that the founding of a new international could not be delayed. A dissenting member of the NAS, Bernard Lansink Jr., got up to state that he truly reflected the majority of NAS members whose referendum had rejected joining the RILU and were in favour of a new international. Rocker remarked that every syndicalist organisation contacted by the International Bureau in Europe and the Americas were in favour of a new international. He said that “We must finally declare clearly: the Third International and the RILU are not organisations of the revolutionary proletariat, they are agencies for the foreign policy of the Russian government”. He warned the French and Dutch that compromise with Moscow would oppose them to other revolutionary syndicalists worldwide. He and other delegates expressed surprise that the NAS leadership had ignored the referendum. The SAC then moved a resolution rejecting an appeal from the RILU to the syndicalists assembled at Berlin to join their international. Upon the passing of the motion, the NAS delegates withdrew from the congress. A resolution from the Argentinean, Danish, German, Italian, Norwegian and Swedish delegations calling for the founding of a new international was then passed unanimously. However, French support was qualified. Besnard declared CDS support for the new International provided that it sought to unite all revolutionary workers willing to overthrow capitalism and the State. A united front should be sought with those organisations outside the new International. This was perfectly acceptable to nearly all delegates, but the CDS delegation went further and called for a formal instruction to the new Secretariat to approach the RILU for united action. This was vehemently opposed by the FORA as represented by Diego Abad de Santillan. The Argentineans believed that the FORA form of organisation, combining elements of Italian and Spanish anarchism, was a truer form of values expressed by Bakunin and his associates within the First International than within the European movement, influenced by socialist political parties and politically oriented union organisations. They were particularly suspicious of elements within the Spanish CNT which had initially joined the RILU. They regarded CNT leaders like Pestaña and Salvador Segui as “chameleons” for their initial support of Moscow. They believed that if the CNT delegates had not been detained, they would have backed the French/NAS motion. They noted “The FORA has clearly signalled its point of view for several years, and if it agreed to the creation of a new international it was with the belief that revolutionary syndicalism throughout the entire world had understood and appreciated its actions over the last several years. In its decision to create a new International of revolutionary workers it absolutely rejects political entities such as those of Amsterdam (Social-Democrats) and Moscow (Communists). Santillan argued vehemently for opposition to the RILU, saying that unity of the proletariat was a “metaphysical illusion” and to drop any moves by the CDS which would only deliver French workers to Moscow. However, an appreciation among delegates of the delicate situation of the CDS led to an endorsement on Revolutionary Unity, with the FORA abstaining. There were unfortunate disruptions by the German police who conducted passport checks and arrested 13 people, including at least three delegates. The Congress agreed to create a revolutionary syndicalist international, emphasising continuity with the past and the First International by calling it the International Workers Association (IWA/AIT). This was on the suggestion of the USI delegate Alibrando Giovanetti, secretary of its metalworkers’ union. It also adopted a ten-point document, the Principles of Revolutionary Syndicalism, drafted by Rocker at the June Congress. The controversy within NAS continued after the congress for a long time. Eventually in a referendum in May 1923, members voted by 53 to 47 per cent for affiliation to RILU. This eventually led to a secession of the dissidents and the founding of the Nederlands Syndicalistisch Vakverbond (NSV), urging NAS members “Do your duty as true revolutionaries, as libertarian communists, as organised syndicalists”. In November 1923 the NSV had won 8,000 out of 23,000 NAS members over and won a lot of support among metalworkers, textile and tobacco workers. It voted by the end of the year to join the IWA. In France, once Monmousseau had acceded to power within the CGTU, the French Communist Party (PCF) started expanding a network of Syndical Commissions controlled by it within the CGTU. This caused uproar among those members opposed to domination by political parties and for autonomy the situation was further aggravated by the murder of two anarchist workers, Poncet and Clos, by Communist thugs at the House of Unions in Rue Grange aux Belles in Paris on 11th January 1924. (1) The RILU, of course, took the side of the PCF. This eventually resulted in the founding of the CGT-Syndicaliste Revolutionnaire (CGT-SR) by Besnard and others in November 1926, which affiliated to the IWA. As to the FORA’s critical stand, any doubts about affiliation to the IWA disappeared when the motion on Revolutionary Unity was rescinded at the IWA’s Innsbruck conference in December 1923. They also felt vindicated by the losses the CDS had sustained in France, which seemed to them to confirm their warning. During 1923 and 1924 the Mexican CGT, the Uruguayan FORU and the Chilean IWW affiliated to the IWA, to be followed later by syndicalist unions in Brazil, Paraguay and other Central and South American countries. There was also a Japanese affiliate. As to the IWW of North America, only its Marine Transport Workers Industrial Union affiliated. The IWW had adopted a position of neutrality as regards to the Berlin congress and said that it would join neither the RILU nor the IWA.

Between 1923 the IWA had affiliates in thirty one countries. However, repression soon began to hit the IWA affiliates. The USI was destroyed by the Mussolini regime between 1922 and 1924. The Portugese CGT, which had a mass membership, was outlawed in 1926 and almost completely destroyed by 1934. The FAUD lost many of its members between 1923 and 1933 and then suffered destruction by the Nazi regime. The CGT-SR remained a minority union and disappeared with the Second World War. In Latin America, the FORA was outlawed after 1930 as the result of a military coup. The Mexican CGT evolved increasingly in a reformist direction from 1928 onwards. Nevertheless the 1922 Congress was important in its affirmation of revolutionary syndicalism, its recognition of class struggle, its avowal of free communism and its stand against Communist Party domination. It should be noted that the key statements emerging from the founding congress of the IWA referred to revolutionary syndicalism rather than anarchosyndicalism. The term “anarcho-syndicalism” was not then currently in use. It had originally been used as a pejorative term by the reformist socialists around Jules Guesde. Shortly after the end of the First World War, the Bolsheviks appropriated the term and continued to use it in a pejorative sense. Eventually the revolutionary syndicalist minority in France decided to reclaim it as a self-descriptor but Pierre Besnard was reluctant to use the term until 1937. Nevertheless, the IWA can be described as an anarcho-syndicalist organisation and it was with the foundation of the IWA that anarchosyndicalism as a current was affirmed on a global level.

(1) see my article at libcom: https://libcom.org/article/shootout-rue-grange-aux-belles-1924

Sources: Baer, James A. Anarchist Immigrants in Spain and Argentina. University of Illinois Press. Damier, Vadim. Anarcho-syndicalism in the 20th century. Black Cat Press Guinchard, Francois. The birth of an international anarchosyndicalist current. Workers of the World: International Journal on Strikes and Social Conflicts, Volume I, Number 4. Thorpe, Wayne. Revolutionary syndicalist internationalism 1913– 1923: the origins of the International Working Men’s Association. 1989 Thesis. Tosstorf, Reiner. “Mission Impossible: Angel Pestana’s encounter as CNT delegate with the Bolshevik Revolution in 1920”. in: David Berry and Constance Bantman, eds, New Perspectives on Anarchism, Labour, and Syndicalism: The Individual, the National and the Transnational. Cambridge Scholars Publishing.

The article above originally appeared in Black Flag Anarchist Review, Summer 2022.

author: Chris Walker
title: Leaked Audio Features MI GOP Candidate Rogers Mocking Affordability Concerns
content:
Rogers minimized worries about rising costs due to Trump administration policies as “derangement.”

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

In newly unearthed audio, Republican candidate for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers (Michigan) appears to dismiss one of the top issues motivating voters in this year’s midterm races: affordability.

In a radio interview from January, Rogers blasted Democrats for highlighting the fact that Americans are facing higher consumer prices on myriad goods and services.

“They [Democrats] say, ‘Trump caused high prices’ — people go nuts, they lose their mind. I do believe there is this Trump derangement,” Rogers, a millionaire, said in the interview, minimizing legitimate concerns about rising costs.

Michigan GOP Senate Candidate Mike Rogers argues that concern over affordability is just 'Trump derangement': Rogers: They say, ‘Trump caused high prices’—people go nuts, they lose their mind. I do believe there is this Trump derangement. pic.twitter.com/VOfDhDYa3b

“[Democrats] have the gall to come out and say, ‘Guess what? We are the only ones that care about how expensive your life is,'” Rogers added.

In separate leaked audio featuring Rogers, the GOP candidate derides worries over higher costs for specific grocery items.

“Oh my gosh, coffee went up,” Rogers says on tape, mocking those concerns. “You know, horror!”

Rogers recently dismissed reporters who asked whether he should “provide an explanation” for those comments, belittling the query as “a couple of DNC talking points.”

Voters across the U.S. are, in fact, concerned about inflation, as prices are significantly higher on many staple items due in large part to President Donald Trump’s tariffs against other countries. Trump’s decision to launch a war on Iran has also resulted in rising fuel costs, which have increased costs of other goods, as diesel is needed to transport items for shipment across the U.S.

The Trump administration likely bears all of the responsibility for rising prices. According to a report from the New York Federal Reserve that was published last week, costs for many goods were actually decreasing before the president implemented an array of tariffs in his first year back in the White House. Because of that policy decision, prices are now increasing.

On a per capita basis, Michigan has been hit the hardest by price increases, with one estimate showing the total per-person household increase in costs being around $5,600 in the state.

Meanwhile, the latest polls show that Michigan voters are more supportive of the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed. In an aggregate of polling data from FiftyPlusOne, El-Sayed garners 48.2 percent of the vote while Rogers receives only 44.8 percent.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: « À trois on vous nique vos mères » : tournant répressif à Lyon avec une manifestation interdite à mi-parcours
content:
Le mouvement lycéen à se démarque depuis le 28 septembre par son intensité. Les lycéen·nes sur les blocages, et en particulier dans les différentes communes de banlieue, ont montré leur détermination avec des actions de blocus offensifs, barricades et manifs sauvages au rendez-vous. Iels ont également dû faire face à une intense répression orchestrée par la Préfecture et exécutée par les keufs et les chef·fes d'établissements. On a vu devant les lycées les flics faire massivement usage de gaz, mais aussi de 

LBD

 et de 

différentes grenades

, notamment les petites nouvelles, «

 

GL

-304 Condor

 

», théoriquement assourdissantes et remplaçantes des tristement célèbres «

 

GM2L

 

». Les blocus ont également donné lieu à de nombreuses arrestations, des lycéen·nes comme de leurs soutiens, tandis que côté établissement, ont été prononcées des expulsions contre les élèves bloqueur·euses, ainsi que des conseils de discipline. Tout, pour mettre fin à la mobilisation.




Premières manifs




Dès la première semaine de mob', les lycéen·nes ont montré leur détermination dans la rue. Le mardi 29 septembre, les lycéen·nes rejoignent la manifestation nationale de la fonction publique. Le jeudi 1

er

 octobre, le rassemblement appelé à Jean Macé par les lycéen·nes débraye en manif sauvage avec dans le viseur le rectorat. Le vendredi, c'est le rassemblement à l'Hôtel de Région Montrochet qui part en sauvage. Les keufs, à chaque fois, s'en donnent à cœur joie. Le 29, on compte 41 interpellations. Le rassemblements de soutien aux interpellés qui a lieu le soir même est nassé et les soutiens contrôlés. Le 30, 17 nouvelles interpelations. Le 1

er

 octobre, les flics répriment salement la sauvage de Jean Macé, et arrêtent 38 personnes dans la journée, en comptant 14 lycéen-nes sur le blocage du lycée Colbert (Lyon 3

e

), aligné·es dans une mise en scène qui rappelle celle de Mantes-la-Jolie en 2018. Le 2 octobre, les flics arrêtent 31 personnes et en blessent de nombreuses autres, notamment dans les attaques de la manif sauvage qu'ils chargent et gazent abondamment jusque dans la gare Perrache. À la fin de la première semaine, on apprend que les keufs ont tiré 

plus de 800 grenades lacrymogènes

 dans l'agglo' pour contenir la révolte, et arrêté 127 personnes.
















 

@la_looutre











La deuxième semaine de mobilisation est marquée par deux grosses manifestations.


Le mardi 6 octobre, près de 30 000 personnes sont dans la rue avec les lycéen·nes. La tête du cortège, lycéenne et étudiante, avance rapidement. Le cortège arrivé à la place Guichard, plusieurs tentatives de sauvage ont lieu, les rues alentours sont retournées et plusieurs barricades enflammées sont dressée, ce qui aboutit à un face à face de près de 2h avec les flics, qui gazent abondamment la foule. Finalement, un cortège de plusieurs centaines de personnes part en manif sauvage dans le 7

e

 et se dirige vers le rectorat. La police, qui avaient perdu sa trace jusque là, occupée par les barricades de Guichard, finissent par gazer très largement les manifestant·es, et effectuent plusieurs charges.
















 







Le 7 octobre, les lycéen·nes tentent de se rassembler à Jean Macé et sont contrôlés en masse par la police. 


Le 8 octobre, la manifestation au départ de Bron réunit là encore plusieurs millers de personnes malgré la pluie. À la fin du parcours, une partie des manifestant·es part en sauvage dans le 8

e

, mais les flics interviennent rapidemment, en gazant et chargeant le cortège, le forçant à se disperser. Ils finissent par obtenir la dispersion complète des manifestant-es en quadrillant le quartier et le noyant sous les lacrymos.
















 







On voit au fil de la mobilisation le dispositif policier changer. D'une repression brutale sur les blocus des lycéen·nes, à un dispositif relâché sur la manif des fonctionnaires, de l'usage abondant de gaz sur les premières manifs jusqu'au recourt à des charges policières sur le cortège...




Manif du 13 octobre




La manifestation de ce mardi change encore une fois le visage de la mobilisation et de sa repression. Rapidemment après le départ, un cortège de tête déterminé se forme. On peut célébrer les caméras défoncées et surtout les quelques onze banques et assurances du parcours dont les vitrines ont été éclatées, le mobilier et la paperasse sortis dans la rue.
















 

@la_looutre











Si la manif a commencé avec un dispositif policier relâché, les flics ont pas tardé à rappliquer et avec des premières salves de lacrymos, on ne compte pas le nombre de charges qui ont été effectuées sur la tête comme le reste du cortège. Les flics ont en outre passé une demi-heure à harceler la manifestation en l'empêchant de franchir le croisement du cour Lafayette et de la rue Baraban et en la coupant en deux. Tout ce temps, des grenades lacrymogènes pleuvaient de tous les côtés afin d'empêcher les deux parties du cortège de se rejoindre. On applaudit d'ailleurs la détermination et l'offensivité du bloc, qui a patiemment renvoyé les palets de lacrymos un à un. En dépit de la mise en place d'un cordon du service d'ordre de l'intersyndical pour permettre à la manfestation de se poursuivre, les flics continuaient à vider leurs chargeurs comme des boeufs. Finalement, voyant l'inefficacité de leurs salves de lacrymogènes, les flics finissent par charger sur une vingtaine de mètre le cortège très mixte, matraquant à tout va les personnes bloquées par la foule dense, et envoyant au passage quelques désencerclantes pour marquer le coup.




Pour autant, c'est au son des slogans toujours plus motivés que la manifestation a finalement réussi faire jonction et à reprendre son chemin... pour une courte durée.




Cet après-midi à Lyon, on a assisté à de véritables mêlées entre les keufs et les manifestant·es, à un cortège divisé et pris en étaux, à des tirs de 

LBD

 sur la foule, l'envoi de grenades désencerclantes.
















 




 

À trois, on vous nique vos mères*

 




Alors que le cortège arrive à Totem dans le calme, la situation prend vite un tour chaotique. Alors qu'une énième banque est en train de se faire soulever, la 

CRS83

 fait une sorte de charge sur le rond point pour effrayer le gros de la manifestation qui s'engage sur le rond point avant de poursuivre en courant la tête de cortège qui s'était déjà engagée cours Tolstoï. Le cortège assiste alors à une centaine de mètres au lynchage par les flics de la tête de cortège et su 

SO

 de l'intersyndicale, pendant qu'un autre groupe de 

CRS

 garde le reste de la manifestation en mire, la dissuadant de venir en soutien de la tête. Contrairement à ce que répètent en boucle les journaleux de la presse locale, ce sont les 

CRS

 qui ont poussé le cortège aussi rapidement vers la station essence du cours Tolstoï, en s'acharnant sur les manifestant-es avec des charges et des matraquages répétés, des tirs de 

LBD

 et un gazage quasi constant.




La manifestation tente alors à plusieurs reprise de rejoindre la tête de cortège en s'engageant à son tour cours Tolstoï. Chaque tentative est marquée par un gazage instantané, des insultes des flics et in fine, plusieurs charges. Les flics s'engagent ensuite dans les rues adjacentes pour partir en chasse aux manifestant-es qui tentent soit de rejoindre l'un ou l'autre des deux bouts de la manifestation, ou d'évacuer la zone.




Dans le cortège, le mot finit par passer qu'au moment de l'arrivée à Totem, et donc en plein milieu du parcours, la préfecture aurait publié sur X l'ordre de dispersion de la manif', ce que les 

CRS

 se mettent à répéter en beuglant dans leurs mégaphones, tout en continuant de s'en prendre à la manifestation, empêchant toute dispersion.




La manif fait de nombreux·ses blessé·es et malaises dus aux gaz. Il y aurait une trentaine d'arrestation (chiffres à affiner...).




L'interdiction d'une manifestation à mi-parcours relève du jamais-vu à Lyon

, et la mobilisation prend visiblement un nouveau tournant repressif ce mardi.




Pour autant, l'offensitivité du cortège aujourd'hui, qui rassemble à nouveau plus de 10 000 personnes montre que le mouvement lycéen et étudiant se fera pas étouffer aussi facilement, et que nous restons plus déterminé-es que jamais. 

Ça continue à bloquer tous les jours, et on se retrouve dans la rue jeudi à 15h aux Terreaux à l'appel des lycéen-nes

 

!




Contre la Pref' et ses laquais casqués, solidarité

 

!




Petit bonus

 : attention, cascade réalisée par des professionnel-les :










copie écran du compte X de la précture du Rhône. 2h après avoir fracassé une manif, une publication qui invite les lycéen-nes au dialogue, youpi

 

!








*parole de keuf rapportée par un manifestant juste avant une charge

author: CMI Argentina
title: El desguace silencioso en el Gran Rosario: desocupación al 11,5% y fábricas en retirada
content:
El derrumbe del poder de compra, el freno total a la obra pública y la apertura indiscriminada de importaciones asfixiaron al mercado interno. Sin demanda, las empresas locales no venden y sus márgenes de ganancia se desploman.




Protesta de los obreros de Pampa Energía tras el cierre de la única fábrica de caucho del país el 21 de julio pasado. Foto: Juan José García, Diario El Ciudadano




Frente a este escenario, las patronales optan por liquidar activos, desinvertir y deshacerse de los trabajadores al menor costo posible. La prioridad es una sola: evitar la chispa de la conflictividad social —tomas de planta, cortes de ruta o huelgas extendidas— que históricamente caracterizó a la región, hoy neutralizada con el auxilio de la reforma laboral.




El cordón industrial asiste al cierre intempestivo de establecimientos con un rasgo de época: la indemnización íntegra e inmediata casi no existe. Se imponen pagos en cuotas o se arrastra al trabajador a juicios interminables. Esta violencia patronal que expulsa a familias enteras de un día para el otro, opera en muchos casos sin resistencias que estén a la altura del daño.




Electrolux cerró su producción y despidió a 200 obreros en septiembre.




La trampa burocrática y el chantaje del desempleo




Ante la primera protesta en los portones, el conflicto se empantana de inmediato en el Ministerio de Trabajo bajo la conciliación obligatoria: no se auditan los números de las empresas, no se reactivan las máquinas y el tiempo ganado no se utiliza para reorganizar la fuerza laboral. La medida opera simplemente como un freezer que traslada el conflicto de la fábrica a los expedientes.




En ese compás de espera, la extorsión económica hace su trabajo. Con miles de desocupados, subocupados e informales golpeando puertas afuera, el miedo disciplina: quedarse a pelear por una fábrica vaciada parece una condena a no cobrar un solo peso.




Dow cerró su planta en Puerto San Martín en octubre de 2024 con 120 despidos.

 

Foto: Soepu.




La soledad del acuerdo y el saldo final




Ahí la resistencia colectiva se quiebra y ganan terreno los “retiros voluntarios”. El obrero queda completamente solo frente al empleador, en una supuesta negociación entre partes “libres e iguales” que en realidad es una rendición forzada por el hambre. El trabajador no elige irse; acepta una suma a la baja para garantizar la subsistencia de los próximos meses. El Estado corona el engranaje: su único rol es homologar el trámite para exhibir una falsa “paz social”.




Al final del circuito, el negocio cierra perfecto: la empresa liquida su planta sin huelgas ni ocupaciones; el gobierno publicita el orden; y los trabajadores quedan en la calle, descartados como piezas que ya no rinden ganancia. Cuando este mecanismo se vuelve la norma cotidiana, el estallido deja de ser una hipótesis y pasa a ser cuestión de tiempo.







Luciana Censi es abogada laboralista y asesora sindical.




La entrada 

El desguace silencioso en el Gran Rosario: desocupación al 11,5% y fábricas en retirada

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Josh Richman
title: Privacy's Defenders Podcast: No Privacy Without Encryption
content:
When we communicate online today – from your personal emails and DMs to secure international commerce – we usually do so with encryption. Encryption converts readable data into unreadable gibberish to protect our privacy and security. This didn’t just happen organically. Three decades ago, the U.S government treated encryption like a weapon, and it took some unlikely heroes to set it free: a grad student, a junior lawyer, and a fledgling digital rights group who sued the federal government.

 




The ruling in 

Bernstein v. Department of Justice

 held that code is speech and so is protected by the First Amendment – a precedent that underpins the internet as we know it today. This landmark case was led by Cindy Cohn, then a young pro bono lawyer working on behalf of EFF, who went on to become EFF’s legal director and then executive director.

 




Welcome to the second episode of “Privacy’s Defenders,” a podcast about the people – lawyers, journalists, hackers, and others – who’ve fought to secure your digital liberties since before most people even knew what the internet was.

 
















%3Ciframe%20height%3D%2252px%22%20width%3D%22100%25%22%20frameborder%3D%22no%22%20scrolling%3D%22no%22%20seamless%3D%22%22%20src%3D%22https%3A%2F%2Fplayer.simplecast.com%2F91542147-6839-46fe-a813-73eb7a5c683c%3Fdark%3Dtrue%26amp%3Bcolor%3D000000%22%20allow%3D%22autoplay%22%3E%3C%2Fiframe%3E










Privacy info.




This embed will serve content from 

simplecast.com













 

 

 




(You can also find this episode on the 

Internet Archive

 and on YouTube.)




In this episode, Cindy – who left EFF in June – speaks with Dan Bernstein, who was a Cal Berkeley grad student when he developed a simple encryption algorithm called “Snuffle.” Because federal law classified encryption as a war munition, publishing Snuffle meant submitting it to the government for review, getting a license as an arms dealer, and being granted a license the government had no intention of granting. Bernstein felt this violated his free-speech rights and in 1995 he sued, represented by Cindy working with EFF.

 




Cindy also talks with Tony Coppolino, the Justice Department lawyer she battled in court – who admits she intimidated him from their very first phone call, and who offers a surprising perspective on the case all these years later.

 




The “Privacy’s Defenders” podcast (new episodes drop every other Tuesday!) is a follow-up to Cindy’s book, “

Privacy’s Defender: My Thirty-Year Fight Against Digital Surveillance

,” bringing to life pivotal moments in the voices of those who fought for your rights. Sales of “Privacy’s Defender” benefit EFF, so 

pick up your copy today

!




Joanne Elgart Jennings co-produced and created this podcast.  

 




Jarod Sport co-produced, mixed, and mastered it.  

 




Corinne Ruff is our story editor.

 




We had additional help from Rachel Estabrook and Alison Broverman.

 




The original music was composed and performed by Nat Keefe of Hot Buttered Rum with Ben Andrews on the fiddle.

title: Δίκη των βασανιστών του Βασίλη Μάγγου: Το θέατρο των «δακρύων», οι 21 διακοπές και μια οικογένεια χωρίς φωνή
content:
Ανακοίνωση του 

Δικτύου αλληλεγγύης και αγώνα Καρδίτσας 

σχετικά με τις εξελίξεις στη δίκη των 6 βασανιστών του Βασίλη Μάγγου:







Δίκη Βασίλη Μάγγου: Το Θέατρο των «Δακρύων», οι 21 Διακοπές και μια Οικογένεια Χωρίς Φωνή










Με την ολοκλήρωση των απολογιών των έξι κατηγορούμενων αστυνομικών τη Δευτέρα, 12 Οκτωβρίου 2026, στο Μικτό Ορκωτό Δικαστήριο Καρδίτσας, ξεδιπλώθηκε πλήρως μια μεθοδευμένη και προκλητική υπερασπιστική τακτική.










Η διαδικασία σημαδεύτηκε από την ακραία στάση των συνηγόρων υπεράσπισης των αστυνομικών, η οποία εξελίχθηκε σε ένα δικαστικό περιβάλλον όπου στην οικογένεια του Βασίλη δεν επιτρέπεται καν να έχει πολιτική αγωγή (υποστήριξη κατηγορίας).










21 Διακοπές σε μια Δίκη χωρίς Πολιτική Αγωγή:




Όπως κατάγγειλε δημόσια ο πατέρας του Βασίλη, Γιάννης Μάγγος, η στάση της υπεράσπισης ήταν εντελώς απαράδεκτη.




Εκμεταλλευόμενοι το γεγονός ότι η οικογένεια έχει αποκλειστεί από τη διαδικασία και δεν εκπροσωπείται από δικούς της δικηγόρους για να τους αντιμετωπίσουν, οι συνήγοροι των αστυνομικών διέκοψαν τη ροή της δίκης συνολικά 21 φορές, προκειμένου να ελέγξουν πλήρως τις εντυπώσεις και να κατευθύνουν τη διαδικασία.










Το Θέατρο των Απολογιών:




Από τον «Τσαμπουκά» και την αλαζονεία της εξουσίας στα Κλάματα.




Η ίδια η διαδικασία των απολογιών των αστυνομικών έφερε στο φως μια προκλητική αντίφαση:




• Το πραγματικό πρόσωπο στον δρόμο: Όπως έχει καταγραφεί σε βίντεο, οι αστυνομικοί έξω από το δικαστικό μέγαρο Βόλου έδρασαν με απροκάλυπτo τσαμπουκά, ασκώντας άγρια βία και ξυλοκοπώντας τον Βασίλη Μάγγο μπροστά στα μάτια του κόσμου και των καμερών.




• Το αφήγημα του κρατητηρίου: Στον αντίποδα, οι αστυνομικοί στις απολογίες τους με όσα προκλητικά ισχυρίστηκαν , μέσα στο τμήμα μετατράπηκαν σε… «αρνάκια» , «μόνο φιλιά δεν του έδωσαν»του Βασίλη , σε μια απεγνωσμένη προσπάθεια να αρνηθούν τον βασανισμό που ακολούθησε.










• Στήθηκαν στις απολογίες τους: Μπροστά στους δικαστές, ο γνώριμος τσαμπουκάς και η αλαζονεία εξαφανίστηκαν και ορισμένοι από τους κατηγορούμενους έβαλαν μέχρι και τα κλάματα, σε μια προφανώς στημένη προσπάθεια να εκβιάσουν τη συμπάθεια της έδρας.




Επιστράτευσαν επίμονα το προφίλ του «καλού οικογενειάρχη» και παραπονέθηκαν ότι η κοινωνική κατακραυγή «διέλυσε» τη δική τους ζωή, αντιστρέφοντας πλήρως τους ρόλους θύματος και θύτη.










Πέρα από το ηθικό προφίλ, στο καθαρά υπηρεσιακό σκέλος οι αστυνομικοί τήρησαν μια στάση πλήρους άρνησης.




Δεν αποδέχθηκαν καμία ευθύνη για τα επιχειρησιακά λάθη και τη βαρβαρότητα της ημέρας εκείνης, στρέφοντας τα βέλη τους προς τις εντολές των ανωτέρων τους.










Η κοινωνία και οι αλληλέγγυοι ξέρουν πολύ καλά τι έκαναν και πώς τους αποκαλεί ο κόσμος. Η μνήμη του Βασίλη Μάγγου δεν είναι σκουπίδι για να παραγραφεί πίσω από υποκριτικά δάκρυα, δικονομικά τερτίπια και τον δικαστικό αποκλεισμό της ίδιας του της οικογένειας.










Τα αιτήματα της οικογένειας είναι και δικά μας αιτήματα:




• Να αποδοθούν πλήρως οι ευθύνες για τον βασανισμό και τον θάνατο του Βασίλη.




• Να υπάρξει πραγματικά δίκαιη δίκη χωρίς συγκάλυψη.




• Να καταδικαστούν οι 6 βασανιστές του Βασίλειου Μάγγου.




Η ακροαματική διαδικασία αναμένεται να συνεχιστεί εντός του μήνα, με τις επόμενες προγραμματισμένες δικασίμους να έχουν οριστεί για τις:




• 26 Οκτωβρίου 2026




• 29 Οκτωβρίου 2026




• 30 Οκτωβρίου 2026




Παράλληλα, για τις 16 Δεκεμβρίου 2026 έχει προσδιοριστεί η εκδίκαση της έφεσης των αστυνομικών σχετικά με την προηγούμενη καταδίκη τους από το Μονομελές Πλημμελειοδικείο Βόλου










ΔΕΝ ΞΕΧΝΑΜΕ, ΔΕΝ ΣΥΓΧΩΡΟΥΜΕ ΤΗΝ ΚΡΑΤΙΚΗ ΔΟΛΟΦΟΝΙΑ ΤΟΥ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΙΟΥ ΜΑΓΓΟΥ










ΣΤΟΥΣ ΔΡΟΜΟΥΣ ΑΝΑΠΝΕΕΙ ΤΟ ΔΙΚΙΟ










ΔΕΝ ΥΠΑΡΧΕΙ ΕΙΡΗΝΗ ΧΩΡΙΣ ΔΙΚΑΙΟΣΥΝΗ – ΔΕΝ ΘΑ ΞΕΧΑΣΤΕΙ ΤΙ ΚΑΝΑΝ ΣΤΟΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΗ










Δίκτυο αλληλεγγύης και αγώνα Καρδίτσας – Για υγεία, ζωή και ελευθερία

Δίκη των βασανιστών του Βασίλη Μάγγου: Το θέατρο των «δακρύων», οι 21 διακοπές και μια οικογένεια χωρίς φωνή

title: ‘Women, Justice and Memory Vigil’ against femicides in its second week
content:
The Amed (tr: Diyarbakır) Network for Combating Violence launched a “Women, Justice and Memory Vigil” against femicides and suspicious deaths of women last Tuesday, October 6. The vigil outside the Diyarbakır Courthouse will continue at the same location every Tuesday for 10 weeks.




Participants displayed a banner reading “Women Hold a Vigil for Justice and Memory,” along with photographs of women who had been killed.  Representatives of numerous political parties and civil society organizations attended the vigil in its second week.




Reading the statement on behalf of the Rosa Women’s Association, Ruşen Yakut said that during this week’s vigil, they were bringing together in collective memory the stories of women who were killed in different cities across Turkey between October 2 and 12 and whose information they had been able to obtain.




Emphasizing that the struggle for justice for murdered women is not limited to any particular period, Yakut stated that they would never abandon their demand for truth and justice. “For us, memory means remembering, leaving a trace, and ensuring that these women are not forgotten. The pursuit of justice means carrying the collective responsibility to protect women’s right to life into the present,” she said.




Following the statement, the stories of Füsun Yuluğkural, Gözde Çelik, Emel Bozkuş, Fadime Akbal, Gülşah Oktay, Sakine Y, Fikriye Cin, Mercan Kaplan, and Canan Bebek, who were murdered or died under suspicious circumstances, were read aloud.

title: Kurdish women’s movement participates in 39th Plurinational Gathering of Women in Argentina
content:
The 39th Plurinational Gathering of Women and Gender-Diverse People, held in Córdoba, Argentina from October 10 to 12, brought together hundreds of thousands of women from across Latin America. Organized by 300 local organizations, the gathering featured workshops, panel discussions, film screenings, and meetings.







 








A delegation from the Kurdish women’s movement participated in a meeting on internationalism, organized jointly with the Abya Yala feminist network, a panel titled “Revolutionary Practices,” and a screening of the film 

In Search of Alina

. The events addressed the experiences of Kurdish women, the women’s revolution in Rojava, the struggle of women guerrillas in the mountains of Kurdistan, and the importance of international solidarity.




At the meeting on internationalism organized by the Kurdish women’s movement and the Abya Yala feminist network, discussions focused on the international dimension of Kurdish women’s struggle and the importance of the “Women Weaving the Future” network. Participants chanted the slogan, “Plurinational, plurinational; from Abya Yala to Kurdistan!”




During the panel titled “Revolutionary Practices,” the delegation spoke about the women’s revolution in Rojava, the struggle of women guerrillas in Kurdistan, and the role of internationalism. Following questions from participants, the delegation also addressed the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




Story of Alina Sánchez told




As part of the event, the film 

In Search of Alina

, which tells the story of the life and struggle of internationalist revolutionary Legerîn Ciya (

Alina Sánchez

), who grew up in Córdoba and was martyred in Rojava in 2018, was screened.




In addition to the delegation from the Kurdish women’s movement, feminist, educator, and journalist Claudia Korol and Alina Sánchez’s mother also spoke at the screening. Her mother’s speech, in which she described her daughter’s life, joy, and determination, moved the participants.




The delegation also addressed an open assembly organized by the Abya Yala Feminists network on Sunday morning. The meeting, attended by representatives of Indigenous peoples and women’s organizations from different parts of Latin America, emphasized the importance of women’s organizing and leadership.




Throughout the gathering, the active participation of the Kurdish women’s movement brought international solidarity and opportunities for joint struggle to the forefront. The events concluded with discussions highlighting women’s liberation as one of the central struggles of the 21st century.

title: Conditions that gave rise to the Kurdish question and the conflict remain unchanged
content:
The conflict between the Turkish state and the PKK has been at a standstill for two years. The PKK has dissolved itself and decided to end its armed struggle against Turkey. The PKK disbanded and took significant steps in 2025 and 2026. All these steps were taken to enable free and unrestricted participation in democratic politics and to achieve a democratic resolution to the Kurdish question.




From the statement issued by the Kurdish Movement Leadership on October 8, we learn that the Turkish state has taken no steps apart from allowing meetings on Imralı Island every few months. More precisely, the Movement Leadership has conveyed this reality, which we have also witnessed, in the form of a polite warning. The statement emphasized that there is no longer any justification for the Turkish state’s failure to act following the significant steps taken by the movement.




The Movement Leadership stated that their leader must be freed and that legislation on freedoms, which would pave the way for a democratic resolution to the Kurdish question, must be enacted without delay. They specifically emphasized that if the Turkish state fails to take steps demonstrating such political will, they will interpret this as an intention to continue its previous policies.




The Movement Leadership made it clear that if the Turkish state takes no action and instead continues to demand further unilateral steps, it will no longer take such demands seriously. It also pointed out that the state’s failure to act would indicate that it is pursuing different objectives. They have thus taken a clear position against the state’s repeated demands to “take this step” or “take that step.”




It appears that the Movement Leadership harbors certain doubts about the Turkish state’s intentions. In short, their message was that they want to move the process forward, but the state is not demonstrating a similar commitment.




The statement issued by the Movement Leadership, along with assessments made to the press by some of its officials, deserves to be taken seriously. They have warned that if the Turkish state is playing a game, it would be the greatest miscalculation in Turkey’s history. Their statements constitute a call for the Turkish state to approach this process seriously. They would not have made such statements if they had not sensed uncertainty and delaying tactics, particularly in the attitude of the ruling AKP.




They consider it extremely important that the Kurdish People’s Leader be able to work under conditions of freedom. It is clear that if İmralı does not maintain continuous dialogue with journalists, intellectuals, politicians, and civil society organizations, they will regard this as a delaying tactic and another form of isolation. In the past, the state would occasionally allow a meeting or make a minor gesture, creating the impression that it was taking meaningful steps in the process. That policy, or game, has now reached its end.




Either this process will make substantial progress, or it will reach a deadlock. If the ruling AKP continues its current approach, it will demonstrate a lack of determination to move the process forward. This is not merely the view of the Movement Leadership; any Kurdish individual or democrat would think the same. After all, months and years are passing, yet the conditions that gave rise to the Kurdish question and the conflict remain unchanged!




The guerrillas are being told to lay down their arms and return, yet no changes have been made to the laws or the legal framework. Under the existing laws, not only returning guerrillas and Kurds but even ordinary democrats cannot freely engage in democratic politics. The prisons are still filled with political prisoners. In fact, even those who have already served the prison sentences imposed by Turkish courts are not being released! How can the guerrillas be expected to lay down their arms and return to Turkey unless the existing laws are changed? If the Turkish state expects them to simply “return home,” that is not going to happen. Indeed, officials from the Movement Leadership have already stated that such an approach is unacceptable.




On the other hand, although the guerrillas have withdrawn from Turkish territory and areas close to Turkey’s borders, the Turkish state is now demanding that they also leave the areas where they are currently stationed. In other words, it is telling them to go somewhere else and live as displaced people or refugees. If the guerrillas are expected to lay down their arms and return to Turkey once the Turkish state establishes the necessary conditions, why is the state also demanding that they leave areas far from the border that have no connection to Turkey? According to information we have received, the Turkish state has reportedly been making such demands.




We do not know whether the Turkish state will continue pursuing this approach following the Movement Leadership’s announcement that the guerrillas have withdrawn from Turkey and pulled back from the border. Judging by the Movement Leadership’s statement, if the Turkish state persists with such demands, the Kurdish movement will not regard it as being made in good faith.




In short, through its comprehensive and striking statement, as well as the remarks made to the press, the Movement Leadership has clearly articulated its position. Devlet Bahçeli has also stated that this is a state policy and that there is no turning back. Bahçeli’s position amounts to a commitment. However, the ruling AKP’s approach is not seen as conducive to advancing the process.




In matters such as these, failure to move forward means moving backward. Indeed, the bicycle analogy is frequently used in conflict resolution processes: the bicycle must keep moving. Yet, for some reason, the AKP is not pedaling!




Source: Yeni Yaşam Newspaper

title: A new chapter in the heart of Paris: Kurdistan House of France
content:
The Kurdistan House of France, which aims to bring together the cultural, social, academic, and institutional activities of the Kurdish community in France under one roof, was officially unveiled to the public at a grand ceremony held at Paris City Hall.




The event, held on the evening of Monday, October 12, in the historic hall of Paris City Hall, located in the political and historical heart of the French capital, brought together politicians, institutional representatives, artists, academics, association leaders, and civil society figures from the Kurdish and French communities.




Three speeches were delivered during the evening. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire gave the opening address, followed by Baran Gürbüz, President of the Kurdistan House of France. Former French President François Hollande delivered the final political address of the evening.




Official launch at historic Paris City Hall




The decision to hold the official launch of the Kurdistan House of France (Maison du Kurdistan de France) at Paris City Hall itself was one of the evening’s most significant symbolic and political messages.




Relations between the Paris municipal administration and Kurdish institutions have become increasingly visible in recent months. In June, Grégoire received representatives of the Democratic Kurdish Council in France and the Kurdistan House of France at City Hall. Their discussions focused on the Kurdish community’s activities in France, youth initiatives, cultural and social programs, and potential joint projects with Kurdish institutions in Paris.




The event on October 12 marked a new stage in the development of these relations.




The official unveiling of an institution bearing the name Kurdistan at Paris City Hall, attended by hundreds of guests, is regarded as a powerful message reflecting the Kurdish community’s decades-long struggle, organization, and institutional development in France.




Baran Gürbüz: The beginning of a new era




Following the opening speech by Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire, Baran Gürbüz, President of the Kurdistan House of France, addressed the participants.




Gürbüz emphasized that the Kurdistan House of France would not merely serve as a venue for events or gatherings but would operate as a permanent institution dedicated to meeting the needs of the Kurdish community in France.




Activities to be carried out in four key areas




The Kurdistan House of France will carry out its activities through four main departments; Culture, Sports and Youth, Social and Legal Affairs, Research and Academia.




Through this organizational structure, the Kurdistan House of France aims to contribute to preserving Kurdish culture, history, language, and collective memory while also building stronger ties with younger generations.




The Social and Legal Affairs Department will provide social, administrative, and legal support to those in need, while the Research and Academia Department will seek to strengthen academic studies on the Kurdish question, the history and culture of Kurdistan, and social developments.




The Sports and Youth Department will play a central role in strengthening ties with younger generations, increasing young people’s participation in social and collective activities, and implementing new projects.




Hollande: Solidarity with the Kurds should not be dependent on political circumstances




One of the evening’s most significant political messages came from former French President François Hollande.




Recalling the struggle against ISIS in Rojava during his presidency, Hollande highlighted the historic role played by Kurdish forces and said: “Victory against ISIS would not have been possible without the Syrian Kurds.”




The former Socialist president emphasized that France’s solidarity with the Kurds should not be dependent on changing regional circumstances or political agreements.




Hollande also recalled that during his presidency, he had received Kurdish women representatives and commanders involved in the fight against ISIS at the Élysée Palace.













‘420,000 Kurds live in France’




François Hollande also devoted particular attention to the role of the Kurdish community in France’s social and economic life.




Stating that approximately 420,000 Kurds live in France, he noted that Kurds have made significant contributions to the country in numerous fields, from science and culture to commerce and healthcare.




Highlighting the contributions of Kurds working in the healthcare sector in particular, Hollande emphasized that the Kurdish community has become an integral part of France’s social fabric.




From pain to institutional development: A legacy of memory in Paris




The official unveiling of the Kurdistan House of France at Paris City Hall also carries profound symbolic significance in the recent history of the Kurdish community in Paris.




While Paris has become one of the most important political and cultural centers of the Kurdish diaspora in Europe, it has also been the site of two major massacres that left deep scars in the collective memory of the Kurdish people.




On January 9, 2013, Sakine Cansız, one of the leading figures of the Kurdish women’s movement, Fidan Doğan, the Paris representative of the Kurdistan National Congress (KNK), and Leyla Şaylemez, a member of the Kurdish youth movement, were murdered in Paris.




On December 23, 2022, three Kurds were killed in another armed attack targeting the Kurdish community in Paris; revolutionary Evîn Goyî (Emine Kara), musician Mîr Perwer (Mehmet Şirin Aydın) and activist Abdurrahman Kızıl.




The Kurdish community’s demand for justice and the attacks that took place in Paris had also been raised during meetings between the Paris municipal administration and Kurdish institutions.




For this reason, the event on October 12 took on significance not merely as the unveiling of a new institution, but also as a new stage in the institutional development of the Kurdish presence in Paris, shaped by struggle, suffering, collective memory, and solidarity.




Four areas, a new institutional model




In the coming period, the Kurdistan House of France will continue its activities in four key areas.




The Culture Department will carry out activities aimed at preserving the Kurdish language, culture, art, music, history, and collective memory and passing them on to future generations.




The Sports and Youth Department will focus particularly on youth organizing, developing sports activities, and strengthening ties between younger generations and the Kurdish community and its institutions.




The Social and Legal Affairs Department will develop support mechanisms to assist people living in France with administrative, social, and legal matters.




The Research and Academia Department will aim to support research on Kurdish history, Kurdistan, social issues, and regional developments, while strengthening relations with academics and universities.




Through these four areas, the Kurdistan House of France aims to establish a permanent institutional structure that strengthens the cultural presence of the Kurdish community in France, responds to its social needs, and serves as a bridge between the Kurdish community, French institutions, and academic circles.




Kurdish music echoes through Paris City Hall




Following the political speeches, the evening continued with Kurdish music.




Koma Rayê took the stage, performing a selection of Kurdish songs for the guests. Later in the program, DJ Aramythos provided music for the evening.




Thus, for one evening, the historic hall of Paris City Hall hosted not only Kurdish political and social representation but also Kurdish culture and music.




This new chapter unfolding in the heart of Paris is set to build a bridge between the collective memory carried by the Kurdish community in France and the institutional legacy it hopes to leave for future generations.
