Doch die israelische Armee wisse genau, wo die Journalist:innen lebten, sagt Omar Nazzal von PJS. «Nehmen wir das Beispiel von Wael Dahdouh.» Ende Oktober wurde dessen Familie getötet. Dann der Angriff auf ihn und Abu Daqqa. Dann, Anfang Januar, wurde sein Sohn, ebenfalls Journalist, im Auto beschossen und getötet. «Das alles ist kein Zufall», sagt Nazzal. Die IDF sagte in einer Stellungnahme zum Tod Abu Daqqas, dass sie Journalist:innen nie gezielt angegriffen habe. Weil Israel bis heute mit einer Ausnahme keine ausländischen Journalist:innen unabhängig nach Gaza liess, ist der Druck auf die Reporter:innen vor Ort umso grösser. «Wir stehen jeden Tag um 6 Uhr auf und arbeiten bis in die Nacht», sagt Al-Jazeera-Korrespondent Zaqout. Die Szenen von toten Kindern und Verletzten, die er täglich sehe, verfolgten ihn manchmal bis in den Schlaf. «Wir halten das nur aus, weil wir keine Wahl haben», sagt er. «Die Menschen sterben. Wir müssen zumindest versuchen, im Fernsehen stark zu sein.»

…“ 

Artikel von Meret Michel, Beirut, in der WoZ vom 15. Februar 2024

 




Journalisten in Gaza: Die Gesichter des Gemetzels




„

Auf dem Friedhof unter freiem Himmel, zu dem der Gazastreifen geworden ist, ruhen die Seelen von mehreren Dutzend Journalisten, die getötet wurden, als sie der von Israel verhängten Medienblockade trotzten. Mediapart hat ihre Geschichten rekonstruiert

…“ franz. 

Bildergalierie vom 11. Februar 2024 in Mediapart

 




„Das Fenster nach Gaza“: Gaza ist zum tödlichsten Kriegsort für Journalisten geworden. Die „Reporter ohne Grenzen“ wollen, dass jeder Tod genau untersucht wird




Im 

taz-Interview von Matthias Ubl vom 14. Januar 2024

 

 äußert sich der Pressereferent, Christopher Resch, von Reporter ohne Grenzen zum zuerst beim Guardian geäußerten Verdacht einer gezielten Tötung des Al-Dschasira-Journalist Hamza Dahdouh und einer seiner Kollegen: 

„Der Fall hat eine besondere Tragik. Hamza al-Dahdouh ist der Sohn des bekannten Journalisten Wael Dahdouh, dem Leiter des Al-Dschasira-Büros in Gaza. Er hat durch die israelischen Luftangriffe schon mehrere enge Familienmitglieder verloren, seine Frau, ein Enkelkind und mit Hamza jetzt auch noch das dritte eigene Kind. Doch der Fall zeigt auch den Kampf um die Narrative, der mit diesem Krieg einhergeht. Die israelischen Streitkräfte haben zwei Raketen auf das Auto gefeuert, in dem Dahdouh und sein Kollege Mustafa Thuraya saßen. Anschließend haben Militärsprecher behauptet, dass sich in dem Auto auch ein Hamas-Terrorist befand, mussten von dieser Darstellung jedoch wieder abrücken. Wir fordern dringend eine unabhängige Untersuchung zu diesem und anderen Fällen. (…) Auch wir haben dazu recherchiert. Von gezielten Tötungen von Journalisten zu sprechen, sind harte Vorwürfe, die man nicht leichtfertig erheben sollte. Aber wir untersuchen jeden Fall, und zumindest in diesem [des Reuters-Journalisten Issam Abdallah vom 13. Oktober] sieht es danach aus. (…) Wir von Reporter ohne Grenzen haben zwei Strafanzeigen beim Internationalen Strafgerichtshof eingereicht, mit denen wir erreichen wollen, dass mögliche Kriegsverbrechen von Israel und auch der Hamas an Journalistinnen und Journalisten untersucht werden sollen. Doch unsere Pressemitteilungen dazu wurden von deutschen Medien so gut wie nicht aufgegriffen. (…) Journalisten kommen seit dem 7. Oktober nur nach Gaza, wenn sie mit der israelischen Armee unterwegs sind. Sie müssen der Armee anschließend ihr Material vorlegen, was für diese Art der Berichterstattung aber nicht ungewöhnlich ist. Wir fordern, dass über die israelischen und den ägyptischen Grenzübergang mehr internationale Medien ins Land gelassen werden. (…) Ich habe den größten Respekt vor dem Mut und vor der Arbeit palästinensischer Journalistinnen und Journalisten, sie sind derzeit das Fenster, durch das die Welt nach Gaza schauen kann. Aber es gibt natürlich Schwierigkeiten, die Menschen vor Ort leben mitten im Krieg, sie haben selbst Angst, vielleicht gibt es Verletzte und Tote im nächsten Umfeld, es fehlt an Strom und Treibstoff. Und natürlich unterdrückt auch die Hamas kritische Berichterstattung, auch wenn es in Gaza immer auch eine lebendige Zivilbevölkerung gab, die kritischen Journalismus ermöglichte. (…) In Gaza sind ja auch die großen internationalen Nachrichtenagenturen wie Reuters und AFP vor Ort, die versuchen im Detail zu berichten. Wenn man alle zusammen schaut, dann entsteht ein Gesamtbild…“




Bis zum 16. Dezember mindestens 64 JournalistInnen und MedienarbeiterInnen im Krieg zwischen Israel und Gaza getötet – JournalistInnen des Gazastreifens sind die HeldInnen 







Opfer unter den Journalisten im Krieg zwischen Israel und Gaza




„… 

Bis zum 16. Dezember ergaben die vorläufigen Untersuchungen des CPJ, dass mindestens 64 Journalisten und Medienmitarbeiter unter den mehr als 19.000 Toten seit Beginn des Krieges am 7. Oktober zu finden sind – etwa 18.000 palästinensische Tote in Gaza und im Westjordanland und 1.200 Tote in Israel. Der tödlichste Tag des Krieges in Bezug auf die Zahl der getöteten Journalisten war der erste Tag, der 7. Oktober, mit sechs getöteten Journalisten; der zweittödlichste Tag war der 18. November, an dem fünf Journalisten getötet wurden.


Die israelischen Verteidigungsstreitkräfte (IDF) teilten den Nachrichtenagenturen Reuters und Agence France Press mit, dass sie die Sicherheit ihrer im Gazastreifen tätigen Journalisten nicht garantieren können, nachdem diese um die Zusicherung gebeten hatten, dass ihre Journalisten nicht von israelischen Angriffen betroffen sein würden, wie Reuters am 27. Oktober berichtete. Journalisten im Gazastreifen sind besonders hohen Risiken ausgesetzt, wenn sie versuchen, während des israelischen Bodenangriffs über den Konflikt zu berichten. Dazu gehören verheerende israelische Luftangriffe, unterbrochene Kommunikationswege, Versorgungsengpässe und umfangreiche Stromausfälle.


Bis zum 16. Dezember:




– 64 Journalisten und Medienmitarbeiter wurden als tot bestätigt: 57 Palästinenser, 4 Israelis und 3 Libanesen.




– 13 Journalisten wurden als verletzt gemeldet.




– 3 Journalisten wurden als vermisst gemeldet.




– 19 Journalisten wurden als verhaftet gemeldet.




–  Zahlreiche Angriffe, Drohungen, Cyberangriffe, Zensur und Tötung von Familienmitgliedern

…“ engl. 

Meldung vom 16.12.2023 bei CPJ

 

 („Journalist casualties in the Israel-Gaza war“, maschinenübersetzt)




Es ist an der Zeit, dass die Journalisten des Gazastreifens wie die Helden behandelt werden, die sie sind




„

Sie berichten unter unvorstellbaren Schwierigkeiten und werden in Rekordzahlen getötet. Die journalistische Gemeinschaft sollte sie jeden Tag ehren. (…)




Lokale Journalisten haben während der beispiellosen Gewalt aus erster Hand über die Bedingungen vor Ort im Gazastreifen berichtet. Die wenigen bestehenden Gaza-Büros der großen internationalen Medien (Reuters, BBC, Associated Press, Al-Jazeera, Agence France-Presse und andere) sind überwiegend mit Einwohnern des Gazastreifens besetzt.




Als Bewohner der Gemeinde, über die sie berichten, haben diese Journalisten Zugang, der anderen Reportern verwehrt ist. Vor fast einem Monat appellierte eine Koalition großer Nachrichtenorganisationen an die Regierungen Israels und Ägyptens (das die Südgrenze des Gazastreifens unter israelischer Leitung verwaltet), ihnen Zugang zu gewähren. Diese Agenturen sind praktisch nicht in der Lage, ihre Mitarbeiter zur Berichterstattung vor Ort zu entsenden. Viele von ihnen haben in Israel gearbeitet und wurden von palästinensischen Strippenziehern, Fixern und Freiberuflern unterstützt, die im Kriegsgebiet leben. Dieselbe Identität setzt sie einer komplizierten Kombination von Zwängen aus: den Anforderungen ihrer ausländischen Arbeitgeber, den Risiken der Wahrheitssuche und -darstellung unter einer autoritären Regierung und dem erhöhten Risiko, wegen ihrer Arbeit der Gewalt der IDF ausgesetzt zu sein. Maalish.




Die Tatsache, dass die internationalen Journalisten, die für kurze Zeit in den Gazastreifen einreisen, um zu berichten, sich der Zensur der israelischen Regierung beugen müssen, macht die Arbeit der palästinensischen Journalisten als Strippenzieher und freie Mitarbeiter für internationale Nachrichtenagenturen besonders wertvoll. Bei ihrer Arbeit in einer humanitären Krise beweisen diese Journalisten die bemerkenswerte Hartnäckigkeit und Anpassungsfähigkeit, die von jedem Kriegsberichterstatter verlangt wird, allerdings mit dem zusätzlichen Nachteil, dass sie zusammen mit ihren Familien im Kriegsgebiet leben. Die Zahl der getöteten Journalisten zeigt, dass vor allem die Palästinenser gefährdet sind. Von den 63 Journalisten, die seit dem 7. Oktober getötet wurden, sind bis auf sieben alle Palästinenser. (…)




Es ist schwer vorstellbar, wie diese Atmosphäre noch feindseliger oder repressiver sein könnte. In seinem jüngsten Bericht stellt das CPJ fest, dass der Ausbruch des Krieges den tödlichsten Monat seit Beginn der Aufzeichnungen im Jahr 1992 für Medienschaffende bedeutet. Die Gesamtzahl der getöteten Journalisten wird bald die Zahl der im letzten Jahr weltweit getöteten Journalisten übertreffen, wobei die höchste Zahl mit 15 Journalisten in der Ukraine und 13 in Mexiko zu beklagen war.




Folglich wird es weniger Journalismus geben. Es gibt weniger Journalisten, die zuverlässige und genaue Daten sammeln und Fakten von Desinformation unterscheiden. Es gibt weniger Stimmen, die dem Rest der Welt beharrlich die Realität im Gazastreifen vor Augen führen. Es gibt weniger Stimmen, weil so viele der Menschen, die diese Arbeit geleistet haben, tot sind, und so viele von denen, die nicht getötet wurden, einen täglichen Kampf ums Überleben mit ihren Familien führen

…“ 12.12.2023 NADIA TAHA The Nation – 

am 15.12. dokumentiert in Portside

 

 („It’s Time for Gaza’s Journalists To Be Treated Like the Heroes They Are“, maschinenübersetzt)










Der gefährlichste Krieg für Journalist*innen im 21. Jahrhundert: Bisher wurden in dem Krieg in Nahost 46 Medienschaffende getötet 




„

Kein anderer Krieg im 21. Jahrhundert hat für Journalistinnen und Journalisten so gefährlich begonnen wie der zwischen Israel und der Hamas. Insgesamt beklagt Reporter ohne Grenzen (RSF) derzeit bereits 55 getötete Medienschaffende, die meisten starben durch israelisches Bombardement. Warum ist das so? Können Medien im Gazastreifen überhaupt noch sicher berichten, und wie glaubwürdig sind ihre Informationen? Wie setzt sich RSF für die Sicherheit der Medienschaffenden ein? Fragen und Antworten gibt es in diesem regelmäßig aktualisierten Beitrag

…“ 

FAQ vom 23.11.2023 der Reporter ohne Grenzen

 

 zur Situation der Medien im Gazastreifen




Angriffe, Verhaftungen, Drohungen, Zensur: Die hohen Risiken der Berichterstattung über den Krieg zwischen Israel und Gaza – auch ARD-Team von israelischem Militär bedroht 







ARD-Team von israelischem Militär festgehalten und bedroht




„

Vorfall im palästinensischen Westjordanland: Ein ARD-Team ist dort von israelischen Soldaten festgehalten und bedroht worden. Die Reporter wollten über die Gewalt radikaler Siedler berichten. Der BR sieht die Pressefreiheit bedroht.


Ein Team der ARD ist im palästinensischen Westjordanland von Soldaten des israelischen Militärs (IDF) festgehalten und bedroht worden. Nach Angaben des ARD-Studios Tel Aviv, das vom Bayerischen Rundfunk (BR) betrieben wird, war Korrespondent Jan-Christoph Kitzler am Samstag, 4. November mit einem palästinensischen Mitarbeiter sowie einer deutschen Mitarbeiterin bereits auf dem Rückweg von einem Interview, als sie von israelischen Soldaten südlich der palästinensischen Stadt Hebron gestoppt wurden.


Wie Kitzler berichtet und Handyvideos des Teams belegen, verhielten sich die Soldaten gegenüber dem ARD-Team überaus aggressiv, mehrfach wurden Waffen in das Teamfahrzeug gehalten. Immer wieder filmten die Soldaten das ARD-Team aus nächster Nähe. Für Kitzler und das Team ein klarer Versuch der Einschüchterung. Bei den Soldaten handelte es sich nach Angaben des Teams vermutlich um Siedler aus der Gegend, die nun als Reservisten eingezogen wurden. Sie waren mit einem Privatfahrzeug unterwegs und trugen zivile Kopfbedeckungen. (…)


Für Christian Limpert, Leiter des ARD-Studios Tel Aviv, handelt es sich dabei um Versuche, die Berichterstattung aus dem palästinensischen Westjordanland massiv zu behindern, auch andere internationale Medien seien betroffen. „Für uns ist es der zweite Vorfall innerhalb einer Woche. Unser Team hat sich klar als akkreditierte Pressevertreter ausgewiesen und war fernab militärischer Sicherheitsbereiche. Wir können das Vorgehen des israelischen Militärs nicht akzeptieren

.“…“ 

Meldung vom 05.11.2023 beim BR

 




Angriffe, Verhaftungen, Drohungen, Zensur: Die hohen Risiken der Berichterstattung über den Krieg zwischen Israel und Gaza




„

Seit Beginn des Krieges zwischen Israel und dem Gazastreifen am 7. Oktober sehen sich Journalisten und Medien in der gesamten Region mit einem feindseligen Umfeld konfrontiert, das die Berichterstattung über den Krieg zu einer besonderen Herausforderung macht.  Das CPJ hat nicht nur die steigende Zahl der getöteten und verletzten Journalisten dokumentiert, sondern auch 18 Vorfälle festgestellt, in denen Journalisten bei ihrer Arbeit in Israel und den beiden palästinensischen Gebieten Gaza und Westjordanland angegriffen wurden. Dazu gehören acht Verhaftungen sowie Angriffe, Drohungen, Cyberattacken und Zensur. (Anmerkung der Redaktion: Diese Zahlen werden aktualisiert, sobald weitere Informationen vorliegen.) Mehrere Journalisten haben während ihrer Berichterstattung über den Konflikt auch Familienangehörige verloren. Am 25. Oktober verlor Wael Al Dahdouh, Leiter des Al-Jazeera-Büros in Gaza, seine Frau, seinen Sohn, seine Tochter und seinen Enkel, als ein israelischer Luftangriff das Flüchtlingslager Nuseirat im Zentrum des Gazastreifens traf, so eine Erklärung von Al-Jazeera und Politico. In Gaza sind die Risiken akut. Israel hat auf den Angriff der Hamas auf sein Gebiet am 7. Oktober mit Luftangriffen und einem Bodenangriff auf den Gazastreifen reagiert, der von der militanten Palästinensergruppe kontrolliert wird

…“ engl. 

Beitrag von Mohamed Mandour am 3. November 2023 bei CPJ

 

 („Attacks, arrests, threats, censorship: The high risks of reporting the Israel-Gaza war“, maschinenübersetzt)







Siehe für die laufende Berichterstattung 

CPJ auf Twitter

 
















Mögliche Kriegsverbrechen: RSF stellt Strafanzeige




„

Reporter ohne Grenzen (RSF) hat vor dem Internationalen Strafgerichtshof (IStGH) Strafanzeige eingereicht, damit dieser mögliche Kriegsverbrechen gegen Medienschaffende im Gazastreifen und Israel untersucht. Am 7. Oktober hatte die Hamas aus dem Gazastreifen heraus brutalste terroristische Attacken auf israelisches Gebiet gestartet. Seitdem bombardieren die israelischen Streitkräfte das abgeschottete Gebiet massiv. Die Strafanzeige ist vom 31. Oktober und nennt acht palästinensische Journalisten, die bei der Bombardierung ziviler Gebiete in Gaza durch Israel getötet wurden, sowie einen israelischen Journalisten, der am 7. Oktober bei der Berichterstattung über einen Angriff der Hamas auf seinen Kibbuz ermordet wurde. Ebenfalls genannt werden zwei weitere palästinensische Medienschaffende, die während ihrer Berichterstattung verwundet wurden. Diese elf Personen wurden Opfer von Angriffen, die nach Ansicht von RSF Kriegsverbrechen darstellen und eine Untersuchung durch den IStGH rechtfertigen. In der Strafanzeige wird auch die vorsätzliche vollständige oder teilweise Zerstörung der Gebäude von mehr als 50 Medieneinrichtungen im Gazastreifen aufgeführt

…“ 

Meldung vom 02.11.2023 bei RSF







_______________




Liebe Kolleginnen & Kollegen!




Israel, das nach westlicher Ansicht bekanntlich 

„die einzige Demokratie im Mittleren Osten“

 ist und das sich alle arabischen Staaten zum 

„Vorbild“

 nehmen sollten, führt aktuell einmal mehr nicht nur Krieg gegen die Hamas und die anderen palästinensischen Widerstandsgruppen sowie gegen die Zivilbevölkerung im Gazastreifen und in der West Bank, sondern auch gegen mißliebige Journalisten. Die seit Jahrzehnten herrschende Militärzensur reicht den Herrschenden in Tel Aviv längst nicht mehr aus.


 


Dass mißliebige ausländische Medien, mit dem Fernsehsender“Al-Jazeera“ an der Spitze, in Israel verboten werden sollen, war der „Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung“ vor einigen Tagen nur eine kurze Meldung im hinteren Teil des Feuilliton wert. Andere bürgerliche Blätter berichteten überhaupt nicht darüber.


 


Noch weniger Erwähnung findet die Tatsache, dass die Armee von Benjamin Netanjahu, seinem neuen Kompagnon und Ex-General Benny Gantz sowie ihren rechtsextremen Kameraden Ben-Gvir, Smotrich & Co. bei ihren massiven Bombardements 

bislang 21 Journalisten umgebracht

 und etliche andere verletzt hat. Weitere Medienschaffende werden im Gazastreifen vermisst oder wurden verhaftet.


 


Außerdem wurden die Büros und Gebäude mehrerer palästinensischer Medien in Gaza durch israelische Bomben dem Erdboden gleichgemacht oder schwer beschädigt. Das berichtet die Internationale Journalisten-Föderation (IFJ) am 26. Oktober 2023 auf ihrer Homepage. Die IFJ vertritt 600.000 Journalistinnen und Journalisten in 146 Ländern:







https://www.ifj.org/media-centre/news/detail/category/press-releases/article/palestine-at-least-twenty-one-journalists-killed-in-gaza

 







Am 20.10.2023 informierte die IFJ über die erwähnte 

Attacke der Regierung Gantz-Netanjahu gegen kritische Medien

, weil diese angeblich 

„die nationale Sicherheit“

 des Kolonialstaats Israel 

„untergraben“

:







https://www.ifj.org/media-centre/news/detail/category/press-releases/article/israel-government-to-shut-down-critical-media-alleged-to-undermine-national-security

 







Da die beiden englischsprachigen Texte sehr leicht lesbar sind, erscheint uns eine Übersetzung unnötig. Die Mitteilung ist unbedingt lesenswert und sollte so weit wie möglich weiterverbreitet werden!


 


Dem Thema 

Militärzensur und Selbstzensur

 beim Mitglied der 

„westlichen Wertegemeinschaft“

 Israel und dem 

Kampf gegen palästinensische Blogger

 widmete das linksalternative, binationale, israelisch-palästinensische Onlinemagazin „+972 Magazine“ am 18. September und 2. Oktober 2023 zwei ebenfalls sehr empfehlenswerte Artikel:







https://www.972mag.com/israel-military-censor-media-interventions/

 




https://www.972mag.com/palestinian-influencers-social-media-persecution/

 







Im 

„World Press Freedom Index 2023“

 

 von Reporter ohne Grenzen liegt die 

„freiheitliche Demokratie“

 Israel übrigens auf Platz 97 von 180 Ländern. Das ist sogar noch eine weitere Verschlechterung, denn im Jahr zuvor rangierte sie noch auf (einem ebenfalls wenig schmeichelhaften) Platz 86!


 


Mit solidarischen Grüßen,




GEWERKSCHAFTSFORUM HANNOVER




Siehe auch/Grundinfos:







palästinensische Journalistengewerkschaft (

Palestinian Journalists Syndicate

 

)

engl.

 von ROG

author: Λουκάς Σταμέλλος
title: Νέοι εκτελεστές, παλιοί υποκινητές
content:
Σύνδεσμος δημοσίευσης: 

Νέοι εκτελεστές, παλιοί υποκινητές




«2 στενά απτό μνημείο σας μένω… Μάντεψε που κατουραω τα βράδια….άντε φλωροι»

 είναι μια από τις απαντήσεις του Ιωάννη Καζαντζόγλου σε σχόλια που τον ειρωνεύονται, σε ανάρτηση μιας εθνικιστικής σελίδας η οποία υπερασπίζεται τους μαχαιροβγάλτες της Ελευσίνας που 

οι ίδιοι δήλωσαν φασίστες

. Σε άλλο σχόλιο απειλεί ευθέως: 

«θα τα πούμε σύντομα»

.













Ο Καζαντζόγλου εννοεί βέβαια το μνημείο του Παύλου Φύσσα στο σημείο όπου ο αντιφασίστας μουσικός δολοφονήθηκε στις 18/9/2013 από τάγμα εφόδου της τοπικής οργάνωσης Νίκαιας της Χ.Α., στην οποία 

επιχειρησιακός επικεφαλής («Υπεύθυνος Ασφάλειας») ήταν ο Καζαντζόγλου

.







Ο Ιωάννης Καζαντζόγλου στο δημόσιο προφίλ του με φωτογραφία όπου διακρίνεται το τατουάζ στον αγκώνα με τον ναζιστικό «Μαύρο Ήλιο».







Η συγκεκριμένη σελίδα εθνικιστικού οχετού φαίνεται να ενεργοποιήθηκε μόλις τον περασμένο Αύγουστο και έχει ελάχιστους ακολούθους, αλλά έχει τη σημασία του το γεγονός ότι ο Καζαντζόγλου είναι ένας από τους πρώτους που την γνωρίζουν και την ακολουθούν.




Σε συνδυασμό με το γεγονός ότι το μαχαίρωμα αντιφασίστα στην Ελευσίνα πραγματοποιήθηκε μόλις λίγες μέρες μετά από τη μαζική διαφήμιση που παρείχαν τα ΜΜΕ της χώρας σε καθοδηγητικό στέλεχος του ελληνικού ναζισμού, αυτό το «ξεμύτισμα» ενός από τους συνεργούς της δολοφονίας Φύσσα δείχνει – εκτός του ότι είναι αμετανόητοι για τις ιδέες τους – ότι είναι αμετανόητοι και για τα μαχαίρια τους.




Επιπλέον, ο ίδιος ο Καζαντζόγλου έχει δημοσιεύσει την παρακάτω φωτογραφία από συνάντησή του με άλλο ένα από τα μέλη του παλιού τάγματος εφόδου χρυσαυγιτών της Νίκαιας, τον Ν. Τσορβά, επίσης συνεργό στη δολοφονία Φύσσα. Με την εύγλωττη περιγραφή 

«Κάποιοι άνθρωποι αν θέλουν δε χάνονται ποτέ.!!!»













Αυτά τα στοιχεία ενισχύουν την υποψία ότι οι μαχαιροβγάλτες που είχαν συσπειρωθεί παλιότερα στο οργανωτικό πλαίσιο της Χ.Α. σήμερα πλέκουν ένα πιο υπόγειο δίκτυο, το οποίο ενδεχομένως λειτουργεί πίσω από διάφορες ομάδες «αυτόνομων εθνικιστών», χωρίς να εκτίθεται σε μια επίσημη κεντρική δομή.




Νέοι εκτελεστές, παλιοί υποκινητές

author: Cas Smith
title: Responding to the far-right threat in Ireland
content:
It’s no secret that the far right is on the rise in several European countries, capitalising on the rising cost of living, health and education and lack of access to housing — largely laying the blame on immigration and the “failure” of multiculturalism.

In Ireland, a wave of far-right protests in 2022 targeting refugee and asylum-seeker accommodation sites was followed by a racist riot in Dublin in November 2023, in the aftermath of a stabbing attack. More recently, pogroms targeting refugees and migrants in Belfast took place between June and September this year.

Paul Murphy – Teachta Dála (a member of the Irish parliament, TD) for Dublin South-West, representing the People Before Profit-Solidarity (PBP-S) alliance, has played a leading role in building the movement against this tendency in Ireland.

Murphy recently spoke to Green Left, explaining that the Irish far right started gaining traction in online spaces during the COVID-19 pandemic, before taking a significant step forward during Europe’s refugee crisis in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

This allowed far-right figures and groups to grow in influence as asylum cases rose, going from “an entirely marginal, entirely peripheral almost entirely irrelevant force in Ireland” to one that had a notable presence on the ground in some communities, being able to elect some councillors and influence populist national parliamentarians.

As the number of Ukrainian refugees arriving in Ireland has declined since its 2023 peak, these groups have maintained their narrative through the targeting of International Protection Accommodation Services (IPAS) centres, which host asylum seekers from various backgrounds.

“They employed very racist rhetoric — suggesting that these people were a danger, tapping into fears that people have,” Murphy said.

Along with scaremongering, the far-right suggested that these centres were “luxury accommodations that homeless Irish people weren't getting — when in fact, they're terrible and overcrowded”.

Murphy said that in response to the scapegoating of refugees, “the government ended up adopting a lot of effectively far-right policies, forcibly making people homeless”, including deciding not to open any more IPAS centres. “Any single man who arrived here was made homeless. Not just homeless, made to rough sleep.”

Murphy said the far right then turned towards a feigned concern for the cost-of-living crisis, which – alongside housing – has been a key challenge in Irish society since the 2010s.

However, although far-right activism around immigration has slowed, it has continued to influence how people understand rising costs and the lack of housing supply.

“If you asked a random person in the street four or five years ago: ‘Why do we have this housing crisis?’, they would have said that this is about the developers, the landlords, the political parties that represent those interests,” Murphy said.

“People would have put forward a basic class analysis of the housing crisis.

“Whereas now, there's a chance that if you ask a random person [this question], they would attribute it to ‘so many people coming in’.”

Murphy said the government “is delighted for this narrative to emerge” and “adds to it significantly because it distracts from its own responsibility”.

Recent protests around the cost of “green” diesel, which is used widely in agriculture and taxed at a different rate, were widely supported, but all of the identified leaders had connections with the far right and or spouted far right ideas, said Murphy.

“They blockaded ports and they won considerable concessions in the context of a generally passive working class and an absence of social movements — with the exception of Palestine,” Murphy said.

“We supported it, [but] we said ‘there's a problem with this leadership, and the trade union movement needs to take the lead’,” said Murphy. Regarding the demand for cheaper diesel, “It can't just be about bringing the price of fossil fuels down, we need free public transport, we need to have retrofitting, we need to get away from reliance on fossil fuels...”

Murphy said that a “big positive” is that the trade unions are now “stepping onto the pitch in terms of the cost-of-living crisis” and there have been “unprecedented turnouts and votes for strike action across the public sector”, in pursuit of demands around cost-of-living protections and wages.

Far-right electoral formations — such as the quasi-fascist National Party, the Irish Freedom Party and a smaller outfit, Ireland First – have been hindered by internal squabbles and disorganisation. However, Murphy said the dominance of far-right narratives has grown the populist right, which now attracts 12–13% of the vote, shared between Independent Ireland and Aontú (Unity), according to opinion polls.

One cultural expression of this is the shifting meaning connected to the Irish tricolour flag. In the past, Murphy said the flying of this flag signified an attachment to the Irish revolutionary tradition, but recently, this has changed.

“There was a campaign linked to the ‘Raise the Colours’ movement in Britain, where people were putting up union jacks in working-class communities, in public streets or lamp posts, but also in people's houses.

“Now, you go into any work class community, you'll still see some of these flags. Definitely some of them may have been to do with sporting events, or maybe put up by old republicans.

“But a significant amount of it is about sending a message, an anti-immigrant message and about making people feel unwelcome in their community.”

In spite of these trends, Murphy contends that there is a growing movement against the far right, with large mobilisations occurring in response to racist attacks and rallies.

“There’s an international phenomenon whereby the pendulum has moved to the right, and that in turn is radicalising a lot of people to the left, who are saying, this is not the type of society I want to live in.

“There have been good mobilisations in response to the upsurge in the far right. In Belfast it was 20,000 people, in Derry there was a big protest, and in the south we’ve also had similar.

“At our biggest, we’ve been able to significantly outnumber them, although our protests happen on different days: the far-right [protest] happens on a Saturday, and the counter protest is called a few weeks later.”

However, Murphy said it was important for the left to try and organise counter protests on the same day, to have the opportunity to speak to working-class people who might be convinced away from far-right talking points.

Murphy said the PBP-S alliance has a three-stage process for addressing the far-right.

“One is building broad, anti-racist, anti-far-right alliances locally and nationally — a broad section of people on a very broad basis,” he said.

“Two, try and build a harder core of anti-racists and anti-fascists who are prepared, for example, to counterprotest against the far-right.

“Three – and this is a really crucial bit – continue to deepen our connections in the working-class communities where the far-right is leading things. That’s essential, to keep open the possibility of discussions with people.”

Murphy said upcoming mobilisations show the left and the unions taking a stand on the cost of living and other social issues and PBP-S is leading the opposition to attempts by South Dublin Council to raise council rates by an average of 25%.

“We’re putting a huge amount of energy into organising street meetings and protests. It’s mainly about countering this increase, and responding to an attack on the more vulnerable parts of the working class.

“But it’s also an opportunity to talk to people about the far right. When you bring people into activities, you enable them to feel more powerful than powerless, and you have the chance of winning the argument that the problem is ‘up there’ as opposed to ‘down here’.”

A full public sector strike is also happening on October 14 – the first in several years. And then there is the movement in solidarity with Palestine, which has “played a role in the past few years in holding the line on things sliding further to the right,” Murphy said.

“It’s the biggest social movement we’ve had over the past three years, [with] thousands of people involved in activism for Palestine. And the far-right clearly doesn’t know how to deal with that.”

author: John Lost
title: Anarcho-syndicalist politics of autonomy - Jonathan Eibisch
content:
Selection from Eibisch, Jonathan (2024): Politische Theorie des Anarchismus, transcript Verlag: Bielefeld, S. 208-233. (open access: https://www.transcript-verlag.de/978-3-8376-7183-4) machined translated text from German to American English.

“Syndicalism arose in France as a revolt against political socialism, and to understand it, we must provide a brief overview of the position that the socialist parties had attained in various countries” (Russell 1971: 57), wrote Bertrand Russell, a prominent advocate of the autonomous labor union movement, in 1918. Following a historical account, he makes a case for recognizing the significance of anarcho-syndicalism, particularly because of its pursuit of a fundamental reorganization of society (ibid.: 75).[1] Similarly, Noam Chomsky, a public intellectual sympathetic to anarchism, emphasized the significance of anarcho-syndicalism, citing the model of the Israeli kibbutzim (Chomsky 1976/2005: 134). Chomsky is particularly fascinated by the large-scale Spanish Revolution, through which successful self-managed structures were created (ibid.: 135). Similarly, in an influential work, Daniel Guérin advocates for anarcho-syndicalism as a practical and constructive implementation of anarchist ideas (Guérin 1969: 41). Guérin makes it clear that Bakunin had already advocated for the proto-trade union organizations—which were still amorphous at the time—conceived in connection with the concept of decentralized, autonomous communes (ibid.: 57–62). However, as rapid social developments overwhelmed the once-influential anarchists, social democracy gained the upper hand in the socialist movement and increasingly oriented it toward parliamentary and party politics. Consequently, the anarchists found themselves

“the 1890s […] into a dead end […]. They were isolated from the world of the working class, where Social Democrats held a monopoly. They huddled in small groups and barricaded themselves in ivory towers to reproduce an unrealistic ideology; or they devoted themselves to (and applauded) individual acts of violence, allowing themselves to be drawn into the cycle of repression and reprisals. […] In order to free the working masses from the influence of the socialists, who were merely deceiving them, the anarchists had to infiltrate the trade unions. […] The workers’ unions were to be reconnected to the “libertarian-communist” society, which remained the ultimate goal of the anarchists” (ibid.: 77f.).

Finally, Guérin sees the revolutionary councils developed during the Russian Revolution of 1905 as the organizational cornerstones of a “libertarian revolution,” precisely because they took places of production as their starting points (Ibid.: 83ff.) and regards the “apolitical” revolution in Spain beginning in 1936 as the most striking example of a radical social transformation based on anarcho-syndicalist ideas, one that was able to build upon a strong tradition (Ibid.: 118–128). For Guérin, self-management remains the key concept of libertarian socialism through which the relevance of anarcho-syndicalism can be revitalized (ibid.: 145–155). This concept is also viewed in the most recent German-language book on anarcho-syndicalism as an essential point of reference, one that must be understood in light of its historical origins. Thus, syndicalism

“starts fundamentally with the material basis. […] Contrary to its materialist worldview, however, the Marxist current did not focus primarily on the economic sphere as the basis of social existence and social change. Ironically, they saw their revolutionary battlefield precisely in the political sphere—which they derived from this and which belongs to the ‘superstructure.’ They sought to participate in the state and ultimately take it over, which was consistent with their centralist orientation. In contrast, the anarchist-oriented wing of the ‘International’ adhered to the premise of overturning the foundations of society through economic struggles; the intermediate goal was direct workers’ self-management, without taking over the structures of the state. This was possible only on a federalist basis, since the state was viewed as an expression of political and military centralism” (Döhring 2017: 20).

More so than other socialist currents, its theory of transformation is derived from practical struggles within class society. Despite some successes in union organizing and labor struggles, the theory of anarcho-syndicalism, at least, seems outdated. Consequently, the substance of the anarcho-syndicalist quest for autonomy must be reconstructed in the following primarily on the basis of historical sources. Thanks to works by, for example, Jule Ehms (2023) and Theresa Adamski, however, historical scholarship on this topic has been brought up to date, including for the German context. The schematic three-step process will be outlined here using the keywords: secession of the autonomous labor movement, strike, and direct action to empower the working class and achieve self-management of production and social functions. This, in turn, involves analysis, distanced criticism, self-organized and empowering social struggles, and finally, the prefigurative path toward the transformation of society as a whole. The sources for this include various texts by Pouget (1903–1907/2014), Cornelissen (1907–1926/2015), Peiró (1931/1986), and Santillán (1936/1986), Rocker (1900–1945), Marcks (2018a, 2018b, 2019), and Schmidt/van der Walt (2009).[2]

One of the defining figures of the second wave of the syndicalist labor movement—which adopted this self-designation with the founding of the French CGT—was Fernand Pelloutier, who was elected secretary of the Federation of Labor Exchanges in 1895 (Cornelissen 2015c: 65). He describes the emergence of anarcho-syndicalism as an eminent quest for autonomy in the sense of actively breaking away from the confined position of the labor movement. It began in 1892 with a critique of social legislation, which, from the syndicalist perspective, essentially represented a shift and a cover-up of exploitation. At its core, this entails a critique of the mode of political reform (Pelloutier 1895/1972: 317). This strategic development was accompanied by an increasing disengagement from politics. Pelloutier writes: “In light of ‘their increasing weakness and their unsuccessful efforts to link politics—which is primarily of interest to the individual—with the economy, which is of social interest,’ the unions finally realized […] that their division had a deeper cause than the conflicts between politicians, and that both […] stemmed from politics” (Ibid.: 320). Due to the perceived ineffectiveness of socialist party politics and its integration into bourgeois parliamentarism, as well as the aforementioned inadequacy of social legislation

“the unions resolved to refrain from any political agitation henceforth, to ruthlessly banish any discussion not purely economic from their educational programs, and to devote themselves exclusively to resistance against capital. The uproar accompanying this shift, however, reached the public. The new motto—“No more politics!”—spread throughout the workplaces […] The unions now seemed sufficiently prepared to the anarchists to embrace and enrich their teachings, and they came to the aid of those who, finally freed from political paternalism, sought to direct their attention—and that of their comrades—toward the study of economic laws” (Ibid.: 321).

Insofar as “pure anarchism” would not be realized in the anticipated socialist revolution, there was all the more need for organization and action in the current historical situation, rather than expecting a “total upheaval.” Therefore, the Federal Committee of the Labor Exchanges has the task of “enlightening the proletariat about the futility of a revolution that is content to replace one form of government with another, even if it were a socialist state” (ibid.: 324). A specific theoretical foundation of the novel autonomous labor movement lay in the dual function of the syndicates as organizations for the working class’s struggle and as the seeds of a new society. This goes far beyond the function of conventional labor unions in aggregating interests and representation. Émile Pouget was the first to articulate this innovative claim, from which the organizational and strategic orientations of anarcho-syndicalist groups were further derived: The syndicate is

“a group such as the ‘reformists’ envision: capable of waging the daily struggle against the employers to secure limited improvements and demands. But beyond that, it is also the appropriate organization for carrying out the expropriation of the capitalists and the reorganization of society—goals that socialists, in their illusory faith in the state, hope to achieve through the seizure of political power” (Pouget 2014a: 53f., cf. Rocker 1947: 25).

In this sense, the trade unions explicitly do not constitute political organizations and combine everyday struggles with a long-term strategy. This is intended to productively resolve the contradiction between reform and revolution that exists in socialist politics, thereby predestining the trade unions as social-revolutionary associations. Through this “dual task” of the trade unions, the overarching goal of social transformation—for which the expropriation of the capitalists is a decisive step—is already being gradually realized through the specific focus of labor struggles on better living conditions (Pouget 2014b: 86ff.). However, what is decisive is “social transformation” achieved “by direct means” (ibid.: 95). According to Pouget, the “group of producers”

“be the nucleus of the new society. It is unthinkable that a genuine social transformation could take place on any other basis. It is therefore essential that the producers prepare themselves for the appropriation and reorganization that lies ahead, because they are the only ones who can carry it out successfully. What we want is a social, not a political, revolution. These are two entirely different phenomena, and the tactics that lead to one take us further away from the other” (Pouget 2014b: 97f., cf. Pouget 2014a: 63).

Rocker later agrees with this (Rocker 1947: 25) and also uses the term “germ cell” (Rocker 1919, Rocker 1924c). Even with a socialist majority, a political path would not make a reorganization of society possible. Starting with the economic base, this must be undertaken by the unions themselves in order to eventually take over production and distribution, as FAUD activist Fritz Kater (1926) also describes. This line of reasoning appears consistent with the assumption that the capitalist class must be completely stripped of power and expropriated, for which the (sometimes idealized) general strike in syndicalism is regarded as a turning point. Pouget further emphasizes that the syndicalist union’s organization for struggle must not be an end in itself, but must engage in confrontation with the capitalist system. The union is “first and foremost a militant organization; its most urgent task is to constantly seek out the causes of social distress, to study them, to combat them, and to eliminate them” (Pouget 2014b: 100). In contrast to political parties, the autonomous labor movement represents the “Party of Labor,” which must orient itself toward the “current demands of the struggle” (ibid.: 130). Precisely because of the simplicity of its theory and its emphasis on practical struggles, syndicalism is superior to other socialist currents (ibid.), provided it is characterized by a unifying “spirit,” as Rocker adds (Rocker 1928). To realize this goal, a decentralized and federative organizational structure was established, in which there were to be no claims to leadership, but which served “to coordinate and intensify the revolutionary struggle of the working class” (Pouget 2014c: 132). In this way, the CGT “represents the exact opposite of democratic organizations, which stifle the vitality of their sections through their centralism and authoritarianism” (ibid.), whereas the CGT allows for the initiative and active participation of its individual members and autonomous unions. Thus, the desired libertarian-socialist form of society is already anticipated. According to Rocker, this is

“entirely natural, for socialism cannot be decreed from above or artificially conjured into existence by laws. It must spring from the depths of the masses as the result of their creative abilities and actions and create its own organization among the people. In the factories, in the fields, in the mines, in the technical and chemical workshops—that is where the new life of the future will develop. […] Here are the forces at work that alone are capable of creating a new world” (Rocker 1924c).

In anarcho-syndicalism, the metaphor of the birth of a new society is elaborated upon in concrete proposals that stem from the definition of its own understanding (→ 5.2.1). Socialism, it argues, is not the attainment of political power, but the autonomous struggle for economic power—and thus the elimination of all political power structures. Revolutionary syndicalism would “therefore be, in its very essence, anti-state and a staunch opponent of any institution of domination, no matter what new guise it may assume” (Rocker 1924b). Furthermore, Rocker explains in this context that the assumption that the state is necessary for the transition to socialism is based on a false understanding of history, insofar as the beginnings of a future, desirable form of society can only be conceived on the basis of the organizations that exist today. Rather than establishing a new “system of oppression” through political revolution, the goal should be to promote the self-organization of the working class (ibid.). In his reference to supposedly new theories of “embryonic forms” that might already contain the logic of utopian social forms within the capitalist present, Holger Marcks points out that such considerations literally draw on syndicalist terminology without making this explicit or even being aware of it (Marcks 2018a). Schmidt and van der Walt underscore this fundamental idea of the syndicalist movement, according to which trade unions “had the potential to perform a dual role: defending and improving workers’ rights, incomes, and conditions in the present; and acting as the key instrument in the destruction of the old order as well as the basic framework for worker self-management of the means of production in the new one” (Schmidt/van der Walt 2009: 135). To achieve this, it would be necessary to explicitly distance oneself from “orthodox” unions, counteract the emergence of excessive bureaucracies, and not focus solely on immediate issues—that is, on the mere representation of interests (ibid.: 181). An important difference from the doctrine of socialist parties of the time lay in the genesis of anarchist syndicalism in its assumption of the plurality of subjects and their interests within the working class. These, however, were to be aggregated into a common class struggle. This starting point drew on the practical experiences of recurring conflicts of interest among various social groups in labor struggles. At the same time, the theory was based on clearly definable class antagonisms, according to which the unions would have to organize themselves (Pouget 2014b: 86ff.). It was also crucial, the theory held, that union members remain individual personalities and unite on the basis of their common interests (ibid.). The syndicalist principle, rather than the democratic one, should apply, as evidenced, among other things, by the granting of imperative mandates. With this anti-political orientation, it is “consequently impossible to draw a parallel between the struggle of the unions and participation in the dismal business of politics—let alone to confuse the two” (Pouget 2014b: 89). Pouget consequently attributes organizational difficulties within the unions to the presence of too much “democratism” and the persistence of “political errors,” and writes of the need to resist the “political virus” (ibid.: 90). This pursuit of autonomy from socialist parties and parliamentary democracy is based on the assumption that plurality and a potential commonality of interests exist simultaneously—a commonality that can only be established through the organization and action of the working class (see Cornelissen 2015b: 57). This process of aggregation and mediation was to take place within the trade unions, which serve to expand workers’ power (Pouget 2014c: 107f.). In the “Party of Labor,” everyone could be admitted, even if they “hold strange philosophical or political views […] [if they] believe, for example, in some god or in the state […]. [W]hat is disapproved of is the interference of the priest or the politician, both of whom have made speculating on the faith of others their life’s work. (Ibid.). The syndicalist movement, therefore, unlike all other alliances: “Interests, not opinions. Thus, there is inevitably a shared perspective within their ranks” (ibid.). Pouget goes on to explain the resulting consequences: “This ability to neutralize individual differences through the consensus that necessarily arises from shared interests gives the Labor Party an advantage in terms of vitality and fighting spirit and protects it from the shortcomings that plague political parties” (ibid.: 108), since they do not aim to engage in politics. It should be noted that this strategic argument is (often unconsciously) linked to specific ideological and worldview-based convictions, which are linked to debates about what anarchism actually is.[3] What is crucial is that within socialist groups, essential anarchist principles such as decentralization, voluntarism, and autonomy would continue to exist and be practiced (Cornelissen 2015b: 56f.; see Cornelissen 2015c: 70). The advocacy for revolutionary groups illustrates a turn toward the political dimension, whereby Christiaan Cornelissen rejects the view that syndicalism “is self-sufficient.” Syndicalism is decidedly opposed to political parties, yet it collaborates with other movements—such as the cooperative movement—that are not formed on the basis of converging economic interests (Cornelissen 2015c: 80f.). The proletarian standpoint is also evident in syndicalism in that it by no means advocates for the “abolition of factories,” as Werner Sombart claims. Rather, the “struggle against the machine” is “wage laborer’s standpoint.” After all, this struggle is not solely or primarily about higher wages, but rather about the abolition of wage labor and better living conditions in general (ibid.: 73; cf. Marcks 2018a, Mueller 2022). In their historical account, Schmidt and van der Walt emphasized that the “broad anarchist tradition”—which was largely syndicalist in orientation—had always referred not only to the working class but also to the peasantry (Schmidt and van der Walt 2009: 6, 15f.). The category of class should not be misunderstood as “crude workerism that fetishizes male factory workers in heavy boots and hard hats. “The working class and peasantry are understood in expansive terms: the working class includes all wage workers who lack control over their work, whether employed in agriculture, industry, or services, including casual and informal workers as well as their families and the unemployed; the peasantry includes all small farmers who are subject to the control and exploitation of other classes, including sharecroppers and labor tenants” (ibid.: 7).

Accordingly, contemporary conceptualizations such as “class struggle anarchism” would also be nonsensical, insofar as they suggest that these are variants of anarchism. However, a class-struggle approach is inherent in anarchism per se. An important question remains: how can syndicalism address those proletarian classes that exist outside of wage labor (ibid.: 181)? The secession of the autonomous labor union movement is not based on dogmatic political abstention, but on historical experiences. Following the French revolution, it could be observed how the working class organized itself autonomously (Pouget 2014a: 59f.). Through this, it was to attain self-awareness—that is, to understand its own position within the social hierarchy and societal constellation—and to empower itself in rebellion against the living conditions imposed upon it.[4] Cornelissen takes a slightly different view in this context. While modern anarchism “stands, in practice, for agitation as ‘direct action,’ as the ‘self-action’ of the masses—not only in open struggle against capitalists, but in every sphere of social life, in the struggle against state and clerical rule (e.g., as antimilitarism, anticlericalism), and in certain forms also in productive association, etc.” (Cornelissen 2015b: 53). But beyond that, its aspirations manifest themselves

“even in the political sphere, directed against all parties without distinction (street agitation against bad laws, mass demonstrations for or against certain political events, etc.). In the latter sphere, today’s anarchists proceed from the premise that all parliamentary parties—from the most rigid conservatives down to the radicals and social democrats—are all the more willing to abolish certain abuses or to implement minor improvements as concessions the more they are compelled to do so from the outside by the direct pressure of the masses. In this way, anarchist tactics in every sphere have gradually taken on the same character—that of striving and acting through the masses’ own power, and not through the actions of those in power” (Ibid.: 53f.).

Unlike Pouget, Cornelissen does not insist on rejecting “politics” in general. His text is dated 1908, while Pouget’s dates from 1903. It is therefore possible that during this period, the relationship to politics within anarcho-syndicalism shifted in general. It seems more likely that Cornelissen did indeed recognize the necessity of considering the political dimension, as was already evident above in his plea for revolutionary groups independent of trade unions. Yet even those groups should not rely on parliamentary politics. They should not confine themselves to the political arena but address their opponents through direct action. In this way, social progress would be won regardless of its legal codification, and the “class struggle would be brought to the forefront” (Cornelissen 2015d: 107). The strategy of exerting pressure on the political establishment—and by no means rejecting the passage of “good laws”—almost resembles that of extra-parliamentary movements. However, it must be regarded as anti-parliamentary because the struggle for “good laws” is not the goal of anarchist syndicalism, and such laws are enacted as a reaction by the state to direct actions and self-organization from below. Therefore, syndicalists considered it “considered it their duty to combat the bad laws introduced in present-day society not in parliament, but outside of it, in free social life. They are also happy to lend their support to any good law, such as international legislation regarding the eight-hour workday, but they do so in daily life and through direct action in factories and workshops” (Cornelissen 2015g: 157). The difference from social movements that are entangled with and linked to party-political approaches is a gradual one and does not resolve the tension in dealing with politics—unlike a dogmatic stance of refusal. Interestingly, Cornelissen also has a different understanding of democracy than Pouget. A “democratic-syndicalist opposition” is making itself felt against the “brutally anti-democratic aspect” of bureaucratic, hierarchical leadership (in political parties as well as in the state itself) (Cornelissen 2015e: 112). In this way, syndicalism opposes social democracy, which undermines class power. The autonomous labor movement experienced a surge in popularity over a short period because it articulated the aversion of numerous workers to “politics” (ibid.: 114f.). Rocker also defines anarchism in contrast to social democracy, which must be distinguished not only because of its “tactical method” but also as “fundamental opposites” with regard to the conception of humanity and the understanding of socialism (Rocker 1900). Rocker rejects parties that claim to “wage a political struggle against the bourgeoisie” (ibid.), even though the social democratic organizations undoubtedly possessed an enormous power base.“Thus, wherever large masses of the working class rallied to its cause, this party developed into a state within a state, and for many years it was able to prevent any other socialist tendency from emerging with systematic and unscrupulous ruthlessness” (ibid.). For Rocker, the quality of socialist organizations and the approach to conflicts in class society—which must not adopt state logic—are decisive, rather than membership numbers. It follows, therefore, that “while the conquest of political power by social democracy appears to be the most important task that must precede the realization of socialism, for anarchism the abolition of all political power is of decisive importance” (ibid., cf. Rocker 1919). In addition to parliamentarism, anarcho-syndicalists also reject nationalism and the drawing of borders, while advocating direct action and an international orientation, writes Rocker in the Declaration of Principles of Syndicalism (Rocker 1919). Secession should take place through the deliberate development of other forms of organization and action. It is interesting that Rocker thereby aims to attain a different political consciousness.[5] This represents a slight shift in his position, with which he responds to the accusation that anarchism is apolitical. On the contrary, his anti-political stance has direct political implications. In summary, the syndicalist premise is that a socialist economic order

“has its natural political complement directly within the workplaces, in the various branches of industrial and agricultural professions […] [and] finds its fullest expression in the council system. However, any external power over the councils and any domination or control of them by political parties or by certain groups of professional socialist politicians must be eliminated from the outset if the social reorganization is not to be disrupted from the very first step and led astray onto the path of state capitalism” (Rocker 1924b).

Rocker thus regards the council system here as an adequate form of political organization, which implies that it must be free from the dominance of parties or politicians (see Senft 2006: 40ff.). Former social democrats like Rocker realized that a void arises when the political dimension is ignored in the name of “pure” syndicalism. Rocker clearly refers to the political dimension of social struggles while insisting that politics should take place outside the state sphere. The goal of “fighting for the greatest conceivable political freedom of movement within today’s system” (Rocker 1924b) makes it clear that he envisions an ongoing process aimed at expanding autonomous spheres of action. Rocker emphasizes that freedom of assembly, the right to strike, the right to form coalitions, etc., were not voluntarily granted by the parliamentary state, but were won through struggle. Because governments must take the demands of the masses into account, this would mean

“indifferently surrendering these achievements, […] surrendering the results of all past revolutionary struggles, and carrying out the agenda of the reactionaries.” As the syndicalists wage the struggle against the business class day after day to improve the living conditions of the proletariat, they never forget for a moment that all these struggles must ultimately aim to put an end to wage slavery and rebuild society on the basis of libertarian socialism. And while they are constantly striving to wrest greater political freedom of movement and opportunities for their propaganda from the governments, they by no means hide the fact that these constant struggles against the political “pressure from governments is merely a step along the path toward increasingly displacing the state from its current positions, with the aim of finally eliminating it from all branches of economic, political, and social life” (ibid.).

This formulation also reflects the anarcho-syndicalist dual approach of simultaneously viewing everyday labor struggles through a social-revolutionary lens. In doing so, Rocker does not treat all political parties equally. They could have a certain value if they act purely as an opposition: “They are always at their best when they can act in a purely critical, i.e., purely negative manner, and this is always the case as long as they confront a despotic system as hopeless minorities and exert a corrosive effect through their agitation” (Rocker 1924c). Once in government, however, they become “slaves of the very same apparatus of power that they supposedly only wanted to conquer” (ibid.). Rocker’s approach can thus be seen as a plea for the possibility of politics free from domination (see Rocker 1947: 3, 30). He insists that anarcho-syndicalism is by no means apolitical and that its adherents

“have no interest in the political structure of the various countries and, consequently, no interest in day-to-day political struggles. This notion is entirely false and stems either from complete ignorance or a deliberate distortion of the facts. It is not the political struggle as such that fundamentally and tactically distinguishes anarcho-syndicalists from modern workers’ parties, but rather the form of the struggle and the goals it seeks to achieve” (ibid.: 29).

Anarcho-syndicalists do not lack “sympathy for political struggle in general” (ibid.: 30); rather, they have experienced it as the “weakest and most helpless form” of action available to workers. Furthermore, in bourgeois democracy, parliamentarism functions as a means of preserving the status quo, which is why class antagonism cannot be abolished through it (ibid.: 31). That this view was widespread in anarchist syndicalism is also evident in the work of Diego Abad de Santillián. Among other things, he points out the absurdity of labeling the Second Spanish Republic as “socialist.” A “workers’ republic” cannot be created in parliament and introduced by decree. Rather, it can only be won by the workers themselves, outside the reach of the state (de Santillián 1986: 103f.). Therefore, private capitalism can only be overcome if state capitalism is not introduced as a supposed intermediate step, which is why democracy must be realized in concrete relationships and in tangible places (ibid.: 106). This requires a far-reaching organization of society along the lines of production sites and chains. For de Santillián, it is not a contradiction to conceive of politics outside the state. On the contrary, he argues for the rejection of the state on political grounds:

“Politically, we must of course reject the dominance of a committee, a party, or a predetermined direction. This means we must also reject the state as an institution that demands obedience from everyone—whether they consent to it or not. Without rejecting this state and the laws it dictates, there can be no true revolution and no social prosperity” (de Santillian 1986: 143).

In this, he agrees with Malatesta, who defines “political struggle […] as the struggle against the government” (Malatesta 2017: 242). This is particularly evident in the course of the Russian Revolution, in which

“[t]he state’s policies […] destroyed socialism […] [and Russia] became an ideal model for bureaucrats […] [and an] imperialist power among other powers, […] which has as little to do with socialism and the ideals of the proletariat as any other state does. This development may surprise some, but not us, for we have consistently pointed out this danger through our criticism. Once again, history confirms our views. The policies of the state are as incompatible with socialism as water is with fire. If one prevails, the other is defeated, and vice versa. Socialism can only be created if, at the same time, the state is destroyed and institutions of the people are established that take direct control over production and distribution” (de Santillian 1986: 149, cf. Cornelissen 2015g: 155).

The CNT’s program, as adopted at the 1936 Zaragoza Congress—during the onset of the social revolution—also states:

“We must all bear in mind that it would be absurd to attempt to construct the society of the future with mathematical precision, for there is often a veritable chasm between theory and practice. Therefore, let us not fall into the error of politicians who present definitive solutions to all problems—solutions that then collapse with a crash in practice. Politicians fail because, without taking into account the development of human life itself, they believe that a single method can apply for all time” (Framework Program 1986: 169).

To the adherents of historical anarcho-syndicalism, what they associated with politics seemed deeply suspect and alien. In this vein, Schmidt and van der Walt also note: “Since its emergence, socialism has been divided into two main tendencies: libertarian socialism, which rejects the state and hierarchy more generally; and political socialism” (Schmidt/van der Walt 2009: 6). At the same time, they view the question of how anarcho-syndicalists deal with the political dimension as a key debate. The issue at hand is “whether anarchists and syndicalists need political groups dedicated to promoting the ideas of the broad anarchist tradition, and if so, what form such groups should take” (ibid.: 22). Accordingly, most anarchists advocated an organizational dualism between popular mass labor union organizations and ideologically committed political groups. In contrast, there was a faction that argued for a unity of the economic and political dimensions within the autonomous labor union movement. For example, in the preamble to the 1937 program of the syndicalist Industrial Workers of the World: “‘The IWW is not anti-political. Nor is it non-political. It is ultra-political’” (quoted in: Ibid.: 141).[6] Based on their research, the two authors therefore conclude that syndicalism is “profoundly political, and takes the state very seriously indeed. Taken to its logical conclusion […], all mass anarchism amounts to a project of taking power in society and creating a coordinated system of stateless governance; this is especially true of syndicalism” (ibid.: 203). There are various concepts and terms for the system of “stateless governance,” all of which ultimately trace back to the fundamental idea of federal self-governance. Experience confirmed what astute observers such as Malatesta (2014: 150–161) had critically pointed out: The labor movement, in and of itself, is not immune to bureaucracy, mere advocacy of interests, and reformism. In other words, its social-revolutionary orientation did not arise eo ipso, but had to be advanced by ideologically committed political activists.[7] This was also archetypically reflected in the practical relationship between the syndicalist Confederación Nacional del Trabajo (CNT) and the anarchist Federación Anarquista Ibérica (FAI). In the tension between anti-politics and politics, Schmidt and van der Walt (2009: 244) argue in favor of politics. Starting from a more direct examination of the understanding of politics in anarchist syndicalism, it is worth taking a closer look at the pursuit of autonomy, which must be understood as a continuous process rooted in a history from below. They accused Marxists of adopting bourgeois historiography—and thus a bourgeois understanding of revolution—with a “Jacobin” orientation in its Leninist manifestations (Kropotkin 1982, cf. Rocker 2012). Pouget describes the long process of achieving autonomy as follows:

“Throughout the 19th century, the proletariat strove to free itself in its struggle from the purely political approach of the bourgeois parties. This required considerable effort, since the bourgeoisie—which depends on the proletariat’s consent or tolerance to govern unhindered—not only fought against and massacred the proletariat whenever it rose up against its exploiters, but tried to make him compliant through clever education, in order to simultaneously dissuade him from engaging with economic issues and to instill in him the illusion of democratism” (Pouget 2014a: 54f.).

The starting point is the historical experience of the bourgeois reaction against the autonomous actions of the labor movement, which the bourgeoisie countered even under the guise of democracy (Pouget 2014a: 55; see also Cornelissen 2015c: 90f.). At the same time, self-organization from below gained strength and, through its relative autonomy, exerted pressure on government policy, as Pouget (2014c: 125–128) and Cornelissen (2015c: 65, Cornelissen 2015a: 39ff.) demonstrate at several trade union and anarchist congresses between 1888 and 1907. The idea of autonomy had been deliberately introduced into the labor movement by those anarchists who were dissatisfied with the dogmatic disputes within the anarchist political scene. Many of them went on to assume leadership roles in the unions (Pouget 2014a: 52). The emergence of anarcho-syndicalism can thus be understood as a fusion of pure trade unionists, disillusioned party socialists, and pragmatic anarchists (Cornelissen 2015c: 66), whereby the pursuit of autonomy in this specific constellation exerted a kind of magnetic pull. Cornelissen explains that trade-union anti-statism should be about principle, not dogma; this becomes clear in Cornelissen’s writing, where he notes that, much like the Christian commandments, it is about a tendency, “as a striving in a certain direction” (Cornelissen 2015c: 77). This statement is surprising in that—similar to Sorel’s Myth (1908)—it emphasizes and reveals the function of the utopia of a society free from domination as a source of inspiration for radical and autonomous social movements, enabling them to take very concrete steps. This also concerns the quality of organizations and actions, rather than, for example, focusing solely on membership numbers and financial resources, as German union leaders are said to do (Cornelissen 2015e: 116f.). Syndicalist efforts toward autonomy thus constitute a specific strategy that emphasizes the importance of self-organized groups which generate alternative concepts, ideas, practices, forms of organization, etc.—a phenomenon that can also be observed historically in other social movements (Cornelissen 2015g: 156). This, in turn, reveals an ambivalence toward politics, which arises precisely from the distance to the ruling order and (organized) autonomy. According to Rocker, the trade unionists realized “that participation in the politics of nation-states did not bring the labor movement one bit closer to socialism, but had, to a large extent, helped to destroy the belief in the necessity of constructive socialist activities. But what is worst of all: it robbed people of their initiative by making them believe that salvation always comes from above” (Rocker 1947: 24). Their emancipation, therefore, can only come about through the proletarian classes themselves, as van der Walt and Schmidt also write. Social movements should represent a genuine counterforce and counterculture to the ruling class, confront the state, and ultimately replace it (Schmidt/van der Walt 2009: 7, 139).

As already mentioned, specific forms of revolutionary everyday struggles were developed within anarchist syndicalism. Pouget emphasizes that reform and revolution must not be pitted against one another; in the syndicalist unions, both come together and thus shape the understanding of social revolution (Pouget 2014c: 96). The same applies to attempts to contain unions through legal frameworks and the association system.

“Yet the fact that the unions view the ‘blessings’ the government wishes to bestow upon them with due suspicion does not in any way mean that they reject the struggle for limited improvements. But these improvements must be real. That is why they prefer not to accept them as a gift of mercy from those in power, but to fight for them themselves through direct action. If, as sometimes happens, the demanded improvement depends on a change in the law, the unions will attempt to force it through by exerting external pressure on the government, not by sending representatives to parliament to act in this regard […]” (Ibid.: 97).

The effectiveness of this strategy, which was developed in large part by anarchists, subsequently led to a renewal of the anarchist scene: Thus, “modern anarchists advocate all means that fall under the term ‘direct action’: strikes, boycotts, systematic obstruction […], sabotage. “But the example set by the revolutionary unions could not help but have a lasting impact on the revolutionary groups as well” (Cornelissen 2015b: 53). The actual developments within the social-revolutionary unions overwhelmed anarchist theory, which, in the assessment of the syndicalists, was implemented on a massive scale in practice. This, however, presupposes maintaining the revolutionary course, which is why Cornelissen, among others, opposes the establishment of socialist collective enterprises that could compete with capitalist firms only in individual sectors. What is needed, he argues, is the syndicalist struggle within these enterprises, which should ultimately lead to their takeover (Cornelissen 2015c: 81f., see Cornelissen 2015g: 158f.). Thus, revolutionary syndicalism positions itself between social-democratic reformism and the often marginal and exclusive groups of anarchists, who frequently stood “outside of real life” (Cornelissen 2015g: 152). In this sense, anarcho-syndicalism can be understood as a socialist, anti-authoritarian, and social-revolutionary mass movement. It thereby resolves the contradiction that a majority of the socialist movement advocates for autonomy and self-empowerment, while a large portion has simultaneously internalized Marxist theories (ibid.: 153). In essence, there had previously been a lack of a social-revolutionary theory that draws from real social movements and flows back into them. In this regard, it is important to point out “that the critique of the revolutionary syndicalists today does not stop at the actions of the Social Democrats and the reformist unions, but is equally directed against the ‘Bolsheviks’ and their ‘state communism’ which leads to ‘state socialism’ or ‘state capitalism’” (ibid.: 154).

Cornelissen places particular emphasis on questions regarding “an organizationally structured, constructive activity” (Cornelissen 2015i: 195); in other words, he believes that the focus on propaganda over the past 40 years has not been productive, since workers find it “uninteresting.” Rather, they would be interested in what anarchism and syndicalism stand for and what “positive organizational and practical work [they] can do” (ibid.: 196). The core element of this should be the takeover of industry through self-management, which would also apply to other social institutions (ibid.: 197; cf. Schmidt/van der Walt 2009: 136, Rocker 1947: 6). In this context, Rocker emphasizes once again that the “claim that the state must remain in existence until society is no longer divided into hostile classes […] appears, in light of all historical experience, like a bad joke” (ibid.: 7). This, however, also raises the question of how leadership could be exercised, for it is not enough—as Malatesta, for example, argues—to say that anarchists do not want to lead anyone (Cornelissen 2015i: 201). Marcks therefore argues, “Great changes occur only at the culmination of many small processes that must be undergone to reorganize a complex society. In this sense, there are ‘no shortcuts’ on the path to a more social world” (Marcks 2019). According to Schmidt and van der Walt, this approach reflects two main concerns of “mass anarchism,” within which syndicalism is the largest strand: First, that immediate improvements in the living conditions of the proletarian classes would contribute to their organization and their self-confidence in their abilities; and second, that the unions could thereby assume a leading role in revolutionary struggles while simultaneously embodying the seeds of the new society (Schmidt/van der Walt 2009: 134). It is understandable that this position stands in contrast to that of insurrectionary anarchism with its maximalist aspirations (ibid.: 138). Reforms, however, should be won in order to move forward. This, on the one hand, refutes the Marxist claim that syndicalism is reduced to economism and, on the other hand, counters the insurrectionists’ assertion that unions cannot be revolutionary (ibid.: 202). Building on the anarcho-syndicalist understanding of social revolution, its implementation through direct action and self-organization can be discussed as the practiced politics of autonomy. After all, the associated practices and principles had already formed the basis of the resolutions of the First International. The syndicalist movement continues these without becoming politically ossified or entangled in ideological turf wars (Pouget 2014b: 93f.). According to its original anarcho-syndicalist understanding, direct action means that

“The working class, in its constant struggle against the existing order, expects nothing from outsiders, from powers or forces external to itself, but rather creates its own conditions for struggle and draws its means of action from within itself. This means that, from now on, the producer rises up against today’s society, which recognizes only the citizen. And that this producer, recognizing that every form of social coexistence is based on its respective system of production, attempts to directly attack the capitalist mode of production in order to transform it, eliminate the entrepreneur, and thereby achieve sovereignty in the workplace—the essential prerequisite for the enjoyment of real freedom” (Pouget 2014d: 137, see Cornelissen 2015e: 110).

According to Pouget, direct action is about the working class taking the initiative while maintaining its independence. This attacks the principle of authority, and thus direct action reveals itself to be “the authentic embodiment of the principle of freedom, its realization among the masses: no longer through abstract, vague, and unclear formulas, but through clear and practical concepts that generate the fighting spirit that is the order of the day. This destroys the spirit of submission and compliance that paralyzes individuals and turns them into willing slaves, and fosters the spirit of revolt that inspires human societies” (ibid.: 136f., cf. Cornelissen 2015d: 94). In any case, direct action is “the normal mode of operation of the syndicates, their essential characteristic” (Pouget 2014d: 137)—the labor struggle in its concentrated “pure form,” without “admixtures” and “compromises with capitalism, without the flirtations with the bosses of which the apologists for ‘social peace’ dream, without ties to the government, without the involvement of ‘mediators’ in the debate” (ibid.: 140). Understood in the context of syndicalism, Cornelissen adopts an almost extra-parliamentary perspective when he further writes that, of course, “the use of direct action to influence government bodies and to support good laws or combat bad ones is not ruled out. But even here, it remains action in real life and not in parliament, and manifests itself as pressure on all political parties without distinction” (Cornelissen 2015c: 86). Instead of political representation and union representation, direct action should be used to address and promote workers’ autonomy. In fact, the tactics and methods of direct action would not be tied to a trade union theory but would simply arise as byproducts of labor struggles (Cornelissen 2015e: 122)—which is also why they are difficult to grasp. With regard to forms of action as well as self-organization, practical solutions—the “least[est] means”—will prevail (Cornelissen 2015f: 139). Through this, the skills necessary for taking over the means of production would already be acquired, and workers’ control of these means would ensure far better production conditions than, for example, imposed Taylorism (Cornelissen 2015h: 180). The strategy of self-organization differs from the political dimension, but the following statement should be understood as suggesting that the former could influence the latter: “In the political sphere, the libertarian communists and anarchists will certainly not be able to achieve much of significance. Nevertheless, they should uphold the principles of freedom, autonomy, and federalism here as well” (Cornelissen 2015i: 204, cf. Peiró 1986: 40ff.). Pursuing this insight further, Marcks sees an implicit syndicalist approach in more recent left-wing theories of transformation—which address “embryonic forms,” “prefigurative politics,” and “modes of relation” (→ 5.4.2)—each of which is intended to be constructed in opposition to the state-capitalist social form. Thus, he even asserts that “the ‘Left’ is therefore, by definition, undergoing a shift toward syndicalism without making this explicit” (Marcks 2018a). He understands a “set” of syndicalist forms of organization and practices as “a constructive social technique capable of strategically mediating between reality and utopia” (ibid.: 3). Syndicalist forms of direct action and self-organization should therefore be understood as a strategic “interaction with reality aimed at agency” (Marcks 2019), which expands the scope for action.
