title: Özkan: ‘Trust in the process rests on Öcalan’s freedom and lasting peace’
content:
Canan Kebenç Özkan, Co-Spokesperson of the Democratic Local Governments Board of the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), spoke to ANF about the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the approach of local governments to the process, communal life, and Abdullah Öcalan’s status and position.




Canan Kebenç Özkan said the call for Peace and Democratic Society issued by Abdullah Öcalan on 27 February had marked a new stage in the conflict, opening a period in which the Kurdish question must be resolved through peaceful means, on a democratic basis and through democratic politics, rather than through conflict.




Özkan said society was undergoing change and transformation, rebuilding itself on a democratic basis, while the state was becoming more responsive to society and democracy. However, she pointed out that the process was encountering obstacles at certain stages.




‘Öcalan’s role is vital’




Canan Kebenç Özkan said Abdullah Öcalan’s role could not be overlooked at this critical stage of the process, stressing that his contribution must be given the recognition it deserves.




Özkan said: “Öcalan’s vital role in this process absolutely cannot be ignored. His role must be properly recognised. At the same time, people across Kurdistan have very high expectations of the process. There is a strong social expectation that lasting peace will be achieved and a democratic foundation established.”




‘Öcalan’s voice must reach the Turkish public’




Canan Kebenç Özkan stressed that Abdullah Öcalan’s voice must reach the Turkish public for the process to advance successfully, achieve its ultimate goal, secure lasting peace and build a democratic society.




Özkan also said: “Öcalan’s role is vital for this process, of which we are all a part, to advance successfully, reach its ultimate goal, establish lasting peace and build a democratic society. First and foremost, Öcalan’s voice must reach the Turkish public. He must be able to meet with journalists, intellectuals and civil society organisations, and maintain contact with his own organisation in a way that enables the implementation of the law as the process of ending the conflict progresses.




For this reason, Öcalan must be provided with conditions in which he can live and work freely as soon as possible, participate directly in the process and oversee its progress. We believe that he must personally carry out this role, particularly in coordinating peace, disarmament and strategy.”




‘Öcalan’s freedom is a key factor in public trust in the process’




Canan Kebenç Özkan said people now wanted Abdullah Öcalan’s physical freedom to be secured and regarded it as one of the most important factors in their trust in the process.




Özkan continued: “The authorities must act immediately to prevent the process from being unnecessarily prolonged and ultimately derailed once again. As local governments, we continue to participate in and organise the actions and events organised by our party. However, the main demand we encounter in our meetings and activities with the public is very clear: People want to see Öcalan free. They believe this is one of the fundamental factors determining their trust in the process.”




‘The public’s main expectations are lasting peace and Öcalan’s freedom’




Canan Kebenç Özkan said the public’s foremost expectation was for peace to become lasting, stressing that one of the essential conditions for achieving this was Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom.




Özkan said: “The public’s most fundamental expectation from the process is lasting peace. One of the essential conditions for this is Öcalan’s freedom. People also want society to be rebuilt democratically and the state to become more responsive to society’s understanding of democracy and that of local communities. In Kurdistan, people want to live as free and equal citizens, with their own language, religion and beliefs. They demand a life of fraternity based on equal citizenship alongside Turkish, Arab, Syriac and Alevi peoples.




Strengthening local democracy is also one of the public’s main expectations. People want the state to become more responsive to local democracy, the conflict between central and local authorities to be eliminated, and local communities to be able to govern themselves. Politically, the fundamental issue is ensuring that Öcalan can live and work freely and that lasting peace is achieved. This is also the foundation of trust in the process.”




‘Appointing trustees is a usurpation of the people’s will’




Canan Kebenç Özkan stressed that a democratic process requires the will of the people to be respected at the local level, saying that the appointment of trustees was not simply a matter of replacing elected municipal officials.




Özkan said: “If a democratic process is to function, the will of the people must be reflected in local governance. The appointment of trustees is not simply about an administrator being appointed to a municipality; it is about disregarding and usurping the will of the people. Our position on trustees is therefore clear.




We have seen that the appointment of trustees has also seriously undermined public confidence and trust in the process. For this reason, we have demanded in our statements that trustees be withdrawn immediately. As an initial step, administrative measures such as the Ministry of Interior refraining from extending trustees’ terms of office could produce positive results in the short term. However, a lasting solution requires the repeal of Articles 45 and 46 of Municipal Law No. 5393, which provide the legal basis for appointing trustees, as well as Decree-Law No. 674, on which this practice is based.”




Canan Kebenç Özkan said they were continuing their democratic struggle through protests and other activities, demanding the withdrawal of trustees and the removal of the legal grounds for their appointment through public statements, demands and diplomatic meetings at every level.




‘Serious ecological destruction is taking place in Kurdistan’




Canan Kebenç Özkan said the geography of Kurdistan had suffered extensive destruction from hydroelectric power plants and dams throughout the period of conflict.




Özkan also said: “Kurdistan has suffered serious destruction from hydroelectric power plants (HPPs) and dams throughout the period of conflict. We are now seeing capital groups embark on a new wave of plunder and exploitation in the region to increase their profits, taking advantage of the process of ending the conflict. Hydroelectric power plants, solar power plants (SPPs), shale gas extraction, gold exploration using cyanide, tree felling and mining activities are causing serious ecological destruction in Kurdistan, as they are in many other cities across Turkey.




We oppose these policies through an approach to local governance based on democracy, ecology and women’s freedom. We carry out various activities together with local environmental organisations, ecological movements and our party’s ecology commission, and we are expanding our struggle.”




Canan Kebenç Özkan reiterated that they were working alongside local environmental organisations, ecological movements and their party’s ecology commission to strengthen and expand their struggle.




‘The plunder of nature is an attack on people’s lives’




Canan Kebenç Özkan said they carried out educational and awareness-raising activities according to local needs, organised public meetings and worked with local communities to develop solutions.




Özkan added: “The plunder of nature does not simply mean the destruction of the environment; it also means interfering with the lives, land, water and future of the people living in those areas. For this reason, we organise discussions and protests together with local communities. We were among the organisers of the vigil against tree felling in Besta. We also supported the protest in Varto (Gimgim).




We recently organised an environmental rally in Diyadin under the slogan ‘I stand up for my land’. Our struggle is not limited to democratic, direct and legitimate forms of protest. We also pursue legal proceedings through our municipalities and closely monitor these processes.”




Communes and the approach to local governance




Canan Kebenç Özkan described a commune, in its most basic form, as a people, society or community governing itself. She said this meant that individuals and communities became active participants in their own lives, with a direct say in their needs, problems and the mechanisms for addressing them.




Özkan said they did not regard municipalities as miniature instruments of central government or the centralised state structure, explaining that this was what they meant by the phrase “Municipalities are communes.”




She said they had long argued that top-down decision-making mechanisms, through which central authorities make decisions on behalf of the people, were inadequate for the societies of the Middle East and the peoples of Turkey and Kurdistan. Rather than allowing municipalities to become miniature states, they advocated transforming them into mechanisms through which people could govern themselves.




Özkan said they were working to develop the means and methods to achieve this. She stressed that people must be directly involved in every area of local life, from identifying their needs and resolving problems to expressing democratic demands, education in the mother tongue, cultural rights, healthy urban living, infrastructure development, combating substance addiction, policies concerning young people and women, and other social needs.




She said municipalities regularly held public and neighbourhood meetings in line with this approach. They were working towards a municipal model in which residents themselves identified their neighbourhoods' needs, demands and expectations and developed their own proposals for addressing them.




Participatory budgeting




Canan Kebenç Özkan said participatory budgeting was an important part of this approach. She explained that initiatives launched last year in Van (Wan) and continued this year in Ağrı (Agirî), Digor and Halfeli enabled neighbourhoods to participate directly in the budget-making process.




Özkan said residents identified their own needs and collectively decided which should take priority, with the participation of women, children, young people and older people. In this way, the budget ceased to be merely a financial document and became a democratic mechanism reflecting the municipality's political direction and society's priorities.




She said combating poverty was another important aspect of communal governance. To address the severe and persistent poverty that remains one of Kurdistan's most pressing problems, they were working to establish cooperatives within the framework of eco-economic policies.




Özkan added that communal gardens aimed at strengthening women's economic independence were also part of these efforts, alongside initiatives addressing social, cultural and mother-tongue needs.




Canan Kebenç Özkan said they developed their activities through direct discussions with women, young people and people with disabilities about their demands.




She explained that they also regarded the commune as a collective governance mechanism encompassing assemblies, city councils, labour and professional organisations, and other local structures.

title: Demo in London says Öcalan’s freedom is fundamental condition for peace
content:
The international conspiracy launched on 9 October 1998 against Kurdish People’s Leader Abdullah Öcalan was protested with a march held in London on its 28th anniversary.




Kurds from Kurdistan and their supporters gathered in front of Wood Green Library for the demonstration, organized under the leadership of the London Communities Union. Flags bearing photographs of Öcalan were carried, while banners and placards calling for the implementation of the right to hope and the securing of Öcalan’s physical freedom were displayed.







 








Speakers at the gathering emphasized that the international conspiracy launched on October 9, 1998, targeted not only Öcalan but also the Kurdish people’s struggle for freedom and their democratic will. The speakers pointed out that, despite the 28 years that have passed, Önder Apo’s freedom has still not been secured. They stated that the Kurdish people have not abandoned their demands for freedom and a democratic solution.




Highlighting the historical significance of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, the speakers stressed that, for the process to lead to a lasting solution, Öcalan must be granted the conditions necessary to work freely, communicate, and engage in negotiations.




The demonstration once again called for the implementation of the right to hope and the securing of Öcalan’s physical freedom, emphasizing his role in achieving a democratic and peaceful resolution of the Kurdish question.




Following the speeches, the crowd began marching toward the Haringey Kurdish Community Centre. Throughout the march, participants carried flags bearing photographs of Önder Apo and banners calling for freedom. They chanted slogans, applauded, and performed zılgıt, traditional celebratory ululations, to protest the international conspiracy.




Songs composed in honor of Öcalan were played during the march, and demonstrators distributed hundreds of leaflets along the route.




An attempt at a racist provocation occurred during the Haringey section of the march. After Kurdish young people reacted to the provocation, a brief tension arose between the police and demonstrators. The march resumed following the incident. The demonstration, during which demands for Öcalan’s physical freedom and the implementation of the right to hope were reiterated, concluded in front of the Haringey Democratic Kurdish Community Centre.

title: Special and psychological warfare propaganda targeting the process
content:
The dialogue and negotiation process surrounding the Peace and Democratic Society Process, which has been progressing over the past two years at what could be described as a painfully slow pace, has reached a critical juncture. The process appears to be experiencing turbulence, while the deepening climate of uncertainty is weakening public confidence.




Devlet Bahçeli's election-related remarks at the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) parliamentary group meeting appear to indicate that a policy is being pursued to extend the process into the election period. As developments unfold in this way, the slow pace or prolongation of the process creates more opportunities for groups seeking to interfere with it. It also provides fertile ground for the complaints of those opposed to the process and the hostile rhetoric of pro-government media.




Alongside attacks on Peoples’ Leader Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement by fascist, nationalist and profiteering groups opposed to the process, the disinformation and aggressive rhetoric spread by pro-government media align with the forces seeking war rather than peace. Their primary objective is to create a sense of resignation and despair among the public and democratic forces.




Throughout world history, major propaganda campaigns have shaken societies, drawing on particular sources and methods.




The political establishment is pursuing its policies by emulating Hitler's propaganda minister, Joseph Goebbels, and adopting his methods. The special warfare media aligned with the government also operate along the lines of National Socialism, following the statement attributed to Hitler's propagandist: “Give me a media without a conscience, and I will organise the whole of society and turn it into an instrument.”




It is important to recognise that the attacks carried out by pro-government media and online trolls, as well as local nationalist and collaborationist groups, within a particular ideological framework are not solely the work of the government itself. The emergence of systematic attacks at this stage appears linked to the shrinking room for manoeuvre of powerful figures behind the war and profiteering lobbies. The outbursts of these groups amount to little more than demands for the continuation of war to preserve the interests of big capital and a system built on profiteering. They therefore conduct most of their attacks through digital platforms and television, seeking to legitimise them through war propaganda.




On one side stands the free press, which represents the language of truth and seeks to reveal the democratic character of social reality. On the other stands the pro-government media network, which represents dominant and ruling powers and seeks to influence society through widespread propaganda, aiming to achieve more lasting and deeply rooted results through psychological warfare. An ideological and political struggle is taking place between these two sides: those who profit from war and those who insist on advocating peace.




The Turkish state has repeatedly introduced censorship and bans to prevent people from following the free press, which reports on the basis of facts. Over the past two weeks, hundreds of social media accounts, including those belonging to free press outlets and related organisations, have either been blocked or shut down on the grounds that they allegedly “threaten national security.”




Institutionalised racism, sexism and corruption are deepening in Turkey. Rather than confronting groups that have lost their moral values and profiteering lobbies, the government and political establishment are targeting free press outlets that practise peace journalism and seek to build public engagement with the process.




To understand what pro-government media are doing today and why psychological propaganda is being used so extensively as part of special warfare, we need to examine what propaganda and agitation actually mean.




As is widely known, propaganda and agitation activities have become increasingly important today. These activities naturally bring to mind the work of the press and broadcasting organisations. Such efforts are primarily carried out within a specific programme and aim to spread a particular idea. The purpose is not simply to talk. The real objective is to put a particular idea into practice through conscious and systematic efforts. We can therefore say that society's emotions, consciousness, perceptions and psychology are being shaped through the media.




To influence people's lives psychologically and intellectually, propaganda first appeals to their emotions and consciousness. A statement attributed to Karl Popper, one of the thinkers of the 21st century, is often used in this context: “Ninety percent of people act according to their emotions, while ten percent act according to their consciousness.” This illustrates how appealing to the psychology and emotions of individuals and societies gives propaganda and agitation an important role in reshaping social life.




Propaganda is developed in connection with an ideology and directed towards a specific objective. The requirements of that ideology and the demands of society are taken into account when determining the objective. In periods of peace and political resolution, legal propaganda and organisations come to the fore, while illegal propaganda and organisations may become more prominent in times of war and conflict.




Agitation, meanwhile, is a method used to increase the impact of propaganda, strengthen it and achieve practical results. It may not extend over as broad an area or as long a period as propaganda. Instead, it primarily aims to influence the masses within a short time and mobilise them in the pursuit of democratic rights and collective action. The methods employed by those carrying out agitation are planned and deliberate.




Today, special warfare and psychological warfare media, seeking to exploit the powerful influence of propaganda more extensively, are pursuing an editorial policy aimed at shaping public opinion by distorting developments on Imrali.




The Turkish state does not want the image it has constructed over decades of Peoples’ Leader Abdullah Öcalan and the Kurdish Freedom Movement to be dismantled. For this reason, it prevents the Peoples’ Leader’s voice from reaching society.




To maintain the impact of the psychological propaganda war waged against Peoples’ Leader Abdullah Öcalan, it obstructs requests by journalists, television broadcasters, academics and representatives of other media outlets to meet with him.




The special warfare media aligned with the political establishment are therefore conducting a highly systematic, calculated, extensive and intensive psychological propaganda war.




It is well known that the state has repeatedly responded with war to the efforts of Peoples’ Leader Abdullah Öcalan since 1993 to achieve a political solution to the Kurdish question and establish peace. For this reason, the state and government continue to prevent Peoples’ Leader Abdullah Öcalan from addressing all the peoples, communities and individuals living in Turkey. This makes it clear that the state and government are deploying their special and psychological warfare apparatuses, giving online trolls and groups opposed to the process virtually unlimited room to operate.




What, then, should the Free Press do in the face of all this propaganda and these attacks?




The Free Press has a tradition stretching back many years. It has remained resilient despite numerous hardships and has established itself as a powerful force against all forms of pressure and attack. This strength comes from its ideological clarity, while it continues to preserve the powerful tradition and legacy it represents.




To conduct effective propaganda against the many forms of systematic attack seen today, weaknesses must be identified and addressed. Developing more effective journalism and broadcasting requires a clear understanding of the relationship between propaganda and social organisation. If the power of propaganda weakens, society becomes vulnerable to manipulation by others.




The economic, social and cultural problems arising from the political establishment’s failures of governance and the crises it faces are being further aggravated by pro-government media propaganda that distorts perceptions and distances society from the truth. At this stage, it is therefore essential for the Free Press to assume a constructive role and regard work concerning women, young people and ecology as a primary responsibility in countering the ruling establishment’s efforts to manipulate society.




There is a need for constructive journalism that informs, educates and organises society across a broad range of activities, from news reporting to shaping public awareness. The Free Press must clearly recognise the methods employed in the special and psychological propaganda war that pro-government media are waging against society.




Moreover, involving broad sections of society in the Peace and Democratic Society Process and encouraging them to take ownership of it are among the important responsibilities of the Free Press and peace journalism. As the responsibility to build public engagement with the process continues to grow, the Free Press, through its commitment to peace journalism, has taken on this task. It is therefore also necessary to remain vigilant against attacks by fascist, nationalist and anti-process groups.




Opposition to the continuation of the Peace and Democratic Society Process is particularly evident across digital media platforms. War and profiteering lobbies appear to be behind this opposition. These groups are known to seek to drag the Kurdish and Turkish peoples back into war and conflict. Attacks on the women's struggle, ecology and existence itself are also continuing.




The mentality that Peoples’ Leader Abdullah Öcalan describes as the “caste-like murderous mentality” has become systematised, fragmenting society and nature. It also functions as a force that deepens social decay, causes environmental disasters, gives rise to various forms of disease and fuels attacks on women's existence. These attacks are profoundly ideological and political in nature.




These developments must be considered as a whole, and the ideological struggle against propaganda, rooted in the Free Press's tradition of resistance, must continue to counter and defeat these attacks.

title: Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan: Society should stand by artists, and artists should stand by society
content:
ANF spoke with artist Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan, one of the signatories of the “1,001 Signatures for a Democratic Republic and Peace” campaign announced on 12 September, about the role of art and artists in the Peace and Democratic Society Process.




We met with Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan at her exhibition titled “Îhtîmaleke Asîman / A Sky of Possibility,” which opened on 22 September. She is the daughter of a family that migrated from Eruh to Istanbul in 1993 during the forced evacuation of villages. The artist, who was held at Bakırköy Women’s Closed Prison from 2017 to 2024, describes the works featured in the exhibition as follows: “In my works, I have depicted my own ten-year journey. This period encompasses three stages of my life: one before prison, another during my time in prison, and the final stage, which is the transition to freedom.”




Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan, who says she works across multiple disciplines, focuses on subjects such as memory, space, freedom, human rights, and ecology in her art.




“Artists must keep the process and its memory alive”




After her release from prison, one of the most important concepts she began to question was freedom. We started our conversation with Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan in front of her work titled “Laş / Body.” In this piece, in which she uses a wall as a metaphor, Dîlan Cûdî portrays the resistance of a body that dissolves into the wall while simultaneously scraping away at it.




Explaining why she felt compelled to sign the “1,001 Signatures for a Democratic Republic and Peace” campaign, Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan said: “Unfortunately, there have been periods when peace was not discussed enough in Turkey. Given that such significant steps are being taken, I considered that I, too, have responsibilities to fulfill. That is why I needed to become a signatory at this point.”




“Artists must be closely connected to the people”




Saruhan added: “I believe artists have a duty to keep this process and its memory alive, document it, expand the space for freedom of expression, and bring out art’s capacity for satire and irony. Softening the harsh atmosphere that currently exists is also among these responsibilities. That is why we artists have a great deal of responsibility.”




She continued: “We are talking about a society in which peace and freedom are discussed and freedom of expression is not restricted. At the same time, I believe the Peace and Democratic Society Process is creating an environment that supports art, opens up space for it, and strives to bring it further into the foreground,” said Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan, adding that art plays a role in advancing society, preserving its memory, and connecting it with its culture.




Emphasizing that artists must remain closely connected to the people and society, Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan said, “And while maintaining that connection, they must find a language that allows them to talk about everything. They must be able to create such a language and open up a channel. I believe that once they open up that channel, they can connect with society and with people, enter every sphere of life, and foster mutual understanding.”




Once again reminding artists of their responsibilities, Dîlan Cûdî Saruhan called on everyone to take responsibility, making the following appeal: “At a time when we need peace more than ever, unfortunately, artists may not occupy a particularly loved or valued place in society, but we are still among those who can transform it. We have roles to play and responsibilities to fulfill.




We are at a point where society must stand by artists, and artists must stand by society. And we are talking about peace at such a time. Talking about peace is a serious matter and truly requires a courageous approach. At this point, I call on everyone to take responsibility.”

title: MHP Deputy Chairman expects results in the peace process by the end of November
content:
As part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process, MHP (Nationalist Movement Party) Deputy Chairman Feti Yıldız expects concrete results by the end of November. Following this, legal procedures are expected to be initiated for prisoners incarcerated for so-called terrorism-related offenses. According to Yıldız, around 2,800 people could benefit from the legal provisions. However, founding members of the PKK are expected to be excluded.




Yıldız spoke to Sabah columnist Yavuz Donat about the next stages of the peace process. AKP Deputy Chairman Hüseyin Yayman also took part in the talk. Both politicians are members of the parliamentary Commission for National Solidarity, Fraternity and Democracy and were among the representatives who met with Kurdish leader Abdullah Öcalan on the prison island of İmralı on behalf of parliament.




“No one can say they are not involved”




Yayman described the peace process as a matter that concerns both the state and society and must be advanced with restraint. “Such things are not achieved through talking, but through silence,” he said. At the same time, he pointed to the government’s existing “red lines.” According to Yayman, a public opinion poll conducted in September showed 73.4 percent support for the process. He described the framework law, adopted by the Turkish parliament with 467 votes, as a safeguard for the next stages of the process.




“After the 467 votes in favor in parliament, no one can say anymore, ‘I am not involved in this matter, in this process.’ It is the responsibility of all of us to resolve this issue and look to the future,” Yayman said. The AKP politician also emphasized that the talks held over the past two years and the contacts with Öcalan had not undermined Turkey’s territorial integrity. He said one of the most important achievements was that families were no longer receiving news of further deaths in the war.




Yıldız reaffirms constitutional limits




Feti Yıldız interpreted the broad parliamentary support for the framework law as an expression of the political will to resolve the conflict. At the same time, he made it clear that the first four articles of the Turkish Constitution, which establish, among other things, the form of government and fundamental principles of the state, are unalterable and cannot even be proposed for amendment. The MHP politician referred to the work of the parliamentary commission, which had listened to numerous social groups over the course of 21 sessions. These included families of fallen soldiers, disabled war veterans, civil society organizations, the so-called Diyarbakır Mothers, the Saturday Mothers, business representatives, and academics.




Regarding the next steps, Yıldız stated: “Results will be achieved by the end of November. After that, legal proceedings will begin for those imprisoned for ‘terrorism-related offenses.’ Around 2,800 people will benefit from the law.” However, he said, the proposed provisions would not apply to members of the PKK’s founding cadre dating back to 1984 or to approximately 230 senior leaders. Yıldız did not provide further details on how the measures would be implemented.

title: Mohamed: Attacks in Heseke an attempt to undermine Kurdish-Arab coexistence and regional stability
content:
Ruksen Mohamed, spokesperson for the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), spoke about the dangers posed by the recent attacks in the city of Heseke. She considered the targeting of women’s symbolism and the denigration of their struggle and sacrifices to be attempts to undermine stability and incite discord among the components of Syrian society, particularly Kurds and Arabs.




Ruksen Mohamed stressed that women have demonstrated their ability to bring about positive change through their struggle and their political, social, organisational, and military participation. She noted that the experience of women in Rojava has established their fundamental role in building a society characterised by peace and stability and respect for diversity.




She also explained that attacks on women’s values, existence, and will reflect a mindset seeking to weaken society and dismantle the bonds between peoples. She emphasised that these practices are not coincidental, but rather part of a plan carrying messages that threaten social cohesion, security, and stability.




The YPJ spokesperson further stressed that targeting Kurdish women, their sacrifices, and their standing threatens coexistence among the peoples of the region and opens the door to further tensions and division.




Ruksen Mohamed affirmed that recognising women’s existence, identity, and will is an essential condition for any serious path towards democratic change in Syria. She called for respect for the rights of all components of society and for ensuring their political and social participation, free from exclusion and discrimination. She also called for those responsible for the attacks and acts of sabotage to be held accountable, stressing that they must not escape legal accountability. She urged the adoption of serious measures to protect civil peace and prevent the incitement of discord.




She concluded by affirming that women’s struggle will continue and that their sacrifices and struggle entitle them to defend their identity, rights, and position, protect their achievements, and work towards strengthening security, stability, and coexistence within Syrian society.

title: Future Syria Party demands justice seven years after the murder of Hevrîn Xelef
content:
On the seventh anniversary of the murder of Kurdish politician Hevrîn Xelef, the Future Syria Party (Arabic: Hizbul Suri Mustakbel, Kurdish: Partiya Sûriyeya Pêşerojê) called on the international community to hold those responsible for the crime accountable. In a statement marking the anniversary on October 12, the party leadership commemorated its former secretary-general, who was murdered in 2019 by members of an Ankara-backed jihadist militia during the Turkish invasion of Rojava.




Commitment to a democratic and decentralized system




Xelef, who was also known as the “Jasmine of Peace,” was killed together with her driver, Ferhad Ramadan, near Qamişlo. The Future Syria Party paid tribute to her as a symbol of the resistance of Syrian women and as a voice for peace, national unity, and opposition to policies of occupation. “Hevrîn Xelef was not only an outstanding political trailblazer but remains a role model for women’s social struggle in Syria,” the party stated.




The party remarked that Xelef’s murder did not break the political will to establish a pluralistic, democratic, and decentralized system, but instead strengthened it. “We reaffirm our goal of a political system in which the rights of all social and ethnic communities in Syria, as well as their participation in shaping their future, are guaranteed.”




At the same time, the party renewed its condemnation of the murder and called on international human rights organizations and judicial institutions to take responsibility for investigating the crime and bringing the perpetrators to justice. “On behalf of all bodies and offices of the Future Syria Party, its women and youth, we renew our pledge to the Jasmine of Syria,” the statement concluded. The party said it would continue to carry the torch of peace and follow the path of those who had fallen until freedom, justice, and equality were achieved in Syria.




Militia leader responsible integrated into the new Syrian army




Hevrîn Xelef (also spelled Havrin Khalaf) was a trained civil engineer and the first secretary-general of the Future Syria Party. On October 12, 2019, just days after the start of the Turkish invasion of Serêkaniyê (Ras al-Ain) and Girê Spî (Tal Abyad), the then 34-year-old politician was ambushed and executed on the M4 highway by members of the Turkish-backed jihadist militia Ahrar al-Sharqiya. The attackers severely abused Xelef and mutilated her body. The autopsy report documented, among other injuries, gunshot wounds, fractures to her legs, face and skull, as well as injuries to her scalp.




In addition to Xelef and her driver, seven other civilians were also killed in the attack. Human rights organizations and the United Nations classified the politician’s killing as a targeted execution. Seven years after the crime, the militia leader held responsible has still not been brought to justice. Ahmad Ihsan Fayyad al-Hayes, known by his alias “Abu Hatem Shaqra,” is now commander of the 86th Division of the Syrian army under the Islamist transitional government of Ahmed al-Sharaa.

title: YRJ commemorates journalists Dilîşan Îbiş and Dilovan Gever
content:
The Association of Women Journalists in Rojava (YRJ) commemorated journalists Dilîşan Îbiş and Dilovan Gever on the anniversary of their deaths. Both journalists were killed while reporting on the war in North and East Syria. In a statement on Monday, the organization paid tribute to their efforts to document war crimes, highlight the suffering of civilians, and convey the realities of society.




Dilîşan Îbiş documented the suffering of civilians




Dilîşan Îbiş was among the media professionals who reported directly from the scenes of events following the beginning of the Rojava Revolution on July 19, 2012. Working under dangerous conditions for the ANHA news agency, she documented developments on the ground and brought the plight of civilians to international attention.




On October 12, 2017, she was killed in an attack by the Islamic State (ISIS) terrorist group while reporting on civilians fleeing the area during the final anti-ISIS offensive in Deir ez-Zor. Other members of the independent press were also killed alongside her.




“Dilîşan Îbiş was among the women journalists who consciously chose to be at the heart of events. Her death exemplified the dangers faced by journalists documenting the truth under wartime conditions,” YRJ stated.




Dilovan Gever reported on the resistance against the Turkish offensive




The association stated that Dilovan Gever (Dilan Ölmez) also regarded her journalistic work as a social responsibility. In 2014, she crossed the Turkish border during the mobilization for Kobanê and joined the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ). Following the liberation of the city, she worked in the morgue’s archives, documenting the lives, struggles, and deaths of thousands of fallen fighters. From 2018 onward, she worked at the YPJ Press Center. As a YPJ correspondent, she took part in the final offensive against ISIS in Deir ez-Zor, among other operations, and reported from the front lines.




Following the start of the Turkish invasion of Serêkaniyê (Ras al-Ain) and Girê Spî (Tal Abyad) on October 9, 2019, Dilovan Gever reported on the war and resistance in the region. On October 13, 2019, she was killed alongside several others in a Turkish airstrike in Girê Spî.




“The memory of our comrade Dilovan Gever will live on in the history of the free press and in the collective memory of women journalists who gave their lives to bring her message to the public,” the association stated.




“The events they documented are an indelible part of our collective memory”




YRJ paid tribute to both journalists as representatives of a form of journalism committed to the truth and to amplifying the voices of women and society. “We remember Dilîşan Îbiş and Dilovan Gever with great pride and respect. The images, testimonies, and events they documented are an indelible part of the collective memory of the press,” the statement said.




“Attacks on journalists cannot silence independent reporting. Rather, the legacy of our slain colleagues carries a responsibility to continue their work. The targeted killing of journalists will not silence the voice of truth or deter the free press from its path,” the YRJ emphasized.

title: Syriac Federation condemns demolition measures in İdil
content:
The International Syriac Federation of Azech has strongly condemned the demolition measures targeting Syriac residents in the İdil district of Şırnak province.




In a written statement, the federation accused Mayor Türkan Kayır and municipal council member Ekrem Şimşek of using the municipal administration as a tool for personal vendettas. The measures reportedly targeted families who had returned to their homeland after decades of displacement.




On October 6, the municipal administration ordered the demolition of a residential and commercial building belonging to Alyet Karagöl. In addition, four other residential buildings and the newly constructed guesthouse of the Syriac Orthodox Church of St. Mary were sealed off. The municipality justified the measures by citing violations of building regulations.










https://twitter.com/gazetesabro/status/2107848754317447376










“We expected impartial municipal governance”




The federation recalled that Türkan Kayır was elected mayor on the DEM Party ticket in the 2024 local elections. “The Syriacs, Kurds, and other residents of İdil expected the elected mayor to govern impartially,” the statement said. Instead, Kayır allegedly began targeting members of the Syriac community who had criticized her policies. According to the federation, she was significantly influenced by municipal council member Ekrem Şimşek, whom the federation accused of personal enrichment and deliberate interference.




The cooperation of the persons in question with the DEM Party ended in December 2024. The party leadership expelled both Kayır and Şimşek for acting “in accordance with anti-party mindsets.” Kayır subsequently refused to resign as mayor and continued in office as an independent. Around 20 months later, she switched to the AKP. On August 14, during celebrations marking the ruling party’s 25th anniversary in Ankara, she officially joined the AKP. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan personally pinned the party badge on her.




According to the federation, Kayır was also expelled from Syriac organizations. It was only after her switch to the AKP that she reportedly began implementing the previously approved measures against Syriac families. First, the guesthouse of St. Mary’s Church was sealed off on the grounds of building regulations. On Tuesday, the building belonging to Alyet Karagöl was demolished. At the same time, the homes of Süleyman Karagöl, Ibrahim Konutgan, Şemun Gösteriş, and Filiz Tokuş were sealed off.




Accusations of double standards in building regulations




“Türkan Kayır and Ekrem Şimşek have disregarded all laws and considered any means acceptable to pursue their own interests,” the federation criticized. According to the federation, neither the will of the voters nor social relations, moral standards, or their responsibility toward the population played any role in their actions.




The federation was particularly critical of the selective enforcement of building regulations. In İdil, nearly 80 percent of buildings, including public facilities, were reportedly constructed outside the framework of regular urban planning and building inspections. According to the federation, the private house Kayır had built after her election was also constructed without a permit and is located in a protected area. Nevertheless, despite complaints filed against it, the building has not been demolished.




Furthermore, the federation has leveled bribery allegations against the mayor. It accuses Kayır of accepting contributions toward the construction of her private home from contractors who had been awarded public contracts. According to the federation, personal conflicts with relatives of Alyet Karagöl and other families were behind the measures taken against them. Kayır and Şimşek apparently believed they could now pursue their interests with the backing of the AKP.




The policy of displacement has taken different forms




The federation places these developments within the historical context of the persecution of Syriacs in Tur Abdin. It recalls the murder of Mikael Bayro in İdil and the 1915 genocide known as Sayfo. “The policy of displacement and extermination has continued in various forms from the years of Sayfo to the present day. As a result of these policies, İdil has been largely depopulated of its Syriac inhabitants,” the statement said. The federation considers it all the more painful that a mayor from the Syriac community is now targeting the few families who have returned to their homeland over the past twenty years.




“The fact that a Syriac mayor is being used as a tool against these families deeply pains us,” the federation stated. Such actions undermine the spirit of solidarity in İdil, the bonds between its people, and their determination to remain in their homeland, it added.




The federation also views the measures as an attack on the prospects of Syriacs returning to their homeland. It accuses certain actors of exploiting state institutions, religious affiliations, and social differences to pursue policies of hostility and ethnic displacement.




Appeal to Syriacs and the public




In conclusion, the federation called on the Syriac population of İdil, their friends, and the Syriac diaspora worldwide to unite in opposition to the measures. “We call in particular on the Syriacs in İdil, our friends, and all Syriacs around the world to stand against this situation, thwart these orchestrated schemes, and expose the mindset and the dirty hands behind the manipulation of Türkan Kayır,” the statement said.




At the same time, the federation urged President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the relevant authorities, political parties, and the Turkish public to take action against those forces that seek to sabotage the return of Syriacs to their ancestral homeland.

title: Talabani says PUK ready to protect Kurdistan amid regional tensions
content:
Bafel Jalal Talabani, President of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), has warned that the region is facing a precarious situation, stressing the need for greater preparedness, political agreements and cooperation to address mounting security and economic challenges.




Speaking during a panel discussion at the Middle East Research Institute (MERI) Forum 2026 in Erbil on Monday, Talabani said the global economic downturn, alongside the security and economic risks facing Iraq and the Kurdistan Region, made it essential for political forces to work towards practical solutions.




“We must all support the peace process,” he said, adding that the PUK was strengthening its historic relationships across different sectors while maintaining strong international ties and engaging with a broad range of political parties.




During the session, titled “

Building a Stronger Kurdistan: Unity, Security, and Regional Partnerships

”, Talabani discussed developments in the Kurdistan Region, Iraq and the wider region, as well as international affairs and possible ways to address current challenges.




Addressing the PUK’s international relations, Talabani said he was proud of the party’s ties with the United States, Iran, Russia, the United Kingdom and other countries.




“However, the PUK has never been, nor will it ever be, subservient to anyone,” he said. “Anyone who claims that the PUK follows the agendas or directives of other countries simply does not understand politics.”




On forming the new Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), Talabani said negotiations were progressing and that a government could be formed quickly if outstanding issues were resolved.




“We could form the government within 24 hours, but we must first resolve the existing issues,” he said.




He noted that constructive meetings had taken place in recent days, including what he described as positive discussions between Qubad Talabani and Masrour Barzani. He also confirmed that he had met Shaswar Abdulwahid, adding that the PUK remained in contact with all political parties while further discussions continued away from the media spotlight.




Regarding the possibility of renewed conflict, Talabani said the PUK had its own plans to protect the people of the Kurdistan Region.




“Should war break out again, the PUK has its own plan. We are capable of protecting our people alongside the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), given the strong coordination between us,” he said.




Commenting on the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq, PUK President said Washington could return to the country relatively quickly, pointing to the presence of US forces in neighbouring Jordan.




Turning to efforts to disarm armed groups in Iraq, he said many were willing to surrender their weapons and that Iran could help bring them under the authority of the Iraqi government.




“With Iran’s assistance, we could bring them under the umbrella of the Iraqi government, although this process requires time and trust,” he said.




Talabani added that Iran has several red lines and argued that avoiding crossing them was important to maintaining regional stability.




During his recent visit to Iran, he said, discussions had included ways to protect the Kurdistan Region in the event of renewed conflict between the United States and Iran.




The President of PUK said Iraq’s current Prime Minister was seeking to introduce fundamental changes and held no negative attitude towards the KRG.




“This is beneficial for the Kurds. Everyone in Kurdistan must understand that today’s circumstances are different from those in 2003 and 2004, when Iraq was weak and the Kurdistan Region was strong. Today, the situation is reversed: a strong and prosperous Iraq means a strong and prosperous Kurdistan,” he said.




Commenting on the agreement between the PUK and the New Generation Movement, he stressed that the understanding was genuine and could benefit the political process, including the KDP.




He said the agreement demonstrated that the largest opposition party recognised the current circumstances and was willing to contribute to forming the new government.




Talabani dismissed media reports suggesting that the PUK was misleading New Generation, describing such claims as unfounded.




“We are ready to reach any fair agreement to form the government, particularly as everyone acknowledges that the previous administration had numerous flaws and shortcomings,” he said.




The PUK President said he had visited Erbil 16 times in an effort to reach an agreement with the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), but the attempts had yet to produce a deal.




“Despite our failure to reach an agreement, we have no major political or strategic differences, and our outstanding issues are not insurmountable,” he said. “We are willing to make concessions on our own rights, but we will not compromise the rights and demands of the people of Kurdistan.” 




Addressing the economic situation and regional developments, Talabani said significant economic progress would remain difficult until the crisis surrounding the Strait of Hormuz was resolved. He added that the financial difficulties facing Iraq were part of a wider challenge affecting other countries, including those in Europe.




He said that if other political parties adopted a clear approach similar to that of the PUK, many of the Kurdistan Region’s problems could be resolved more easily. He stressed that the PUK did not engage in behind-the-scenes political manoeuvring.




“We can reach agreements with Turkey, Baghdad, Iran and the United States, yet we have been unable to reach an agreement with our brothers and sisters in the KDP. Why is that?” he said.




Talabani reaffirmed that the PUK remained committed to dialogue and was ready to reach an agreement, but warned that time was running out.




Turning to developments in Syria, he said the PUK had always been ready to respond to requests for assistance from the Kurds in Western Kurdistan (Rojava). He expressed optimism about their future but urged them to accelerate their efforts.




On relations with Turkey, Talabani said ties had improved and returned to normal, adding that both sides needed one another. He said Turkey had increasingly recognised that the issues concerning the Kurds, the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and those in the mountains could be addressed through dialogue and diplomacy.




“We will also cooperate in this process,” he said, adding that the PUK was engaged in discussions with Iran to pursue a similar approach to resolving issues affecting the Kurds there.




In his concluding remarks, PUK President Bafel Jalal Talabani delivered a direct message to the KDP, urging its leaders to resume negotiations in good faith and reach an agreement on forming the Kurdistan Regional Government.




“I have a special message for the KDP. Dear brothers and sisters, I am not speaking about partisan politics, but about several comrades within the KDP whom I consider friends, as well as others whom I regard as friends of President Mam Jalal, Hero Khan and Kak Kosrat,” he said.




Talabani stressed that the PUK neither wished nor was able to govern the Kurdistan Region without the KDP, adding that the two parties had an opportunity to reach an agreement and work together.




“Look at our relations in Baghdad, and compare them with yours. If we join forces, we can govern Iraq and transform the Middle East,” he said.




He added that the differences between the two parties were not insurmountable and called for formal talks to resume with sincerity and mutual trust.




The MERI Forum 2026 opened in Erbil on Monday, 12 October 2026, under the theme “

In Our Shared Region: Promoting Stability, Cooperation and Prosperity

”. The two-day event will address a range of pressing local and regional issues.

title: MSD remembers Hevrîn Xelef, calls for the perpetrators to be held accountable
content:
The Syrian Democratic Council (MSD) released a statement marking the seventh anniversary of the assassination of Kurdish politician Hevrîn Xelef (Hevrin Khalaf), Secretary General of the Future Syria Party and member of the Syrian Democratic Council’s Presidential Council. Xelef was extrajudicially executed on October 12, 2019, by Turkish-backed Syrian armed groups during the military offensive targeting Serekaniye (Ras al-Ayn) and Gire Spi (Tal Abyad).




MSD said that Xelef’s targeted killing remains a stark reminder of the systematic abuses committed against civilian political leaders during that campaign, stating: “Hevrîn Xelef championed political engagement as the key to uniting Syria’s diverse ethnic and religious communities and advocated for women’s full participation in public life. Her work was driven by a commitment to inclusive dialogue, mutual respect, and minority rights. She dedicated her career to building a democratic, pluralistic Syria where all citizens have a voice in shaping their nation’s future.”




The Syrian Democratic Council emphasized that Xelef’s political legacy is more relevant today than ever: “Achieving long-term stability requires establishing a democratic, decentralized state grounded in equal citizenship, political pluralism, protected civil rights, and women’s leadership. A stable Syria cannot be built on power monopolies or political exclusion; it demands genuine power-sharing and institutional respect for human rights.”




The MSD stressed the urgent need to establish the truth regarding the assassination of Hevrîn Xelef, hold the perpetrators accountable, and bring them to fair trials to ensure an end to impunity. It also underscored that all individuals responsible for crimes and violations across Syria—including those committed by figures of the former regime—must be held accountable based on the specific facts of each case.




“Achieving justice, providing redress for victims, and guaranteeing their right to the truth are essential pillars for upholding the rule of law. Together, these steps are necessary to build a democratic state that respects human dignity and prevents future abuses,” the Syrian Democratic Council underlined.

title: Father of journalist Ahmet Polad: My son is not receiving medical treatment in prison
content:
Kurdish journalist Ahmet Polad (real name Mehmet Nizam Aslan) is not receiving adequate medical care at Marmara Prison in Silivri, in Istanbul, despite serious health problems. His father, Adil Aslan, who visited him on October 6, told Mezopotamya Agency (MA) about his son’s untreated injuries and the consequences of eight months in captivity under the Islamist group HTS in Syria. The journalist was handed over to Turkey’s National Intelligence Organization (MİT) in early September and subsequently imprisoned in Istanbul’s Metris Prison.




Months of uncertainty about his fate




Adil Aslan described the desperate search for his son, who had been abducted while working as a journalist in Syria. For a long time, the family did not know whether he was still alive. The first clues came from former prisoners. One eyewitness reported the abduction of Polad and his German colleague Eva Maria Michelmann. On April 11, a released prisoner confirmed having seen the journalist in detention. At the same time, the family learned that he had been injured. “For days, I did not know whether my son was still alive. The fact that former prisoners came forward as eyewitnesses gave us at least a little hope. I never gave up searching for him,” Adil Aslan said.




By late April, evidence increasingly suggested that Polad was being held captive by HTS. The family hired a lawyer in Damascus and issued a power of attorney through the Syrian consulate in Istanbul. According to his father, however, the documents were confiscated. HTS subsequently once again denied holding Polad captive. “We began to fear more and more that Mehmet had been killed. Those were extremely difficult days. His mother and I could not sleep at night.”




Handover to Turkish intelligence




On September 8, the family finally learned that Aslan had been taken to Idlib with his hands tied and his eyes blindfolded, where he was handed over to the Turkish National Intelligence Organization (MİT). “My son was forced to remain in MİT custody for two days with a sack over his head. After that, he was taken to the police in Ankara,” his father reported.




On September 11, Adil Aslan received a phone call from the Istanbul police. He was informed that his son was being held by the counterterrorism unit. Initially, he was denied permission to visit him. The journalist is now being held at Marmara Prison in Silivri, which is regarded as a detention facility for political opponents. As a confidentiality order has been imposed on his investigation file, the family still does not know the specific charges against him.




“Journalism is never a crime”




“Mehmet was detained in a place where he was conducting research for his reporting. When he was abducted, he had nothing with him except his camera,” Adil Aslan explained. He said that only civilians had been held in the cells and that nothing was known about their subsequent fate. The father condemned HTS violence against the people of Syria, referring in particular to the massacres of Alawites and Druze. “Two years ago, these people were still considered terrorists, and now they have supposedly formed a government. They oppress and massacre people.”




The father stated that his son had been subjected to physical and psychological torture during his eight months in captivity. “These are all crimes against humanity. We do not accept this. No one should accept it. Everyone must speak out. Journalism is never a crime,” he stated.




Polad forced to treat his own wounds




During his visit on October 6, Adil Aslan observed that his son’s health had continued to deteriorate. However, Polad was trying to downplay his condition to avoid worrying his family. “He says he is fine so that we won’t worry. But he still has shrapnel embedded in his hip. He went on a hunger and thirst strike for months, and his health is not good. He also suffers from scabies. He has not been taken to a hospital for treatment for any of these conditions.”




The journalist also has to care for his wounds himself. “When I asked him about his injuries, he told me that he changes the dressings himself. As a result, his wounds keep becoming infected.”




Finally, Adil Aslan appealed to the public and human rights organizations to stand up for the prisoners: “I call on all humanity to put an end to this oppression. There are many people in the same situation as us.”

title: Iran launches drone attack on Azadî Camp in Koye
content:
Iran has once again carried out a drone attack on the Azadî Camp in the Koye district of the province of Hewlêr (Erbil) in southern Kurdistan (northern Iraq). It is not yet known whether anyone was injured or killed or what damage was caused.




The camp is home to members of the Democratic Party of Iranian Kurdistan (KDP-I) and their families. Since the beginning of the war between Iran, the United States, and Israel, the camp has been targeted dozens of times by drone and missile attacks.




Other Rojhilat parties and their facilities in southern Kurdistan have also repeatedly been targeted by Iranian drone and missile strikes. Bases and camps belonging to the Komala factions and Sazmanî Xebat have been particularly affected.

title: Le tournant de la guerre
content:
Aucune des sept précédentes expéditions militaires ordonnées par Poutine et débutées par la seconde guerre de Tchétchénie n'avait été officiellement déclarée et nommée comme telle.

 [

1

]

 Or, dans une interview accordée au journaliste Pavel Zarubin le 5 juillet 2026, le porte-parole du Kremlin Dmitri Peskov a dit que la Russie était désormais entrée en guerre contre l'Ukraine « à cause du soutien des Occidentaux »

 [

2

]

.




Cette dénégation des faits

 [

3

]

 se transforme en une inversion accusatoire comme les soviétiques en ont acquis la maîtrise depuis très longtemps. Mais ce qu'il faut entendre par là, c'est que le Kremlin est en guerre contre ce qu'il appelle « l'Occident collectif ». Où l'on constate une fois encore que ce n'est pas nous qui décidons qui est notre ennemi, c'est lui qui nous désigne, comme le dirait Julien Freund. Et de fait, il nous désigne de manière de plus en plus fréquente, systémique et violente : cette guerre est en train de prendre un autre tour, aussi bien en Ukraine qu'en Europe.




Depuis cet été 2026, une très nette inflexion de l'agression russe vers une guerre totale vise délibérément, massivement et quotidiennement la population civile ukrainienne, en même temps qu'il se produit une indéniable extension des interventions de tous types sur le sol européen et son internationalisation croissante : entre trente et quarante mille Nord-Coréens s'entraînent sur le sol de la fédération russe quand autant travaillent dans ses usines de drones

 [

4

]

. Sans parler des aides iraniennes et chinoises en tous genres.







 

 




 

Rassemblement en mémoire des disparus et prisonniers de guerre, Ukraine, août 2026.


 




I – EN UKRAINE, MOSCOU MÈNE DÉSORMAIS UNE GUERRE TOTALE

 [

5

]




 

Des têtes de missiles à l'uranium appauvri

 




Le 20 mai 2026, les services ukrainiens ont trouvé près du village de Kamka, à 50 km au nord-est de Tchernihiv, une tête de missile durcie à l'uranium appauvri en détectant des niveaux de radiation élevés

 [

6

]

 sur l'épave d'un missile R-60 lancé lors de l'attaque de cette région le 7 avril précédent. Par la suite, en juillet, au moins six autres cas similaires ont été documentés dans la même région

 [

7

]

. Rappelons que cela fait suite à l'utilisation du phosphore blanc, de bombes thermobariques, d'obus à sous-munitions et de mines anti-personnelles, soit des armes interdites ou dont l'usage est réglementé par des traités et conventions internationales.







 

 










 

 




 

Le SBU a neutralisé l'ogive et l'a transportée vers un site de stockage de déchets radioactifs. 

Ukrinform

, 23 juillet 2026 et Julie Bernichan, 

Le Parisien

, 25 juillet 2026.


 







« Compte tenu de la toxicité et de la radioactivité de l'uranium appauvri, nous exhortons les citoyens à la plus grande prudence s'ils découvrent des fragments de drones, de missiles ou d'autres munitions ; ceux qui sont endommagés ou brûlés présentent un grand danger, car ils peuvent émettre des poussières radioactives dangereuses pour la santé et l'environnement. Si vous découvrez de tels objets, ne les approchez pas, ne les touchez pas et ne les déplacez pas. Il est nécessaire de se mettre à une distance de sécurité et de le signaler immédiatement en appelant les lignes d'assistance »

 [

8

]

.







 

 




 

Kiev bombardée, le 15 mai 2026.


 










 

Missiles et drones visent les civils et leurs infrastructures

 


Depuis le début de l'agression à grande échelle, les bombardements russes ont prioritairement visé les infrastructures civiles ou les immeubles d'habitation

 [

9

]

. Plus de 3 000 services de santé ont été atteints, si bien « qu'avec le temps, ces impacts cumulés érodent la santé des populations, creusent les inégalités et compromettent les perspectives de récupération bien au-delà des zones de front »

 [

10

]

. Plus de 4 400 établissements d'enseignement ont été touchés ou détruits, ce qui entraîne certaines municipalités à inventer des écoles en sous-sol de manière à ce que les enfants ne restent pas isolés à la maison

 [

11

]

. À la fin du mois de juillet 2026, 545 sites culturels avaient été endommagés selon l'UNESCO

 [

12

]

 et près de 13 millions de livres ont été détruits depuis le début de l'été 2026

 [

13

]

. L'Ukraine a d'autre part répertorié 211 000 crimes de guerre en quatre ans

 [

14

]

. Le système de transport a lui aussi été impacté : durant les huit premiers mois de 2026, au moins 1 500 attaques ont été perpétrées contre les chemins de fer ukrainiens et plus de 250 locomotives ont été détruites.




En avril 2026, il y avait eu une inflexion de la guerre globalement favorable aux Ukrainiens : les attaques de drones à longue portée touchaient les infrastructures militaires, pétro-gazières et économiques

 [

15

]

 ; les offensives russes sur le front étaient en grande partie défaites ; les Ukrainiens mettaient hors jeu plus de soldats que ce que Poutine était capable de mobiliser et ils regagnaient un peu de terrain ; les routes d'approvisionnement et les centres logistiques russes dans le Sud, étaient rendus quasi inopérants. Mais depuis le mois de juillet les bombardements russes avec des missiles balistiques et des drones à réaction, notamment sur la capitale, ont fait d'énormes dégâts matériels et humains

 [

16

]

. Durant ce seul mois, 467 civils ont été tués et 4 600 blessés. Sauf à ce que l'hiver prochain soit bien plus clément que celui de l'an dernier, les mois qui viennent s'annoncent comme les plus difficiles depuis le 24 février 2022, le pays étant en manque d'intercepteurs 

ad hoc

, de notoriété publique. À ce propos, il était étonnant de trouver nombre d'informations militaires sensibles en source ouverte à ce sujet, mais il semble que les autorités ukrainiennes en aient pris conscience ces dernières semaines.







 

 




 

30 morts et 22 blessés à un arrêt de bus délibérément bombardé. Kramatorsk le 8 octobre 2026.


 







 

La situation est critique à Kherson et Kyiv depuis le 27 août

 




Les forces russes ont attaqué la centrale de cogénération de Kherson. L'installation a subi de très graves dommages et le responsable militaire de l'oblast a exhorté les habitants à évacuer la ville. Selon lui, Kherson pourrait rester sans électricité ni chauffage pendant une période prolongée. Depuis le 1

er

 juillet, les forces russes ont lancé plus de 1 700 drones d'attaque en utilisant plus fréquemment les engins à réaction et 170 bombes aériennes guidées ont été larguées sur les infrastructures critiques de l'oblast de Kherson, soit plus en deux mois que pendant toute la première moitié de 2026. En outre, le nombre d'attaques par de petits drones FPV (notamment utilisés dans les tristement célèbres « safaris humains ») est passé à 6 500 en une seule semaine

 [

17

]

.




Alors qu'auparavant les frappes massives et combinées se concentraient principalement durant la nuit et qu'elles étaient espacées de huit à dix jours, la capitale ukrainienne fait désormais face à un pilonnage 24 heures sur 24, depuis le 27 août 2026

 [

18

]

. Lors d'une semaine de cette campagne de bombardement continu, la ville a enregistré un record historique de 76 alertes, du jamais vu depuis les tous premiers jours de l'invasion en 2022. Les sirènes de la ville retentissaient en moyenne 10 fois par jour et jusqu'à 13 fois par période de 24 heures. Les habitants passaient régulièrement plus de 15 à 17 heures par jour confinés dans les abris ou le métro

 [

19

]

.




Le 4 septembre 2026, un drone russe a précisément frappé la fenêtre du bureau du chef du SBU (qui était absent) dans un immeuble du centre de Kiyv, ce qui est nouveau et suppose un « agent répéteur » à moins de 5 kilomètres de là.




 

Le pays fait face à des difficultés de tous ordres

 




Surtout lorsqu'elle a été longue et s'est accompagnée de violences meurtrières massives, la colonisation d'un pays laisse des traces pérennes dans tous les domaines, y compris politiques évidemment, longtemps après qu'elle a été officiellement abolie

 [

20

]

. Mais, pour la deuxième fois en un an, des manifestations publiques ont eu lieu en Ukraine à l'été 2026, en réaction à une décision du gouvernement du 15 juillet. Et pour la deuxième fois, celui-ci a dû céder à la pression populaire quelques jours après ses débuts, en remplaçant le chef d'état-major Oleksandr Syrski – représentant de la vieille école militaire soviétique (encore un legs du colonialisme) – par Mykhaïlo Drapaty.




Il est utile de répéter à ce propos que, parmi les pays de l'ex-empire soviétique, c'est en Ukraine qu'il s'est produit le plus d'alternances gouvernementales et de révoltes populaires victorieuses depuis 1991. Par ailleurs, nous ne connaissons pas, dans l'histoire contemporaine, d'exemple comparable de manifestations d'opposition massives en temps de guerre, la population encourant à ce moment-là le risque d'être bombardée.




Également démis le 15 juillet, Mykhaïlo Fedorov, le jeune ministre de la Défense n'a pas été réintégré. Mais qui est-il ? Il est né en 1991, avait fondé en 2013, sa propre agence numérique spécialisée dans le marketing en ligne et la publicité ciblée sur les réseaux sociaux. En 2014, il s'est présenté sans succès aux élections législatives sous l'étiquette d'un parti libéral. Cinq ans plus tard, il dirigeait l'équipe numérique de la campagne présidentielle de Zelensky, puis est devenu ministre de la Transformation numérique. Il était donc dans le gouvernement depuis sept ans lorsqu'il a été remercié. Jusqu'au 17 août au soir, il était loisible de manifester pour la réintégration de Fedorov dans le gouvernement. Mais dans son allocution du mardi 18 août 2026, Fedorov a défendu l'idée – après Poutine et Trump – d'organiser des élections en temps de guerre

 [

21

]

, une grave erreur politique, suivie de plusieurs autres. À ce sujet, examinons un cas historique exemplaire en Europe.







 

 




 

32

e

 jour de manifestation, Ukraine, août 2026.


 







 

Pendant dix ans, il n'y a eu aucune élection dans ce pays

 


On l'oublie trop souvent, notamment en France : le seul et unique pays européen qui a résisté en tant que nation et qui a gagné la guerre contre le nazisme, c'est le Royaume-Uni. Tous les autres, y compris ceux qui ont joué de leur neutralité (Suisse et Suède), ont collaboré avec le III

e

 Reich à divers titres. Même une ancienne directrice de l'ENA avouait sincèrement l'avoir compris tardivement et de manière fortuite

 [

22

]

. Il serait donc mal venu – et en aucune manière légitime, on le verra – de reprocher aux Britanniques de ne pas avoir tenu d'élections de 1935 à 1945. Précisons que la législature élue le 26 novembre 1935 aurait dû se terminer en novembre 1940, mais que l'entrée en guerre de septembre 1939 avait rendu l'organisation d'un scrutin national inopportune : des millions de citoyens étaient mobilisés dans les armées, dans l'économie de guerre ou déplacés par les bombardements. Les inscriptions sur les listes électorales, l'accès aux urnes de millions de personnes aurait été très difficile et risqué. De plus, la tenue de ces élections aurait nécessité une infrastructure logistique et administrative, du personnel formé et des lieux de vote qui devaient être sécurisés. On imagine quels efforts supplémentaires cela aurait demandé à la population qui subissait les terribles bombardements de la Luftwaffe

 [

23

]

. Tout cela rendait impossible la garantie d'un vote démocratique, sûr et régulier.




Plus généralement, toutes les limites à la liberté des médias, au débat politique, à la participation des citoyens, compromettent l'intégrité d'un scrutin. C'est pourquoi dans de nombreux pays, des cadres juridiques divers interdisent explicitement la tenue d'élections durant un état d'urgence d'origine naturelle (séismes, pandémies…) ou humaine (guerres et conflits de tous types). Ainsi, le Covid-19, a entraîné le report des élections dans plus de 80 pays.







 

 




 

Chaque jour des centaines de repas déshydratés partent pour le front. Cuisine internationale des volontaires, Ukraine, août 2026.


 







 

Les autres erreurs de Mykhaïlo Fedorov

 


Commençons par dire que nous lui faisons crédit de sa volonté de lutter contre la corruption par la passation de marchés réguliers et de sa volonté de réformer les contrats de service armé. C'est important. Mais d'une part, aucune initiative ou plan militaire ne devrait être mis en place par le ministère de la Défense indépendamment de l'état-major des armées (point 3 de son bilan)

 [

24

]

. D'autre part, il est dangereux de répandre l'idée que la guerre serait essentiellement une question technique car elle est avant tout politique. Cela a toujours été et le restera, nous ne tarderons pas à le savoir. Par ailleurs, Fedorov a dit dans une interview à l'agence Reuters le 25 août que son pays pouvait perdre la guerre cet hiver. Quels que soient les arguments avancés, ces propos ne peuvent en aucun cas être tenus par quelqu'un qui a des responsabilités dans la défense de son pays. À l'évidence les problèmes sont nombreux mais mieux vaut œuvrer à les résoudre que d'en faire une dénonciation politicienne. Enfin, il a accepté un contrat avec le ministère de la Défense italien, c'est-à-dire avec un gouvernement d'extrême droite

 [

25

]

.




II – LES ATTAQUES RUSSES EN EUROPE OCCIDENTALE




 

Des pays de l'UE sont régulièrement survolés par des avions russes

 




Des avions russes effectuent des vols au-dessus de la mer Baltique ou du couloir terrestre de Suwałki

 [

26

]

 (c'est-à-dire qu'ils survolent l'espace aérien polonais ou lituanien) sans plan de vol, transpondeurs éteints et sans contact radio. Ces comportements déclenchent des missions d'interception d'urgence qui se comptent par centaines chaque année. Par exemple, pour la seule journée du 2 juin 2026, des Rafale français ont dû intercepter six chasseurs, bombardiers ou avions de reconnaissance russes qui s'approchaient de la zone balte

 [

27

]

. Mais il n'existe pas de chiffre qui rende compte des survols de l'ensemble de l'espace aérien européen par des avions russes depuis le 24 février 2022. Il y en aurait eu au moins neuf en Finlande, cinq en Suède et des dizaines d'appareils russes espions IL-20 auraient été interceptés en Estonie. Mais une chose est certaine : même après plusieurs minutes de survol sans autorisation, aucun n'a été abattu alors qu'en 2015 la Turquie (membre de l'Otan) avait détruit un Sukhoï 24 qui avait survolé son territoire pendant 17 secondes, sans que cela prête à conséquence. Ainsi, depuis le début de cette guerre, l'armée russe teste les temps de réaction des pays occidentaux, enregistre les fréquences des radars et maintient une pression militaire et politique constante sur les populations visées. Elle ne manquera pas de main-d'œuvre pour cartographier tous les sites sensibles en UE : 170 000 Russes y résident de manière régulière, sans parler des agents d'occasion ou jetables et de groupes sympathisants qui s'empressent de l'aider.







 

 




 

Partie Est du mur des victimes de la guerre russe, devant le monastère St Michel à Kiev.


 







 

Les missiles russes s'affranchissent des frontières européennes.

 


En Pologne, à plusieurs reprises

 [

28

]

, des missiles de croisière russes ont pénétré l'espace aérien polonais avant de s'y écraser ou de faire demi-tour, sagement suivis par les radars du pays.




L'Ukraine a plusieurs fois rapporté le survol de son territoire à revers par des missiles russes provenant de l'espace aérien roumain

 [

29

]

, notamment en février 2023, bien que Bucarest n'ait pas confirmé ces trajectoires, du moins jusqu'en 2026. 

A contrario

, la Moldavie a constaté et dénoncé à plusieurs reprises le survol de missiles russes traversant son espace aérien lors de frappes contre les infrastructures ukrainiennes.




Selon les bases de données compilées par des centres de recherche et des analystes de défense, on recensait environ 4 à 6 survols de l'espace aérien européen par an entre 2022 et 2024. Une accélération très nette a été constatée par la suite, avec une multiplication des intrusions, recensées par dizaines depuis 2025

 [

30

]

.







 

 Il y a toujours plus de drones russes dans le ciel de l'UE.

 




En 2025, la Roumanie a enregistré un grand nombre de survols et de chutes de drones russes qui attaquaient à revers les infrastructures des ports ukrainiens sur le Danube. En septembre 2025, des F-16 ont suivi un drone russe durant cinquante minutes au-dessus de l'espace aérien roumain, avant qu'il ne le laisse repartir vers sa cible ukrainienne.
