author: B Camminga
title: We are not a novelty
content:
Trans and gender-diverse people are routinely told that what they are is new — a sudden emergence, a recent contagion. In South Africa, this claim circulates with increasing force: In the 

surge of Christian fundamentalist organizing against trans rights

, in the transphobic slurs directed at a trans contestant on 

Big Brother Mzansi

 earlier this year, and in the pronouncements of 

prominent political figures

 who have characterized transgender rights as a form of 

“woke” ideology

. The implication is always the same: that we are a novelty. And novelties do not deserve the weight of rights.

The historical record tells a different story.

In 1815, a young British military surgeon arrived at the Cape Colony. 

James Barry

 was cantankerous, flamboyant, and conspicuously short. During his time at the Cape, he performed what is believed to be the first cesarean section in southern Africa in which both mother and child survived. The child was named after him: James Barry Munnik, who would grow up to become the grandfather of J. B. M. Hertzog — founder of the National Party in 1914 and one of the principal architects of apartheid.

J. B. M. was also the namesake of the hertzoggie, the apricot-jam-filled tartlet. When he reneged on promises, the Cape Malay community responded with the 

twee gevreetjie

: a coconut-topped protest cookie whose name means, in Afrikaans, “two-faced” or “hypocrite.” On the eve of his death, Barry made one request: that no clothing be removed and that he be buried as is. The request was not honored. It was discovered that Barry was what we might now understand as a man of trans experience. His legacy is deeply ambivalent — he was a colonizer, an agent of empire. But his presence in the historical record asks us to complicate our timelines.

In 

1966, Joan Kruger, Edna Hobles, and Sonia Kola

 were arrested under legislation known as the Disguises Acts — a set of pre-Union laws dating back to 1891 that criminalized “masquerading as women.” The three were well known enough to have been featured in 

Drum

 magazine that same year. Joan and Edna were eventually released. Sonia was charged. The distinction was this: Joan and Edna had no prior arrests. Sonia did. And she would not stop wearing dresses. 

S v. Kola

 (1966) became the case that set the precedent for what would later be amalgamated into the Prohibition of Disguises Act (1969).

Access to alternatives was starkly racialized. Gender-affirming surgery had been available to white people in South Africa since at least the early 1950s, and by 1974 the state had become directly involved — funding reassignment surgery under the belief that it constituted a cure for homosexuality. For Sonia, as a South African of color convicted in 1966, none of that access was available. She had her dresses.

What the case produced was a legal trace that ran forward through decades of jurisprudence — cited by Edwin Cameron in arguments that extended constitutional protection of sexual orientation, and by Justice Laurie Ackermann in the majority judgment that gave that protection a broad reading. A case about a woman who would not stop wearing dresses became part of the constitutional fabric of the new South Africa.

In 1992, Michelle Emmerich — a trans woman, an ANC member, and a civil servant — faxed a proposed 

Gender Rights Article

 to the 

Convention for a Democratic South Africa (CODESA)

, hoping it would be included in the Bill of Rights. No one responded. She was told she was too emotional and should tone it down. In her own words: “I for one sticks out like a sore thumb. I have decided to call it a day. Just imagine, being the only [transgender] human rights activist in the ANC.” And so she quit, leaving almost no trail. That unanswered fax, now archived at 

Constitution Hill in Johannesburg

, is a marker in the record, evidence that the argument for an expansive understanding of gender was already being made in 1992, long before it found a hearing.

Before any formal trans organization in South Africa, there was a small group known as 

the Phoenix Society

 — founded in the 1980s and composed of white transvestites, crossdressers, transsexuals, and those who called themselves “transgenderists.” They communicated through veiled messages in magazines and their own publication, 

FanFare

. A short documentary about the group was made for the South African Broadcasting Corporation program 

50/50

 — and never aired. Some members believe this was the result of an intervention by the apartheid security police.

The Phoenix’s membership is largely lost to history. But one name has survived: 

Charl Marais

, who in his own words was “the only female to male person that they knew of and also, in that day and age, I was the only Coloured there.” Charl would go on to become a pioneering writer and editor of 

Trans: Transgender Life Stories from South Africa

 — one of the first works to put trans South African lives on the record, in their own words.

These are not the famous names. They are not the landmark cases. They are not even necessarily people with uncomplicated politics. But here is what their stories show: trans and gender-diverse people in South Africa have not merely survived its history — they have shaped it. The claim that trans identity is new is not only historically inaccurate; it erases a history of people doing the quiet, stubborn, necessary work of existing, and who, in doing so, shaped something larger than themselves.

author: Barbara Rodriguez
title: Measles in Pregnancy Care Is a Novel Concern for Many US Doctors Amid Outbreak
content:
Soaring cases expose the vulnerabilities of pregnancy and postpartum care in an era of lowering vaccination rates.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

A deadly measles outbreak in Pennsylvania, which has infected more than 975 people this year and been linked to five deaths, has also infected at least 50 pregnant women in the state. Doctors in outbreak areas are making changes to how they care for pregnant patients and their babies, offering a glimpse of what may be in store across the nation as cases spread.

Among the deaths were two infants in Lancaster County, an area about 60 miles west of Philadelphia and the epicenter of the Pennsylvania outbreak. A newborn had congenital measles, which was passed in utero through an unvaccinated mother who was infected. It is not clear whether the other infant, who was reportedly 6 weeks old at the time of death and had a genetic birth disorder, was exposed in utero or after birth.

Some Pennsylvania-based doctors have experienced an uptick in anxious questions from patients about the implications of measles on just about all aspects of pregnancy care: What do more cases mean for a current pregnancy? Are additional precautions needed for someone planning to get pregnant soon? How concerned should parents with a newborn be about public outings?

It all depends, doctors in Pennsylvania and nationally told The 19th, on preventative care measures taken prior to pregnancy and a person’s proximity to an outbreak. What is certain is that new cases of congenital measles and increasing exposure risks are putting a spotlight on the vulnerabilities of pregnancy and postpartum care in America in an era of lowering vaccination rates.

“Air doesn’t know that there’s a border between Pennsylvania and Ohio, or that there’s a border between New Jersey and New York,” said Dr. Sharee Livingston, an OBGYN in Lancaster County. “We are dealing with a respiratory illness, and even if we weren’t dealing with a respiratory illness, none of us live in a vacuum.”

Livingston never came across a single case of measles during her medical training in the mid-2000s, and neither did many of her peers.

But in the past six months, Livingston estimates that she has treated at least a dozen patients infected with the highly contagious disease. Livingston did not share more information about the patients, including whether they were all women or if any were pregnant.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) told The 19th that, as of Friday, a total of 977 measles cases had been reported in 2026, and 53 of those were among pregnant women. As of early October state health officials have reported nearly 40 percent of Pennsylvania’s cases were coming from Lancaster County. The five measles-associated deaths — the infants, a 40-year-old woman, an 18-year-old and a 20-year-old with leukemia — were the first in the state in 35 years.

“Measles wasn’t a conversation we were having before, but it is now,” said Dr. Kisha Davis, president-elect of the American Academy of Family Physicians.

DOH told The 19th it could not confirm any estimate of the number of congenital measles cases in the state or provide more details about the infected pregnant women, citing state privacy laws. The department said there is no nationally standardized definition for congenital measles and that it is working with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to develop a system for tracking and reporting cases. They have been tracking cases during pregnancy and in “very young children” and said that since Oct. 2, more than 100 measles cases in the state have been in children under the age of 4. NBC News reported that at least six newborns in the state have been infected with measles during the outbreak, citing a Pennsylvania doctor.

There have been more than 3,800 confirmed measles cases in the United States this year, the highest number in decades. Roughly 95 percent of the infections are among unvaccinated people or individuals whose vaccination status is unknown. It is unclear how many of those people were pregnant or postpartum at the time of infection. But Dr. Kevin Ault, an OBGYN who recently started working at Penn State Health in Hershey — about 30 miles northwest of Lancaster County — noted that more than a quarter of cases were in adults of childbearing age.

“At any given time, about 1 percent of Americans are pregnant. So there’s an intersection there of unvaccinated adults and pregnant people that are going to be in this scenario,” said Ault, who is a fellow with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and serves in the organization’s expert group on infectious diseases and immunization.

Doctors do not recommend that pregnant patients get the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine because it carries a live virus, making immunization prior to pregnancy critical. Vaccinated pregnant people pass antibodies to their infants and have an immune system that is better positioned to keep a future fetus and baby safe from measles or to reduce complications in the rare event of a breakthrough infection.

Livingston has been trying to reassure vaccinated patients who may still worry about infections, reminding them of these robust protections. But, she noted, “if the pregnant person believes that they’ve had an exposure and they’re unvaccinated, that’s where it becomes a problem. Because then there’s a risk to both the fetus and the mother.”

An infection in an unvaccinated person during pregnancy has a host of complications including pregnancy loss, premature delivery and low birth weight. New guidelines on congenital measles released last month by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) warn of a 25 to 30 percent rate of infection if measles is passed through the birth parent within days of a birth. The guidelines had been in the works for some time but carried more urgency after the infant fatalities in Pennsylvania, said Dr. Pia Pannaraj, a member of the AAP’s Committee on Infectious Diseases and a professor of pediatrics at the University of California, San Diego.

“Many doctors that are practicing right now might never have seen measles in their lifetime, so they know it from the textbooks, but that’s not the same as having a patient,” she said. “So we’re having to educate providers: ‘How do you recognize measles? This is what the rash looks like.’”

The AAP guidelines break down different scenarios for monitoring congenital and newborn measles infections. In some cases, babies without overt symptoms of measles birthed by an infected parent can be given a post-exposure antibody known as immune globulin — but it may not help if infection has already occurred. Treatment in general for infected babies is limited and includes monitoring possible complications, like a fever or pneumonia.

“There’s only basically what we call supportive care,” Pannaraj said. “So we treat the symptoms as they arrive as best we can, but there’s no way to basically kill the measles virus, and there’s no way to prevent the complications that will occur.”

Infected babies can be at higher risk for encephalitis, a type of brain swelling, as well as a rare but fatal brain inflammation that can appear later in life.

“Mom takes the hit of getting the disease, but the infants are at the highest risk for measles complications of anybody that could get measles,” Pannaraj added, noting that babies’ immune systems are incredibly underdeveloped.

Dr. Holly Cummings, an OBGYN in Philadelphia and the chair of Pennsylvania’s section of ACOG, said she’s increasingly ordering bloodwork to check the measles immunity of patients who are thinking about getting pregnant.

This hasn’t always been Cummings’ approach. She already assesses her patients’ immunity for other viruses but relied on the general understanding that most people have received the MMR series, which is 97 percent effective at preventing measles. Several doctors told The 19th that they’ve worked under an assumption that children growing up in the 1990s and onward went through public schools that mandated the MMR vaccine. Those mandates are still in place, but exemption laws have been expanded since then.

ACOG, which has guidelines on measles that it developed more than a decade ago, recommends that doctors assess a patient’s immunity with either proof of vaccination or through bloodwork. For patients born in the ‘90s, electronic medical records of their childhood vaccinations may also be more readily available to doctors.

A measles immunity check before pregnancy may become a necessity in the future, but it will depend on circumstances like community spread and declining vaccination rates, Davis said.

“The vast majority of folks are still vaccinated — the fact that we are having to have that conversation again feels a little disconcerting,” she said.

These clinical considerations will carry more weight as more adults choose not to vaccinate their families, and as their children reach childbearing age. Vaccination rates for routine vaccines continue to decline among kindergartners, according to new CDC data. In Pennsylvania, more than half of counties have an MMR vaccination rate below 95 percent, the threshold for herd immunity. That includes Philadelphia County and some groups of children in Lancaster County.

While some of the most impacted areas in the state are far from Philadelphia, Cummings doesn’t want to make assumptions about her patients’ vaccine status. In September, public health officials reported a measles exposure at several locations within the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia complex, including a NICU lounge.

“In the context of this current measles outbreak — and particularly for me right now given that there’s such a high number of cases in Pennsylvania — it does feel important for me to bring it up and ensure that my patients are protected,” she said.

There are implications for future care beyond the frequency of immunity testing. Doctors may reexamine how they advise parents about early MMR vaccination for their babies.

Infants as young as six months old can be approved for an early MMR shot if they will be in an area with potential measles exposure. This option, Pannaraj said, used to be reserved for infants traveling internationally to high-risk exposure areas. But doctors are increasingly recommending an early shot if a child is living in or traveling domestically to an outbreak region. An early shot doesn’t negate the need for two shots later, which have been timed for maximum effectiveness.

“Is there going to be a time where we need to think about earlier vaccination?” she said. “Now, I hope that’s not the case, because currently the outbreaks are still limited within the United States. We’re all working hard to make sure it stays that way and to try to get rid of the outbreak.”

Emphasizing the importance of vaccination has been complicated in recent years. The politicization of pandemic-era mitigation policies gave rise to a new wave of online misinformation about the safety and efficacy of vaccines, including the MMR vaccine.

Disinformation over the disputed link between the MMR vaccine and autism flourished in the late ‘90s, but vaccine disinformation has a more powerful megaphone now through the federal government. Both President Donald Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have spread false information about routine childhood vaccines. In August, Trump claimed without evidence that the MMR shot can be “quite lethal.” And while Kennedy’s department has occasionally promoted the MMR vaccine, he falsely said last year that the shot causes annual deaths. In 2021, Kennedy gave a speech in Lancaster County where he downplayed the threat of measles.

His record shapes public perception: New polling shows 40 percent of adults are unsure whether or not Kennedy recommends the MMR vaccine, and another 29 percent think he does not recommend it. Kennedy oversees the CDC, which has not recognized all five deaths reported in Pennsylvania. The department says on its measles dashboard that it is working to standardize a definition for measles deaths.

“These are not new efforts. What is new today is the fact that there’s been a corporatization of the anti-vaccine movement,” Chelsea Clinton, vice chair of the Clinton Foundation and assistant professor at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health, told The 19th. “There are deep profit motives frequently fueling many of the loudest voices. I think some have deeply painful personal experiences and extrapolated out of those without scientific evidence or data and yet really believe they’re trying to save other families.”

Still, public health officials in Pennsylvania are seeing a response to the outbreak. In August, health providers reported administering more than 46,000 doses of the MMR vaccine — a massive jump from the roughly 25,000 doses they recorded monthly during the first half of the year.

Doctors say a person who is thinking about getting pregnant should get the MMR vaccine or check their immunity through bloodwork prior to conception. Someone who is pregnant and not vaccinated should consult with health providers about any special precautions to take to avoid an infection.

“We should be talking to women and to anyone whose partner may be thinking about being pregnant so that being caught up on your vaccines is just part of what someone is thinking about while also maybe trying to stop smoking, and drink more water, and eat healthier and all the other things that people often say they’re trying to optimize for their health before getting pregnant,” Clinton said.

Livingston credits state and federal public health officials for being responsive to the outbreak in her county, but she sees opportunities for more equitable care that helps people walk into pregnancy the healthiest version of themselves — which in turn can help to mitigate future adverse outcomes.

For now, Livingston is leaning on evidence-based best practices. She believes recent lessons from the pandemic around immunization will ultimately help her community move forward.

“I don’t mean to sound really flowery or overly positive, but I am hopeful,” she said. “I believe that most people want to be healthy during their pregnancies. They care tremendously about their unborn child, and so I think when people understand that that’s our angle, it makes it a little bit easier to have the conversation and maybe adopt best practices.”

Additional reporting by Isabela Espadas Barros Leal.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

title: Kulüpler Birliği’nden yayın ihalesi açıklaması: Teknik kriterler belirlendi
content:
Kulüpler Birliği Vakfı Başkanı Ertuğrul Doğan, Süper Lig yayın hakları ihalesine ilişkin hazırlıkların sürdüğünü belirterek yeni yayın sözleşmesinde yer alacak yayın standartları ve teknik kriterlerin belirlendiğini açıkladı.

Kulüpler Birliği Vakfı Başkanı Ertuğrul Doğan imzasıyla yapılan açıklamada, Süper Lig’in yayın hakları ihalesine yönelik çalışmaların titizlikle yürütüldüğü bildirildi.

Açıklamada, Süper Lig’in ekonomik değerini artırmak amacıyla uluslararası alanda uzman bir danışmanlık firmasıyla kapsamlı bir değer analizi çalışması yapıldığı belirtildi.

Yayın ve görüntü kalitesinin artırılması amacıyla çekim kriterleri, kamera özellikleri ve teknik şartların Avrupa liglerindeki uygulamalar esas alınarak değerlendirildiği aktarılan açıklamada, Türkiye’deki uzmanlarla işbirliği yapıldığı kaydedildi.

Açıklamada, çalışmalar sonucunda yeni yayın sözleşmesinde yer alması gereken yayın standartları ve teknik kriterlerin belirlendiği ifade edildi.

Yayın ihalesine ilişkin diğer hazırlıkların kulüpler ve ilgili paydaşlarla koordinasyon içinde sürdüğü belirtilen açıklamada, ihalenin öngörülen takvim doğrultusunda sonuçlandırılması hedefi vurgulandı.

Kulüpler Birliği Vakfı, Süper Lig yayın hakları ihalesinin Türk futbolunun ve kulüplerin çıkarlarına en uygun koşullarda başarıyla sonuçlandırılması için çalışmaların devam ettiğini bildirdi.

author: Ruhi Bhasin
title: How Gen Z Protests Are Reshaping Politics in Asia
content:
Asia has seen a surge of “Gen Z protests,” led by a generation tired of accepting the status quo and increasingly using social media to drive change in deeply entrenched political systems. In India, protests over the education system helped force the education minister’s resignation in 2026. Protests in Bangladesh and Nepal in 2024 and 2025, respectively, led to government changes. These protests have helped expose fractured political structures in these countries.

Governments in several South and Southeast Asian countries have done little to address the economic distress and corruption plaguing them. The Gen Z citizens, who are facing the brunt of these crumbling systems, are increasingly demanding accountability and justice, using social media to fight back, organize, document events, and press their demands. Despite efforts to suppress them, these protests have brought political change. Whether these movements can sustain solidarity and organize beyond immediate demands to pursue lasting reforms remains to be seen.

In India, the Bharatiya Janata Party-led government has been in power for more than 12 years, having first been elected in 2014. Press freedom and other democratic safeguards have come under pressure during its tenure; Sweden’s V-Dem Institute has classified India as an “electoral autocracy.” As stated by an August 2026 Time report, “Modi has consolidated his grip on all manner of national institutions in recent years: from the media, where pliant owners have repeatedly bent the knee to the administration, to election authorities, which in a recent state poll erased millions of names from voter rolls in a move widely seen as benefiting Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).”

India has been facing increasing unemployment among its educated youth, even though the government has consistently maintained these claims to be false. The country’s youth have also been contending with an education system marked by repeated paper leaks. In May 2026, the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test for undergraduate medical admissions was canceled over paper-leak allegations, fueling anger over the examination system.

Meanwhile, during the same month, the Supreme Court Chief Justice’s comparison of unemployed youth to “parasites” and “cockroaches” led to the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) by Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student from Boston University who graduated in 2025 with a master’s in public relations. The CJP’s Instagram account amassed 20 million followers within days, according to Time. Dipke eventually returned to India on June 6. Anger over the government’s mismanagement of the education system soon moved from social media to the streets as thousands of Gen Z showed up at Jantar Mantar, a popular protest site in India’s capital, New Delhi, with their main demand being the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

As the protest gained momentum and spread, authorities resorted to force against demonstrators. Young protesters used social media to document events on the ground and responded with “humor and grit.” For them, the protest wasn’t about any political party but rather about ensuring accountability for a broken education system. They finally succeeded in forcing Pradhan to resign on July 25, 2026.

“In the end, the young cockroaches proved so resilient because Modi’s regime of control had no punishment or humiliation to threaten them with beyond what the system already inflicts on them every day. These young men and women had reached a point where they felt they had no voice in the existing order—and nothing left to lose,” explains the Time report. Allegations of links to foreign funding were also made against the movement, but the Ministry of External Affairs said it had “no information” to confirm these allegations.

In July 2026, after the protest ended, the government introduced a bill to amend the public examinations law, and Modi announced an examination reform task force. Whether these actions succeed in reforming the education system and whether the CJP can keep pushing for their proper implementation remains to be seen.

The CJP announced another campaign in September 2026 demanding chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over alleged manipulation of voter rolls. Street protests followed in October, with opposition parties and civil society groups participating. The Election Commission denies the allegations. These protests will test the CJP’s ability to sustain pressure and the authorities’ response to demands for electoral reform.

The CJP has already split internally, resulting in the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party—Democratic.

In September 2025, Gen Z protests erupted in Nepal after the government banned social media platforms that had not met its registration requirements, according to a Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health article. Gen Z saw this move to ban social media as an attempt to trample their freedom of expression, while the politicians were hoping to use their traditional tactics to also stop hashtags like #NepoKids or #YouthAgainstCorruption targeted against their children and the privileged life they led, in sharp contrast to the hardships being faced by ordinary youths daily. The government further shut down the internet, thinking that would muzzle the protests. However, they drastically underestimated the youth’s power and frustration.

While the ban triggered the protests, several larger unresolved issues had been simmering for years, including unemployment, corruption, and nepotism, which strengthened the agitation. “In a country where 56 percent of the population is below the age of thirty, a geriatric leadership whose average age was seventy was woefully out of touch. In the last decade, internet connectivity had rapidly expanded to cover more than half the population. Young Nepalis were online—on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit, Discord—but offline, they saw none of the better future promised by the 2006 revolution against the monarchy. Instead, they saw widening inequality and corruption, and on their social media feeds, they saw the children of elites flaunting their privilege,” writes author Amish Raj Mulmi for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

The protesters demanded Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli’s resignation. He finally heeded their demands on September 9, 2025.

Since democracy was restored in Nepal in 1990, the country has seen political churn, having witnessed “twenty-seven prime ministers, each averaging barely a year in office,” according to Mulmi. The government collapsed after the protests, leading to an interim government, with elections eventually taking place in March 2026. Balendra Shah’s Rastriya Swatantra Party won the election, and Shah became the prime minister.

While the Gen Z movement has succeeded in changing the political system, the government’s inexperience is a critical roadblock as it tries to fix a dysfunctional system. It remains to be seen whether it can use the popular mandate to ensure stability. Deadly floods in August 2026 gave Shah’s government an early test of its ability to respond to a national crisis. “While early moves such as arresting former leaders and launching an ambitious reform agenda signal change, the government faces risks of internal fragmentation, personality-driven politics and bureaucratic resistance. Its success will depend on delivering economic opportunities, maintaining public trust, and translating its populist momentum into stable, rules-based governance,” writes Anil Sigdel, a lecturer at the University of Vienna, Austria, in a May 2026 article.

The Gen Z revolts in Nepal reflect the dilemma faced by 21st-century democracy, according to the journal Society. “On the one hand, it exposes the exhaustion of a political order sustained by elite capture, corruption, and exclusion. On the other, it demonstrates the enduring vitality of democratic ideals, the capacity of ordinary citizens, and especially the young, to demand accountability, dignity, and change. The uprising of 2025 was not only a fleeting eruption of anger; it was also a generational awakening with decades of unfulfilled promises.” Mulmi argues that earlier generations in Nepal toppled governments without leading to lasting change. Whether the Gen Z movement will result in such reforms remains unclear.

Bangladesh saw an uprising primarily led by student protesters in 2024, which was also called the July Uprising. The initial protests followed the court’s reinstatement of the quota system. “The protests began in early July as peaceful demands from university students to abolish quotas in civil service jobs—a third of these are reserved for relatives of veterans from Bangladesh’s war for independence from Pakistan in 1971,” according to the BBC. But the protests soon grew into a broader anti-government movement over unemployment and corruption, turning violent amid police crackdowns and clashes between demonstrators and student groups supporting Sheikh Hasina’s government. This was followed by curfews, shutting down the internet, and mass arrests.

Eventually, the government had to cave in, and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina resigned and fled to India on August 5, 2024, after ruling the country for 15 years. The “weeks of bloody protests and brutal action by government forces killed nearly 1,400 people and wounded more than 20,000, according to the country’s International Criminal Tribunal (ICT),” stated Al Jazeera.

The protests also prompted allegations of involvement by the United States, China, and Pakistan. BBC Monitoring documented these claims and the responses to them without establishing foreign involvement. In a commentary published by New Eastern Outlook, Brian Berletic argued that the uprising reflected a US-backed effort at regime change.

Meanwhile, an interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus took power in Bangladesh after the protests. In October 2025, Yunus’s interim government introduced the nonbinding July National Charter that several major parties signed; Hasina’s banned Awami League was excluded from the process. The signing of the charter was met with protests as agitators “wanted the document to include more provisions for the activists who helped oust the previous government,” according to PBS.

While the Yunus-led interim government received support initially, “the enthusiasm and aspiration for transformative change appears to have faded. Instead, the country now faces uncertainty, political fragmentation and instability,” states the Institute of South Asian Studies, adding that the initial uprising “laid bare the flaws of the existing political and socio-economic order by casting them in moral terms and promoting a collective stake in democracy. Through their expression of dissent, protesters sought to demonstrate that democracy is not a singular or monolithic entity confined to those in power.”

Eventually, Tarique Rahman was sworn in as Bangladesh’s new prime minister in February 2026. He is already facing pressure to implement the promised changes as people took to the streets in September 2026 amid rising living costs and energy prices. Whether his government can deliver economic reforms remains an open question.

Can the Gen Z Protests Lead to Long-Term Changes?

In Nepal, the protests paved the way for new political actors to lead the country; in Bangladesh, the long-established Bangladesh Nationalist Party came to power, showing how similar protests can have different political outcomes. Political scientist Arijit Mazumdar contrasts how the two countries’ electoral systems absorbed the protests: “In Bangladesh, elections continued to exist, but confidence in electoral competition had weakened and established parties retained overwhelming organizational advantages. In Nepal, despite significant political instability and extra-constitutional developments, elections remained the broadly accepted mechanism through which political conflict was ultimately resolved. These differences shaped whether protest energy produced rupture without substantial electoral renewal or was absorbed into party competition.”

Youth-led protests have also taken place in Indonesia and Madagascar, as well as in other parts of Africa. These protests have showcased the courage and determination of young people. Whether their demands lead to lasting change also depends on political organization and the institutions that carry out reforms. “[G]overning a state requires skills that no revolution alone can teach. … At the same time, examples like Thailand and Sri Lanka demonstrate that youth-led political transformation is not impossible. What distinguishes relatively successful cases is not merely public enthusiasm but organizational continuity. Political movements gradually evolved into structured parties, built alliances with civil society and engaged existing institutions rather than relying exclusively on street mobilization. Sustainable reform required more than revolutionary legitimacy,” writes H.M. Nazmul Alam for Scroll.

The youth protests in Sri Lanka in 2022, known as the Aragalaya (struggle), resulted from a major political and economic crisis. The protests helped force Sri Lankan President Gotabaya Rajapaksa’s resignation in July 2022; the National People’s Power (NPP), led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, formed a government in 2024. Under his rule, some positive economic changes have taken place, but promises of a “system change” take time and vision.

Social media has helped young protesters bypass traditional media gatekeepers, amplify their grievances, and build solidarity. But visibility and a change of leaders do not, on their own, remake political institutions. The different outcomes in India, Nepal, and Bangladesh show why the real test of these movements extends beyond the protests. As the article in the journal Society points out, “[without] institutional pathways to translate protests into policy, such uprisings risk being co-opted by populist leaders or dissipating into chaos.”

Ruhi Bhasin is a senior journalist and features editor with the Independent Media Institute. She previously worked for The Times of India and The Indian Express, where she covered politics, law, and social issues.

author: anred
title: Histórico: Buenos Aires será la sede del 40° Encuentro Plurinacional en 2027
content:
Tras cuatro décadas de recorrido federal y de manera ininterrumpida, el máximo evento de los feminismos y las disidencias regresa al territorio donde nació en 1986. La elección se realizó mediante el tradicional «aplausómetro» durante el cierre de la edición número 39 en Córdoba. 

Por ANRed

 







CÓRDOBA — En una jornada cargada de mística, debate y organización colectiva, la Comisión Organizadora del 39° Encuentro Plurinacional de Mujeres, Lesbianas, Travestis, Trans, Bisexuales, Intersexuales y No Binaries anunció que la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires albergará la próxima edición del evento en 2027. La decisión se tomó a través del histórico sistema de «aplausómetro», el mecanismo asambleario y masivo con el que este espacio federal define democráticamente sus destinos año tras año. Tras la elección de la sede, se procedió a la lectura de las conclusiones de los más de 100 talleres que funcionaron durante el fin de semana.




Este regreso a las callee porteñas tiene una profunda carga simbólica y política. La última vez que el Encuentro se realizó en Buenos Aires fue en su edición fundacional de 1986. En aquel momento, apenas unas 600 mujeres provenientes de diferentes provincias y de diversas comunidades de pueblos originarios se congregaron para sembrar la semilla de una experiencia asamblearia y colectiva que terminaría transformando por completo la historia de los feminismos en la Argentina.




Cuarenta años después de aquella primera convocatoria, el espacio se ha masificado, transformado y complejizado. Con la única y lógica excepción del parate obligado por la pandemia de COVID-19, los Encuentros se sostuvieron de forma ininterrumpida durante cuatro décadas. Su persistencia en el tiempo consolida un formato único en el mundo: un espacio completamente autónomo de los gobiernos y los partidos, federal, plural, autofinanciado y autoconvocado que sirve como usina de organización, debate y posterior lucha en las calles.




De cara al próximo año, el desafío se traslada al centro político del país. En un contexto que demanda la articulación constante frente a las violencias y opresiones, el 40° Encuentro Plurinacional abrirá un nuevo capítulo en Buenos Aires con el objetivo de seguir reconociendo diversidades, compartiendo experiencias desde los territorios y fortaleciendo el tejido social hacia una comunidad más justa e igualitaria.




Todo en pleno año electoral, en el marco de una profunda crisis política social y cultural, en el gobierno de la Libertad Avanza. «Vamos a Buenos Aires a sacar a Milei, contra todos los fascismos. Seremos Nostres quienes les pongamos un freno a estas politicas de precarización de nuestras vidas» cerro una encuentrera.

title: Nazır Kapusuz’dan Katılımevim iddiası: 24 milyar TL kamu kaynağı mı aktarıldı?
content:
İktisatçı Nazır Kapusuz, Katılımevim hisselerinin Tera’dan Emlak Katılım’a devredildiğini öne sürerek fon soruşturması kapsamında kamu kaynaklarının kullanıldığı iddiasını gündeme getirdi. Kapusuz, güncel fiyatlarla yaklaşık 12 milyar TL değerindeki Katılımevim hisselerinin ardından Pusula’daki hisselerin de benzer şekilde devredilmesi durumunda kamu kaynaklarından toplam 24 milyar TL aktarılmış olacağını belirtti.

Nazır Kapusuz, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı paylaşımda, Emlak Katılım’ın Tera’dan 1,5 milyar adet Katılımevim (KTLEV) hissesi aldığını belirtti. Kapusuz, söz konusu hisselerin güncel fiyatlarla yaklaşık 12 milyar TL değerinde olduğunu belirtti.

Tera’nın Pusula’ya da hisse satışı yaptığını öne süren Kapusuz, Pusula’nın Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu (TMSF) yönetiminde bulunmasına dikkat çekti. Kapusuz, önümüzdeki günlerde Emlak Katılım’ın Pusula’daki hisseleri de yaklaşık 12 milyar TL karşılığında alabileceğini tahmin etti.

İki işlemin de gerçekleşmesi halinde kamu kaynaklarından fon havuzuna toplam 24 milyar TL aktarılmış olacağını savunan Kapusuz, iddia ettiği gelişmelerin ekonomi basınında yeterince yer bulmamasını eleştirdi.

Kapusuz, Katılımevim’in olağan yükümlülüklerini sürdürebilmesi için daha önce 45 milyar TL’lik kamu zararı oluştuğuna dikkat çekti. Söz konusu tutarın fonlara değil, taksit ödeyen yurttaşların yükümlülüklerine ilişkin olduğunu belirten Kapusuz, ayrıca 24 milyar TL’nin Türkiye Varlık Fonu üzerinden TMSF’ye aktarılmış olacağını ifade etti.

Kapusuz, paylaşımını “Atın artık manşeti” sözleriyle tamamladı.

Evet ilk kamu zararı ile fona destek geldi Emlak katılım 1.5 milyar adet Ktlev hissesini Tera’dan aldı. Güncel fiyatlarla yaklaşık 12 milyar TL Tera aynı şekilde Pusula’ya da satış yapmış (ki şu anda TMSF yönetiyor) tahminim 2-3 gün sonra emlak katılım o payları da 12 milyara alacak Böylelikle 24 milyar TL fon havuzuna kamu kaynaklarından para aktarılmış olacak Neden hala manşet olmadı bilmiyorum ekonomi basınında! Böylelikle Katılımevin normal yükümlülüklerini devam ettirmek için 45 milyar TL’lik kamu zararından sonra (bu fona değil taksit ödeyenler içindi) 24 milyar TL bizzat Türkiye Varlık Fonundan TMSF’ye para aktarılmış oldu. Atın artık manşeti!

author: Publicación Abierta
title: El verdadero holocausto silenciado
content:
Introducción: Un nombre negado




En 1992, cuando se cumplían quinientos años de la llegada de Colón a América, el historiador David Stannard publicó un libro que sacudió el debate académico: American Holocaust. En sus páginas sostenía que la destrucción de los pueblos indígenas del continente americano constituía “el acto de genocidio más masivo en la historia del mundo”. La cifra que manejaba era escalofriante: hasta cien millones de personas desaparecidas entre 1492 y el final del siglo XIX. La reacción no se hizo esperar. Buena parte de la academia estadounidense rechazó la comparación con el Holocausto judío, argumentando que las enfermedades habían sido la causa principal y que no existía una intención exterminadora comparable a la de los nazis.




Ilustración del siglo XVI de Theodor de Bry para la “Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias” publicado en 1552 por el fraile dominico español Bartolomé de las Casas.




Más de tres décadas después, la disputa continúa. Pero lo que está fuera de discusión es que el término “holocausto” sigue reservado, en el imaginario colectivo y en buena parte del discurso académico, para un solo evento histórico. Mientras tanto, la destrucción de las sociedades indígenas americanas —un proceso que se extendió por cinco siglos y que, en muchos aspectos, continúa en el presente— permanece en un limbo semántico. No es negada. Pero tampoco es nombrada con la radicalidad que su magnitud exige.




Este artículo sostiene una tesis incómoda: la resistencia a aplicar el término “holocausto” a la catástrofe indígena americana no es una cuestión meramente académica. Es una operación política de memoria que jerarquiza el sufrimiento, distribuye responsabilidades y, en última instancia, legitima la continuidad del despojo. Porque el verdadero holocausto silenciado no es sólo el del pasado. Es el que sigue ocurriendo cada vez que una comunidad mapuche es desalojada en la Patagonia argentina, cada vez que se deroga una ley que protegía tierras ancestrales, cada vez que un título de propiedad “trucho” pesa más que la preexistencia de un pueblo.




Ilustración del siglo XVI de Theodor de Bry para la “Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias” publicado en 1552 por el fraile dominico español Bartolomé de las Casas.




La magnitud del colapso: cifras y controversias




Cualquier discusión sobre el “holocausto indígena” tropieza de inmediato con un problema: las cifras. No hay consenso sobre cuántas personas vivían en América antes de 1492, y sin ese punto de partida, cualquier cálculo de mortalidad es especulativo. Las estimaciones varían de forma dramática. El historiador Ángel Rosenblat calculó que la población del Nuevo Mundo en 1492 era de aproximadamente 13 millones de personas, cifra que algunos elevan a veinte millones. Otras estimaciones, sin embargo, hablan de decenas de millones solo para México central, y de una población hemisférica que podría haber alcanzado los noventa o cien millones.




Esta disparidad no es un detalle menor. Si la población precolombina era de trece millones, la mortandad de cincuenta millones sería imposible. Si era de noventa millones, la desaparición de sesenta o setenta millones se vuelve plausible. La elección de una cifra u otra determina, en buena medida, la magnitud del cataclismo que se está dispuesto a reconocer.




Lo que sí está documentado es el ritmo y la profundidad del colapso en regiones específicas. En México central, la población pasó de unos veinticinco millones en 1519 a poco más de dos millones y medio en 1568. En el Perú, de nueve millones en 1532 a un millón trescientos mil en 1570. En La Española, la población taína prácticamente desapareció en menos de cincuenta años. No se trata de estimaciones abstractas: son procesos documentados por cronistas, funcionarios coloniales y registros de tributos que muestran una caída vertical de la población indígena en las primeras décadas tras el contacto.




“Conquista de México por Cortés”. El sitio de Tenochtitlan por el conquistador español Hernán Cortés, durante la conquista española de México. Autor desconocido




Las causas de esta catástrofe son múltiples y entrelazadas. Las epidemias —viruela, sarampión, tifus, gripe— fueron devastadoras, y afectaron incluso a poblaciones que no tuvieron contacto directo con los europeos. Las enfermedades viajaron por rutas comerciales indígenas mucho antes de que llegaran los conquistadores a determinadas regiones. Pero reducir el colapso a un “choque viral” es insuficiente y, en muchos casos, engañoso. Como señala el antropólogo Romain Simenel, la idea de que los indígenas eran “vulnerables” a las enfermedades europeas ha servido históricamente para construir un discurso que despolitiza la catástrofe, presentándola como un accidente biológico inevitable en lugar de como el resultado de condiciones impuestas: esclavitud, trabajos forzados, desnutrición, hacinamiento, destrucción de sistemas de salud tradicionales y prohibición de plantas medicinales.




La explotación fue, en sí misma, una máquina de muerte. El sistema de encomiendas, la mita minera, las plantaciones de azúcar en Brasil y el Caribe, el traslado forzado de poblaciones enteras: todo ello produjo una mortalidad masiva que no puede atribuirse a “gérmenes” abstractos. Los encomenderos necesitaban mano de obra, y la obtenían a un costo humano que las leyes intentaron limitar sin éxito. Cuando Carlos V promulgó las Leyes Nuevas de 1542 para abolir los servicios personales y las encomiendas, la reacción de los colonos fue tan violenta que en el Perú se produjo una guerra civil y el virrey fue asesinado. La Corona podía legislar, pero no podía contener los intereses económicos que se habían desatado.




El debate sobre el genocidio: definiciones en disputa




La discusión sobre si lo ocurrido en América constituye genocidio depende, en gran medida, de cómo se define el término. La Convención de la ONU de 1948 establece que el genocidio requiere “la intención de destruir, en todo o en parte, un grupo nacional, étnico, racial o religioso”. El elemento clave es la intención. Sin ella, los actos pueden ser crímenes de lesa humanidad, pero no genocidio en sentido jurídico estricto.




Aquí es donde el caso americano se vuelve complejo y donde las posiciones se dividen. Raphael Lemkin, el jurista que acuñó el término en 1944, incluía la colonización europea de América como un caso paradigmático de genocidio. Para Lemkin, el concepto central era “un plan coordinado de diferentes acciones dirigidas a destruir los fundamentos esenciales de la vida de los grupos nacionales”. Bajo esa definición, la destrucción de las sociedades indígenas —no solo la matanza directa, sino la destrucción de sus formas de vida, sus sistemas de creencias, sus estructuras sociales— encaja sin dificultad.




Sin embargo, la definición de la ONU, más restrictiva, ha sido utilizada para excluir el caso americano. El argumento es que la mayoría de las muertes se debió a enfermedades no intencionales, y que la intención de exterminio total —como la que existió en el Holocausto nazi— no estuvo presente de manera sistemática. Steven T. Katz, uno de los defensores más influyentes de la “singularidad” del Holocausto judío, sostiene que el término debe reservarse para “la implementación, cualquiera sea su resultado, de la intención de exterminar totalmente un grupo… definido por los propios criminales”. Bajo este criterio, ni la trata de esclavos ni la desaparición de millones de indígenas americanos califican como genocidio, porque la mayoría sucumbió a enfermedades y no a una política explícita de exterminio total.




Esclavos africanos en América. Grabado de Joseph Swain, 1835




Esta posición ha sido cuestionada desde múltiples frentes. El historiador Christophe Giudicelli señala que, incluso sin pronunciarse sobre el carácter general de la colonización, es posible detectar en cada proceso colonial operaciones que califican como genocidas según los criterios restrictivos de 1948. Las campañas de “guerra a fuego y sangre” en el Norte de México, las guerras de “pacificación” en la frontera argentina y chilena, las reducciones forzadas, la esclavitud indígena en Brasil y el Caribe: todos estos fueron actos deliberados, con intención de destruir total o parcialmente grupos humanos específicos.




El problema, entonces, no es que el caso americano no cumpla con los criterios del genocidio. El problema es que la definición dominante —construida en un contexto histórico y político muy específico— está diseñada de tal manera que hace excepcionalmente difícil aplicarla a procesos coloniales prolongados. Como señala A. Dirk Moses, la “doctrina del Holocausto único” ha funcionado como una forma de jerarquizar el sufrimiento y, en la práctica, de blanquear otros genocidios. Al reservar el término para un solo evento, se establece una escala implícita de valor humano en la que algunas víctimas merecen ser recordadas con una radicalidad que se niega a otras.




La continuidad del despojo: el caso argentino




Si algo demuestra la persistencia del holocausto silenciado es que no terminó. No es un evento del pasado remoto, confinado a los siglos coloniales. En Argentina, la lógica del despojo territorial se ha reactivado con una intensidad que no se veía desde las dictaduras militares.




Fragmento del cuadro “Conquista del desierto” de Juan Manuel Blanes




La Conquista del Desierto, entre 1879 y 1884, fue el momento fundacional del genocidio estatal argentino. El eufemismo “desierto” designaba territorios densamente poblados por los pueblos mapuche, ranquel, tehuelche y otros. La campaña militar, financiada en parte por grandes estancieros que esperaban obtener tierras a cambio, masacró a la población civil, encarceló y esclavizó a los sobrevivientes, y expulsó a miles hacia tierras estériles. Como señala el investigador Javier Serrano, en el campo académico la Conquista pasó de ser considerada una “epopeya” a ser ampliamente concebida como “asimilable al genocidio de los pueblos indígenas”, aunque en el discurso político y mediático persisten las justificaciones del viejo marco de “civilización contra barbarie”.




La Masacre de Napalpí, en 1924, fue condenada judicialmente en 2022 como un crimen de lesa humanidad cometido en el contexto de un proceso de genocidio. La sentencia del Juzgado Federal de Resistencia (Chaco) estableció que el Estado argentino fue responsable de la planificación, ejecución y encubrimiento de la matanza de entre cuatrocientas y quinientas personas de los pueblos Qom y Moqoit. Se ordenaron medidas de reparación: la designación del 19 de julio como Día Nacional de Conmemoración, la continuación de las excavaciones forenses, la incorporación del caso en el currículo educativo y el reconocimiento público de responsabilidad estatal. Es uno de los pocos casos en América Latina donde un tribunal ha pronunciado la palabra “genocidio” en relación con la violencia contra los pueblos indígenas.




Masacre de Napalpí. Mural. Foto: 

Revista Cítrica




La Patagonia Rebelde, entre 1920 y 1921, mostró la intersección entre origen étnico y clase. La mayoría de los trabajadores rurales que participaron en las huelgas de Santa Cruz eran indígenas huilliches provenientes de Chiloé, Chile. Fueron fusilados por el ejército argentino en una represión que dejó alrededor de mil quinientos muertos. Durante décadas, su origen indígena fue invisibilizado en la narrativa histórica, que los presentaba simplemente como “chilotes” o “peones”. La dimensión étnica del conflicto quedó sepultada bajo la categoría de “lucha de clases”, como si ambas cosas pudieran separarse.




Pero lo que verdaderamente revela la persistencia del holocausto es el presente. En diciembre de 2024, el gobierno de Javier Milei derogó por decreto la Ley 26.160, que declaraba la emergencia territorial indígena y suspendía los desalojos mientras se realizaran los relevamientos de tierras comunitarias. El decreto 1083/2024 dio por finalizada la emergencia y, con ello, abrió la puerta a la ejecución de sentencias de desalojo que habían estado paralizadas. En el último informe presentado al Congreso, se destacaba que, de las 1870 comunidades identificadas, aún restaban relevar 607 —un 32% del total—. Es decir, se puso fin a la protección antes de completar el trabajo que la ley misma ordenaba.




Los desalojos no tardaron en llegar. En agosto de 2026, comunidades mapuche en Neuquén, la comunidad Santa Rosa en Jujuy y la comunidad Mbya Guaraní Puente Quemado II en Misiones enfrentaron operativos policiales de desalojo. En el caso de las comunidades mapuche Kinxikew y Melo, en la Patagonia, cientos de policías —incluyendo el Grupo Especial de Operaciones— participaron en el desalojo. El lonco Lucas Melo Piñén lo expresó con crudeza: “Acá tengo a mi padre enterrado y a mi abuelo lo asesinaron aquí. Nos quieren sacar con un título trucho. Estas tierras nos pertenecen, tenemos pruebas de preexistencia y reconocimiento del Estado”.




El desalojo de la comunidad por efectivos de la policía de Misiones. Foto: Prensa EMiPA




El Instituto Nacional de Asuntos Indígenas (INAI) había reconocido en 2023 la ocupación actual, tradicional y pública de la comunidad Kinxikew, aunque no otorgó el título comunitario. El litigio fue iniciado por una familia belga de apellido Broers, que detenta un título de propiedad desde la década de 1970. Es ese título —cuestionado por la comunidad como “trucho”— el que la justicia utilizó para justificar el desalojo.




Detrás de estos conflictos hay intereses económicos concretos. La legisladora jujeña Natalia Morales lo señala sin ambigüedades: “La situación de conflictividad es permanente debido al interés geopolítico que hay en los bienes comunes naturales, como el litio o el agua. Jujuy funciona como el laboratorio de lo que Milei quiere extender a nivel nacional”. En Misiones, el desalojo de la comunidad Mbya Guaraní fue pedido por un empresario forestal. En Salta, la comunidad Lule denuncia que se pretende ceder casi nueve hectáreas a un club de rugby privado, con notificaciones para demoler viviendas que afectan a más de cincuenta familias.




A esto se suma el debate en el Congreso de una Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada, que permitiría desalojos “exprés” mediante juicio sumarísimo y restitución anticipada de inmuebles. El Centro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS) ha alertado que esta norma aceleraría las expulsiones sin resolver previamente la titulación de los territorios indígenas. Es la misma lógica de siempre: el título de propiedad privada —a menudo obtenido durante dictaduras o mediante irregularidades— pesa más que la posesión ancestral documentada.




El silencio como complicidad




¿Por qué importa el nombre? ¿Por qué insistir en llamar “holocausto” a lo que ocurrió —y ocurre— en América?




La respuesta es que el nombre determina la memoria, y la memoria determina la justicia. Cuando el Holocausto judío fue nombrado y reconocido, se convirtió en un imperativo moral universal: “Nunca más”. Se construyeron museos, se instituyeron días de conmemoración, se dictaron leyes contra el negacionismo, se establecieron reparaciones. El nombre “holocausto” no solo describe un evento: crea un mandato de memoria y una obligación de reparación.




Nada de eso ha ocurrido con la catástrofe indígena. No hay un “Nunca más” que se aplique a la Conquista del Desierto. No hay reparaciones masivas por la expropiación de tierras ancestrales. No hay un día internacional que conmemore a los cien millones de muertos. Lo que hay, en cambio, es un silencio que se reproduce en los currículos escolares, en los medios de comunicación y en el discurso político.




Ese silencio no es neutral. Es funcional. Si la destrucción de los pueblos indígenas no se nombra como holocausto, entonces los Estados que la perpetraron y que la continúan no tienen que enfrentar la misma exigencia de reparación que enfrentó Alemania después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Si las muertes se atribuyen principalmente a “enfermedades”, entonces la responsabilidad se diluye en la biología. Si la Conquista del Desierto fue una “epopeya civilizatoria”, entonces los desalojos actuales son simplemente “restitución de propiedad privada”.




Sobrevivientes mapuche de la “conquista del desierto” en un 

campo de concentración en las cercanías de Valcheta, en Río Negro. Fuente: 

Felipe Pigna, El Historiador




El filósofo e historiador A. Dirk Moses ha argumentado que la “doctrina del Holocausto único” ha servido para que las potencias occidentales —y sus herederos en América— puedan invocar el Holocausto judío para justificar sus propias violencias coloniales o imperiales. El reconocimiento del Holocausto se convierte en una credencial moral que exime de rendir cuentas por otros genocidios. Israel puede invocar el Holocausto para legitimar su tratamiento de los palestinos. Estados Unidos puede invocarlo para legitimar sus guerras. Argentina puede invocarlo —o al menos, no necesita invocarlo explícitamente— para legitimar el desalojo de comunidades mapuche.




La negación del nombre es, por lo tanto, una forma de complicidad con la continuidad del despojo. No es que no se sepa lo que ocurrió. Es que no se quiere extraer las consecuencias morales y políticas de saberlo.




Conclusión: Nombrar para no olvidar




La pregunta que queda flotando es incómoda: ¿qué se gana con llamar “holocausto” a la catástrofe indígena? La respuesta es que no se trata de ganar nada, sino de dejar de perder. De dejar de perder la memoria, la verdad y la posibilidad de justicia.




Stannard tenía razón en 1992, y sigue teniéndola hoy: la destrucción de los pueblos indígenas de América es el acto de genocidio más masivo de la historia. No es una exageración retórica. Es una descripción factual de un proceso que duró cinco siglos, que involucró a todas las potencias europeas y a los estados que las sucedieron, y que produjo una mortandad que ninguna otra catástrofe histórica ha igualado.




Pero el verdadero holocausto silenciado no es solo el de los muertos. Es el de los vivos. Es el de las comunidades que hoy, en el siglo XXI, siguen siendo desalojadas de tierras que sus abuelos habitaron antes de que existieran los estados que las expropian. Es el de los títulos “truchos” que pesan más que la preexistencia. Es el de las leyes que se derogan para facilitar las expulsiones. Es el de los gobiernos que, como el argentino, hablan de “inseguridad jurídica” para referirse a los derechos indígenas y de “legítimos dueños” para referirse a quienes obtuvieron la tierra durante dictaduras.




Nombrar ese proceso como holocausto no es un ejercicio de victimismo. Es un acto de precisión histórica. Es decir, lo que es, con el nombre que merece. Porque mientras no se nombre, seguirá ocurriendo. Y mientras siga ocurriendo, el silencio será su mejor cómplice.




La memoria no es un lujo. Es una necesidad. Y en el caso de los pueblos indígenas de América, es una necesidad urgente, porque el holocausto no ha terminado. Solamente ha cambiado de forma.




La entrada 

El verdadero holocausto silenciado

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

title: Wenn Satire Beleidigung und Not zur Würde verwandelt: Die „Cockroach Janta Party“ der jungen Faulen und Erwerbslosen in Indien scheint ununterdrückbar
content:
Dossier




„

Indiens „Kakerlaken-Partei“ begann als Scherz. Dann schlossen sich Millionen an. Der Aufstieg der Bewegung geht auf Äußerungen eines Richters am Obersten Gerichtshof zurück, der einige junge Menschen und Kritiker der Institutionen mit „Kakerlaken“ und „Parasiten“ verglich. Im Internet schließen sich Inder der „Cockroach Janata Party“ (CJP) an – einer parodistischen politischen Bewegung, die als Online-Satire begann, sich aber rasch zu einem Ventil für die Wut über Arbeitslosigkeit, Korruption und den Zustand der indischen Demokratie entwickelt hat. Die Bewegung, eine freche Anspielung auf den Namen der regierenden hindu-nationalistischen Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) des indischen Premierministers Narendra Modi, hat die sozialen Medien mit Memes, parodistischen Wahlkampfbotschaften und Witzen überschwemmt, in denen sich die Frustration der Bevölkerung widerspiegelt

…“ engl. 

Artikel von Jay Ganglani und AP vom 23. Mai 2026 auf NBC News

 

 (maschinenübersetzt) – siehe mehr Informationen, auch zur versuchten Unterdrückung:







Modi setzt 30.000 Polizisten und Angehörige paramilitärischer Einheiten gegen die Protestbewegung in Indien, die er weder lange festsetzen noch verhindern kann 







„

Modi hat den Verstand verloren. „Die Regierung hat darauf mit einer massiven Verstärkung der Sicherheitspräsenz in der Hauptstadt reagiert. Rund 30.000 Polizisten und Angehörige paramilitärischer Einheiten wurden eingesetzt, das Internet wurde unterbrochen, Zugverbindungen nach Delhi wurden gestrichen, U-Bahn-Stationen und Straßen wurden gesperrt

.“…“ 19teiliger engl. 

Thread von Albert Pinto vom 10.10.2026 auf bsky

 




Indien: Festnahmen in Delhi: Protest-Anführer freigelassen – neue Demonstrationen geplant




„

Wegen umstrittener Streichungen in Wählerverzeichnissen fordert die Kakerlaken-Bewegung (CJP) Konsequenzen. Die Polizei lässt die meisten der Festgenommenen wieder frei. Die wollen wieder auf die Straße.


Die indischen Behörden haben den Gründer sowie zwei weitere führende Vertreter der sogenannten Kakerlaken-Protestbewegung einen Tag nach ihrer Festnahme wieder freigelassen. Das zuständige Gericht ordnete am Sonntag nach Angaben der Bewegung als Auflage an, dass der Gründer Abhijeet Dipke und seine beiden Mitstreiter „ein Jahr lang nicht den Frieden brechen“ dürften. Der Polizei zufolge wurden zudem die meisten der am Samstag in Gewahrsam genommenen rund 2000 Protestteilnehmer wieder auf freien Fuß gesetzt. Die Sicherheitskräfte hatten mit einem Großaufgebot versucht, eine geplante Großkundgebung in Delhi zu unterbinden. Am Sonntag wurden weitere Demonstrationen in der Hauptstadt erwartet. (…)


Zahlreiche Protestteilnehmer seien am Kundgebungsort im Zentrum der Hauptstadt aufgegriffen und abgeführt worden, berichteten die Zeitung The Hindu und andere einheimische Medien. Auch im Finanzzentrum Mumbai, heißt es, seien rund vierhundert Demonstranten festgehalten worden. Das UN-Menschenrechtsbüro äußerte sich besorgt über die Berichte von Massenfestnahmen.


Fernsehsender berichteten, dass auch oppositionelle Abgeordnete und ehemalige Regierungschefs mehrerer Bundesstaaten festgenommen worden seien, ebenso wie kurzzeitig mehrere Journalisten. Um die Demonstranten aufzuhalten, boten die Behörden Zehntausende Sicherheitskräfte auf, errichteten Barrikaden und ließen in Teilen Delhis das mobile Internet abstellen sowie Dutzende U-Bahn-Stationen und Märkte schließen

…“ 

Agenturmeldung vom 11. Oktober 2026 in der Süddeutschen Zeitung online

 




Proteste in Indien – Gründer der «Kakerlaken»-Bewegung vorübergehend festgenommen




„

Die Protestbewegung wirft der Modi-Regierung Korruption vor. Die wichtigsten Antworten zur jüngsten Eskalation

. ..“ 

SRF-Beitrag vom 10.10.2026

 

 

 mit Video




Jugendproteste in Indien: Aktivistin Neha Bora gibt trotz Festnahmen nicht auf




„

Neha Bora ist die Vorsitzende der linken Studierendenorganisation AISA. Sie ist eine der bekanntesten Stimmen der indischen Jugendproteste.




Neha Bora lässt sich nicht aufhalten. Am Sonntag ruft die 29-Jährige erneut zum friedlichen Protest in Indiens Hauptstadt auf. Um halb drei treffe man sich an der Metrostation RK Ashram, schreibt die Doktorandin auf X: „Wir sehen uns dort. Kommt nicht zu spät.“ Bora läuft mit einer Gruppe Richtung Zentrum. „Wir haben die Barrikaden überwunden und Connaught Place erreicht“, meldet sie.




Wenig später veröffentlicht sie ein Video aus einem Bus mit vergitterten Fenstern. Sie wurde erneut gestoppt. Am Samstag hatte die Polizei Delhi mit einem massiven Aufgebot abgeriegelt. Zeitweise wurden der Internetzugang eingeschränkt und Metrostationen geschlossen. 7.000 Personen wurden festgenommen. Die Gen-Z-Bewegung rund um die Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) hatte zum Protestmarsch zum Jantar Mantar aufgerufen. Ihre Führung wurde bereits bei der Ankunft am Flughafen festgesetzt, ebenso der bekannte YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.




Neha Bora, die Vorsitzende der linken Studierendenorganisation AISA, die sich mit der CJP solidarisiert, schaffte es auf die Straße. Auch am Samstag marschierte sie, bis sie von Beamten eingekreist und in Verwahrung genommen wurde. „Ich bin in Gewahrsam. Die Bewegung ist es nicht“, meldete sie später. Sie trug ein Shirt mit einem Aufdruck des Anime „One Piece“. Der Manga tauchte bei Jugendprotesten von Nepal bis Indonesien auf.




Neha Bora, die Vorsitzende der linken Studierendenorganisation AISA, die sich mit der CJP solidarisiert, schaffte es auf die Straße. Auch am Samstag marschierte sie, bis sie von Beamten eingekreist und in Verwahrung genommen wurde. „Ich bin in Gewahrsam. Die Bewegung ist es nicht“, meldete sie später. Sie trug ein Shirt mit einem Aufdruck des Anime „One Piece“. Der Manga tauchte bei Jugendprotesten von Nepal bis Indonesien auf.




Immer neue Verhaftungen




Die Proteste setzen Premierminister Narendra Modi und seine hindunationalistische BJP-Regierung unter Druck. Im Zentrum steht die Überprüfung von Wählerlisten, kurz SIR. In den Entwurfslisten fehlten zunächst rund 130 Millionen Einträge. Oppositionelle und Ak­ti­vis­t:in­nen befürchten, dass dadurch Wahlberechtigte, insbesondere Angehörige von Minderheiten, von Wahlrecht ausgeschlossen werden könnten. Sie werfen der Wahlkommission vor, die BJP zu begünstigen. Die Kommission weist Manipulationsvorwürfe zurück. Die Forderung nach dem Rücktritt des obersten Wahlkommissars Gyanesh Kumar ist ungebrochen. (…) Die ebenfalls von der CJP angeleiteten Proteste richteten sich gegen die Bildungspolitik, Prüfungslecks und die fehlenden Perspektiven vieler junger Menschen. Mit kämpferischen Reden und Aufrufen in den sozialen Medien rückte Bora selbst ins Zentrum der Aufmerksamkeit. Auf Instagram folgen ihr inzwischen rund 1,5 Millionen Menschen

…“ 

Artikel von Natalie Mayroth vom 11.10.2026 in der taz online

 




Hindunationalismus: Ultrarechter »Macher«




„

Indien: Vor 76 Jahren wurde Narendra Modi geboren, seit 25 Jahren regiert er in Spitzenämtern und hat dem Land seine neoliberale und fundamentalistische Agenda aufgedrückt  (…)




Human Rights Watch (HRW) hat schon in der Einleitung seines Berichtes 2026 für das vorige Jahr für Indien ein »Abgleiten in Autoritarismus« konstatiert. Die Nationale Menschenrechtskommission leide unter politischer Einflussnahme, zahlreiche Aktivisten säßen – oft auf Grundlage der drakonischen Antiterrorgesetze – ohne Prozess im Gefängnis. Die NGO Freedom House stufte das Land bereits 2021 in den Kategorien von »frei« auf »teilweise frei« herab. Und auch die britische Webseite »The Human Rights« kam in ihrer jüngsten Bestandsaufnahme von April zu dem Schluss, dass sich die Menschenrechtslage unter Modi seit Jahren im Niedergang befindet, was vor allem »Muslime, Christen, Dalits, Adivasi und andere Minderheiten« zu spüren bekämen. (…) Modi ist nicht um harsche, kontroverse Aussagen verlegen. Echte verbale Ausfälle sind aber eher selten, offene Hetze gegen Minderheiten überlässt er vorrangig anderen. Doch all die Einschnitte, die es über die Jahre an bürgerlichen Freiheiten, Toleranz und der grundlegenden Atmosphäre im Land gab, hat in letzter Instanz der Doppeljubilar zu verantworten. Seine Breitenwirkung nimmt ab, ist aber noch immens. Die »Marke Modi«, konstatierte The Economic Times schon vor einem Jahr, kombiniere »Ideologie, Charisma, administratives Talent und ein tiefes Verständnis für das Mindset der Massen«. Der spürbare BJP-Stimmenrückgang zur nationalen Wahl 2024, die vor allem von der Jugend getragene Massenbewegung der »Kakerlakenvolkspartei« vor wenigen Monaten, die den Bildungsminister zum Rücktritt zwang, und auch die aktuellen Proteste sind aber klare Zeichen, dass die Modi-Ära ihren Zenit überschritten hat. Noch sitzt er aber fest im Sattel

.“ 

Artikel von Thomas Berger in der jungen Welt vom 12.10.2026

 










Indien: »Primär kämpfen wir gegen strukturelle und politische Gewalt«. Cockroach-Proteste: Was verstehen Studierende in Delhi unter Friedensarbeit?




„

Frieden – was bedeutet das eigentlich? Ist Frieden nur die Abwesenheit von Gewalt, oder gehört dazu auch gesellschaftliche Veränderung? In Delhi setzen sich Studierende gegen Diskriminierung, Korruption und politische Gewalt ein. Mit den Cockroach Protesten wird die Frage von Gewalt und Gewaltlosigkeit für einen gesellschaftlichen Frieden neu gestellt. Ronja Mann und Lotte Leibner haben Studierende gefragt: Was bedeutet Frieden für sie – und wie kann Friedensaktivismus aussehen?

…“

Die indische Jugend sieht sich heute mit einer beispiellosen Krise konfrontiert, die von drastisch hohen Lebenshaltungskosten und Erwerbslosigkeit geprägt ist. Laut der periodischen Arbeitskräfteerhebung der Regierung liegt die allgemeine Arbeitslosenquote landesweit bei etwa 3,1 Prozent. Unter jungen Hochschulabsolventen beträgt sie 11,2 Prozent, übersteigt in ländlichen Gebieten sogar 11,8 Prozent – ein Hinweis darauf, dass die Anzahl erwerbsloser Personen mit hohen Bildungsabschlüssen jene der allgemeinen Bevölkerung um das Dreifache übersteigt. Die Menge an Bewerbungen, die zwischen 2014 und 2022 für Stellen bei der Zentralregierung eingereicht wurden, veranschaulicht die Misere: Auf fast 220 Millionen Bewerbungen folgten letztlich nur rund 722.000 Anstellungen.


Darüber hinaus zeigen Daten des Arbeitsamtes und des indischen Statistikamtes, dass die jährlichen Wachstumsraten der Reallöhne im informellen Sektor seit 2015 auf nahezu null Prozent gesunken sind. Der von der Azim Premji University veröffentlichte Bericht »State of Working India 2026« ermittelte einen Rückgang des durchschnittlichen Monatsgehalts eines indischen Hochschulabsolventen von etwa 30.000 Rupien im Jahr 2011 auf nur noch 28.000 Rupien (rund 255 Euro) in den vergangenen Jahren. Bereinigt um die erdrückende Inflation und die explodierenden Lebenshaltungskosten verdienen die jungen Menschen von heute effektiv weniger als die vorherige Generation. Die Forderung nach dem Rücktritt von Bildungsminister Dharmendra Pradhan (BJP) binnen sieben Tagen ist ein konkretes Anliegen, mit dem die Bewegung einen wunden Punkt trifft. Hintergrund sind Unregelmäßigkeiten bei der landesweiten Zulassungsprüfung NEET für medizinische Studiengänge, die nun rund zwei Millionen junge Menschen wiederholen müssen. (…)


Am Wochenende kam es zu Festnahmen von Protestierenden, sonst blieb es weitgehend friedlich. Daher fragt die Journalistin Arfa Khanum Serwani: „Warum werden Wasserwerfer nur gegen Kongress-Protestierende eingesetzt?“. „Hat die Regierung Angst vor einer neuen Gen-Z-Bewegung (…) oder nimmt sie diese einfach nicht ernst?“. Dipke dagegen zeigt sich gestärkt: „Mit unserer friedlichen Demonstration haben wir der Regierung gezeigt, wozu wir fähig sind“. Die Kakerlaken-Partei steht vor der Herausforderung, sich von einem digitalen Phänomen in eine reale politische Bewegung zu verwandeln. Von außen betrachtet ist es Indiens erste größere neue politische Protestbewegung seit vielen Jahren. Die „Stimme der Faulen und Arbeitslosen“ kratzt dabei am Image der Hindunationalisten

…“ 

Artikel aus Mumbai von Natalie Mayroth vom 7.6.2026 in der taz online

 




Kakerlaken-Partei: Warum sie der Regierung in Indien gefährlich werden könnte




„

Riesiger Zulauf für die Cockroach Janta Party (CJP): Das indische Online-Projekt mit einer Kakerlake als Symbolfigur zieht Millionen junge Menschen an. Sie sind von schlechten Jobaussichten und steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten frustriert. Was hinter der CJP steckt und wer nun nervös wird. (…)




CJP: Sarkasmus, aber mit Inhalt




Auf ihrer Webseite beschreibt sich die Partei als „Stimme einer ausgebrannten Jugend“ und hebt die positiven Seiten der Schädlinge hervor: Sie sind ausdauernd, anpassungsfähig und überleben selbst unter extremen Bedingungen. Die CJP scherzt mit Aufnahmekriterien wie Arbeitslosigkeit, Faulheit und ständige Online-Präsenz und nennt ihre Mitglieder „überqualifiziert, politisch frustriert und finanziell verwirrt“.


Doch in und neben Memes, KI-generierten Inhalten und Kurzvideos gibt auch handfeste politische Forderungen: So fordert die Bewegung beispielsweise eine Frauenquote von 50 Prozent im Parlament und Kabinett und will künftig verbieten, dass indische Oberste Richter nach ihrer Pensionierung politische Positionen etwa im indischen Oberhaus, der Rajya Sabha, erhalten können. Den Milliardären Mukesh Ambani und Gautam Adani, die einen Großteil der indischen Medienlandschaft dominieren, sollen Lizenzen entzogen werden, damit die Medien unabhängiger werden können. …


Die Jugend in Indien fühlt sich von der Politik nicht gesehen, hat schlechte Jobaussichten bei steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten. Sie beklagt wachsende Ungleichheit, religiöse Polarisierung und Probleme im Bildungssystem. Offiziell liegt die Jugendarbeitslosigkeit bei über 15 Prozent, bei Hochschulabsolventen noch deutlich höher. (…)


Bei Straßenprotesten waren bereits als Kakerlaken verkleidete Menschen zu sehen, sodass sich die Bewegung aus dem digitalen Raum auf die Straße verlagern könnte. Auf ihrer Webseite kündigt die CJP an, eine Partei, für eine Generation aufbauen zu wollen, die mit leeren Versprechen, ständigen Benachrichtigungen und Warnungen vor niedrigem Batteriestand aufgewachsen ist. Auch plant sie bereits Proteste gegen die Regierung

…“ 

Analyse von Marie Illner am 07.06.2026 auf web.de

 










„

Die korrupte indische Regierung unterdrückt die Stimme der Generation Z, indem sie die Seiten der Cockroach Janta Party auf Twitter, Facebook und Instagram sperrt. Folgt uns und erhebt eure Stimme




#CorruptIndianGovernment #CockroachJantaParty

“ engl.

Inzwischen haben sich mehrere Videos von gewalttätigen Protesten, Vandalismus und Brandstiftung im Internet verbreitet. Angeblich zeigten diese Clips junge Anhänger der Cockroach Janta Party, die für Chaos sorgten. Ein X-Nutzer teilte die Videos und schrieb: „EILMELDUNG – ‚Cockroach Party‘. Demonstranten der Generation Z geraten in der Nähe von Armeebüros aneinander, während die Wut auf das Modi-Regime wächst.“

Sonam Wangchuk bezeichnet sich selbst als „Ehren-Kakerlake“: „Ich bin sehr beeindruckt“




„… 

Eine „Partei“, die eigentlich nur als „Satire“ gedacht war, hat mittlerweile Millionen von Anhängern und „Mitglieder“ in „Lakhs“! Inmitten dieses Online-Hypes hat die „Partei“ offenbar ihren ersten „Ehren-Kakerlak“ erhalten, da der vielgepriesene Umweltschützer und Pädagoge Sonam Wangchuk seine Unterstützung für die sensationelle „Cockroach Janata Party“ (CJP) bekundete. Indiens Generation Z hat die verachtete Kakerlake zu einem Symbol des Widerstands gemacht




„

Die stachelige, langbeinige und oft verachtete Kakerlake ist zu einem unerwarteten Symbol des Widerstands unter Indiens Generation Z geworden – eine scharfe Zurechtweisung für das herrschende Establishment in der größten Demokratie der Welt.




Die „Cockroach Janta Party“, deren Name eine satirische Anspielung auf die regierende Bharatiya Janata Party ist, hat in weniger als einer Woche mehr als 19 Millionen Instagram-Follower gewonnen – fast doppelt so viele wie die Regierung. 

Es verdankt seine Entstehung Äußerungen des Obersten Richters Surya Kant, die weithin so verstanden wurden, dass er die arbeitslosen Jugendlichen des Landes als „Kakerlaken“ bezeichnete. (…)




Die Äußerungen lösten einen viralen Protest aus, und die Generation Z verwandelte die Beleidigung in ein Symbol des Stolzes. KI-generierte Bilder des virtuellen Kakerlaken-Maskottchens der Partei tauchen nun überall in den Social-Media-Feeds, Nachrichtensendern und Zeitungen des Landes mit 1,4 Milliarden Einwohnern auf. Auch wenn es sich nicht um eine offizielle politische Partei handelt, dient die Cockroach Janta Party als lautstarkes, jugendliches Forum, um Missstände wie die steigende Jugendarbeitslosigkeit sowie das, was sie als politische Dysfunktion und Korruption ansehen, anzusprechen. (…) 

Mit einem Durchschnittsalter von 29 Jahren hat Indien eine der jüngsten Bevölkerungen der Welt. Die jungen Menschen des Landes sind zunehmend besser ausgebildet und ehrgeizig, doch das Land ist noch nicht in der Lage, die potenziellen wirtschaftlichen Vorteile daraus zu nutzen

…“ engl. 

Artikel von Rhea Mogul und Esha Mitra vom 22. Mai 2026 auf CNN
