author: Juliet Jacques
title: UK Universities Are Smashing Humanities and Arts Subjects to Pieces
content:
In June 2026,

 Exeter University announced plans to cut 150 jobs

. These redundancies would barely touch management, or teaching and research in STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) subjects. Unsurprisingly to those who have followed the assault on the UK’s universities over the last two decades, they would reduce support and especially academic staff, with 85% of the posts under threat being in HASS (humanities, arts and social sciences). 




Nor would they be surprised to hear that, as 

an English lecturer told the New Statesman

, the decision made no financial sense as the extra work for remaining staff would reduce their contribution to the

 Research Excellence Framework

 that determines their funding. 




More than 40,000 people have 

signed a petition

 against the cuts,

 staff voted no confidence in their vice chancellor

, and

 Exeter UCU have declared a trade dispute

 with the university.




The outcome remains to be seen, but the proposals fit into a long-term pattern of cuts to HASS departments at British universities, in a political and media climate hostile to the pursuit of such subjects, or public funding of art and culture. 




The introduction of tuition fees for domestic students in 1998 (after

 Thatcher announced them for overseas students

 during her first year in office) and their trebling under the coalition government in 2010 were crucial in shifting the universities’ primary function from the creation of knowledge to the generation of capital, with the introduction of new layers of management to facilitate it. 




This

 disincentivises students

 from less wealthy backgrounds from pursuing degrees without an obvious career path, with fears that they will never make enough money to clear their debts increasing since the financial crisis and austerity, and the imposition of interest on student loans. (For example, I owe more now than when I graduated in 2003 because my repayments cannot keep up with the interest, so it functions as an extra tax.)




The instilling of this depressing logic into the student body has been reinforced by the policy and rhetoric of every government since Thatcher’s – be it Conservative or Labour. Installed as prime minister to at least look as though he might mitigate some of the catastrophic inequality and injustice of the last 50 years, and to hopefully save his party as an electoral vehicle, Andy Burnham has taken a classically New Labour approach to the access issue 

by announcing changes

 in how loans are presented to students, rather than any cuts to tuition fees or renewed university funding. 




Both are much needed: in 2024, 

nearly 4k HASS jobs were cut

, with all but 110 in non-Russell Group universities. This reduced student choice, and now Russell Group institutions are making similar cuts. Burnham has had little to say about this. His

 emphasis has been

 on telling schools to adapt their curricula to ‘local business needs’, with prioritised funding for technical and vocational qualifications for 14 to 19-year-olds.




This isn’t a bad thing in itself: attending university at the height of the

 Blair government’s 50% in higher education plan

, I met plenty of people who were passionate about their subject, and plenty who were there because they didn’t know what else to do – and who may have been better served by another option. Coming after the previous government’s repeated attacks on HASS, and the arts more broadly, however, it suggests a Labour administration that has little intention of dealing with the issues, and which has followed the last Conservative government’s lurch to the right as much as New Labour followed that of Thatcher and Major.




The

 white paper

 produced under Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership proposed no serious changes to a model dependent on higher fees from international students, increasingly put off the UK by its ever-more xenophobic attitudes, manifested in laws such as the one introduced by the Conservatives in 2024 and tightened by Labour, 

against Masters students bringing dependants

. (For disclosure, I teach Masters students at the Royal College of Art, who are predominantly from overseas – we have far fewer students from EU countries since Brexit, and any significant political or economic changes in China would cause us and many other institutions big problems.) 




A downturn in numbers of international students will further imperil university finances, and entrench their reliance on private funding, putting them even more at the service of corporate interests. The lack of noise, let alone any policy suggestions, from the Labour government about any of this – or about similar job losses in arts industries 

such as television

 – reinforces a state of hopelessness, with staff feeling that no one will stop the constant decline.




As might be expected, the

 University and College Union

 (UCU) are holding plenty of ballots, some of which have resulted, or will result, in strike action. The University of Dundee has cut 675 jobs through voluntary redundancies in the last two years, with plans announced to 

remove 154 more

; the innovative

 Cooper Gallery

, attached to the university, is also threatened with closure. Staff began a

 five-week strike

 on 21 September, backed by 79% of UCU voters. 




Staff at Edinburgh went on strike over £140m cuts and 1,800 job losses, while university 

announced plans to scrap 90 degree programmes

, with over half in languages, literatures and cultures. Essex, Sussex, Nottingham, Glasgow and others have also

 announced strike dates

, and more universities will surely follow suit. 




Shockingly, the

 University of Brighton

 announced the termination of all collective agreements with UCU 

and Unison

 by June 2027, coinciding with proposals to close its Falmer campus by 2030. The UCU branch has resolved to fight the plans, and industrial action looks a near-certainty.




None of this has happened by accident, given the relentless devaluation of the arts. During the New Labour period, it felt more possible to argue that the arts were good because they generated employment and income, and soft power for the United Kingdom – both through the universities themselves and the popularity of the music, films, art, comedy and other cultural works produced by people who had studied at them. That was before the Conservatives blew up the university sector out of class hatred. The whole concept of soft power has gone out of the window in recent years, rejected by an international far-right bloc which increasingly regards political diplomacy and cultural exchange as a waste of time and money.




Amidst the rise of the British far right – an inevitable product of the austerity programme that has smashed HASS courses, universities in general, the arts and wider society to pieces – it feels like time to go back to the cultural democracy arguments of the 20th century: that the arts and humanities are inherently good rather than just economically profitable, and they should be funded because they make life more enjoyable and interesting. (This is an argument

 Stewart Lee has made

, compellingly, for years.) 




The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy – of whom I, for one, have been critical for

 not fulfilling her remit

 – has

 written about

 how the Conservative government “virtually erased arts and culture from our classrooms and communities”, and how this needs to change, with the working class access to the arts that was hard won in the post-war period being restored. 




It’s a very slow, small step in the right direction, and it needs to be connected to the huge challenge of rebuilding and refinancing HASS courses and reiterating the social uses of the arts – both things that Labour’s manifestos did in 2017 and 2019. Having rejected these manifestos under Starmer, Burnham is going to have to do the Corbynism without Corbyn that Starmer promised if there to be any hope to saving British universities – but if Nandy’s logic can be extended, then improved secondary arts education can put people on a long path to a life in the arts, and give the country a more diverse and vibrant culture.

author: Johnnie Jae
title: Indigenous People Are Resisting Erasure From Schools, Media, and Our Land
content:
Joining the fight against our erasure helps Native communities defend our right to be seen, heard, and counted.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas that the Indigenous Lucayan people called Guanahani. He continued on to Cuba and Hispaniola and, on later voyages, to other parts of the Caribbean, but he never set foot in what is now the continental United States. It makes little sense for a country to honor a man who never reached it, and even less to credit him with discovering a place that millions of people already called home. And it makes even less given what Columbus actually did in the places where he stepped foot: He rounded up Indigenous people in the Caribbean, chained them, and sent them as slaves to Spain. And when Indigenous communities rose up in resistance, he ordered his soldiers to “spread terror,” maiming and slaughtering civilians en masse using firearms, dogs, swords, and pikes.

But despite all this, in 1937, the United States established a federal holiday in his name anyway.

Native people have been fighting the sanitization of Columbus’s story for decades. The idea of replacing Columbus Day arose as early as 1977, when Indigenous representatives raised it at a United Nations conference in Geneva.

In 1990, South Dakota renamed the day Native Americans’ Day. The change began with Oglala Lakota newspaper publisher Tim Giago, whose columns challenged Governor George Mickelson to mark the centennial of the Wounded Knee massacre with a “Year of Reconciliation” and to give the October holiday to Native people, proposals Mickelson took to tribal leaders and then to the legislature.

Two years later, as the country marked 500 years since Columbus landed, the city of Berkeley, California, adopted Indigenous Peoples’ Day. Bay Area Native organizers and their allies, returning from a 1990 gathering of Indigenous nations in Quito, Ecuador, formed a coalition called Resistance 500 and won official taskforce status from the City Council, which then unanimously adopted their recommendation to replace Columbus Day. Today at least 17 states and more than 100 cities recognize it, and in 2021, Joe Biden became the first president to formally proclaim it.

Then, the next White House reversed course. In October 2025, President Trump moved to “reclaim” Columbus’s legacy from those he termed “left-wing arsonists,” though he never mentioned Indigenous Peoples’ Day by name.

Native people have been fighting the sanitization of Columbus’s story for decades.

Columbus Day tells a story that skips what came before 1492 and what came after. Before the United States existed, Indigenous nations governed and cared for these lands. Colonization brought land theft, forced removal, and government policies designed to break those nations and sever Native people from their languages, cultures, communities, and homelands.

The people carrying out those policies often stated their intentions openly. In 1851, California’s first governor, Peter Burnett, told state legislators that a war of extermination would continue “until the Indian race becomes extinct.” In 1892, Richard Henry Pratt, founder of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, described the purpose of federal boarding schools in one line: “Kill the Indian in him, and save the man.”

Indigenous Peoples’ Day marks that failure. It also arrives during a new wave of attempted erasure across Indian Country. The methods are different, but the questions are familiar. Who gets counted? Who gets to tell our history? Who gets to speak for Native people? Who decides what happens to Indigenous land, water, and culture?

When this country attempts to count Native people, it always seems to fall short. Pollsters ostensibly skip us because oursample size is too small to report. On election night in 2020, a national network put Native voters on screen as “something else.”

The U.S. census, for all its flaws, at least asks. It lets us check a box and write in the name of our tribe.

Now the federal government wants to stop asking altogether. On September 10, 2026, the Census Bureau proposed dropping the race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 census. Race has been on the form since the first count in 1790, though for much of that time we were left out. Until 1940, the government excluded “Indians not taxed” (meaning Natives living in the jurisdiction of their sovereign nations) from the census, which is used to decide where federal money goes and how voting districts are drawn.

Even with the question on the form, the census can’t get us right. In 2020, it missed an estimated 5.64 percent of Native people living on reservations, a higher undercount than any other racial or ethnic group.

Taking the question off the form won’t change who we are or how our nations determine citizenship. But census numbers help determine what the federal government owes us — and it does. Native nations signed hundreds of treaties with the United States and were dispossessed of nearly all of the land the country now sits on. In return, the government promised to protect tribal lands and to provide health care, education, and housing.

The courts have long held that the United States has a “trust responsibility” to tribal nations — a permanent government-to-government obligation bound by the U.S. Constitution, treaties, federal statutes, and Supreme Court rulings. Without a count, our tribal governments have a harder time holding Washington to its word, and Washington has an easier time breaking it.

Our history is getting the same treatment. A treaty is easier to break when nobody is taught that it exists. After years of lobbying by tribal educators, states including Connecticut, North Dakota, and Oregon began requiring Native history be taught in schools. Then came the backlash. Laws against so-called “divisive concepts” began to spread through statehouses in 2021, and tribal educators say some teachers now skip Native history for fear of breaking them. In August 2021, South Dakota state officials cut much of the Native history and culture from draft social studies standards.

A treaty is easier to break when nobody is taught that it exists.

The federal government under Trump has gone further under the banner of fighting Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) policies. In January 2025, the president signed an order ending federal DEI programs. In the purge that followed, the Pentagon deleted web pages honoring the Navajo Code Talkers — veterans who helped win World War II — and restored some only after tribes objected. Later that month, the Smithsonian closed its diversity office, and a second order in March 2025 directed it to remove what the president called “improper ideology.” The National Museum of the American Indian is among the museums under review.

Native history shouldn’t be treated as optional or controversial; it is foundational to American history. Students who are never taught about our nations, our governments, or our sovereignty will grow up with ideas about us that someone else gave them. Eventually, some of those students become the people making decisions about Indian Country.

Tech companies control how much of us the youth can learn about online. In 2015, Facebook locked Native users out of their accounts after flagging names like Lone Hill and Creepingbear as fake. On May 5, 2021, a national day of awareness for missing and murdered Indigenous women, Instagram stories marking it were wiped from the app, which the company blamed on a technical bug. Later that year, Native creators who livestreamed arrests at the Line 3 pipeline protests in Minnesota told the Daily Dot that TikTok suspended their accounts and their views dropped from tens of thousands to a few thousand. In Canada, Meta’s 2023 news block left Indigenous outlets unable to reach their own communities.

While real Native people and news outlets get buried, fake ones are filling the space. Nunatsiaq News found a site called We-News running 121 AI “correspondents,” including a fabricated Inuk reporter named Leah Qammaniq. She doesn’t exist. CBC turned up two more fake AI correspondents presented as Dene and Yukon First Nation “journalists.” Every story under their names had been taken from real newsrooms in Canada’s northern territories. The frightening reality is that anyone with a phone can make a “Native elder” in seconds, and Native technologists say social media is now full of AI images that come from no real community, reversing decades of work by advocates to combat racist stereotypes promoted by old movies and TV shows.

Colonization was always about land, and it never stopped at removing the people. Colonizers also went after the plants and animals that knew us, the ones that carried the memory of who belonged to a place and who had looked after it for thousands of years. On the plains, hunters cut the bison from tens of millions to a few thousand by the early 1880s, with Army generals cheering them on. The tallgrass prairie our nations once tended across roughly 25 percent of the North American continent now survives on about 1 percent of its former range. Plowing it up released carbon the grasses had stored deep in the soil for centuries, and that loss fed the climate crisis we live in now.

We are living with the worst of it. Native nations in the United States have lost nearly 99 percent of their historical lands,according to a study in the journal Science, and the lands we were forced onto face more extreme heat, less rain, and, for nearly half of tribes, greater wildfire danger. We are paying the most for a crisis we did the least to cause.

We still don’t get the final say over our land. Western Apache people have prayed and held ceremonies at Chi’chil Biłdagoteel, also called Oak Flat, for longer than the United States has been a country. In March 2026, the Forest Service handed it over to a mining company, Resolution Copper, even though the government’s own initial environmental reviewfound the mine would destroy the site’s sacred springs, oak groves, and burial grounds.

Native nations in the United States have lost nearly 99 percent of their historical lands.

Big Tech is next in line. Companies are actively scouting reservations for data centers, and a single large one can use more than a million gallons of water a day on land where water is already an endangered resource. A few tribes are receptive to deals.

Meanwhile, other tribes want nothing to do with data centers, and they’re fighting back. Muscogee Nation leaders said no to a facility on their Looped Square Ranch in November 2025. Four months later, the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma became the first tribe to impose a moratorium on AI data centers, and by August 2026 the Cherokee Nation had banned data centers outright on its lands. The Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation have taken the fight to federal court to keep a project for powering a data center off a sacred site.

Indigenous Peoples’ Day exists because Native people organized for decades to be acknowledged and to honor the authentic history of this land. Honoring Indigenous Peoples’ Day requires picking up some of that work.

Anyone can call their school district to ask what students are learning about nearby tribes, and be in the room when the curriculum comes up for a vote. The Census Bureau is taking public comments on its proposed rule to drop race and ethnicity questions from the 2030 census until October 13, 2026, and the bureau must consider those comments before the rule is final. Leaving a comment in support of Native communities helps us defend our right to be seen, heard, and counted.

Find out whose land you’re on and what issues they may be up against, whether it’s a pipeline or data center. Then follow their lead.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Journalists Arrested Under Terrorism Act at Protest Against Israeli Arms Company
content:
Police in Leicester arrested at least five journalists under the Terrorism Act while they were reporting on a protest outside a drone factory owned by an Israeli arms company.




The 

journalists

 were detained for two hours last Thursday at a UAV Tactical Systems factory 

owned by

 Elbit Systems, which makes weapons that are used in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.  




Those arrested included two reporters for the Leicester Gazette and three freelance photojournalists. Police only let them go once they shared information to prove they attended the protest in their capacity as journalists, Press Gazette reported. 




A photographer who goes by the name Just Barold on social media was 

among those detained

. 




“Multiple journalists including myself were arrested under section 13 of the Terrorism Act for going to work,” he wrote. “An officer told me that I would be de-arrested as soon as I gave my details despite identifying myself as a journalist with a press card.




“Our arresting officer was unable to articulate what caused the suspicion but it did instantly vanish when they got my name, address and date of birth.” 




Press advocacy group Reporters Without Borders said in a statement that it was “deeply concerned to hear of the arrest of journalists covering a protest in Leicester, particularly given they had identified themselves as such to police.”




It added: “No journalist should have to weigh the risk of arrest against their duty to inform the public. If reporters cannot cover protests freely, the public is left in the dark about events it has a right to know about. Policing and government must ensure that journalists are free to do their jobs without interference.”




In total, police 

arrested 35 people

 at the protest under section 13 of the Terrorism Act. Some of the protesters held signs reading, “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action”. The proscribed group has frequently targeted and damaged factories owned by Elbit Systems.

author: Patrick Bond
title: Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize Spotlights South African and Global Battles for Justice
content:
Judge Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize award on October 9 was a rare bit of very good news. “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” she said, laughing, alongside Nuremberg Forum members in Germany, upon hearing the news. She was attending a commemoration of the Nazi war-crimes prosecution that ended in October 1946. Pillay’s willingness to attack broader socio-political conditions reflects a long history of fusing ideological radicalization and practical reforms.

Yet at the very same time, a xenophobic movement – ‘March and March’ – was rioting and burning cars both in Pillay’s native Durban and in Johannesburg next to South Africa’s Constitutional Court. The vigilantes were both trying to influence the November 4 municipal elections (and will do so again and again in the next few weeks), and specifically protesting the state’s new implementation of a ConCourt ruling that empowered immigrants through a more generous interpretation of asylum regulations.

And the same day, their own Zulu nationalist leader, 84-year old Jacob Zuma – who was SA President from 2009-18 – was reported to be on his last legs at a KwaZulu-Natal hospital. If he passes on, that could inflame matters further this week, requiring a more extensive army deployment to the province.

These local crisis conditions mean Pillay’s sudden high profile could help society figure out what to do next, to shift momentum back to progress. But her global role is vital, too. The lead organizer of South Africa’s Boycott Divestment Sanctions campaign, Roshan Dadoo, explained:

“South Africa is the largest exporter of coal to Israel, fuelling genocide, ethnic cleansing, illegal settlements and the military-industrial complex. Scandalously, just last month, the South African government granted an Israeli oil company, Navitas Petroleum, offshore oil and gas exploration rights in the Orange Basin, off our west coast. We urge our government, in honour of Nobel Prize laureate Navi Pillay, to immediately implement policies of academic, cultural and sporting boycott, to impose an embargo on sales of South African coal to Israel and a ban on all trade that benefits the economy of genocidal Israel, including the rejection of Navitas Petroleum”.

Since August 2025, Glencore and African Rainbow Minerals – the latter owned by Patrice Motsepe, who is President Cyril Ramaphosa’s brother-in-law and potential replacement – have been supplying close to 100% of the coal that the Israeli genocidaires need to run around a fifth of their own grid. The two firms’ export contracts with Israel are more than two decades old, including a period before 2014 when coal-mining tycoon Ramaphosa himself was in league with Glencore to sell to South Africa’s electricity parastatal, Eskom.

Not all the great leaders of the anti-apartheid movement – like Ramaphosa, who was the founding president of the National Union of Mineworkers and then African National Congress (ANC) General Secretary before losing an internal battle to succeed Nelson Mandela, to Thabo Mbeki – have such fast-disappearing ethics. Pillay is among the most principled.

Increasingly respectable radicalism

An active 85-year old judge, Navi Pillay witnessed apartheid’s racial, class and gender oppressions at a young age, one of eight children in a low-income Indian ghetto of Durban. Her grandparents cut sugar as indentured laborers, and her father drove a municipal bus.

Pillay began her social justice career as a working-class student cadre of the quasi-revolutionary Non-European Unity Movement in Durban during the early 1960s, in spite of most nationalist anti-apartheid leaders of Indian origin refusing to join due to its radicalism. She shook off the Unity Movement’s purist ‘militant abstentionism’ and went on to start her own law firm in 1967 when Durban’s white-run firms refused her employment applications for predictable racist reasons – although she was the local university’s top student.

Pillay then learned courtroom tactics while defending heroic anti-apartheid activists including armed guerrillas from the New Unity Movement in 1971, the imprisoned Mandela and others from the ANC in 1973, and members of (Steve Biko’s) Black Consciousness Movement from the mid-1970s. In the 1980s, in addition to earning a Harvard law doctorate, she co-founded an office committed to women’s defence against domestic violence.

In 1995 she was nominated by Mandela to join a UN tribunal on the 1994 Rwanda genocide. As its chair, she guided a crucial ruling against one defendant (Jean-Paul Akayesu) which established rape as a feature of genocide that had not been previously recognised. By 2003, Pillay rose to the very highest ranks of global jurists at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where she worked for five years.

Her United Nations work on Palestine and Burma has been formidable. At the ongoing Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory she has not hesitated to term Israel attacks on Palestine as genocidal.

From 2008-14 as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, she twice expressed outrage at Burma’s (Myanmar’s) treatment of the Muslim Rohingya people by the army. Then in 2020 she ruled against a government led by her fellow Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi (from 2016-21, prior to a military coup); since 2019 Pillay has served the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on The Gambia v. Myanmar, the other ICJ genocide case under consideration.

Pillay has also looked hard at the xenophobia that has long raged in rightwing-populist South Africa, including in 2015 at the Isipingo neighbourhood near her South Durban childhood home of Clairwood. Xenophobia was first noticed as a major problem shortly after Mandela became president in 1994, but his successor Mbeki arrogantly denied its existence in late 2007 – resulting in mass violence six months later. Nearly all the immigrant victims were from neighbouring countries: hence ‘Afrophobia’.

Pillay led a local commission in 2015 that began to reverse her prior support for the Pretoria government. For in 2010 she had remarked from a faraway UN perch,

“South Africa has taken some steps in the right direction to address aspects of its migration problems. The creation of a High Level Inter-Ministerial Committee on xenophobic violence against non-nationals is a welcome development. Moreover, the South African Police Services are working with the UN to understand and tackle the root causes of anti-migration sentiment and to establish appropriate mechanisms to combat violence.”

All this occurred under Jacob Zuma’s rule, and in retrospect Pillay’s framing appears overly-optimistic. Today, the police insist on bribes if they meet immigrants – even with formal paperwork in order – in streets like those of bohemian Melville here in Johannesburg, which I’ve witnessed twice in the last six months.

And today, Zuma’s Zulu-nationalist support base takes the form of the ANC-breakaway ‘MK Party’ (named after the largest black military force against apartheid prior to 1994, uMkhonto weSizwe). It garners 15% support in the national polls, and will potentially win the mayorality of its stronghold Durban next month.

In the same city, Zuma-supporting rioters in July 2021 did massive damage, and 350 lives were lost (and $3 billion in damage) in episodes of arson, looting, stampedes and pogroms. MK Party leaders are explicitly supportive of the March and March Afrophobes, providing one of four driving forces behind South Africa’s locally-distinctive proto-fascism.

(Three others that may in future align are the Afrikaner fanatics claiming they suffer oppression and even ‘genocide’; the evangelical Zion Christian Church members who – facilitated by Motsepe – are ardently pro-Israel; and the ‘Smutby Group‘ network combining smut and rugby, led by mining-billionaire heir Rob Hersov who firmly supports the main xenophobe in the current Government of National Unity, Gayton McKenzie of the Patriotic Alliance.)

Of course, the police and other state agencies never dared ‘tackle root causes,’ which include massive and rising unemployment (more than 43% this year), a housing crisis that pits current residents against immigrants, retailer chaos in low-income areas (where immigrant wholesale bulk-buying networks undercut local spaza shops), and South African corporate subimperialism in the region which results in blowback against refugees suffering from Johannesburg extractive corporations and climate criminals.

(Another feature of hometown degeneracy is that the Durban street where Pillay grew up – Houghton, in Clairwood – has for years been under a double wrecking-ball attack: industrial rezoning by an uncaring Durban municipality, and an invasion of container trucking depots that are ripping out 120-old homesteads. The latter process is largely due to the incapacity of the fast-privatizing parastatal Transnet railroad, which has lost vast market share to truckers abusing the roads and back-of-port zone. Hence Transnet’s Durban harbour infrastructure is rusting away, while expansion of port-petrochem activities is continually resisted by local activists.)

One reflection of the potential importance of Pillay’s role came hours after her prize: the oft-compromised International Criminal Court (ICC) – which to its credit did finally get around to issuing arrest warrants for both Vladimir Putin (in 2023) and Benjamin Netanyahu (in late 2024) – was paid a kind of tribute by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. He applied extreme financial sanctions confirming that, as Trump himself bragged this year, “We’re like pirates… We’re not playing games.”

The ICC and ICJ do have an aspiring protector against naked yankee imperialism: the Hague Group of a dozen countries formed in 2024 to support international justice. However, as Middle East Eye reported last week, that network is fading, not only because of the right-wing electoral wave sweeping Latin America, ousting three member-states since March: Colombia, Bolivia and Honduras. Also, Ramaphosa’s hypocrisy in permitting genocide fuel for Israel (resulting in war profiteering by his own family), in spite of the promise to ban exactly that.

With Hague Group co-chair South Africa blatantly violating the network’s commitment without accountability, why would anyone take it seriously (even if committed staff at Progressive International make up its secretariat)?

Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize is certainly of great value to progressives in South Africa today. To be sure, the often-nonsensical character of Oslo decision-making is revealed in its award to several serious imperialists – Teddy Roosevelt, Henry Kissinger, Barack Obama, the European Union – and three Israelis: Menachem Begin, Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.

Leaders from the periphery and semi-periphery have also engaged in brutal acts after winning the Peace Prize: Ethiopia’s Abiy Ahmed, Burma’s Aung San Suu Kyi and apartheid’s FW de Klerk. Or a stupid act, in the case of 2025’s right-wing Venezuelan winner María Corina Machado, who cravenly donated her physical prize to the narcissist Trump, but then got nothing in return after he kidnapped Nicolas Maduro and Cilia Flores on January 3. One banker who in 2006 incongruously won the Nobel Peace Prize, did enormous damage to poor people through predatory microfinance: Mohammed Yunus (subsequently the de facto leader of Bangladesh).

In an essay celebrating Pillay, Matt Meyer from the International Peace Research Association – also a Nobel nominee this year – spells out the awkwardness of Oslo’s see-saw strategy. So in contrast to those dud winners, three other great South African Peace Prize laureates – Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu and Nelson Mandela – fought tirelessly for political liberation. And Tutu also fought for economic liberation after 1994, often against Mandela, who became a free-trade neoliberal at Mbeki’s insistence, never applying the BDS strategy against Israel that had worked so well for the ANC and international allies during the fight against apartheid.

Another chance for global justice

However, on that front, a ray of hope shines within the country’s largest working-class organization, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), which holds a major conference this week. The 1.6 million member federation will not only choose leadership and decide whether or not to support Ramaphosa’s ANC in the municipal elections across the country – a task that split the federation last month. More positively, a compelling conference resolution stands before the workers:

“To campaign for the immediate and complete prohibition of all South African coal exports to Israel. The federation shall campaign for the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition to utilize its existing legislative powers to prohibit all South African coal exports to Israel. COSATU shall actively engage its affiliates in the relevant sectors, to campaign for and implement the non-handling of South African coal destined for Israel.”

If passed, and if action accompanies words, it would be long overdue. Thousands of South African mineworkers’ labor entails coal digging for Israeli power plant consumption – even though a $98 billion ‘Just Transition‘ fund should prevent workers’ income losses if halted. Rail, truck and port transport workers facilitate coal movement to the Richards Bay harbour and then to Israel’s Hadera and Ashdod ports. Other mineworkers provide diamonds. And grape pickers and packers near Cape Town ensure autumn harvests sweeten genocidaire mouths.

An ossified COSATU is likely to disappoint, if indeed the conference occurs. But there are other impressive social resistance campaigns now struggling in unity, e.g. against Israel’s Navitas on the country’s Atlantic Coast. One huge battle was won in the ConCourt in August against offshore methane exploration by Shell and a local Zionist oil man.

Following Pillay’s lead, such ongoing campaigns do have the potential to link struggles for Palestine solidarity, Pan Africanism (Siyafana Sonke and Kopanang Action Against Xenophobia), labor democracy, climate justice, marine conservation, women’s safety and working-class households’ electricity access.

So even if Pillay has operated mainly within legalistic, slow and often useless UN institutions the last 30 years, a revival of her longer-term progressive traditions could provide more durable inspiration. For as grassroots fascism rises here, seemingly inexorably within the most unequal country in the world, with no hope of solutions from Ramaphosa and his corporate friends, and as Trump, Rubio and their ilk push the contradictions of their own vacillating paleoconservative/neoconservative/neoliberal versions of imperial capitalism to the breaking point, here at least is a stable rock to lean on for leverage: Navi Pillay.

Patrick Bond is a political economist, political ecologist and scholar of social mobilisation. From 2020-21 he was Professor at the Western Cape School of Government and from 2015-2019 was a Distinguished Professor of Political Economy at the University of the Witwatersrand School of Governance. From 2004 through mid-2016, he was Senior Professor at the University of KwaZulu-Natal School of Built Environment and Development Studies and was also Director of the Centre for Civil Society. He has held visiting posts at a dozen universities and presented lectures at more than 100 others.
